Fuerunt autem virorum praeter mulieres parvulos, centum septuaginta quinque millia, sexcenti quinquaginta octo ad bellum promptissimi : principum nomina qui cũ Marcomiro erant, de prosapia eius defcenderant, Nicanor dux, patruus Marcomi- ri regis: Sunno, Panthenor, Priamus, fratres Marcomiri, dicti iam regis: Helenus dux, Antenor dux, Menander dux, Edrasius dux, Gethenus dux, Priamus dux, Marenus dux, Er- mon dux, Nicanor dux, Pyndari dux, Helam dux, Marcomir dux, Colam dux, Masan dux, Antenordux, Ancreasius dux , Bengoth dux, Calomer dux, Rodanus dux, Malda dux, Kylã dux, Solas dux, Colo dux, Bremus dux, Sunno dux, Melanus dux, Nicamor dux, Thaphon dux, Salon dux, Meodarus dux. Quantas vero difficultates in itinere habue- rint, quae bella cū obsistentibus sibi populis gesserint, quantaque pericula vel inciderint, vel euaserint, si quis ad plenum scire desiderat, memoratum scriptorem legat in libro hi- storiarum gentis Francorum.cuius initia sicuti sunt miranda, sic mihi videntur (silua pa- ce iudicantium melius) in pluribus esse fabulosa. Compendium, Book I.

... which we call April, King Marcomir himself, with Sunno, Panthenor, and Priam, his brothers, the leaders left beyond the Danubian sea, circling for a long distance through the borders of Scythia and toward the north, and then turning their route toward the region of the Teutons, began his migration westward with the whole people of the kingdom, their wives, children, and all their goods, with great labor, difficult and long-lasting.

There were, apart from women and little children, 175,658 men most ready for war. The names of the princes who were with Marcomir and had descended from his lineage were: Duke Nicanor, uncle of King Marcomir; Sunno, Panthenor, Priam, brothers of Marcomir, the aforesaid king; Duke Helenus, Duke Antenor, Duke Menander, Duke Edrasius, Duke Gethenus, Duke Priamus, Duke Marenus, Duke Ermon, Duke Nicanor, Duke Pyndari, Duke Helam, Duke Marcomir, Duke Colam, Duke Masan, Duke Antenor, Duke Ancreasius, Duke Bengoth, Duke Calomer, Duke Rodanus, Duke Malda, Duke Kylan, Duke Solas, Duke Colo, Duke Bremus, Duke Sunno, Duke Melanus, Duke Nicamor, Duke Thaphon, Duke Salon, Duke Meodarus.

The number of the whole people, as Hunibald bears witness, men, women, and little children of both sexes together, was 489,360, not counting the servants attending them. But if anyone desires to know fully what great difficulties they had on the journey, what wars they waged with the peoples opposing them, and what great dangers they either fell into or escaped, let him read the writer mentioned in the book of histories of the people of the Franks. Just as its beginnings are remarkable, so they seem to me, saving the judgment of those who judge better, to be fabulous in many respects.

At length, after many labors and countless difficulties, King Marcomir came into Germany with his leaders and the whole people. They were kindly received by the Saxons as brothers, and among them received the desired settlements by the Rhine, namely that province in which those now dwelling there are called the West Frisians, and also the Gelderlanders and Hollanders: that is, around that region where the Rhine flows into the sea by three mouths, although at first they received rather narrow settlements, which in a short time they made wider westward by force of arms.

Indeed, in the twentieth year of his reign, King Marcomir, provoked by an injury from the Transrhenane Gauls, gathered an army and, after crossing the river, subjected to his rule that land which, enclosed by islands of the Rhine, is nearest to the sea, expelling its inhabitants; and he entrusted it to his brother Sunno to guard. He brought in by ship people of his own nation to inhabit and cultivate it.

But when the Gauls took ill the incursion of the new foreign people into the borders of the Hollanders, and were provoking it with various attempts, King Marcomir, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, having gathered a great army both of his own people and of the Saxons, crossed the Rhine by ship, entered western Gaul, devastating everything with sword and fire, and reached as far as the Meuse. Thereafter he fought many battles with the Gauls, triumphing everywhere as victor, and his name was terrible to the conquered Gallic peoples; all who heard of Marcomir feared him. He made a treaty with the Britons dwelling on the island.

From that time, for almost nine hundred years, the kings of the aforesaid people of the Scythians never ceased from harrying the Romans and the Gauls, sometimes defeated, yet more often victors, until at last they compelled by arms into their power not only all Gaul, but also all Alemannia, Swabia, Bavaria, Burgundy, Italy, Sclavonia, Thuringia, Austria, Saxony, the Teutons, Cimbri, Danes, Cisrhenanes, Mosellans, Treveri, Metz people, Austrasians, Liege people, Morini, Tournai people, people of the Meuse, Atrebates, Cologne people, Mainz people, Vangiones, Nemetes, Strasbourg people, Helvetii, Rauraci, Bohemians, and Sorbs, together with the Spaniards, all the Germans, and almost all Europe.

After this King Marcomir died, when the twenty-eighth year of his reign had been completed, namely in the year 412 before the birth of Christ, in the twenty-first year from the entry of the people into the borders of Saxony at the Rhine. He left three sons, dukes, Antenor, Priam, and Nicanor, and twelve daughters.

Down to this year Wasthald the Scythian, or Sicamber in his native speech, carried down, as it were, the historical work of the people, through more or less 758 years, beginning from the fall of Troy. In it he describes the various dwellings of his race, their settlements, and also their leaders, wars, kings, and the different deeds of the Pori in order. After him Hunnibald the Frank, from the written songs of the flamens, continued the history of the people of the Franks for 1,426 years, down to the last year of King Clovis, who, first of the kings, received Christ, baptized by Saint Remigius, in the year of the Lord 498. Mortuam vero post annos reginam, Sicambri retulerunt inter deas, in me- moriam eius regum procerumque decreto, qui prius Nouimagi, id est, Neumagi, quasi no- 30 ui cognati dicebantur à Saxonibus amicis, deinęps vocabantur Sicambri, per annos fer- me quadringentos, donec tandem à Franco rege quodam suo (quemadmodũ dicemus) nuncupati sunt Franci, vsue in praesentem diem, licet cum admixtione gentium. Interim vero quod fuerunt cum suis Troianis, etiam dicti sunt Troiani: cum Ar- menis, Armenĩ: cum Scythis, Scythe: cum Germanis, Germani: cum Gallis, Galli; ab a- lis frequenter aliud nomen consecuti, mores, linguam, idioma loquelae, vocabulum crebro cum sedibus mutauerunt. Anno Antenoris duodecimo, patruus eius Sunno moritur, duos relinquens filios, 40 Marcomirum Hectorem, quorum primus postea cum equo super glaciem curritans, in Rheno fuit submersus: junior vero, ducatum patriis in Hollandia sub regis imperio guber- nabat. Reliquit alios quatuor filios, ex quatuor aliis concubinis procreatós, qui non computantur inter duces, lege Sicambrorum vetante, quae interdixit liberis de prima v- xore superfutibꝰ, filios sequentium principes vel esse vel nominari, quam legem Cambra tulit regina, ne regnum confunderetur. Priamus autem frater Antenoris regis, ducatum apud Grunes, in ea videlicet regione mari finitima, quae nunc dicitur Friasia, in qua oppidum Priami filius dux, anno ante Christi nativitate m trecentesimo septimo condidit nouum, quod ex suo nomine Groningen nuncupatur vsue in praesentem dièm. Erat enim duci nomen Grunus, à quo etiam populi (quamuis origine Franci) ad tempus dicti sunt Grunes. Antenor autem post multa fortiter gesta, moritur anno regni sui tricesimo: domi- nicae vero natiuitatis, ccc.lxxxii.quem Sicambi, more gentilitio, ingenti pompa prosequentes, iussu reginae in deos retulerunt. TERTIVS. 50 PRIAMVS regis Antenoris ex Cambra regina vnicus filius, post patrem regnauit su- per Sicambros, qui postea Franci sunt dicti, annis sex viginti, cuius tempore Sicam- bricus populus sermonis patrii paulatim coepit obliuiisci, Saxonum vt lingua, in quo- rum confinibus morabantur. Remanserunt nihilominus ex vsu veteris sermonis plura cum eis vocabula, quae Graecam resonare originem potius videntur, quam proprietatem linguae Theutonicae siue Germanorum, quod facile discernet, qui plenam linguae vrtriuf- que habet notitiam. Nec subita fuit prisci sermonis in gente mutatio, quae tempore coe- pit, vsu tandem peruenit in naturam. Anno Priami regis sexto, mortuus est Marcomir dux, qui nepos fuit primi Sunno- nis, de quo supra dictum est, quod cum aliis ducibus gentem perduxerit in Germaniam. A 3

The Second of the Annals of Trithemius.

Antenor, the elder son of King Marcomir, raised to the kingship in the same year, reigned after his father for thirty years. He was held in the highest honor among his people; he secured for himself the very firm friendship of the Saxons, with whose help, as victor, he engaged in many battles with the Romans and the Gauls. His brothers Priamus and Nicanor assisted him, together with the rest of the dukes, with steadfast loyalty; after crossing the river, they often inflicted many troubles upon the Gauls. Sunno too, the king's uncle, with his sons, always adhered to Antenor himself with the utmost fidelity in all things, and instructed him in government as his own son, while nevertheless venerating him as lord.

King Antenor had a wife named Cambra, who was the daughter of Belinus, king of Britain. She was a woman of surpassing beauty above all the daughters of the whole kingdom, and of such great prudence that the king was always accustomed to obey her counsel in all matters, no otherwise than that of some deity, before the princes of the Franks. The manners of the people, still excessively rude with Scythian savagery, she rendered more cultivated by laws; she taught the nobles to build cities and castles. There she introduced adornment of the forehead, gave women likewise the practice of sowing flax, committing hemp to the earth, and weaving and preparing it for clothing and various uses. She composed laws, pronounced judgment, and presented herself as a prophetess and priestess of Diana, an Aliruna.

And since, though a woman in sex, she bore in mind the character of a king and priest, it came among the Saxons from laughter into a proverb that, whenever they heard someone exulting or speaking with more than customary prudence, as if wishing to imitate the prudence of Cambra, they would say reproachfully: "Behold Cambra." This in their language is said thus: "Si Camber," as though they were saying, "Do you understand the prudence of Cambra?" Thus in time the proverb became established, because the last two words, that is, the adverb and the name, "Si Camber," made one word, which as a whole makes "Sicambrus."

After the queen had died years later, the Sicambrians, by a decree of the kings and nobles, counted her among the goddesses in her memory. They had formerly been called by their Saxon friends Novimagi, that is, Neumagi, as it were "new kinsmen"; thereafter they were called Sicambrians for almost four hundred years, until at last, from a certain king of theirs named Franco, as we shall say, they were called Franks, down to the present day, although with an admixture of peoples.

Meanwhile, however, because they were with their Trojans, they were also called Trojans; with Armenians, Armenians; with Scythians, Scythians; with Germans, Germans; with Gauls, Gauls. Frequently acquiring one name after another from others, they often changed their customs, language, idiom of speech, and name along with their settlements.

In the twelfth year of Antenor, his uncle Sunno died, leaving two sons, Marcomir and Hector. The first of these afterwards, while riding on horseback over the ice, was drowned in the Rhine; the younger governed his father's duchy in Holland under the king's authority. He left four other sons, begotten by four other concubines, who are not counted among the dukes, since the law of the Sicambrians forbade it; this law prohibited, while children by the first wife survived, the sons of subsequent women from being or being called princes. Queen Cambra enacted that law so that the kingdom would not be thrown into confusion.

Priamus, brother of King Antenor, held the duchy among the Gruni, namely in that region bounded by the sea which is now called Frisia. In it the duke, Priamus's son, founded a new town in the year 307 before the birth of Christ, which from his own name is called Groningen down to the present day. For the duke's name was Grunus, from whom the peoples also, although Franks by origin, were for a time called Gruni.

Antenor, after many deeds bravely performed, died in the thirtieth year of his reign, and in the 382nd year before the Lord's nativity. The Sicambrians, escorting him with great pomp according to pagan custom, counted him among the gods by order of the queen.

The Third.

Priamus, the only son of King Antenor by Queen Cambra, reigned after his father over the Sicambrians, who were later called Franks, for twenty-six years. In his time the Sicambrian people gradually began to forget their ancestral speech and to use the language of the Saxons, on whose borders they dwelt. Nevertheless, from the use of the old speech many words remained among them, which seem rather to echo a Greek origin than the property of the Teutonic or German language; anyone who has full knowledge of both languages will easily discern this. Nor was the change of the ancient speech among the people sudden: what began with time at length, through usage, passed into nature.

In the sixth year of King Priamus, Duke Marcomir died. He was the grandson of the first Sunno, of whom it was said above that, with the other dukes, he led the people into Germany.

6. COMPENDIUM, BOOK I. [Margin: Theocalus, pontiff and historiographer of the Sicambri. The sacred rites were performed in the Greek tongue.]

Among his many children he had one son, by name Theocalus, a man most outstanding in all the wisdom of the Greeks, the Scythians, and the Germans, whom the Sicambri [made their] great pontiff.

In the eighth year, therefore, of Priam, king of the Franks—Cambra his mother and queen, and Theocalus the pontiff, commanding [it]—the Sicambri built two cities between the mouths of the Rhine, of which the one they called Neopagus, the other Neomagus, in memory of their acquired name. In these two cities, and especially in Neopagus, was the residence of the king of the Franks for a long time.

They also established in the same city of Neomagus a great and most strong temple to Jupiter, in which Theocalus the pontiff, dwelling with the priests, instructed the sons of princes and nobles in morals and knowledge, spoke prophecies to the people, and wrote in songs the brave deeds of the kings—which the youth, compelled to learn by heart, were wont to sing in the temple on feast days. Yet at certain seasons of the year the priests dwelt not in the cities but in the wilderness, whose food too was sparing, and [whose] exercise of talent [was] the continual learning of the course of the stars, and songs, and the histories of the ancients.

But king Priam, after many incursions had with the Gauls, after battles and victories, at last dies, in the twenty-sixth year of his reign, 356 years before the nativity of Christ from the Virgin Mary, leaving several sons and daughters from four wives, whom he had had at once and together.

HELENUS, the elder-born son of king Priam, succeeding [his] father, reigned among the Sicambri nineteen years, a man severe against [his] enemies—whose infants, as often as he could capture [them], he immolated to Pallas and other demons. But to his own people he was not cruel, but mild, and very humane, grievous or troublesome to no one, and therefore pleasing to all.

In the first year of his reign he had a war with the Transmosan Gauls and the Tungri, in which he laid low more than sixteen thousand of the enemy, and turned the rest to flight. He slew also, with his own hand, the first-born of the king of the Morini, by name Guedo, and subjected to his dominion a great part of the land beyond the Meuse, which he commended to his dukes to be guarded. Frequently thereafter he fought with the Gauls with varying fortune, now victor, now vanquished; of whose battles and deeds we have written more in the first volume of the annals.

At last, after many [things] bravely done with the Gauls and other enemies round about, Helenus, king of the Sicambri, dies, in the nineteenth year of his reign, 337 years before the nativity of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

DIOCLES, the elder son of king Helenus, after [his] father reigned twenty-nine years, a man tall of stature in body, harsh in morals, and, by excessive gravity, severe, bold, brave, and most warlike, who waged many battles.

In the twelfth year of his reign, a multitude of the Gothic people went out from the Scanzian islands, which are now called Gothic, and, poured into the borders of the Saxons, began to exercise a most grievous devastation, consuming with iron and fire whatever it could find. Against this most savage people, which was wont to spare no one, five kings advanced to war—namely, the king of the Thuringians, the king of the Teutons, the king of the Rugii, and Diocles himself of the Sicambri, with princes, dukes, and many warriors, whose army was numbered at two hundred and sixty thousand men.

The war is waged; a fierce battle is joined with the enemy, in which there fell of the Gothic army more than one hundred thousand warriors. But on the part of the five kings, twenty-five thousand fell, among whom Heriman also, king of the Thuringians, perished. But the Saxons, having gained the victory, divided the spoils of the enemy among [their] allies with an equal balance, and, the enemy having been put to flight afar, the kings returned to their own [lands].

Meanwhile, when the Gauls dwelling beyond the Meuse had understood that king Diocles had stripped [his] country of the army,

ANNAL. TRITHERMIL. Anno regni sui tricesimo sexto, Basanus Sicambrorum rex maximus, in solen- nitate sui natalis apud Neomagum convocavit suos filios, fratres, duces, proceres, & nobiles familiarum, ad coniunium: cum quibus septem diebus epulatu opipare, patriis diis facra peregit, louem in aere supra templum cum et visibilem ostendit. O etaua die filium suum Clodomirum, de omnium consensu procerum, Sicambris regem designavit: mul- ta carmine patrio genti futura praedixit, filios et regnum principibus commendavit, in- stitiam praecepit, introgressuque facellum templi nusquam comparavit. Nefcio quid his contribuam fabellis, indignationem an risum: dolo an arte sublatus sit, incertum manet: sed vnum hoc exstitimo fuisse in causa, hominis vel ingenio, vel daemo- nis spontanea indubitante voluntate subducti, cupidinem aestimationis consequenda diunitatis. Nam (vt scribit Amerodacus Sicambrorum philosophus) rex Balan divinita- ris appetentissimus fuit, iustitiam coluit, gentem dilexit, hostem proflavit, pientissimus bonis, semper crudelis et leuerus iniquis. Euanuit autem, siue (vt rectius dicam) subtraxit se, vt Amerodacus est author, de proce- rum cōsistorio publico, vt diximus, anno regni sui tricesimo sexto: ante vero natiuitatem domini, anno cc. XLVIII. quem Sicambris translatum in decorum consortium aetiman- tes, sub nomine Balangot coluerunt. OCTAVVS. Clodomirvs Basani maior natu filius (sicut pater de consensu principum ordin- uerat) in regno succedens, regnavit annis decem et octo. Cuius anno primo statim vt Galli cognoverunt euauisfe Basanum, quem ipsi mortuum non dubitabant, missis ad Clodomirum nuncijs, omnem ab eo terram inter Mosam et Rhenum, pergyrumque in circuito, quam Sicambrìa primo corum introitui in fines Cilichenanos, contra iustitiam sibi violenter et surpascent, repetebant. Quam si redderec ōtemneret, gladio se recuperare omnia paratos fore, comminati sunt, siue responsum per nuncios destinatos negatiuim remittat, siue nihil omnino respondeat. Rex autem Clodomir Gallorum nuncios, tanquam consilium super instanti negotio habitus, cum principibus suis, prudenter et studiose protractos, apud se diutius retinuit, & summa cum diligentia cauens, ne consilij mentis sua arcuam in corum deueniret notitiam, suis praeceptis ministris, vt cos copiose cibarent, laetosque habere dies di- spone- Interim rex Clodomir misis nuncijs ad reges Saxonum, & Doringorum, vt copias in auxilium secretius, & cito mitterent Sicambris amicis cōtra Gallos communes aduer- sarios, instantifime postulavit. Venerunt Saxones cum Doringis in subsidium, vt rogab- eij. Saxones et Doringi Sic- ambrorum fo- 40 quod terram à nobis repetitis, quam progenitores nostri dudum ture bellī à vestris, tanquam iniurio- sis vicinis, & manifestis hostibus suis, iustissima ratione gladio vindicarunt. Cogitate vires nostras longe vobis superiores, & cessate ab hac temeritate stultitie et iniqua. Memores eftote cladium, quas à canis. diuo genitore nostro (inter Deos relato) eiusque parentibus, olim pro merito fuscceptis, & quiescite in caneis cum vulpibus latantes. Nostrum est imperare vobis: vestrum autem, nostris humiliter obe- dire preceptis. Quod si venire contra nos praesumperitis, decreuimus vobis potenter occurrere, & que nobis maiores nostri tradiderunt, gladio defensare. His literis et nuncijs Galli fufcepris, in iram concitati sunt, & se quantotius de Sicam- bris vindicare flatuerunt, ponte super Mosam artificiose fabricato, pugnatorum ingen- tem traduxerunt exercitum, quibus rex Clodomirus cum ducentis sexaginta quatuor 50 millibus potenter occurrit, diuifque in partes exercitu, alteram locavit ad insidias: alteram vero, misit è regione procul, vt necatis Gallorum cultodibus, pontem praeoc- cuparet: terriam vero partem, qua numero militum erat maior, duxit in aduer- sarios. Congriuentur Sicambrì cum Gallis in loco nō procul à Mosā flumine, qui Delon vocatū et martē ancipiti aliquādiu pugnatur. Postremo simulantes fugam Sicambrì, retro cedere paulatim coeperunt, donec Gallos tandem longius à Mosā flumine prōtraxerunt ad locum insidiarum. Vbi tunc immobiles feterere Sicambrì, & qui prius fugam simulae- rant, vt gigantes fortifìsime repugnabant. Interea milites circumgyrando veneruntad

led against the enemy, they divided into three parts: two of these they arranged each as a battle-line, but the third they placed in hiding-places for ambush. As the Gauls approached and brought forward one battle-line, when they saw the Sicambri coming against them with two, they were thrown into confusion; but there was no time to order their forces otherwise, since their adversaries were hastening to close battle.

For as soon as the Gauls came within sight of the Sicambri, the Sicambri, impatient of delay, directed one battle-line against the enemy wedge. When the battle had already begun, wheeling the second line around at Neomagus against the enemy from the flank, they threw their order into confusion. And when the fighting was fierce on both sides, and the army of the Gauls was already inclining toward flight, suddenly the Sicambri burst forth from ambush and, making an attack, held the Gauls enclosed among themselves, so that no place for flight lay open to those ready to flee. Thus the wretched Gauls, enclosed in the midst of the Sicambri, were butchered to death like cattle, and they suffered so great a slaughter that, out of eighty-eight thousand of them who had assembled for the war, scarcely ten thousand escaped, saved by the benefit of night, in flight. Of the Sicambri, Duke Marcomir, Duke Helenus, and Duke Antenor fell, with about four thousand men. Nevertheless the victory, with the spoils of the enemy, fell to the Sicambri.

Diocles the king, throughout all the days of his reign, stood bravely in contest with the Gauls, and scarcely in the meantime was there a year in which he did not trouble them by some incursion or battle. At last he died in the thirty-ninth year of his reign, 298 before the birth of the Lord. By the queen he had four sons, Henus, Priamus, Nicanor, and Basanus; by other wives he had several sons.

The Sixth.

Helenus, the eldest son of the aforementioned king Diocles, succeeding his father, reigned fourteen years: a sluggish, wanton man, and memorable for no activity of virtue. In his time the Gauls, making incursions several times, stirred up no few disturbances for the Sicambri. Against them his brothers, with the nobles of the kingdom, often led out the army, and, fighting with varying fortune, were sometimes defeated, sometimes victorious. But the king sat at home, idle among the gatherings of concubines, dissolving in lust, useful neither to the kingdom nor pleasing to the people, stupid for peace and unfit for war.

Therefore, before the fourteenth year of his reign had yet been completed, the nobles of the kingdom, gathering at Neopagus, together with the whole soldiery of the army, by the common decree of all deposed him from the kingdom as useless and harmful to the people, in the year 284 before the birth of the Lord.

The Seventh.

Basanus, the younger son of the above-mentioned king Diocles, after the deposition of his brother Helenus from the kingdom, was raised to the kingdom of the Sicambri by the common election of the dukes, nobles, and soldiers, and reigned thirty-six years: a man in his generation most prudent, brave, bold, and exceedingly warlike.

When Theocalus died, the Sicambri appointed him chief priest of Jove; because of the greatness of his prudence and the magnificent deeds accomplished by him, they called him Basanus the Great. The Sicambri held him in such reverence that they paid him honors not only royal but almost divine. No one was ever allowed to contradict his commands with impunity, whether in a small matter or in a great one, under the undoubted penalty of bitter death. For he was most eager for the estimation of divinity; on that account he both did and said great things. Hence, wherever he went, he ordered a rope and a sword to be carried before him, as a manifest sign of justice; and he was accustomed to preserve it so tenaciously that he would spare neither his own son nor any of the princes who, knowingly, had offended even a little against the law of equity which he had established.

He had a son named Sedanus. Accused of adultery, he was soon judged by his father to death, according to the law which he had established for the Sicambri. When the nobles pleaded for the youth, the father answered: “Do not, O noble men, fight against justice and the laws which I decreed with you as mature witnesses; for it is easier to bind by hand the wind blowing in the air than to turn the mind of King Basanus away from the execution of equity.” When this had been heard, the princes fell silent; but the father himself said to his son: “I do not kill you, son, but the law of the fatherland, which you knowingly transgressed”; and, seizing him, he cut off his head with his own hand.

At that time the Sicambri began to fear their king Basanus to such a degree that no one among them, great or small, presumed to say or do anything evil against the law. Hence the priests of the gods, by a Greek word [unclear], that is, called the king Just Basanus. But the common people called him Theobasanus, which in the German tongue is Basangoth [unclear].

signifies, because all revered him as a friend of the gods who was afterward to be deified.

From this a proverb arose among the Sicambri: whenever one man saw or heard from another anything contrary to the law, he would say, “Hort opp lieffman, kent gyn nit dy grote kunig Basan.” As if he had said, “Cease, good men, from such things; do you not know how just the great King Basanus is? If he perceived you saying or doing such things, he would without doubt kill you as transgressors.”

In the fifth year of King Basanus, the king of the Orchades, having many island petty kings as auxiliaries, declared war on the Sicambri because of the rejection of his daughter, whom King Basanus, having had her as wife, had repudiated and sent back to her father. The reason for her repudiation we described in the first volume of the annals. But King Basanus, having learned of the approach of his adversaries, advanced against them with a great multitude of fighters to the seashore, not far from the place where the Franks later built Mesoburg. Seeing from their ships so great an army of the Sicambri, the Orchades did not dare to advance onto land.

When the Gauls and Morini again broke eastward, where the Sicambri had placed settlements in the region of the Tungri, King Basanus met them with the strong hand of his men and laid them low with such slaughter that scarcely a few escaped out of many. Having won the victory, he built many castles and very strong fortifications on both sides of the river Meuse, in which he stationed garrisons of the Sicambri.

In the upper part of the river, moreover, he built a very strong castle, which from his own name he called Basanburg; in it the kings of the Sicambri and Franks after him resided for a long time, because of the pleasantness and strength of the place.

In the twenty-sixth year of his reign, King Basanus, after many battles bravely fought with various nations round about, wishing to present himself as pontiff of the gods, renewed their rites with much superstition. He appointed many priests most skilled in the worship of the divine powers, attentive to the course of the stars, trained after the manner of the ancients in prophecies, in foreknowledge, in the interpretation of dreams, in ethical and physical doctrines, and also very well practiced in composing and singing, in both languages, the songs and histories of the ancient kings and heroes only of their own people. Among these Heligastus, once the son of the pontiff Theocalus, surpassed the others in talent and practice of writing; he was in charge of educating the sons of the dukes and nobles, and described the deeds of heroes in verse.

Concerning this man Hunibaldus, historian of the Franks, writes many marvelous things; unless they are granted to have been done by the artifice of some demons, they should be thought rather to have been fabricated by some writer than performed by a man devoted to idols. He foretold to the Sicambri many future things; he presented Jupiter visibly to the priests; he brought men’s secret counsels into public view; and he disclosed to King Basanus the hidden plans of the enemy in difficult causes and affairs. It seemed that nothing escaped him of all the things that the enemies, even in most secret counsel, had discussed against the Sicambri. This matter inspired confidence in friends, but despair in enemies.

For King Basan, with all the princes of the kingdom, depended wholly on the counsel of Heligastus; what he ordered, all did; whatever he forbade, no one dared attempt. At his command the Sicambri met the enemy; and if he commanded the contrary, they remained peacefully at home. As often as he foretold victory to the Sicambri, they conquered; as often as he foretold otherwise, they were conquered. While he lived, the Sicambri prospered in all things; whenever their name was heard, it terrified enemies and made them dreadful to all throughout [unclear].

After he had spent thirty-two years in his office, on a certain solemn day of Jove, standing in the midst of the priests, hurling thunderbolts in the temple and troubling the air with his voice, resounding with frenzies in the manner of soothsayers, he suddenly disappeared, and, vanishing completely, no one was ever found who could know where he had gone. The Sicambri, thinking that he had become a god, proclaimed that he had been taken up into marriage with Diana, and they decreed sacred rites for him each year.

In the thirty-third year of his reign, Basanus moved a mighty army to the upper parts of the river Rhine, to the region called Tegaraña, which lay toward the south between the Saxons and the Cisrhenane Mainz people, under the protection of the Treviri, having its own petty king named Thaborinus. King Basanus killed him along with many others and subjugated his whole region to his own dominion. These things were done in the year 251 before the birth of Christ. The place in which the aforesaid King Thaborinus of the Tegaranes fell was called Mount Thabor from his name; it is about four miles distant from Confluentes. There Basanus, king of the Franks, founded a very strong castle, which, as a perpetual memorial of the victory, he named Mount Thaborinus; but, the word having been corrupted, it is today called Monthahur by the inhabitants.

ANTHARIVS regis Cassandri filius, post patrem regnauit annis x x x v. de quo scribit Hunibaldus, quod Moguntinos Romanorum colonos, miserabili clade attruit, urbem incendit et subvertit, qua postea in colo vbi nunc transfrapam Cianam et vallem, in declivo montis ad Rheni littus translat et constructa cernitur. Facta est haec Moguntinorum miseranda desolation, anno regis Anthari sextodecimo, qui fuit ante Christi nativitatem quinquagiesimus sextus annus, vt ex serie temporum ostenditur. Rex Anthari cum auxilio Germanorum intrauit Galliam, vicos incendit, praedas et spolia infinita sapis reportauit, magnam per Galliam defoliationem fecit, incendit urbes, vicos destruxit, castella subvertit, gentis robur contruit, & regionem diu fructiferam, in solitudinem redigit. Verum cum senuisset rex Antharius, annoregni sui ultimo, qui fuit ante Christi nativitatem septimus atque tricesimus, denuo irruptentibus in regionem Sicambrorum Gallis, & Mosam transeuntibus, occurrit eis cum suorum exercitu ad pugnandum, vbi cum dimicaret in cantius, ab hostibus circumseptus, cum viginti millibus Sicambrorum interit, anno regni sui x x x v. & Galli magnam ea vice Sicambris calamitatem induxerunt. FRANCVS Anthari regis maior natu filius, a quo Sicambris deinceps dicitur Franci (vt Hunibaldus est auactor) post patrem regnauit annis xxviii. homo ferox, audax, & bellicosus, gentis sui defensor acerrimus, qui mortem genitoris dure satius vindicavit in Gallos, & multa cum externis nationibus bella constituit, semper victor et triumphator gloriosus, quem gens Francorum et nominis et honoris sui principem fuisse, nō immeritogloriarus. Pugnare Francus rex iste coeuerit non fugere, qui amabilis suis et mirabilis fuit: hostibus autem cunctis nimium semper metuendus. Anno regni sui primo cum Germanis, Saxonicibus, atque Doringis, perpetu foedus contraxit, de consentu omnium ducum et procerum Sicambrorum, tabulis argenteis (iuxta 30 morem gentis antiquum) amicitiam confirmans, ita videlicet pactorum conditiones statuentes, vt Sicambris et Germani, Saxones atque Doringi, sub distinctis regibus atque principibus, tanguam fratres et germani, unus deinceps populus cenferentur, & in axuum permanerent, & bellum quod uni ex his immineret regno, quacunque à gente, omnes concerneret, atque coniunctis armis, communibusque propullaretur impennis. Terruit haec regnum confederatio plus quam potest, senatum, populumque Romanum: & variis modis, diuerfis ingenij, & multiplici ad inuentione contractum Germanorum foedus dissoluere, quanquam frustra, laborant. Exo tempore virtus et potentia Francorum Romanis semper fuerunt suspicata, metuentibus illis (quod postea contingit) ne Germani totius Europae monarchia potirentur. Et haec fuit causa, quod Octavia nus Romanorum Caesar postea sub Christi nativitate vnuerfum orbem Romanis obediens per capita fecit describi, putans multitudine gentium Francos esse delédos, quos co adhuc tempore scriptores historiarum nationum Germanos appellantur. Anno autem tertio regni Franci, cum viderent Romani, quod foedus regum Germanorum nullo possent ingenio dissoluere, rursus Gothos in fines Saxonum submisserunt, qui per annos ferme decem in finibus Germania coelidentes, paulatim et successive cogitabant foe in interiora nationis memoriae diffundere. Interea rex Francus crebro praelabilatur cum Gallis, & necé patri dura vicifilitudine in eos vindicabat, multaque corú millia per illud tempus occidebat. Verum cum Gothi quotdie magis ac magis ad interiora Germania irrumpent, Saxones cum Theutonibus tande necesseitate compulsi, bellum in eos mouere statuerit. Convocatis in auxiliu, iuxta compacta socijs, Sicambris atque Doringis, exercitum ducentorũ ac triginta millium virorum ad praelium eduxerit. Scanziani autẽ, qui et Gothi, convocatis et ipli socijs, innumerabile poene multitudinem Germanis veniaeribus, opposuerit. Bellum atrocissimum in eo loco, qui dicebatur Colmasũ, inter partes committitur, & cadéribus hincinde multis, à mane vique ad noctem martie ancipiti pugnatur. Postera die Germani exercitum diuiserit in tres partes, singulis duces singulos prefeuerit: Sicambris autẽ sub corum regé Franco audaciffime dimicatae, nomẽ sui ducis Franci, quasi numẽ quoddã crebrius vociferantes, clamabat: Hie Franci! Hie Franci! Postremo victi sunt Gothi, & plusquae octoginta corũ millia perempti, caeteri fuga lapși cu liber.

Annals of Trithemius

In the thirty-sixth year of his reign, Basanus, king of the Sicambri, at the solemnity of his birthday at Nijmegen, summoned his sons, brothers, dukes, nobles, and distinguished members of his household to a very great banquet. With them, feasting lavishly for seven days, he performed sacrifices to the gods of his country, and showed Jupiter visible in the air above the temple [unclear]. On the eighth day, with the consent of all the nobles, he designated his son Clodomirus king over the Sicambri; in his native song he foretold many future things to the people, commended his sons and the kingdom to the princes, enjoined justice, and, entering the chapel of the temple, appeared nowhere again.

I do not know what I should assign to these little tales, indignation or laughter. Whether he was removed by deceit or by art remains uncertain; but this one thing I judge to have been the cause: the desire of a man, undoubtedly withdrawn either by his own ingenuity or by the voluntary will of a demon, to attain the reputation of divinity. For, as Amerodacus, philosopher of the Sicambri, writes, King Basan was most eager for divinity; he cultivated justice, loved his people, overthrew the enemy, was most dutiful to the good, and always cruel and severe to the unjust.

He vanished, however, or, to speak more correctly, withdrew himself, as Amerodacus is the authority, from the public assembly of the nobles, as we have said, in the thirty-sixth year of his reign; but before the birth of the Lord, in the year 248. The Sicambri, judging that he had been translated into the company of the gods, worshipped him under the name Basangot.

The Eighth

Clodomirus, the elder son of Basanus, succeeding in the kingdom, as his father had ordained with the consent of the princes, reigned eighteen years. In his first year, as soon as the Gauls learned that Basanus had vanished, whom they did not doubt to be dead, they sent messengers to Clodomirus and demanded back from him all the land between the Meuse and the Rhine, and around the [unclear] in circuit, which the Sicambri, from their first entry into the Cisthenan borders, had violently usurped for themselves contrary to justice. If he disdained to return it, they threatened that they would be ready to recover it by the sword, whether he sent back a negative answer through the appointed messengers or made no answer at all.

King Clodomirus, however, prudently and deliberately detained the messengers of the Gauls with him for a long time, as though he were going to take counsel with his princes concerning the urgent matter; and, taking the greatest care that the secret of his counsel and mind should not come to their knowledge, he ordered his servants to feed them abundantly and arrange that they should have cheerful days.

Meanwhile King Clodomirus sent messengers to the kings of the Saxons and Thuringians, urgently asking that they very secretly and quickly send forces to aid the Sicambri, their friends, against the Gauls, their common adversaries. The Saxons came with the Thuringians to assist their friends, as they were asked, bringing forward an army of one hundred thousand fighters. When matters had been arranged most secretly at his command, King Clodomirus allowed the messengers of the Gauls, furnished with gifts, to depart; and, lest anything of the foregoing could come to their knowledge on the road, he assigned escorts for a safe journey to those setting out, who would accompany them and observe them more carefully, with letters of this sort:

“Clodomirus, great king, to the Gallican satraps. We marvel at your rashness, that you demand back from us the land which our forefathers long ago, by right of war, most justly vindicated by the sword from yours, as from wrongful [unclear], their manifest enemies. Consider that our strength is far superior to yours. Cease from this rashness of unjust folly. Remember the defeats which you long ago deservedly received from our begetter, translated among the gods, and from his parents. Rest in your caves, hiding with foxes. It is ours to command you; yours, however, humbly to obey our precepts. But if you presume to come against us, we have decreed to meet you powerfully and to defend by the sword what our ancestors handed down to us.”

When the Gauls received these letters from the messengers, they were stirred to anger and resolved to avenge themselves upon the Sicambri as quickly as possible. Having skillfully built a bridge over the Meuse, they led across a huge army of fighters. King Clodomirus met them most powerfully with two hundred sixty-four thousand men; and, having divided the army into parts, he stationed one part in ambush; another he sent from the region at a distance so that, after killing the guards of the Gauls, it might seize the bridge first; the third part, which was greater in number of soldiers, he led against the adversaries.

The Sicambri and the Gauls engage in a place not far from the river Meuse, which is called Delon; for some time they are driven back in an uncertain battle. At last the Sicambri, pretending flight, began to withdraw little by little, until at length they drew the Gauls farther from the river Meuse to the place of ambush. There the Sicambri then stood immovable, and those who had previously feigned flight fought back most bravely like giants. Meanwhile the soldiers, circling around, came to [unclear].

Compendium, Book I.

...the crossing of the river, and, after the enemy guards had been killed or driven far away, they seized the bridge in advance. The rest at once burst out from the ambushes and, attacking the enemy bravely, cut them down from the rear, slaughter them, and kill them without pity. At last those who could, seeking safety in flight, since they did not know that the bridge had been occupied in advance by the Sicambri, were shut in on every side and were cut down by the enemy; nor was there any place to escape the death pressing upon them before their eyes. A few, with night coming on, escaped safe out of many, those who were able to flee into the dark groves and forests.

Thereafter the kingdom of the Sicambri rested from the turmoil of wars for a few years; but afterwards, when peace was broken, the people more often took up arms on a great scale. The other deeds and wars of King Clodomirus, which he had with foreign nations, following Hunibald we have written down in the first volume of our annals.

King Clodomirus died in the eighteenth year of his reign, 230 years before the birth of the Lord, leaving three sons by Queen Ermendrude, who had been the daughter of the king of the Teutons: Nicanor, Helianus, and Helenus.

Ninth.

Nicanor, the elder son of King Clodomirus, succeeding his father, reigned for thirty-four years. He was a stern man, just in his generation, warlike, and most impatient of any injuries from enemies, especially from the Gauls; for this reason, with varying fortune, he very often fought against them very fiercely.

For from that time when this people, sprung from the stock of the Trojans, first came from the borders of the Scythians into Germany, to the mouths of the Rhine, it never ceased from the harassment of the Gauls, until at last, not without much bloodshed among its own people, it powerfully brought all Gaul under its yoke. No one was ever able fully to overcome the Franks or Sicambri; no one imposed the bridle of subjection upon these most fierce men, but they did not lay aside the desire of ruling, which they had once drunk in, before they had brought all Gaul, and Italy as well, into their power, after the Roman empire had been annihilated and many kings destroyed.

For, as was said above, it is clear from the calculation of the times that, from the beginning of the Franks’ entry, as they are now called, into the lands of Germany on this side [of the Rhine], down to Clovis the great king, who, first as victor over the Alemanni, believed in Christ, 930 years elapsed. During these years the Sicambri fought with the Gauls, never ceasing to make war upon them, although more often defeated in part, until finally they overcame them all.

It should be known, however, that they were not always called either Franks or Sicambri, but frequently changed their names along with their settlements. For indeed, as Hunibald bears witness, when after the destruction of Troy they wandered among various nations for many years and did not long have fixed settlements in one place, among the Scythians they were called Scythians; among the Armenians, they were called Armenians. When they dwelt at the mouths of the Danube, they were called neither Franks nor Sicambri; but because they were neighbors to the Scythians, they received the name of the Scythians’ languages. Afterwards, driven out through the Goths by the envy of the Romans, as Amerodacus is the authority, they descended into the territories of Germany, and, settled in their seats, as has often been said, at the mouths of the Rhine, they learned the speech of the German Saxons. At first they were called Neomagi, afterwards also Germans; then, named Sicambri from Cambra, they changed even that name with time, stirred by love of King Francus, from whom the name of the Franks, as will be said later in its proper order, took its beginning. Hence it has happened that the writers of other peoples, whenever in the descriptions of their histories they introduce mention of the deeds of this people, often call them Germans rather than Sicambri, or Franks. This has usually brought no small harm of error to those who do not know the true origin of the Franks, while they believe that the Franks were either natives or began from a conspiracy of a few men.

King Nicanor, joined with the Saxons and Thuringians, in the fourteenth year of his reign advanced to war with a great multitude against the Goths, who were again breaking into the lands of the Teutons and Saxons. In the first encounter they were superior to the Goths and crushed the Germans with great slaughter. But soon, when the army had been restored, they were defeated by the Goths; many thousands of them perished, both by the edge of the sword and submerged in the waters; the rest sought safety in flight.

In the twenty-first year of his reign he waged a naval war against King Orhadus, in favor of the king of Britain, whose sister, named Constantia, he had as wife. But he did not wage the war successfully enough, because many of his men, on account of their inexperience in naval combat, in

At length he died in the thirty-fourth year of his reign, in the one hundred ninety-sixth year before the birth of Christ, leaving five sons: Marcomirus, who succeeded to the kingdom; Antenor, who ruled the maritime region; Priamus, who died at his uncle’s in Britain; Helenus, who held the Cisthenan duchy, between Saxony and the Rhine, over the Tegarani; Clodius, duke of the Mosani.

Tenth.

Marcomirus, son of King Nicanor, the elder by birth, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-eight years, a prince singular in modesty and prudence in his generation: pious, mild, and beneficent toward his subjects, but severe toward enemies at all times. Instructed from youth by the priests of the gods sufficiently in all the wisdom of this world, he became a most learned astrologer, augur, seer, interpreter of dreams and events. As often as he could, in leisure, he ordered the brave deeds of his ancestors to be sung before him, both in the palace and in the temples, so that by their example his spirit might be stirred to the defense of his people and always to the increase of the kingdom. This was the custom among our ancestors, the Franks and Germans: that the deeds or sayings of heroes worthy of remembrance should be entrusted by the priests of the temples to songs in the fatherland’s tongue, in the learning, remembering, and singing of which the talents of the young were exercised. This custom lasted for many years, until at last it failed.

But King Marcomirus, in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, which was the one hundred sixty-eighth year before the incarnation of our savior Jesus Christ,

Eleventh.

Clodius, first-born of Marcomirus king of the Sicambri, reigned after his father for eleven years. In his time the sword of the Romans, directed into Gaul, brought no small harm upon the Sicambri. For in these times the Romans increased the strength of the Gauls, who, making an incursion beyond the Meuse, very grievously and often afflicted the foreign people. The Sicambri, fierce in spirit, meeting them, repelled force with force.

After many battles joined with the Gauls, King Clodius, in the last year of his reign, having gathered a huge army both of his own men and of Saxons, again fought with the same not far from the fortress of Basanburg. In this battle, while he was reconnoitering too incautiously, he was slain in the line by the adversary. But the Sicambri, encouraged by the exhortation of their leaders, notwithstanding the death of the king, continued the war, and fighting bravely at length defeated the Gauls; after killing many of them, they put the others to flight. King Clodius died, slain in the war of the Gauls, as has been said, in the eleventh year of his reign, and in the one hundred fifty-seventh year before the birth of Christ.

Twelfth.

Antenor, son of King Clodius, the elder by birth, reigned after his father for sixteen years. He made truces, which our people call Treugae from the pledge of faith interposed, with the Gauls for ten years. This one thing was also [pleasing?] to the Romans: because, being more humane than the rest, he forbade human beings to be sacrificed to the gods. This displeased many nobles of the Sicambri, who thought that the fear of them among foreign nations was diminished. But because this pious measure had been decreed with the counsel of the priests, the constitution itself remained inviolable. For priestly authority among them was always greater and more excellent than that of all leaders and princes. King Antenor died in the sixteenth year of his reign, and in the one hundred forty-first year before the birth of the Lord.

Thirteenth.

Clodomirus, son of Antenor, reigned after his father for twenty years. In his first year the Romans, overthrowing the Numantines through Scipio, reduced them into their power. In his sixth year, the truces which they had made with his father now ended, the Gauls, having gathered a great army of their men, resolved to move against the Sicambri; and, crossing the river Meuse, first [unclear]

The ancient [unclear] always pursued the Gauls in war. Marcomirus reigned twenty-eight years. A praiseworthy custom in a prince; [unclear] instructed in memorable matters. Marcomirus brought down the kingdom of the Sicambri. Clodius reigned eleven years. Clotharius reigned sixteen years. Truces were made between the Sicambri and the Gauls. Antenor reigned ten years. Truces were made between the Sicambri and the Gauls. The priests of the Sicambri had great power. Clodomirus reigned twenty-eight years. The ancient [unclear] always pursued the Gauls in war.

12. Compendium, Book I.

The war of the Sicambri with the Gauls; the Gauls are overcome by the Sicambri.

They declare [war] upon their enemies. Clodomir, supported by the aid of the Germans, confidently met the Gauls without delay. A very fierce battle was fought for people and kingdom; many fell on both sides. At last the Gauls turned their backs, and the Sicambri pursued them as far as the river, and laid low the greater part of the army by the edge of the sword. If they had either destroyed the bridge or seized it beforehand, as Clodomir the king, son of great Basanus, had once done, not even one of the Gauls could have escaped. After the Gauls had suffered this disaster, as long as Clodomir survived they no longer crossed the Meuse with an army, though they often committed raids in their usual fashion. King Clodomir, after many battles fought with the Romans, the Gauls, and the peoples farther up around the Rhine and the Moselle, died in the twentieth year of his reign, which was the one hundred twenty-first year before the birth of Christ.

The Fourteenth.

Merodacus, son of Clodomir, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-eight years. He was a high-minded, vigorous, and very bold prince; how warlike he was the Romans and the Gauls could perceive, for he often fought bravely with them, even with his own hand. For with the Saxons, Doringi, and Germans bringing auxiliaries, he led into Italy against the Romans an army of two hundred and twenty thousand fighting men; and, devastating everything round about, he came with his forces as far as Ravenna, and returned victorious, enriched with many spoils. On his return he also severely afflicted many colonies of the Romans, subjected them to very grave hardships, and made his name formidable to all.

Greatly stirred by these events, the Romans, having joined many nations to themselves, declared war on the Sicambri; the necessary preparations having been made, they assembled for battle. And lest the Saxons or Doringi bring aid to the Sicambri, the Romans had first induced the Goths and Slavs, by promised gifts, that at one and the same time these should attack the Saxons and they themselves the Sicambri. King Merodacus, therefore, being necessarily abandoned by the Saxons and Doringi, called upon the king of the northern island, whom today we call Danes; he came with one hundred thousand men as auxiliaries and increased the number of the Sicambri.

And so, in the twenty-second year of his reign, he learned that a great army of the Romans was coming against him. For Marius, prince of the Romans, sent the Roman legions with the Gauls, under Duke Theodomenus, beyond the Meuse. They boldly engaged the Sicambri, whom they themselves called Germans, and fought fiercely together; many thousands of men fell on both sides, and the Sicambri fled, having lost more than twenty thousand fighting men. After this, Merodacus, his army restored, became more powerful than the Gauls and Romans and afflicted them with much slaughter, as, following Hunibald, we have said more fully in the first volume of our histories or annals. But afterwards, when he had fought many battles with the Gauls and Romans and had enlarged the borders of his people by no small amount, King Merodacus died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, but in the ninety-third year before the birth of Christ.

The Fifteenth.

Cassander, the elder son of King Merodacus, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-one years. He was a very warlike man, in whose time the Gauls, with the aid of the Romans, more often crossed the river Meuse and invaded the borders of the Sicambri. Cassander, the aforesaid king of the Sicambri, gathered the armies into one and advanced to battle against them; when the clash had taken place, the fighting was fierce for a long time, and many fell on both sides. For all the days in which he ruled the Sicambri he was in conflict with the Gauls and Romans.

In these times Borbista, king of the Goths, with an innumerable multitude of fighting men, entered the borders of Saxony, devastating the region with fire and sword. Against him three very powerful kings, namely Arthari king of the Saxons, Hamer king of the Doringi, and Cassander, the aforesaid king of the Sicambri, gathered their armies into one and advanced to battle. When the clash had taken place, the fighting was fierce for a long time, and many fell on both sides. At last King Borbista turned his back, and the Germans obtained the victory. On another occasion after this, King Borbista again entered Saxony with a very great multitude of Goths, and cruelly devastated the region with fire and sword as far as the river Vistula; and, having seized many spoils of the Germans, he withdrew, nor did he presume to advance farther that day. For he knew the forces of the Germans to be unconquerable, although at the Romans’ urging he had often tested them. The Sixteenth.

[unclear] in the twenty-first year of his reign, but in the seventy-second year before the birth of the Lord; he was buried at Neopagus with many treasures.

Antharius, son of King Cassander, reigned after his father for thirty-five years. Hunibald writes of him that he crushed the people of Mainz, Roman colonists, in a wretched disaster, burned and overthrew the city, which afterward is seen transferred and built in that place where now [unclear] and the valley are, on the slope of the mountain by the bank of the Rhine. This pitiable devastation of the Mainzers took place in the sixteenth year of King Antharius, which was the fifty-sixth year before the birth of Christ, as is shown from the sequence of times.

King Antharius entered Gaul with the help of the Germans, burned villages, very often carried off boundless plunder and spoils, caused great devastation throughout Gaul, burned cities, destroyed villages, overthrew castles, broke the strength of the people, and reduced a region long fruitful to solitude.

But when King Antharius had grown old, in the last year of his reign, which was the thirty-seventh before the birth of Christ, the Gauls again burst into the region of the Sicambri and crossed the Meuse. He met them with the army of his own men to fight; there, while he fought too incautiously, he was surrounded by the enemy and [unclear] with twenty thousand Sicambri. This Frankish king was accustomed to fight, not to flee; he was very gentle and beloved by his own people, but always exceedingly to be feared by all enemies.

Francus, from whom they are called Franks, reigned 28 years.

In the first year of his reign he contracted a perpetual treaty with the Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians, with the consent of all the dukes and nobles of the Sicambri, confirming the friendship on silver tablets, according to the ancient custom of the people: namely, establishing the terms of the agreements so that the Sicambri, Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians, under distinct kings and princes, should thereafter be regarded as one people, like full brothers, should remain so forever, and that any war which threatened the kingdom of one of these, from whatever people, should concern them all and be repelled with united arms and common expenses. This confederation of kingdoms terrified, more than can be said, the senate and people of Rome; in various ways, by different devices, and with manifold contrivance, they labored, though in vain, to dissolve the treaty contracted by the Germans. From that time the courage and power of the Franks were always suspect to the Romans, who feared, as later happened, that the Germans would gain possession of the monarchy of all Europe. And this was the reason why Octavian Caesar of the Romans afterward, under the birth of Christ, caused the whole world obedient to the Romans to be registered by heads, thinking that by the multitude of the nations the Franks were to be destroyed; at that time the writers of histories still called them peoples of Germany.

But in the third year of Francus’s reign, when the Romans saw that they could by no device dissolve the treaty of the German kings, they again sent the Goths into the borders of the Saxons. Settling for almost ten years in the borders of Germany, they gradually and successively planned to spread themselves into the interior of the aforesaid nation. Meanwhile King Francus often fought with the Gauls, avenged upon them with harsh retaliation the death of his father, and killed many thousands of them during that time. But when the Goths broke more and more each day into the interior of Germany, the Saxons with the Teutons, at last compelled by necessity, resolved to make war on them. Having summoned as allies, according to the agreements, the Sicambri and Thuringians, they led out to battle an army of two hundred and thirty thousand men. But the Scanzians, who are Goths, having themselves summoned allies, set against the approaching Germans an almost innumerable multitude. A most savage battle was joined between the parties in that place which was called Colmasus; with many falling on both sides, they fought from morning until night with doubtful fortune. On the next day the Germans divided the army into three parts and set individual commanders over each; but the Sicambri, fighting very boldly under their king Francus, more frequently shouted the name of their leader Francus as if it were some divine power, crying: “Here Frank! Here Frank!” At last the Goths were defeated, more than eighty thousand of them were slain, and the rest slipped away in flight with [unclear].

Antharius reigned 35 years.

Mainz destroyed.

The Sicambri burned [unclear] Gaul.

The Seventeenth.

Francus, the elder son of King Antharius, from whom the Sicambri were thereafter called Franks, as Hunibald is the authority, reigned after his father for twenty-eight years. He was a fierce, bold, warlike man, a most vigorous defender of his people, who avenged the death of his father harshly enough upon the Gauls, waged many wars with foreign nations, always a victorious and glorious triumphator; the people of the Franks not undeservedly boast that he was the first author of their name and honor. This king Francus was accustomed to fight, not to flee; he was very gentle and beloved by his own people, but always exceedingly to be feared by all enemies.

In the first year of his reign he contracted a perpetual treaty with the Saxons and Thuringians of Germany, with the consent of all the dukes and nobles of the Sicambri, confirming the friendship on silver tablets, according to the ancient custom of the people: namely, establishing the terms of the agreements so that the Sicambri, Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians, under distinct kings and princes, like full brothers, should thereafter be regarded as one people, should remain forever, and that the war which threatened the kingdom of one of these, from whatever people, should concern them all and be repelled with united arms and common expenses. This confederation of kingdoms terrified, more than can be said, the senate and people of Rome; in various ways, by different devices, and with manifold contrivance, they labored, though in vain, to dissolve the treaty contracted by the Germans. From that time the courage and power of the Franks were always [unclear] to the Romans, who feared, as [unclear].

Compendium, Book I

...and wives, returned to their former hiding-places; thus the Saxons, with the aid of the Franks and Thuringians, joyfully recovered their own territories, devastated and occupied by foreigners for ten years.

From that time the Sicambri, laying aside their ancient name, began, out of love for their king, to call themselves Franks. Indeed, as Hunibald bears witness, not only the nobles, but also all the soldiers, the whole people of the entire nation, were so delighted by the very novelty of the name that they induced the king by entreaties to decree by public edict that thereafter they were forever to be called not Sicambri but Franks. This the king established all the more gladly, the more eagerly he loved the immortality of his own name. Therefore they were called Franks, who previously by some were called Sicambri, and by others, by reason of their alliance, Germans. And it is indeed remarkable how they gloried in the novelty of this word, since for many times thereafter, whenever they met one another, they greeted one another thus: “A good day, free Frank.” Nevertheless, not suddenly, but at last after much time, this name came into unity, so that the people itself were called Franks even among other nations; for to the Romans and especially the Gauls the name of the Franks was hateful. Hence among their writers they were more often called Germans than either Sicambri or Franks. Hunibald did not pass over in silence whence, or from whom, the name of the Sicambri had its origin.

Whence the Franks are called free, “Die fryer Francken”; by what names they were known.

That the Franks were previously called Sicambri is attested not only by Hunibald, but also by the blessed archbishop Remigius, who, as Gregory, bishop of Tours, records, when he was to baptize Clodoveus, king of the Franks, the first of the kings of the Franks converted to Christ, as we shall say in its proper place, said before the assembly of nobles, while he was putting off his royal ornaments and humbling himself for the sacred washing, with all hearing: “Gently bow your neck, Sicamber; worship what you burned; burn what you worshipped.” Of the history of this matter I have already spoken more fully, after Hunibald, in the first volume of the Annals.

The Franks were previously said to have been Sicambri.

The saying of St. Remigius to Clodoveus.

The Frankish name was always distasteful to the Romans and Gauls.

And so in the twenty-fourth year before the birth of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, which was the fourteenth year of King Francus, the Sicambri changed their ancient name to a new one, although both before and afterward they were more often called Germans, or Sicambri, among writers. For although they themselves wrote and always retained the name Frank, taken up under the aforementioned king, nevertheless it could not immediately come into use among foreign nations, [unclear]

King Francus, after the Goths had been overcome, returns.

He attacks the Gauls, joining battle.

Three hundred thousand Franks and Germans against the Gauls.

...a people hostile to us, or to die fighting.

Gladdened by these words, the king at once sent messengers to the Saxons, the Germans, and also the Thuringians, asking aid by right of alliance against the assault of the Gauls. All these, with great eagerness, sent the requested supports of soldiers: the Saxons, namely, eighty-four thousand fighting men; the German Theutones, sixty thousand; and the Thuringians, forty-six thousand. Joined with these, the Franks with great forces very hastily brought out an army of three hundred thousand men against their adversaries. But King Francus, seeing the desolation of the region which the Gauls had made, moved with great indignation of spirit, said: “See, my bravest fellow-soldiers, you who rightly grieve for the shed blood of your fathers, what these most treacherous Gauls have done. I swear by the head of my little son Antharius, whom these most wicked men killed, that I shall give no rest to my head until I have avenged myself on them in a notable way.” And they all praised his swift resolve.

Therefore, after a bridge had been constructed with boats and many timbers, in two days he led the army across, leaving forty thousand men to guard the crossing; with the remaining multitude he advanced into Gaul, and he made such a slaughter as no one of the Sicambri before him was able to make, or is believed to have conceived in his mind. For, having advanced as far as the river Tabul, [and] the western sea...

Francus, after constructing a bridge over the Meuse, devastates Gaul.

[the southern] than the northern, the Tungri, the Tarubani, and the people of Liege, and whatever lies between or adjacent to these, he savagely laid waste with fire and sword.

When the Gauls joined battle with him, he overcame, routed, and destroyed them with such ease that he was thought to be not a man, but some divine power sent from heaven. Hence all the nations round about, excessively terrified, feared thereafter to engage the Franks, as though they were the fiercest monsters. In that encounter and devastation, more than two hundred thousand of the Gauls themselves fell by the sword of the Franks, together with children, infants, and women. For just as the Gauls had previously done when they devastated the Sicambri, sparing no parents, so they received from the same.

Then the Senate and People of Rome, moved with indignation, [unclear] an expedition of legions of soldiers against the Germans, under the command of Marcus Lollius. For they did not think it would be safe to engage the Franks, whom they themselves called Germans, before they had subdued the Saxons and the Doringi. The Romans therefore entered Saxony; at first they indeed conquered, killing eighteen thousand Germans.

The Sicambri, sparing none, so received from the same.

But Francus, hearing this, weighed down by labors and old age, sent a legion of soldiers against the Saxons into Germany, under the command of Marcus Lollius. For he did not think it would be safe if they engaged the Franks, whom he himself called Germans, before they had subdued the Saxons and the Doringi. The Romans therefore entered Saxony; at first they indeed conquered, killing eighteen thousand Germans.

The Romans are overcome by the Franks in war.

Then in the twenty-fourth year of King Francus. Finally King Francus, weighed down by labors and old age, after many battles most victoriously fought with the Romans, Goths, Gauls, and other nations, and after the kingdom of the Franks had been increased not a little and its territories enlarged, died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, in the ninth year before the birth of the Lord. His wars, character, institutions, laws, and victories were written by Clodomirus, high priest of the Franks, in German verse, and by Hunibald in prose, in the Latin language; under their guidance we have treated them thus in the first volume of the annals of German and Frankish affairs which we wrote.

Clogius the Eighth.

Clogio, the eldest son of Francus the king, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for thirty years: a most cunning man, versatile in talent, an augur, a magician, and a most inquisitive astrologer. Concerning him the aforementioned high priest, counselor, and seer of the Franks, Clodomirus, arranged many astonishing and wonderful things in verse, of which we made mention in the first volume.

His mother, named Lothildis, daughter of the king of the Doringi, was the chief officiant, or priestess, of the temple of Pallas, devoted to magical arts, by the practice of which she did many marvelous things. For, as the authors already named wrote, by her songs and incantations she destroyed whichever enemies of her son she wished, made them unfortunate, and slew them through the ministry of demons, however far away they were; by sorcery she procured victory for the Franks and fear, terror, and flight for their enemies; rains, thunder, lightning, and horrible storms in the air were brought on by her spells whenever, wherever, and against whomever she wished. In the fourth year of his reign, the Romans again launched an expedition into Germany; the allied kings, meeting them energetically, did not cease bravely to drive back force with arms, until they compelled the enemies to retreat and flee. [unclear] the Franks, but called Germans, fought with Tiberius the Roman and most bravely for his people; finally, after many had fallen on both sides, the Romans departed without victory.

In the tenth year of the reign of the aforementioned Clogio, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, the Lord, savior of the whole universe, Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, was born in Bethlehem of Judah from the ever-virgin Mary. In that year, as Hunibald bears witness, by the edict of Caesar Augustus, the world subject to Roman rule was registered by heads. This, apart from the meaning of the mystery, accomplished by divine providence, was not without literal significance, since the Franks supplied the cause. [unclear] and from the name of its leader Phirisia it is called Phirisia, as Hunibald holds, down to the present day.

Again after ten years, with the consent of the aforementioned King Clogio and all the princes, all the kings of Phirisia, like the other leaders, were to remain forever subject to the king of the Franks, and each year were to pay a tribute of two hundred sixty oxen; and, in the manner of the Franks’ other friends, they were to fight against any enemies whatsoever.

King Clogio of the Franks died after many brave deeds, in the thirtieth year of his reign, which was the twentieth year of the Lord’s nativity. Concerning his character, prophecies, oracles, and wars, Hunibald writes many things.

Compendium, Book I.

Nineteenth.

Herimer, the elder son of King Clogio, succeeding his father, reigned for twelve years, a warlike man and excessively bold. In the third year of his reign, the Gauls, making an incursion, came as far as the Meuse, devastating with hostile rashness everything that belonged to the jurisdiction of the Franks, except fortifications and castles, and after this they quickly withdrew to their own lands with plunder and spoils.

But afterwards, when this incursion of the Gauls became known to King Herimer, he was moved to anger; and, having summoned to himself the dukes beyond the Meuse, through whose negligence the Gauls had broken in, [unclear] according to the laws of the Franks: whoever is established in ducal authority shall diligently protect the province entrusted to him. But if through his negligence enemies enter the region, if they injure our people, or if they despoil the inhabitants of the land of their property, let him pay half of his goods into the king's purse, and let him no longer be duke, but live deprived of honor. If he willingly permitted entry to the enemies, let him be buried alive or be punished capitally; and let his wives, with his children and all his property, pass to the king's service.

Then, having called to his aid allies, Germans, Theutonici, and Thuringians, King Herimer entered against the Gauls with a heavy multitude and subdued them with so great a slaughter that for many years they could not recover their former strength. Finally, however, in the last year of his reign, when he had again led an army across into Gaul, being excessively bold, not to say rash or presumptuous, and fighting rather incautiously, he was killed by them in battle, in the thirty-second year of the Lord.

Twentieth.

Marcomir, brother of the aforementioned King Herimer, who had been slain by the Gauls, succeeding his brother in the kingdom of the Franks, reigned for eighteen years: a man tall in stature, harsh in manners, yet favorable to friends, but feared and terrible to enemies. He engaged in many battles with the Roman Gauls, and often severely afflicted the people of Mainz, Trier, and the Agrippinians together.

In the second year of his reign, the only-begotten Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, Savior of the world, born man from Mary, ever a most pure virgin, without mixture with a man, according to that same humanity was crucified at Jerusalem, the city of the Jews, under Pontius Pilate, governor of the Romans; he suffered, died for our salvation, and was buried. He descended to the lower world, snatched the righteous from there, rose from the dead on the third day, and, ascending into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, to judge the living and the dead; he lives forever.

In the tenth year of King Marcomir, Claudius Caesar of the Romans led an army into Britain, which we now call England by the customary term, and by force of arms made it, together with the islands of the Orkneys, tributary to the Romans. On the journey there and back, he severely afflicted the Franks dwelling between the Meuse and the Rhine, though not without bloodshed among his own men.

At that time Guiderius, son of the late King Kymbelinus, was reigning in Britain. When he had been slain in battle by the army of Claudius, his brother Arviracus at once rose up in his place; putting the royal diadem on himself and killing many of the Romans, he pursued Claudius as far as the ships. Caesar, seeing that he could not overcome Arviracus, offered peace and gave him his daughter as wife. He recovered the tribute denied to the Romans, and with the help of his son-in-law also led his army across to the islands of the Orkneys.

But Marcomer, the aforementioned king of the Franks, died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the fiftieth year of the Lord's nativity, in the eighth indiction of the Romans.

Twenty-First.

Clodomer, son of the aforementioned King Marcomir, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for twelve years, a restless and very warlike man. Hunibald reports of him that he was most hostile to the Roman Gauls; he desired nothing more than to erase the memory of them. There was scarcely a year in which he did not move an expedition into Gaul at least once.

In the first year of his reign, three suns appeared at the same time, which gradually returned into one. There followed throughout all Europe a great and immense famine, and a mortality not only of men but also of draft animals.

Mainz, destroyed by the Romans, is repaired.

In the ninth year, however, King Clodomer, with a great army of his men, crossed the Rhine and the Meuse and expelled the Gauls, recovering everything previously lost. With the help of the Germans he fought with the Romans at Mainz, but he could not prevent them from repairing the city. He died in the twelfth year of his reign, and in the sixty-second year of the Lord's nativity, in the fifth indiction of the Romans.
