VICESIMVSSEQVNDVS. 17 ANTENOR regis Clodomeri filius, post patrem regnauit annis sex, qui toto tempore quo regnauit, bellum gessit cum Galli atque Romanis, cuius tandem et occasione cum multis regni proceribus, miserabiliter interijt, quando (sicuti dicemus) ponte fracto in Mosa flumine, submersus est. Anno siquidem regni sui vltimo, ponte supra naues veterum more fabricato ex lignis, exercitum trans flumen duxit in Galliam, vastata regione, cum praeda et spolijs multis re- Antenor rex regnauit anni 6. ditum maturauit in Franciam. Cumque iam flumen pars maior transisset exercitus, & rex ipse cum proceribus et reliquis vltimis adhuc resideret ad littus, subitopons, equitum numero grauatus, cecidit, solutae que naues ab inuicem funibus ruptis, miserablem cunctis dedere spectaculum, pluribus in flumine cadentibus. Attonitus rex et animo nimirum turbatus, de ponte reparando cum his qui aderant coepit habere consiliũ, cum ecce mox Galli nunciantur in magna pugnatorum multitudine, post tergum venire, parati ad pu-gnam. Quibus auditis consternati sunt omnes qui erant cum rege, quibus fugam tempus negabat et locus: pugnam vero interdixit minor exercitus. Igitur cum euafionis nulla patefeceret nisi natandi via per flumen, arma et quicquid potuit grauare, proiecerunt in a-quam, & salutem natando tentabant. Rex etiam proiecta lorica, foloque super tunicam baltheo praecinctus et enfe, fese cum equo submisit in vndas. Similife periculo, necessi-tate compulsi, omnes reliqui submiferunt. Natare simul coeperunt vniuersi, alij super 20 equos, alij manibus ac pedibus aquarium impetus fulantes. Ex eis plures natando per-uenerunt ad littus, multi etiam qui natandi non habuere peritiam, prefocati ab aquis in medio fluctuum perierunt. Annals of Trithemius. The Twenty-Second.

Antenor, son of King Clodomer, reigned after his father for six years. During the whole time in which he reigned he waged war with the Gauls and the Romans; and at length, on account of this, he miserably perished with many nobles of the kingdom, when, as we shall say, the bridge broke and he was drowned in the river Meuse.

In the last year of his reign, then, after a bridge had been built of wood over boats in the ancient fashion, he led his army across the river into Gaul. Having laid waste the region, he hastened his return into Francia with much booty and many spoils. And when the greater part of the army had already crossed the river, while the king himself with the nobles and the last of the rest was still waiting on the bank, suddenly the bridge, weighed down by the number of horsemen, collapsed; and the boats, released from one another when the ropes broke, gave all a miserable spectacle, with very many falling into the river. The king, stunned and surely troubled in mind, began to take counsel with those who were present about repairing the bridge, when behold, at once the Gauls were announced to be coming behind them in a great multitude of fighters, ready for battle. On hearing this, all who were with the king were thrown into consternation; time and place denied them flight, while the smaller army forbade battle. Therefore, since no way of escape lay open except that of swimming through the river, they threw into the water their arms and whatever could weigh them down, and tried for safety by swimming. The king also, having thrown off his cuirass and being girded over his tunic only with belt and sword, committed himself with his horse to the waves. Compelled by necessity, all the rest committed themselves to like danger. They all began to swim at once, some on horses, others with hands and feet sustaining the force of the waters. Many of them reached the bank by swimming; many also who had no skill in swimming, choked by the waters, perished amid the waves. Among them King Antenor too was drowned, with nine princes, whose names are these: Duke Priam, Duke Clodius, Duke Richimer, Duke Antenor, Duke Marcomer, Duke Walther, Duke Clogio, Duke Herimer, and Duke Rutwicus, with sixty-three other nobles of the Franks. Thus King Antenor of the Franks perished in the sixth year of his reign, in the sixty-eighth year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the eleventh indiction of the Romans.

The Twenty-Third.

Ratherus, or, as he is written by others, Rhatherius, the eldest son of the aforementioned King Antenor, after the death of his father reigned over the Franks for twenty-one years. He was a great-souled, bold, and brave man, who always most vigorously defended the people of the Franks by his sword from every incursion of the Gauls, fearing no one, dreading no one, but himself to be feared by all. In his second year, Nero, the wicked emperor of the Romans, stirred up the first persecution against the Christians, killed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, at Rome, and throughout the whole empire cruelly destroyed many thousands of believers.

Ratherus, moreover, king of the Franks, crushed the Gauls repeatedly; he avenged his father’s death with arms, fire, and sword; he restored the borders taken from his people; he built castles, cities, and fortifications; he renewed the treaty with the kings of the Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians, which King Francus had once struck a hundred years before, as we said above; and he enlarged the boundaries of the kingdom of the Franks.

After these things he finally died in the twenty-first year of his reign, in the eighty-ninth year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the second indiction of the Romans, and was buried in the city of Ratherdama, which he himself had newly built from the foundations and dedicated to his own name. His magnificent deeds [unclear] Arebaldus, pontiff of the Franks, [unclear] Saxons and Thuringian kings, which King Francus had once [unclear] Arebaldus, chief priest established as pontiff by the people of the Franks, which he willingly accepted.

In his twelfth year the Goths again poured into the borders of the Saxons, [unclear] the region in their custom [unclear] in all things magnificent, bold, warlike, excessively superstitious in the worship of the idols of his people, indeed one who wished not only to equal the Romans in the number of gods, but even to conquer and surpass them. Wherefore, when divinities had been multiplied by him, after [unclear] was dead, Richimer himself, king of the Franks, together with the German brothers and the Teutons, in accordance with the ancient treaty renewed a few years before, as we said, quickly led out a great army; and when a gathering had been made, they killed more than twenty thousand Goths, and turned the rest, wounded and stripped, to flight.

Compendium, Book I.

After the Goths had again been driven out of Saxony, the Franks held a conference with the Germans and the Teutons, debating among themselves how they might thereafter bar the Goths and the Scanzian peoples from returning into the territories of the Saxons or Germans. At last it pleased all the kings and nobles that from the people of the Franks, Saxons, Thuringians, Germans, and Teutons, who around the sea were nearer neighbors to the Dacians and Goths, they should gather one nation, with children, wives, and beasts of burden, to inhabit the land beyond furthest Saxony, nearest to the Scanzians, and to prevent the incursions of enemies.

When this agreement had been concluded, Richimer, king of the Franks, sent eighteen thousand men, with children and wives, into that region; over them he appointed as leader and prince Sunno, his second-born son. To him, according to the agreement, many then came together from the Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians; from diverse peoples they became one, and within a short time they grew into a great nation, and thereafter did not permit the Scanzians to devastate Saxony. Yet they were rather often harassed by the Romans.

This duke Sunno established the seat of his nation with power in the borders of Saxony, having to the east the Sarmatians; to the south the Slavs of Bohemia; to the west Saxony and the Teutons; and to the north the Cimbri, the sea, the Dacians, the Scanians, the Goths, and island-dwelling men inhabiting marshy places.

Sunno duke, Clodomer, Sunno duke of the Franks.

Sunno increased not a little the possession he had received. After him Sunnon received [unclear] his principate, who in the year of the Lord’s nativity one hundred forty-six, indiction [unclear], received the nation, who in the year of the Lord’s nativity one hundred forty-six, on the banks of the river Oder, built a new city, which, out of love for his forefathers, he called Frankfurt. After this he also founded another city at the mouth of the aforesaid river, not far from the sea, which from his own name he called Sunda, or, as Hunibald testifies, Domicianus.

The name of the Franks remained for some time in these lands, until at last, when the dukes had multiplied, the region was divided into several parts, and each division received its name from individual princes or events. From Marcomer and his son Brando, who founded the city [unclear] Brandenburg, some were named [unclear]; from Brando his son, who founded the city [unclear] Brandenburg, others were named Braburgi; and others took other names from others.

Previously, in the fifth year of King Richimer, Domitian Caesar had worn down the Sarmatians and Dacians who dwelt on the borders of Germany toward the east, and afflicted them greatly. And, adding sin to crime, after the most impious Nero he stirred up the second persecution against the Christians; he was the first of all the Caesars to command that he be called God and Lord by all.

In the eleventh year of his reign Richimer, king of the Franks, had a war with the Romans and Gauls, not far from the city of Basana, aided by the common votes of the Germans, in which many fell on both sides. Meanwhile, when the Roman legions had returned to Cologne Agrippina, word was brought that Nerva Caesar was dead; in his place the soldiers raised Trajan, a man of Spanish nation, to be Caesar. He ruled nineteen years, six months, fifteen days.

But Richimer, king of the Franks, after many brave deeds, finally died in the twenty-third year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 113, the eleventh Roman indiction. Ruthvicus the Frank wrote in verse of his life, character, deeds, and worship of the gods.

ODEMARS, the elder son by birth of the aforesaid Richimer, king of the Franks, reigned after his father for fourteen years, a prince of the Franks very beloved by the people, who refrained from wars as far as could be done without damage to the commonwealth. For he made truces, which the Franks, because of the pledge interposed, call, as it were, “confidences,” with the Gauls and the Romans, to whom thereafter he showed himself so much a friend that he compelled all to lament his death.

Thus as long as he lived among men he kept the promised peace, and devoted all his zeal to the honor and adornment of his nation; he [built/adorned?] very many castles, cities, and fortifications throughout the kingdom. For the Franks, Saxons, and Germans at that time were still subject to the vanity of idols and far removed from knowledge of the Christian faith. They worshiped Mars as a fierce god of war, from whose divine power they sought victory at all times. To each of their gods also they [made] not only individual altars

Annals of Trithemius

[groves?] and temples, but also individual cities and villages; nor was there any number of senseless gods.

In these times the chief priest of the Franks, pontiff, elder, and prophet was named Vechtanus, born from the ancient stock of kings, eloquent in the Greek and Latin tongue; most skilled in astronomy, music, medicine, and the philosophy of the Greeks, since he had spent much time both at Rome and at Athens in the study of the writings of secular men, together with certain other fellow students of his. At length, having returned to his homeland, he taught the sons of kings and nobles, according to the ancient custom of the Franks, under an oak.

He wrote many things, in Greek poems, on the sacred rites of the gods; and he composed histories of the ancient kings, ten in number, in German, with which he exercised the talents of the young and greatly strengthened their memory. In the fifth year of King Odemar this man perished in a small river, to which, having been drowned in it, he gave his name, so that it is called in German, from Vechtanus, the Vecht down to the present day. Over his tomb King Odemar founded a new city, which he named Odemarsheim from his own name; it remains to the present in the territory of the diocese of the church of Utrecht.

But where Odemar, king of the Franks, among the Nitrians was [unclear] by the duke, called Marcoburg: Clogio, who perished in Britain; Francus, who was duke on this side of the Rhine among the Hogii, from Confluence as far as the mouth of the river Main toward the east, between the Mainz people and the Saxon Germans, who, restoring an ancient city, named it Frankfurt. And Meroda, struck by a [unclear] in hunting, died; Nicanor, who was an island duke at the mouths of the Rhine; and Odemar, whom his father, after the death of Vechtanus, [made?] pontiff [unclear] of the Romans the tenth, whose body is buried at Odemarsheim beneath a pyramid, as he had ordained while alive.

The Twenty-Sixth

Marcomer, son of King Odemar, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-one years. He had a wife named Athildis, daughter of Marus king of Britain; by her he begot seven sons, whose names were these: Clodomer, the firstborn, who succeeded his father in the kingdom; Marcomer, who held the duchy among the Nitrians, where he founded a city of his own name, called Marcoburg; Clogio, who perished in Britain; Francus, who was duke on this side of the Rhine among the Hogii, from Confluence as far as the mouth of the river Main toward the east, between the Mainz people and the Saxon Germans, who, restoring an ancient city, named it Frankfurt. And Meroda, struck by a [unclear] in hunting, died; Nicanor, who was an island duke at the mouths of the Rhine; and Odemar, whom his father, after the death of Vechtanus, [made?] pontiff [unclear] of the Romans the tenth, whose body was buried at Odemarsheim beneath a pyramid, as he had ordained while alive.

Doracus, prophet and writer of the Franks, flourished at that time, a former hearer and disciple of Vechtanus, born from the noble lineage of kings. Afterwards, when Odemar had died, he succeeded in the highest pontificate by the election of the governors. He obtained such authority among the Franks, and was held in such esteem, that he was worshipped by all almost as some divine power, and commanded not only the common people as he wished, but also the kings of the Franks and all the nobles. Writing in verse, he continued the histories of the nation.

The Franks had peace throughout all the days in which Marcomer reigned, and under his direction they greatly increased in riches, power, and honor. Doracus writes in the annals, as Hunibald testifies, that the Romans always held the Franks suspect both in peace and in war, as future overthrowers of the empire, having long since been forewarned by the oracle of Phaedrus, and that for this reason they often conspired with all their forces for their destruction, though in vain. For afterwards under King Faramund and his successors they both obtained all Gaul by their own forces and overcame the Roman empire.

Marcomer, king of the Franks, died in the twenty-first year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 148, in the first indiction.

The Twenty-Seventh

Clodomer, eldest son of the aforesaid Marcomer, king of the Franks, reigned after his father for seventeen years, a man of singular prudence, modest and most humane toward his own people. He had a wife named Hasildis, daughter of the duke of the Rugii; by her he begot three sons, Faraertus, Nicanor, and Roricus. The first of these, as we shall say, succeeded his father in the kingdom; the second was king of Frisia; the third, drowned in the water not far from Neuss, died and left his name to the river, which is called the Rur down to the present day. The place of Roricus’s drowning was between the Neocum castle [eischenanū?] and the old city which the inhabitants called Moradunum. In those times both Francia and all Germany were estranged from knowledge of the Christian faith.

Clodomer, king of the Franks, died in peace in the seventeenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 165, in the third indiction of the Romans. In his time the Gauls were preparing an inroad

Compendium, Book I.

The Twenty-Eighth.

Farabertus reigned 20 years.

Farabertus, the elder son of King Clodomer, succeeded his father and reigned twenty years, beginning in the aforementioned one hundred sixty-fifth year of the Lord’s nativity, in the third Roman indiction. He renewed and again ratified with the Germans, Saxons, Thuringians, Theutons, Marcomanni, and Cimbri the treaty and friendship formerly contracted by King Francus, as we said above, and then confirmed by other kings, renewed, and often strengthened and continued by a new ordinance. This greatly displeased the Romans and stirred them to arms.

The legions of the Romans into Germany [unclear].

For in the sixth year of this King Farabertus, which was the one hundred seventy-first year of the Lord’s nativity, in the times of Lucius Aurelius Commodus Caesar, the Romans, not bearing calmly so great a concord of the Franks with the Theutons and Germans, tried with every effort to overthrow it. And so, having sent legions through Sarmatia into Germany against the Dacians, Marcomanni, Theutons, Saxons, and Franks, they brought forth a great army of their men. Against their incursion the kings of the aforesaid peoples sent out such great forces of fighters that the said Romans were compelled to withdraw without victory, with loss and confusion.

Another expedition of the Romans into Germany, in the time of Antoninus Pius.

In the eleventh year of King Farabertus, under the emperor Antoninus Pius, the Romans again led an army back into Germany by way of the Sarmatians, and fierce fighting went on for a long time, and many on both sides fell wounded by the sword. Concerning the circumstances, outcome, and miracles of rains in this war, which were then reported on behalf of the army of the Romans, following Hunibald we have set out a sufficient narrative in the first volume of the Annals; we judge it superfluous to repeat it here.

Farabertus, king of the Franks, after many brave deeds, died in the twentieth year of his reign, in the 185th year of the Lord’s nativity, in the eighth indiction.

The Britons, who are now called English, receive the faith of Christ.

Faganus and Diuanus, bishops of the Britons.

In the times of this reign of Farabertus, namely in the one hundred eighty-second year of the Lord’s nativity, Eleutherius, pope of Rome, at the request of Lucius king of Britain, son of Coillus, sent into that Britain itself, which is now named England, the bishops Faganus and Diuanus, so that they might announce the word of salvation to the said king, and also to the nobles and the whole people of the British kingdom of his island, and baptize them, converted to the faith of Christ, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. When they came to the appointed place, in a short time they converted not only King Lucius but also the people of the whole island to the faith of Christ.

Priests of idols in Britain: pontiffs, 28; archflamens, 3.

[unclear], the aforesaid apostolic preachers consecrated their temples of idols to the honor of the one God, the almighty Father, appointing as many bishops in place of the flamens, and archbishops in place of the archflamens. Gildas wrote of these matters more fully in the book which he entitled On the Victory of Aurelius Ambrosius, king of the Britons; and after him Geoffrey of Monmouth, a Briton, who, for Duke Rupertus of Claudiocestria, completed in ten books the history of the Britons and the successions of all their kings, from the first entry of the people, with Brutus from the Trojans, into that island itself, down to the six hundred eighty-ninth year of the Lord’s nativity. His contemporary Caradocus of Llancarfan also described the successions, years, times, and deeds of the kings of the Franks in lucid speech.

Gildas and Geoffrey of Monmouth, historiographers.

Caradocus, writer of the Franks.

Sunno reigned 28 years.

Sunno, the elder son of Farabertus king of the Franks, succeeded his father and reigned twenty-eight years. He was a strong, vigorous, and bold prince, who fought many battles against the Romans and also the Gauls. In his time, when Lucius king of Britain, whom we said had first most humbly received the Christian faith, died without children, the Romans sent the senator Severus into Britain with two legions. He fought many battles with Fulgenius, by whom at last, in the siege of the city of Eboracum, he was killed along with many Romans; his son, named Bassianus, they accepted as king.

Severus the Roman is killed in Britain.

In the same year in which Severus was slain in Britain by Fulgenius, Sunno king of the Franks, with the Germans and Saxons bringing aid, after crossing the river at the fortress of Delonum,

The Franks [devastated?] Gaul.

HILDERICVS Sunnonis regis maior natu filius, post patrem regnauit annis qua- draginta: vir magnanimus, prudens, audax, bellicosus, qui non minus prudentia, 10 quam armis, gentem suam omni tempore fortiter defensauit, regni terminos longe lateque potenter extendit. Tantae namque virtutis potentie fuit, vt non modo Gallis, sed etiam Romanis esset haud medioeriter metuendus: quibus Francum nomen vfque adeo iuuifum erat odiofum, vt eam gentem nunquam aliter quam Germanam vel seri- bere vel nominare consueuerint. Gloriabantur fuo nomine Franci: quorum odio laborantes Romani vocabulum inuidebant: nec prius gentium vicinarum (Romanorum maxime Gallorum) scripto res historiarum, Francum nomen communi voto Sicambiae populo concesserunt; quã armis virtutibus Franci totam pene Europam suo dominio subiecierunt. Nam antea (sicut diximus) Romani, Galli, reliquae nationes inimicae, Francos(testante Hunibal- 20 do) liuore commoti, non alio nominauere vocabulo, quam Germanos. Sic etenim dicit auctor iam memoratus: Maiores nostri non minorem pro nomine gentis fuce, quod olim à Franco rege suo acceperunt, communi decreto curam habuerunt, quam pro regno; quis gloriosum sibi fore ar- bitrabantur, Francum nomen non amplius in aliud commutare, semel à suis progenitoribus cum sum- mo honore assumptum. Tantaeque apud suos aeftimationis auctoritatis fuit, vt eius imperio euncti semper obedirent. 30 Hic die natalis Hiderici regis Francorum stans in templo louis, apud Neopagum, multitudinem Francorum gentis, magno in precio Hildegast, philosophus, consiliarius, coram ipsius dei simulacro post preces pro impetratione vaticinii fusas, repente furere vates, parens regum, senior, omnium doctiffimus, quia sua tempefate miranda dixit,fecit, coepit (vt moris est dementatis) carmine alirunarum, agi ratoque capite ae manibus recur- uatis, ita vaticinabatur, non versibus lege metrorum compofitis vtens, sed rithmis abs- 40 que mensura furore fatis confufe prolatis, quorum interpretationem fic fecit Huni- baldus: Veniet ab occiduo Francis victoria Deo, Dardanique veteres quem coluere maiores. Aquilam Romani habuerunt pro signo dimicantes, quorum superbam arrogan- tem potentiam suprimere annihilare per fortitudinem fimul prudentiam cupien- tes, pro altera sumpferunt leonem: pro altera vero, serpentem. Annals of Trithemius.

He laid waste [unclear] the Gauls, and, after devastating the region round about, returned victorious, enriched with spoils. The rest, however, which Hildegast, philosopher of the Franks and distinguished seer, described in a German song, and afterward Hunibald in prose in the Latin language, we too have spoken of in the first book of the Annals.

Sunno, king of the Franks, died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, but in the year 213 of the Lord’s Nativity, in the sixth Roman indiction.

The Thirtieth.

Hilderic, the elder son of King Sunno, reigned after his father for forty years: a high-souled, prudent, bold, warlike man, who at all times stoutly defended his people no less by prudence than by arms, and powerfully extended the boundaries of the kingdom far and wide. For he was of such virtue and power that he was to be feared in no small degree not only by the Gauls but also by the Romans; to them the Frankish name was so hateful and odious that they were never accustomed to write or name that people otherwise than German.

The Franks gloried in their name; the Romans, laboring under hatred of them, begrudged them the word. Nor did the written histories of neighboring peoples, especially of the Romans and Gauls, by common consent grant the Frankish name to the people of Sicambria before the Franks, by arms and virtues, had subjected almost all Europe to their dominion. For previously, as we have said, the Romans, the Gauls, and the other hostile nations, as Hunibald testifies, moved by envy, named the Franks by no other word than Germans. For the author already mentioned says thus: Our ancestors had no less care, by common decree, for the name of their people, which they once received from their King Francus, than for the kingdom; for they thought it would be glorious for them no longer to exchange the Frankish name for another, once it had been assumed by their forefathers with the highest honor.

In these times there flourished under King Hilderic [unclear], also [unclear], [unclear] Hildegast, seer and philosopher, [unclear], most learned of all, who in his own time said, did, and wrote marvelous things. And he was of such esteem and authority among his own people that all always obeyed his command.

On the birthday of Hilderic, king of the Franks, standing in the temple of Jove at Neopagus, before a multitude of the Frankish people, Hildegast, philosopher, counselor, seer, father of kings, elder, most learned of all, because in his own time he said and did marvelous things, after prayers poured out before the image of that very god for the obtaining of a prophecy, suddenly began to rave, as is the custom of the frenzied, with a song of [unclear], and, with head tossed and hands bent back, he prophesied thus, not using verses composed according to the law of meters, but rhythms without measure, uttered very confusedly in prophetic frenzy; Hunibald made their interpretation thus:

Victory will come to the Franks from the western God, whom the old Dardanian ancestors worshiped. Whatever the Gaul possesses, whatever all Germany possesses, all will yield to your right, warlike Sicamber. When he gives you first a king from the name, whom the leaders, then without a king, shall appoint, then, with him victorious, the Frank shall reign without end.

He also added thus concerning the empire of the Romans:

Behold, the great God will give the brothel-camps to the Frank, and the lion will break the eagle, crushed together with the serpent.

Hunibald explains this meaning concerning the standards of the Franks, which they used in battles, which we call the insignia of princes.

The kings of the Franks, he says, from that time when they began to have war with the Romans, on the advice of the pontiffs of their people, took these new arms or insignia: after throwing away the three frogs which they had once brought from Scythia on a white fleece, they depicted a lion with the forepart of its body on a fleece of blue color, its feet stretched out for seizing, its mouth open in the manner of one roaring, whose lower part of the body ended in the tail of a serpent; with this it seemed strongly to bind, press, and choke the neck of an eagle depicted beneath on a golden fleece with wings spread.

The Romans had the eagle as their sign when fighting. Desiring to suppress and annihilate their proud and arrogant power by strength and at the same time prudence, the Franks took the lion for one part and the serpent for the other. For by the lion the Franks mystically designated their strength, but by the serpent their wisdom and prudence.

Hildegast, seer and philosopher.

The Romans always begrudged the Frankish name to the Sicambri.

Later they counted the Franks as Germans.

22 COMPENDIVM LIB. I. volebant, quibus indubitanter se Romanos tandem superaturos sperabant. Quibus infi- gnijs, siue armis, (quanquam improprie dicantur) omnes deinceps Francorum reges vsi fuerunt, vsque ad Clodouem Christianum, qui pro leone, tria legitur lilia demissa coeli- tus assumpsisse, quod suo loco dicetur. Regno tandem Francorum per filios Ludouici primi in duo diuiso, liliorum inter- signe cum Francis remansit Gallis, siue occidentalibus: propria vero leonis, atque caudae serpentis arma regnum Francorũ orientale siue Germanicum retinuit, quod cũ imperiũ sibi Romanum habeat annexum, interfigniis prioribus in obliuionem deductis, aquila imperij nota duntaxat vtī consueuit, ab illo tempore diuisionis vsque in presentem diem. Hildega- sta mobi- lium Fran- corum do- cter in omni scientia. Franci mo- ribus adi- ficisq́; que cultores ef- fectuꝑ erant. Hildegast etiam sapiens Francorum memoratus, nobilium filios docuit in eitharis, &amp; in diuerfis alijs instrumentis musicis, gesta maiorum carminibus lingua decantare ma- terna, motibus gentem viuere ciuilibus, aedificare domos, &amp; habitu incedere cultiores monuit, &amp; ferocitatem deponere iussit. Enimuero Franci parum eatenus cultum siue or- natum curabant, tam in structuris, quam in indumentis. Quae omnia Hildegast instituit cultiora, &amp; Romanorum superbiam non armis modo, verum etiam rebus et amp; moribus contundere ac domare sapientissime praecepit. Ex eo tempore Franci domos et amp; amplio- res et amp; pulchriores aedificare coeperunt, variisq́; distinctas mansionibus. Quicquid enim prioribus construxere temporibus, nimia simplicitate sui contemptibile fuit et amp; rusticum: quippe cum propter crebras mutationes sedium, habitare in campis assueti magis fuerint, quam in civitatibus. Hinc Germani sumentes prouerbium, quoties viderunt aliquid ve- tusta simplicitate fabrefactum, siue depictum, sie laudantes antiquitatem dicere consue- uerunt: Das ist ein gut alt Fränckisch Werk. Reliqua Hildegasti mirabiliter dicta, scripta, feu facta, Hunibaldus commemorat. Anno Hilderici regis Francorum vicesimoquarto, Alexander Mammeae filius, Caesar Au- gustus Romanorum, apud Moguntiam Germaniae vrbeṁ, militari tumultu perimitur, anno regni sui decimotertio. Hildericus autem rex Francorum, eius nominis primus, post multa fortiter et amp; ma- gnifice gesta, moritur tandem anno regni sui quadragesimo: Dominicae vero natiuitatis, ducentesimo, quinquagesimo tertio: indictione Romanorum prima. TRICESIMVS PRIMVS. Bartherus regnauit anno. 48. BARTHERV S Hilderici regis filius, patri succedens, regnauit annis X VIII. cuius tempore Romani bellum gesserunt cum Gothis, qui Istrum fluuium transmeantes, eorũ ciuitates deuastabant et amp; vrbes: quorum triginta millia occiderunt, sub ducatu De- cii Caesaris, &amp; filii eius. De Romanis etiam multi ceciderunt, inter quos et amp; filius ipse Decij Caesaris occupuit. Decius vero Caesar, iniquissimus Christianorum persecutor, dum fu- geret, in gurgite eiusdam paludis submersus est, cuius cadauer inueniri à suis nunquam potuit. Anno Bartheri regis decimo, cum Romani sub Gallieni lasciuientis imperio tor- perent ocio, tempus rati adesse conueniens Franci, quo siueas in eos contumelias vindica- rent, auxiliantibus Germanis, Saxonibus, Bauaris, atque Doringis, magnum adunauerũt bellatorum exercitum, &amp; ingressi hostium fines, omniaq́; igne deuastantes, &amp; ferro, vs- que ad Rauennam incursione peruenerunt hostili, praedaque locupletati ad sia reuersi- ssunt, Anno sequenti, qui fuit regis Bartheri vndecimus, Alemanni contractis copiis, ex- ercitum fortem duxerunt in Galliam, vastaq́; regione ferro et amp; igne, cum spoliis et amp; praeda multa in sua redierunt. Eodemq́; anno expeditionem contra Romanos mouerunt in Italiã, &amp; multa eis damna intulerunt, vindicantes iniurias, quas multiplices susceperant abeidem. Anno Barheri regis tertio decimo, qui fuit Dominicae natiuitatis ducentesimꝰ sexagesimus sextus annus: indictione Romanorum quartadecima, Franci, auxilio Ger- manorum, &amp; Saxonum, ingentem contraxerunt exercitum, &amp; Rheno, Mosaque trans- missis, sub Anthario, Luthero ducibus, intrauerunt Galliam, hostiliter omnia depopulã- tes: Antharius dux, filius erat Bartheri regis iam dicti Francorum: &amp; Luther, filiius exitit Marbodi regis in Saxonia: à regione Tungrensibus proxima incipientes, &amp; inde per Bel- uacos vltra Sequanam hostiliter procedentes, vsq́; in Hispania peruenerunt, Terra- conensem vrbeṁ nobilem obsidione cingentes, funditus eam destruxerunt. 22. Compendium, Book I.

...they wished, by which they hoped without doubt that they would at last overcome the Romans. These insignia, or arms, although they are improperly so called, all the kings of the Franks thereafter used down to Clovis the Christian, who is read to have adopted, in place of the lion, three lilies sent down from heaven, as will be said in its proper place.

At length, when the kingdom of the Franks was divided into two by the sons of Louis the First, the emblem of the lilies remained with the Gallic, or western, Franks; but the eastern or German kingdom of the Franks retained its own arms of the lion and the serpent’s tail. Since that kingdom has the Roman Empire annexed to itself, the earlier insignia having been brought into oblivion, it has been accustomed to use only the eagle, the mark of the empire, from that time of division down to the present day.

Hildegast, teacher of the noble Franks in every science.

The aforesaid Hildegast also, the wise man of the Franks, taught the sons of the nobles to sing in their mother tongue, with citharas and various other musical instruments, the deeds of their ancestors in songs; he advised the people to live by civil customs, to build houses, and to go about more cultivated in dress; and he ordered them to lay aside ferocity. For indeed the Franks until then cared little for cultivation or adornment, both in buildings and in clothing. Hildegast made all these things more cultivated, and most wisely instructed them to crush and subdue the pride of the Romans not only with arms, but also with possessions and manners. From that time the Franks began to build larger and more beautiful houses, divided into various chambers. For whatever they had built in earlier times was contemptible in its excessive simplicity and rustic, since, because of their frequent changes of settlement, they had been more accustomed to live in fields than in cities. Hence the Germans, taking up a proverb, whenever they saw something made or painted with ancient simplicity, were accustomed, praising antiquity in this way, to say: “That is a good old Frankish work.”

The Franks had become more cultivated in manners and buildings.

Hunibald records the remaining marvelous sayings, writings, or deeds of Hildegast. In the twenty-fourth year of Hilderic, king of the Franks, Alexander, son of Mammaea, Caesar Augustus of the Romans, is killed at Mainz, a city of Germany, in a military disturbance, in the thirteenth year of his reign.

But Hilderic, king of the Franks, the first of that name, after many brave and magnificent deeds, at length dies in the fortieth year of his reign, and in the two hundred fifty-third year of the Lord’s nativity, in the first Roman indiction.

The Thirty-First.

Bartherus reigned 48 years.

Bartherus, son of King Hilderic, succeeding his father, reigned eighteen years. In his time the Romans waged war with the Goths, who, crossing the river Ister, were devastating their cities and towns. The Romans killed thirty thousand of them under the command of Decius Caesar and his son. Many of the Romans also fell, among whom the very son of Decius Caesar [unclear]. But Decius Caesar, a most wicked persecutor of Christians, while fleeing, was drowned in the whirlpool of a certain marsh; his corpse could never be found by his men.

In the tenth year of King Bartherus, when the Romans under the wanton rule of Gallienus were sluggish in idleness, the Franks, thinking that a suitable time was at hand to avenge the insults committed against them, with the assistance of the Germans, Saxons, Bavarians, and Thuringians, gathered a great army of warriors; and, entering the borders of their enemies and devastating everything with fire and sword, they reached Ravenna in a hostile incursion, and, enriched with booty, returned to their own lands.

In the following year, which was the eleventh of King Bartherus, the Alemanni, having assembled their forces, led a strong army into Gaul; and, after laying waste the region with sword and fire, they returned to their own lands with much spoil and booty. In the same year they set an expedition in motion against the Romans in Italy, and inflicted many losses on them, avenging the manifold injuries which they had received from the same.

In the thirteenth year of King Bartherus, which was the two hundred sixty-sixth year of the Lord’s nativity, in the fourteenth Roman indiction, the Franks, with the aid of the Germans and Saxons, assembled an immense army; and, after crossing the Rhine and the Meuse, under the leaders Antharius and Luther they entered Gaul, laying waste everything in hostile fashion. Antharius the leader was the son of Bartherus, the aforesaid king of the Franks; and Luther was the son of Marbod, king in Saxony. Beginning from the region nearest to the Tungrians, and from there proceeding hostilely through the Bellovaci beyond the Seine, they reached as far as Spain; and, surrounding the noble city of Tarragona with a siege, they destroyed it utterly.

But Bartherus, king of the Franks, at length dies in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the year 50

namely in the year of the Lord's Nativity 181, in the fourth Roman indiction; his many deeds Hunibald adequately sets forth.

The Thirty-Second.

Clodius reigned 27 years. War occurs between the Romans and the Alemanni.

Clodius, the elder son of King Barther, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for twenty-seven years. In his third year the Romans, sending legions and mindful of the earlier injury, attacked Alemannia in war. Against their incursion the Alemanni advanced armed, having in their army thirty thousand fighters. A very hard battle was joined not far from Lake Benacus, in which almost fifteen thousand of the Alemanni were killed.

[unclear]

In the twelfth year of King Clodius, the Franks under their dukes invaded Gaul, and slew many thousands from the Roman guards as well as from the Gauls; and, occupying a great part of inner Gaul, they inhabited the north.

The Franks laid waste Gaul [unclear].

Clodius, king of the Franks, died after these things, in the twenty-seventh year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord's Nativity 317, in the first Roman indiction.

[unclear]

The Thirty-Third.

Great disturbances in Britain. The tenth persecution of the Christians occurred. Walther reigned 8 years. Severus. Churches and divine books they burn with fire, and the Christians in the tenth persecution after Nero...

Walther, son of King Clodius, after his father reigned over the Franks for eight years; a magnanimous, brave, and warlike prince. In the time of his reign, when persecution had been proclaimed everywhere, Diocletian in the east and Maximian in the west overthrow the churches of Christ, burn the divine books with fire, and miserably afflict the Christians in the tenth persecution after Nero; and Diocletian, in the first year of the aforesaid King Walther, commanded himself to be worshipped as God; he also at the same time subjected Alexandria with all Egypt to the Romans.

[unclear]

The Thirty-Third.

Diocletian with all Egypt.

In the first, second, and third year of Walther king of the Franks, there were great disturbances in Britain, which is now called England. For, some years before, King Lucius had died, who first received the faith of Christ with his people from Pope Eleutherius, as we said above.

[unclear]

The Thirty-Third.

In the one hundred eighty-fifth year, in the times of Farabert king of the Franks, the Romans sent Severus the senator into Britain to take up the kingdom. When he too had been killed at York by Fulgenius, Bassianus, the son of this same Severus, was admitted as king. When he also was killed, Carausius seized the kingdom, and despised the commands of the Romans.

[unclear]

The Thirty-Fourth.

The kingdom of Britain [unclear]. Asclepiadotus, powerful king of Britain. Dagobert reigned 11 years.

Dagobert, the elder son of Walther king of the Franks, succeeding his father, reigned for eleven years, a man toward his subjects pious, [unclear], and very humane; whom they [unclear] with singular love. [unclear] with two Roman legions he killed, and placed upon himself the diadem of the kingdom; and against the will of the Caesars and the senate, he reigned for ten years, cherished justice, [unclear] the province.

[unclear]

The Thirty-Fourth.

Against him Asclepiadotus, a warlike, brave, and bold man, rising up, killed him with the two Roman legions, and placed upon himself the diadem of the kingdom; and against the will of the Caesars and the senate, he reigned for ten years, cherished justice, and [unclear] the province.

Walther, king of the Franks, in these times rested from wars, and at last finally died in the eighth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord's Nativity 306, in the ninth Roman indiction, before which there was an earthquake.

ANNALS OF TRITHEMIUS. 23.

…namely in the year of the Lord's nativity 181, in the fourth Roman indiction, whose manifold deeds Hunibald sufficiently sets forth.

THE THIRTY-SECOND [king]. CLODIUS, the elder-born son of king Barther, succeeding [his] father, reigned over the Franks twenty-seven years; in whose third year the Romans, sending legions, attacked Alemannia in war, mindful of the former injury. Against whose incursion the Alemanni advanced armed, having in their army thirty thousand warriors. A battle hard enough is joined not far from Lake Benacus [Garda], in which nearly fifteen thousand of the Alemanni perish.

In the twelfth year of king Clodius, the Franks under [their] dukes invaded Gaul, and slew many thousands both of the Roman guards and of the Gauls, and, occupying a great part of interior Gaul, inhabited the north.

But Clodius, king of the Franks, dies after these [things], in the twenty-seventh year of his reign, [and] of the Lord's nativity 317, in the first Roman indiction.

THE THIRTY-THIRD. [Margin: a tumult in Britain; the tenth persecution of Christians.] WALTHER, son of king Clodius, after [his] begetter reigned over the Franks eight years, a magnanimous prince, brave and warlike, in whose reign—the persecution being everywhere published—Diocletian in the East and Maximian in the West overturn [the churches of Christ], burn the divine books with fire, and miserably afflict the Christians with the tenth persecution after Nero; and Diocletian, in the first year of the said king Walther, commanded [himself] to be adored as God, who also at the same time subjected Alexandria with all Egypt to the Romans.

In the first, second, and third year of Walther, king of the Franks, there were great tumults in Britain (which is now called England). For king Lucius—who first with his people received the faith of Christ from Pope Eleutherius (as we said above)—having died some years before, in the year 185, in the times of Farabert, king of the Franks, the Romans sent the senator Severus into Britain to undertake the regency. He too being killed at York by Fulgenius, Bassianus, son of the same Severus, was admitted as king. He too being slain, Carausius invaded the kingdom, who despised the commands of the Romans.

THE THIRTY-FOURTH. [Margin: Asclepiodotus, powerful king of Britain. Dagobert reigned 11 years.] DAGOBERT, the elder-born son of Walther, king of the Franks, succeeding [his] father, reigned eleven years, a man [kind] to [his] subjects, gentle, very humane, whom they loved with singular love. Against him Asclepiodotus, a warlike, brave, and bold man, rising up, killed [the usurper] with two Roman legions, and placed the diadem of the kingdom upon himself, and, against the will of the Caesars and the senate, reigned ten years, cultivated justice, [and] shut out the [Roman] province.

WALTHER, king of the Franks, in these times rested from wars, and at last finally dies, in the eighth year of his reign, [and] of the Lord's nativity 306, in the 9th Roman indiction; before which there was an earthquake.

ANNAL. TRITHERMII. 29 suam vxorem, cum qua, Octauiio mortuo, totius insularis regnum obtinuit. Venerat autem vocatus in Britanniam cum exercitu militis Romanorum, & maior pars militum cum eo remanuit, paucioribus numero in Italiam reueris. Deinde post mortem Valentini et Valentis Caesarum, anno regni sui Britannici quinto, in superbiam elatus mente, & quietis impatiens, Caesarem se constitui Romanorum fecit ab his, qui cum eo remanerant militibus, contra Gratianum, quem sibi Romani praefecerant. Moxitaque ut Caesar militibus salutatus est, Britaniae regnum vicario procurandum commisit, omnemque nobilitatem et iuuentutem militiae totius insulae Britanniae (quae nunc Anglia dicitur) in unum convocans, cum eis in Galliam navigavit, talem habens intentio- nem animi, ut deuictis Gallis, Romanam proficiceretur, sibique imperium subijeceret. Anno igitur Marcomiri regis Francorum nono, dominice vero nativitatis CCCCXXXVII, indictione Romanorum quindecim, Maximus Britanniae rex, cum ingenti multitudine suorum navium intrauit Gallias, & omnia per circuitem regionis hostiliter vastavit. Et primo quidem applicuit cum navibus ad littus terra Armorica, qua ab illo tempore et deinceps Britannia nova, sive minor dicit, sive in praesentem diem, quam tunc in habitabant Franci, sub moderamine ducis Lubalchi, quem reges Francorum vicarium regni illis in locis constituerant. Dux autem Lubalchus introitum tantae multitudinis gentium haud mediocriter turbatus, copias ut potuit suorum contraxit, procedensque obuiam venientibus, cum eis bellum commisit, in quo ipse cum quindecim Francorum millibus fuit occisus, ceteris fugâ salutem quarentibus. Denique ut nominis sui terrorem cunctis pergyrum incineret, magna crudelitate vus est: quippe qui mulieres, & virgines, senes et iuvenes, paruulos et infantes, quotquot reperit, sine misericordia trucidavit. Erant autem Franci reges, duces, nobiles, milites, & populus omnis, idolorum vana superstitione adhuc obcecati atque polluti. Maximus vero, et si Tyrannus, tamem cum omnem militia, & populo suo fuit Christianus. Hac de Lubalcho et Francis obtenta victoria, Maximus principatum illum Armoricum contulit duci Conano, qui fuit ex fratre nepos Octauii regis Britanniae supradicti, relictaque cum ca bona parte exercitus Britannorum ad custodiam, ipse cum reliqua multitudine copiarum discedens inde, per universamque Galliam discurrens, contradicentes suo imperio non minus crudeliter quam potenter bello et armis fecit obedientes. Interea Gratianus Romae Caesar, intelligens Maximus sibi nomen et diadema Romani usurpasse imperii, egressumque magno cum exercitu de Britannia vastare coepisse Gallias, contractis et ipse copiis, contra eum mouit in Galliam, & urbem Parisiensem cum exercitu intrauit. Congressus postea cum Maximo, proditio Merobaldi magistri militum superatus est, & fugâ lapidis, venit Lugdunum: vbi postea fuit occisus. Conanus autem, quem Maximus regem in Armorica regione constituerat, frequentes a Gallis et Romanis, qui erant in Aquitania, incursiones sustinebat, quibus ille fortiter occurrens, viriliter cum eis dimicabat, multique corum peremptis, reliquos in fugam convertit. Consecutus postremo pacem, & quietam Armorici regni possessionem, cum nobilibus suis coepit habere consilium, quomodo vxores et liberos, quos in Britannia dimisserant, ad se quantotius facerent cum omni fuppelleciti perduci domes- tica, ne generis propagis deficeret. Militum vero numerus, qui de Britannia venerant cum Conano in Armorican, fuit triginta millium pugnatorum: Plebanorum vero et agriculturarum (vt Galfredus est auctor) fuerunt centum millia, qui omnes iussione Maximi de Britannia in Armorican navigauerant. Ex his multi non habebant vxores: ceteri vero qui habebant, cas in Britannia dimisserant cum paruulis, quando Maximum sequi cogebantur. Conanus autem et omnis populus eius, cum essent Christiani, filias Paganorum idola muta colentium vxores et filias Christianae, cum Gallis tamem commissiones nupialis nullum eis placuit habere commercium. Fuitin diebus illis subregulus quidam in Britannia (quae nunc Anglia vocatur) nomine Dionotus, qui, mortuo Caradoco fratre suo, Cornubia tenebat principatum, cui et Maximus rex profecturus in Galliam, ut viro prudentissimo, commendauerat regnum. Is filiam habebat unicam nomine Vrfulam, inter omnes Britannia virgines cunctorum iudicio speciosissimam, & valde Christo deuotam. Compendium, Book I.

The thirty-fifth.

Chlogio reigned for only two years.

Chlogio, son of King Dagobert, succeeding his father, reigned for only two years. For in the second year of his reign, the Romans and the Gauls fiercely invaded the kingdom of the Franks in the Cismosanian regions and began to lay everything waste with fire and sword. But King Chlogio, having gathered what forces he could, went to meet the enemy with the help of the Germans; and, when he fought too incautiously, he was killed. Yet the Franks did not on that account shrink from the battle, but fought bravely. For Clodomir, brother of the slain king, drew his body back from the battle-line and clothed himself in his arms, so that all might think that he himself was the king, lest either his friends, once the king’s death was known, should lose heart, or the enemies, exulting, should conceive certain hope of victory. And so Duke Clodomir, clothed in the king’s arms and returned to the battle-line, since he was thought by everyone to be the king himself, inspired steadfastness in his own men and fear in the enemy. By fighting very bravely he restored the battle, turned the Gauls together with the Romans at last to flight, obtained the victory, gathered the spoils of the enemy, and freed the kingdom from destruction.

Accordingly Chlogio, king of the Franks, fell in the second year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 309, in the seventh indiction of the Romans. He left two sons, of whom the elder by birth, Helenus, was then in his twentieth year, while the younger, Richimer, was in his eighteenth. But by law the Franks were forbidden to advance anyone as king before he had completed the twenty-fourth year of his age. Hence it came about that neither of the sons of Chlogio came to the kingdom, but their uncle Clodomir was chosen as king.

The thirty-sixth.

Clodomir, brother of the slain King Chlogio, chosen as king by the common decree of the Franks, thereafter reigned eighteen years, a distinguished, prudent, and strong prince, who kept his people in peace and enlarged the kingdom of the Franks.

For in these times, when the Suevi were being grievously afflicted by the Romans, they resolved to call the Franks, Saxons, and Thuringians to their aid; and they trusted that they would find them willing all the more easily because they knew that they had always hated the Romans. But the Franks, otherwise ancient enemies of the Romans, after holding counsel among themselves, readily gave consent to the petition of the Suevi, judging it more wholesome to fight with their enemies in lands far from their own borders than in their own territories.

Therefore Clodomir, king of the Franks, appointed his brother Genebald as commander of the army that was to go, and entrusted to him eighty thousand fighters. The other kings called by the Suevi to their aid did likewise; the soldiers assembled into one and arranged made up a sufficiently great army. Then, having joined battle with the Romans, they fought most fiercely, killing many thousands of them, while the rest sought safety in flight; and so the Romans were driven from the territories of the Suevi.

When the Germans had gained this victory and were dividing the spoils in the camp according to custom, a dangerous quarrel arose between two soldiers, of whom one was named Adelbert, while the other was a Sueve named Doringus. The cause of the disturbance was this: that the Sueve soldier had accused Doringus of having secretly taken something or other from the common booty. When he denied it, a serious sedition arose, the Thuringians defending Doringus and the Suevi the Sueve. For each had many adherents from his own people, whose minds were stirred up. But when Doringus steadfastly denied the theft, the Sueve offered to prove the truth by duel. When the princes had permitted this, single combat was arranged between them on the appointed day; and in it Doringus, at the second encounter, was killed by the Sueve. When, on account of this matter, he had been stripped of his clothing and arms, the theft too, concerning which he had been accused, was found hidden upon him. After receiving this disgrace, the Thuringians were exceedingly angry; but, concealing their anger, they afterward held secret counsel among themselves as to how they might avenge Gunther’s fall upon Adelbert. When the plan had been settled, namely that they should kill the Sueve that same night, one hundred twenty of them conspired together concerning the matter to be kept secret. Therefore on the following night they silently rushed upon the tent in which they suspected Adelbert to be, demanding that the murderer be handed over to them to be killed. Roused by these voices, the Suevi ran to arms, firmly resolving either to defend their innocent soldier from death or to die with him. When the deed was presently reported in the camp of the Thuringians, they were greatly moved and, as if turned to fury, immediately seized arms; and, having formed a column, they rushed upon the Suevi, who suspected no such thing, raising shouts on high like men raging. But the Suevi were not idle: when they could not call the Thuringians back from the tumult with fair words, they themselves put on arms and strove to resist bravely. A fierce battle was joined between friends, in which more than two thousand of the party [unclear]

COMPENDIVM LIB. I optime nouerat, sed etiam valde amabat. Vnde missis ad eum nuncijs et epistolis, petiuit cam sibi in vxorem transmitti. Secundo petiit, quatenus vxores liberosque militum et plebanorum in Britanniā, cum exirent mariti Maximi iussu, dimissas navibus imponebant cum earum suppellectili, & in Armoricum ad se regnum transmitteret. Tertio mandauit, vt secundum numerum, quem expresserat literis, mitterentur virgines, promilitibus de nobili prosapia, nobiles: & pro plebanis, quoque plebanae, quas sibi vxores ducerent singuli, qui tunc coniuges non habebant. Dionotus viso Conani nuncio, & cupiens satisfacere ipsius desiderio, collegit ex diversis Britanniae provinciis filias nobilium undecim millia: de ceteris vero, ex inferiori genere sexaginta millia, virgines et mulieres, quas omnes ad certum diem intra Londiniam conuenire praecipit. Naues quoque ex cunctis Britanniae littoribus iussit adducere, quae sufficiant ad tantae multitudinis euectionem. Quid, licet multis in tanto coetu placuiffe, displicebat nihilominus et multis, quae maiore parentis et patriae diligent affessu. Nec defuerunt alioe forsan, quae caslitatem nuptiis praeferentes, in qualibet terra maluiffe vitam amittere quam maritari. Parat standem ad euectionem necessarijs, mulieres praefectura naves ingrediuntur, & per Tamensem fluvium maria penetrant. Postremo cum vela infleuerent versus Armoricanos, hoc est, ab aquilone ad austrum, subito grandis in mari tempestas exortatur, & divisa clasfe, naues ab inuicem separantur. Magnum cunctis infatbat periculum, & maior pars navium in profundum maris dissipata, & cum mulieribus submersa est. Quae vero tantum euafere periculum, appulsae sunt in Barbaras nationes, & insulas maris, & ab ignota gente siue trucidata, siue perpetuam in servitutem sunt mancipata. Inciderant enim in exercitum nefandorum principum, Wanij et Melgae, qui mercede conduci Graiani, Britanniā primo, acdeinde maritimas nationes, & insulas circumiacentes, in odium Maximi deuafabant, à quibus cruelditer pro caslitatis amore perierunt. Erat autem Wanius (aut fi malueris Gnauius mōre Gallorum) rex Hunorum: Melga vero Pictorum, quos Gratianus imperator mercede conduci, miferat in fines Germaniae simul et Galliae, vt affligerent cos qui partes Maximi sequebantur. Circa maritima ergo pedestri simul et nauali seuentes incursu, praedictis mulieribus et puellis in eas regiones à vento proiectis securrunt: quas, cum effent et pulchrae et Christianae, suam in commissionem sollicitabat. Verum vbi nephandorum turpitudini consentire mulieres in Christo fideles recufarent, ab impijs miferabiliter occife sunt. Hanc autem lamentabilem sanctarum vnius et septuaginta millium virginum ac mulierum, praeter infantes et paruulos, historiam Hunibaldus non refert, sed memora- tus austor Galfredus Monemutensis in fine quarti libri, de origine gentis, & gessis regum Britannie insulae, qua primo dicebatur insula Gigantum: deinde à Bruto rege primo di- ēta fuī Britannie: postea nuncupata est Albion: & postremo nomen Anglia sortita, retenit in hunc diem. Marcomitus vero supradictus Francorum rex, quia vir prudens erat, sic principatus sui temperabat habenas, vt nec partes Maximi sequeretur, nec Gratiani, propter ea quod ille Francis abstulerat, multis eorum cruelditer et sineratione peremptis, Armorican: & ifte Romanos regeret, gentem ab origine Francis inimicam. Continuit ergo se pru- denter in terminis regni, malens hostem consumsi ab altero, quam fauorem patrare in- nimico. Post caedem puellarum, praedicti duo reges, Gnauius Hunorum, & Melga Pictorum, ad complacentiam Casaris Gratiani, Britanniā omni militia (ficut diximus) per Maximum deflituram, hostiliter inuadentes, igne et ferro stragem fecerunt ingentem, & innumerabilem populi multitudinem cruelditer occiderunt. Quod cum nunciatum fuisset Maximo regi, eo tempore apud Treuiros commoranti, milit Gratianum quen- dam municipem, cum duabus legionibus in Britanniā, vt hostes inde propelleret. Erat autem cum Hunis et Pictis, Scoti, Daci, & Norvegij, quos Gratianus omnes facta con- gressione fugavit in Hiberniam. His temporibus Maximus rex Britonum, & Romani vsurpator imperii, superata iam vniuersa Gallia, peremptoque apud Lugdunum Gratiano Casare, sed de regni sui col- locavit in urbe Treuirosu: vbi et synodum couocauit epifcoporum, in qua sanctus Marti- nus praeful Turonentis personaliter comparuit, signique et miraculis pluribus corru- scavit. Aderant et Ambrofius epifcopus Mediolanus, Aulonius quoque praeful Bur- degalensis,

Erant eo tempore mag-ni gentium motus in Britanniae et in cunctis adiacenti-bus insulis, Francorum regno viciniae quorum consideratione rex Clodomirus angustiaba-te tur metuentes Romanorum infidialiae ne absentè pugnato-res exercitu nouam aliquam in 30 regnum molirentur incursione. Propterea cautum Francorum nequaguam est visum consilio, his praefertim periculosis temporib-us populum diuidere, neglectisque propriis aliena defensione, cum ad alterum dei propitia-tibus forsan possimus sufficere: etiam rúmque autem hoc est nostrum regnum vestrum hîs diebus ab-hostium incursione tueri nostra non sit in potestate. Nimia denique locorum distantia nos plu-rimum impedit, ne vobis contra Sueuos tam crebro possimus conferre suffragium, cu-m illi principium Rheni fluminis teneant et ortum; nos vero ultimate ostia occasum. Veruntamen ne vobis omnino francorum interuen-ti-pax refor-matur. videamur de fusse amiciis nostro consilio placuit vt nuncios ad Sueuos dirigamus nostros atque legatos, per quos triennales rursum vobis inducias obtineamus treugas. Interea consilium habeant Dorigi, vt cum Suenius vel pacem conseguit valeant aeternam, vel alio quoquùm̃ medio necessarium-de-fensionis murum interponent, hoc est, vel ex suis vel ex alienis gentibus amicis. 40 Quibus à rege Francorum prolatis respondere legati: Optima est, ô rex Doringo-vum legari sententiam laudant.. &amp; vos principes Franci, consultatio vestra, si tamen inducias triennales à Sueuis poteritis impetrare franconibꝰ. Quod vero consuluisse, vt vel ex nobis, vel ex gente qualibet aliena defensionis inter nos mu-rum ponamus et Sueuos, regis nostri sententia est, et procerum omnium gentis Doringorũ, super quo nostrum precamacur consultationem audite, simul auxiliu-m fideles amici pre-bete. Terra noīs est amplitudine contra meridiem lata, fructuum vbertate fuerunda, cuius ultimi fines disterminant inter Sueuos atque Dorigos. In quam si ex vestris ponerè incolas volueritis ducem, erunt vobis regno Francoru-m proculdubio perpetuum in honorem commodum: Dorigis vero defensionis in murum: et Suenius in metum. Nulla difficultas donationis interuenti-repoterit, qua minus principum gentis Doringorum oblatione voluntaria in vestra fit potestate. 50 Super his consultatione praehabita, Franci consenfere libenter, vt pote quibus nihil magis cordierat, quam nomen Francum dilatare simul regnum. In primis igitur mi-fis epistolis ad Sueuos atque legatis, pacem Dorigis ad triennium impetrarunt, con-fi-lium de noua possessione suscipienda secreterum tenentes. Deinde suos cu-m legatis ami-corũ praedictis miserunt in Dorigiam, vt propositum super donacione promiffae re-gionis negotium de regis procerum sententiâ confirmarent. Quibus omnibus rite per-actis, quae feribimus secquebantur. QVANDO ET VNDE FRANCI PRIMVM VENERINT AD Menigauium Peopolitanum, sequitur. C

Annals of Trithemius.

men of each side were slain. Yet the Thuringians lost more men than the Suebi, and, defeated, at last withdrew, compelled by necessity.

This conflict had remained hidden from the Franks and the Saxons until the contest came to an end; they had pitched their camps not in the same place, but in different stations. But afterwards, when the Franks, together with the Saxons, had learned the cause, they labored with many negotiations for peace and concord between those at variance. Yet since each party complained that it had been gravely injured by wrong, they could not restore full concord between them. They did, however, establish truces, or armistices, of three years between them, in which they ordered the parties to abstain from war until anger should cool with time and the disturbance be quieted.

From that time the Suebi always held the Thuringians suspect of treachery, as Hunibald says, and they were troubled by a hidden and manifest hatred against them, although many do not know the cause of this mutual hostility.

[unclear] to the present day, as we learned long ago from the report of Hunibald, our dearest brother, what the cause of dissension was between you, friends, Thuringians, and the Suebi, and what is the occasion of those disturbances which today stand at the doors. We confess to you that for a long time [unclear].

The [Thuringians] sent to [Clodomir], king of the Franks, and to the nobles of the realm, begging with great urgency that, in view of the former alliance, they should bring them the owed and friendly aid against the Suebi. At that time there were great movements of peoples in Britain and in all the adjacent islands neighboring the kingdom of the Franks; in consideration of these, King Clodomir was distressed, fearing the treachery of the Romans, lest, while the army of fighters was absent, they should contrive some new incursion into the kingdom.

After counsel had been held with the nobles of the realm, King Clodomir gave the envoys of the Thuringians this answer in a public assembly of the magnates. From the report of Duke Henebald, our dearest brother, we learned long ago what the cause of dissension was between you, friends, the Thuringians, and the Suebi, and what is the occasion of those disturbances which today stand at the doors. We confess to you that for a long time [unclear].

They sent to the king of the Franks and to the nobles of the realm, begging with great urgency that, in view of the former alliance, they should bring them the owed and friendly aid against the Suebi. At that time there were great movements of peoples in Britain and in all the adjacent islands neighboring the kingdom of the Franks; in consideration of these, King Clodomir was distressed, fearing the treachery of the Romans, lest, while the army of fighters was absent, they should contrive some new incursion into the kingdom.

Therefore it in no way seemed prudent to the counsel of the Franks, especially in these dangerous times, to divide the people and, neglecting their own affairs, to undertake the defense of others, since perhaps with God’s favor we might suffice for one of the two; for even to protect this our kingdom from the incursion of enemies in these days is not in our power. Moreover, the very great distance of places greatly hinders us from being able to bring you aid so often against the Suebi, since they hold the source and beginning of the river Rhine, while we hold its farthest mouths and its western end. Nevertheless, lest we seem to have been altogether lacking to you in the friendship of the Franks, it has pleased our counsel that we direct our messengers and envoys to the Suebi, through whom we may again obtain for you three-year truces and armistices. Meanwhile let the Thuringians take counsel, so that they may either obtain a lasting peace with the Suebi, or by some other means interpose the necessary wall of defense, that is, either from their own people or from friendly foreign peoples.

When these things had been set forth by the king of the Franks, the envoys answered: Excellent, O king and you Frankish princes, is your counsel, if indeed you will be able to obtain three-year truces from the Suebi. But as for your counsel that we place between ourselves and the Suebi a wall of defense, either from ourselves or from any foreign people, this is the judgment of our king and of all the nobles of the Thuringian people. Hear our consultation concerning this matter, we beg, and at the same time, as faithful friends, provide aid. We have a land broad in extent toward the south, fertile in abundance of fruits, whose furthest boundaries separate the Suebi and the Thuringians. If you wish to place inhabitants from among your people in it, with a duke, this will certainly be a perpetual honor and advantage to you and to the kingdom of the Franks, but to the Thuringians a wall of defense, and to the Suebi a cause of fear. No difficulty concerning the grant will be able to intervene, by which it should not, through the voluntary offering of the princes of the Thuringian people, come into your power.

After consultation had been held on these matters, the Franks gladly agreed, as men who had nothing more at heart than to extend the Frankish name and kingdom at the same time. Therefore, first sending letters and envoys to the Suebi, they obtained peace for the Thuringians for three years, keeping secret their plan concerning the new possession to be undertaken. Then they sent their own men with the aforesaid envoys of their friends into Thuringia, so that they might confirm, according to the judgment of the king and nobles, the proposed business concerning the grant of the promised region. When all these things had been duly completed, the events which we shall write followed.

When and whence the Franks first came to the Menigau of the [People?], follows.

ANNAL. TRITHEMII. degalensis, qui de laudibus patriae urbisque Treuriorum, opus metricum scripsit, quod Mosellam, a praeterfluente fluvio, prenotavit. Hieronymus etiam presbyter Bethleemitanus librum beati Hilarii episcopi Pictauiensis de synodis eodem tempore apud Treuiros rescripsit. Maximus autem cum maximo exercitu mouens a Treuiris, Victorem filium suum infantulum, regem Galliarum constituit, eique tutores Quintinum et Nanncum principes urbis Treuiorum deputavit. Ipse deinde cum exercitu profectus in Italiam, a Theodosio peremprus est, anno Marcomiri regis Francorū tertio decimo. Nec diu postea etiam filius eius Victor, in gratiam et fauorem Theodosii, gladio perit. Post Maximi autem interitum, Marcomirus rex Francorum cotractis copijs, magnum suorum exercitum transmisit in Galliam sub ducibus Sunnone, Genebaldo, Priamo, & Antenore, quatinus non solum recuperarent amissa, sed omnem quoque Galliam Francicis redderent subiectam. Et breui quidem tempore multa recuperantes, qua Maximus abstulerat, etiam Gallia partem non modicam regno Francorum addiderunt. Veruntamen Armoricanorum regnum, quod Britones inhabitabant (vt diximus) sub Conano, illa vice obtinere non poterant, quod tamet postea receperunt. Interim vero quod hi duces bello intendunt Gallicano, Romani Francorum regnum duce Valentiniano Caaeare, qui cum Theodosio imperabat, exercitum grandem miserunt in Germaniam, Francos (vt sperabant) penitus deleturi. Contra quos Marcomirus rex Francorum, cum Germanis atque Saxonibus procelit ad bellum, & facta congreßione ab hostibus peremptus cecidit cum multis, alijs fuga labentibus, anno regni sui xv. Dominica vero natiuitatis cccc. xciii, indictione Romanorum sexta. Valentinianus autem ulterius progredivolens, & omne regnum Francorum, quod in partibus erat Cisrenanis, suo cupiens subjugare imperio, propter Longobardorum incursionem, in Italiam retrocedere compulsius fuit. Sed aflu necessitatem occultans retro abeundi, nuncios misit ad eos qui remanerant in regno, Francos, per quos mandavit, vt denuo aut bellum eligerent, aut Romanis penderent tributum. At Franci iam regedestituti, roboreque militia cum ducibus in Gallia constituto, cum Imperatoris necessitatem receulis nescirent, atque nihil alind quam bellum imminere putarent, & viribus impares se viderent esse, Romanis promittere tributum, quod tamet nec promittere sine principum consensu et voluntate, tunc (sicur diximus) procul absentium, potuerunt, nec solueru. His Valentinianus imperator cum Francis, vt voluit peraetis, in Lombardos profectus est. Interea ducibus Francorum, Dagoberto, Sunnoni, Genebaldo, Priamo, Antenori, & caeteris natu maioribus, qui bella gentis tractabat in regione Galloru, nunciantur omnia, qua Romani, duce Valentiniano, egissent cum Francis, quomodo et regem morti, & gaetem addixissent tributo, qua semper fuit libera, & nulli ab origine Troiana fuisset subiecta. Irati sunt, commoti sunt, & turbati sunt valde, multique deliberauere consultationibus, quemadmodum hanc prudenter vindicarent inuironam. Post multam igitur et diurnam eorum consultationem, postremo in vnam conuencere sentiant, vt magis patriam in libertate conferuare deberent auita, quam rebus urger Gallicanis. Relinquentes ergo in finibus Gallicanis Priamum ducem cum sufficiente praesidio militi, caeteri principes in Franciam Germanicam reuersti sunt cum exercitu. Vacuitur autem regnum Francorum deinceps, post interitum regis Marcomiri, sine regre, sub ducibus duntaxat duobus, annis fere viginti sex. QUADRAGESIMVS PRIMVS. Dagobertus frater Marcomiri regis Francoru a Valentiniano perempti, & filius regis supradicti Clogionis, post interitum germani consensu Francoru interrex, sive gubernator fuit regni, annis feme (vt Hunibaldus insinuat) quinque, vir magnanimus et belicosus, cuius tempore ducatum tenuit apud Francos Orientales Marcomir filius Clo- dij annis sedecim. Cepit autem gubernacula regni sub ducis nomine Dagobertus, anno dominica natiuitatis cccc. xciii, indictione sexta. Anno Dagoberti ducis secundo, Valentinianus Caesar missis nunciis ad populum Francorum in Germaniam, tributum priore anno exegit impositu. Cui duces populus regni per cosdennuncios ita remandarui; Francoru semperena libertas tributu imporere nationibus ca- teris consuuit, non solueru. Tu autae qui robore Francorum al fente, cum paucitate inermi pugnasti, & dolo non fortitudine viceisti, sitae a Francis exigendi tributu ius habere considis, veni cum volueris, & gant Valen- gladio nos liberrimos et esse semper futiis. Et scru oßedemus. His te facimus certiori, ne super hac re inuiano quaequam ad nos mittas inermem, quippe qui vita potius dare contendimus, quam perdere libertatem.

26 COMPENDIVM LIB. I. Hic capit ducatus O- rientalis et Francorum. Francorum 32580. ve- nient Her- bipoli. Anno igitur Clodomiri regis Francorum septimo : Dominice autem natiuitatis CCCCXXVI. indictione Romanorum XIII. nona die mensis Aprilis, iussione memoria regis, exiuerunt ab ostijs Rheni, vbi primas in Germania sedes olim habuerunt Sica- bri, cum vxoribus, liberis, suppliciis simul atque iumentis viri armati triginta sex, agricultores, & diuersarum artifices distributionum duo millia sextenti octoginta sex, profecturi ad nouas sedes Francis promissas à Doringis. Exiuerunt autem non simul vna vice omnes, sed successiue per turmas, die praescripta incipientes, donec tandem in mensse Septembri numerum compleuere praesignatum; Hunibaldo Francorum testante historico. Ducem vero populi Franciae Orientalis rex Clodomirus, Genealdum fratrem su- 10 um constituit, cui exercitum simul et administrationem totius ducatus sub his conditio- nibus, Francorum more, commendauit, vt videlicet tam ipse quam eius filij haeredes et successores perpetuo sub ditione regum Francorum permaneat, eorumque mandatis in cunctis fideliter obediant, cum ipsis ad bellum contra quoscunque aduersarios proce- dant, & reliquorum consuetudine ducum regni Francorum seruitutem ipsis regibus et honorem vbique debitum impendant. His conditionibus datis et acceptis, Genebaldus dux Franciae Orientalis cum de- putata sibi gente, ad Menigantium proficiescitur, & oblato sibi principatiui annis ferme tri- ginta dominatur. Erat enim vir prudens, audax, & bellicosus, qui terram Franciae duca- tus, non solum prudenter rexit atque distribuit, sed etiam terminos possessionis valde 20 augmentauit. Audientes Sueui Franciae Orientales fines aduentum, satis aegre tulerunt, me- tuentes futurum, quod accidit, ne multiplicati numero et viribus, etiam terminos acce- ptae possessionis in eorum perniciem dilatarent. Verum vbi sevident coeptis Francorum posse nequaquam resistere, congregationem aduentus eorum simulante, missisque ora- toribus pacem rogant, ex necessitate magis (vt videbat ut multis) quam ex intentione. Causam quoque dissensionum omnem, quam praetendebant, aduersum Doringos, Sueus cum Francia pa- 30 cern firmari. Marcouar dux Fran- corum Orien- talium. cercantur Do- ringa omnes. Eodem anno in mensse Septembri Marcomirus, ducis Genebaldi filius, cum reli- qua Francorum turma, quaead transmigrandum regis Clodomiri iam prius mandato su- crat selecta, per familias, domos, atque personas, venit in Dorigiae fines meridianas, & circa Menum fluium, cum fratribus suis maniones accipere promissas: ab oriente, Boios habentes atque Boemos à meridie, Sueuos: ab occidente, Rhenanos, Moguntiacos, & A- podas: ab aquilonè vero, Fagophagos atque Doringos. Francis in- 40 troansibuis cadunt Do- ringi omnes. Ad Francorum introitum Dorigi. praecepto Heuroli regis eorum, vltra nemus re- trocesserunt, omnes relinquentes cunctam nouis hospibus annonam sequentem an- num sufficientem. Franci ergo noui aduenia, in finibus Dorigorum primo consede- runt, inter Salam (vt nunc appellatur à Salagaasto) fluuium, & Neccari partes inferiores, circà Meni fluminis littora: In eo paganio,* qui prius Meningau, postea dictus est Francia Orientalis. In qua cum tempore vicis et vrbes non paucas numero construxerunt, & breuiribus et potentia creuerunt. Genealogia ducùm Fran- ciae Orientalis. Faramun- dus dux G. Francorum Orien- talium. Marcoumer Faramunds filius dux. Genebaldus autem dux, genuit Marcomirum et Dagobertum, qui annis praefuit Francis Orientalis vno et viginti : Dagobertus autem genuit Clodium, qui praefuit populo annis decem : Clodius autem genuit Marcomirum; Faramundus autem, cum pa- tre et solus ducatum administrauit, annis quindecim, & postea electus fuit in regem Fran- corum, vt ordine suo dicemus. Ducatum vero Franciae Orientalis, Marcomiro fratri commendauit, quem annis exit XVIII. Quo in venatione ab apro percusso et interempto, Clodomir filius praedicti ducis Sunnonis successit in ducatu, & prae- fuit annis XXXI. Clodomir autē genuit Hugbadum, qui praefuit annis XXVI. Hugbadus autē genuit Helenū, qui praefuit annis triginta: Helenus autē, genuit Gotfridū, qui praefuit annis XXIV. Godfridus autē, genuit Genebaldū tertiū, qui praefuit anni XX.
