Compendium, Book I.

Here begins the duchy of the Eastern Franks. 32,580 Franks will come to Herbipolis.

Therefore, in the seventh year of Clodomir, king of the Franks, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 426, in the thirteenth Roman indiction, on the ninth day of the month of April, by command of the aforesaid king, there went out from the mouths of the Rhine, where the Sicambri had once had their first settlements in Germany, with their wives, children, household goods [unclear], and pack animals, thirty-six armed men [unclear], farmers and craftsmen of various trades, two thousand six hundred eighty-six, setting out for the new settlements promised to the Franks by the Thuringians. They did not all go out together at one time, but successively by bands, beginning on the prescribed day, until at last in the month of September they completed the number previously designated, as Hunibald, the historian of the Franks, attests.

King Clodomir appointed as duke of the people of Eastern Francia his brother Genebald, to whom, according to the custom of the Franks, he entrusted both the army and the administration of the whole duchy on these conditions: namely, that both he himself and his sons, heirs, and successors should remain forever under the authority of the kings of the Franks, should faithfully obey their commands in all things, should go forth with them to war against any adversaries whatever, and, according to the custom of the other dukes of the kingdom of the Franks, should everywhere render to those kings the service and honor owed to them.

When these conditions had been given and accepted, Genebald, duke of Eastern Francia, set out with the people assigned to him for Menigantium, and ruled the principality offered to him for almost thirty years. For he was a prudent, bold, and warlike man, who not only governed and distributed the land of the duchy of Francia prudently, but also greatly enlarged the boundaries of its possession.

When the Suebi heard of the arrival of the Eastern Franks at their borders, they bore it rather ill, fearing that what did happen would come to pass: that, multiplied in number and strength, they would also extend the boundaries of the possession they had received to the Suebi’s ruin. But when they saw that they could in no way resist the undertakings of the Franks, pretending a welcoming gathering for their arrival and sending envoys, they asked for peace, more from necessity, as it seemed to many, than from intention. They also [unclear] every cause of dissension that they alleged against the Thuringians.

Peace is established between the Suebus and Francia. Marcomir, duke of the Eastern Franks. All the Thuringians [unclear].

In the same year, in the month of September, Marcomir, son of Duke Genebald, with the remaining band of Franks which had already earlier been chosen by King Clodomir’s command for migration, by families, households, and persons, came into the southern borders of Thuringia, and around the river Main, with his brothers, to receive the dwellings promised to them: having to the east the Boii and Bohemians; to the south, the Suebi; to the west, the Rhenish people, the people of Mainz, and the Apodae; and to the north, the Fagophagi and Thuringians.

At the entrance of the Franks all the Thuringians fall [unclear].

At the entry of the Franks, the Thuringians, by command of their king Heurolus, withdrew beyond the forest, leaving behind for the new guests all the grain sufficient for the following year. Therefore the newly arrived Franks first settled in the borders of the Thuringians, between the river Saale, as it is now called from Salagaast, and the lower parts of the Neckar, around the banks of the river Main, in that district which was formerly Meningau and was later called Eastern Francia. In it, in the course of time, they built not a few villages and cities in number, and grew in [unclear] and power.

Genealogy of the dukes of Eastern Francia. Faramund, duke [unclear] of the Eastern Franks. Marcomer, son of Faramund, duke.

Duke Genebald begot Marcomir and Dagobert, who ruled over Eastern Francia for twenty-one years. Dagobert begot Clodius, who ruled over the people for ten years. Clodius begot Marcomir. Faramund, however, governed the duchy with his father and alone for fifteen years, and afterward was chosen king of the Franks, as we shall say in its proper order. He entrusted the duchy of Eastern Francia to his brother Marcomir, who held it for eighteen years. Duke Marcomir begot Priamus, who ruled for twelve years. Duke Priamus begot Genebald the second, who ruled for twenty-one years. When he was struck and killed by a boar while hunting, Clodomir, son of the aforesaid Duke Sunno, succeeded in the duchy and ruled for thirty-one years. Clodomir begot Hugbad, who ruled for twenty-six years. Hugbad begot Helenus, who ruled for thirty years. Helenus begot Gotfrid, who ruled for twenty-four years. Godfrid begot Genebald the third, who ruled for twenty years. Genebald begot Clodomir, who ruled for twenty-four years. After him Heribert, his nephew, succeeding in the duchy, ruled for thirty years. When he too had died, Clodoveus, son of his brother, ruled in the duchy

COMPENDIVM LIB. I. Hoc nuncio Valentinianus accepto, Francorum mirabatur constantiam, & circunstan- tibus dixit: Franci Frane, durus es populus, & a ferocitate potius, quam a libertate nominandus. Et quieuit anno currente negotium, propterea quod a diversis nationibus Romanorum respublica multas et varias illo in tempore pateretur incursiones hostiles. Anno autem sequente Valentinianus deceptus consilio suorum denuo misit ad Fran- cos Sisinnium comitem aulicum, vt eos bonis induceret persuasionibus ad solutionem tributi, firmissimamque amicitiam Romanorum. Sed Franci non immemores eorum, quae prius Valentiniano remandauerat, necemque Marcomiri regis sui amantissimi vin- dicare cupientes, misium ad se comirem cum tota societate quam adduxerat, gladio per- emerunt, in contemptum Valentiniani, & omnium Romanorum. Post haec Franci maximo fuorum in vnum adunato exercitu, sub ducibus Sunnone et Genebaldo (quem Galli Gundebadum nuncuparunt) cum impetu Rheno transmisso in fines Romanorum irruptentes, & omnia depopulant, etiam Coloniësibus metum incusserunt. Omnia enim qua fuerit inter Rhenum, Mosam, & Tabulam, fluuios, suo co- tendebat subiugare domino. Vetur posteaquam excursus Francorum innotuit apud Treuiros, Nannenus et Quintinus principes Treuiorum (quis, fucut et Coloniës, Roma- norum partes fequebantur) collecto exercitu impetum in eos facere constituerit. Nam interea Franci regione Gallorum vastata, multique illorum peremptis, ad fedes patrias cum exercitus parte spolia transmisserunt vtlerius procedentes. Cum Nannenus et Quintinus Treuiorum principes cum exercitu venissent, & Fran- ci (vt diximus) in bono numero iam praeda onusi Rhenum transsillent, intentionem habentes reuertendi ad socios, & quod reliquum erat Gallis intactum pro viribus defol- adi, secuta est Francos confusio magna propter inconsultam et minus cautam partitio- nem exercitus. Erant enim prima Francorum sedes (quod sepe diximus) circa fines et o- stia Rheni, vbi nunc est Hollandia, Selandia, & populi Traieçeses, Gelrenfes, & Frifii, quo- rum pars nomen postea Westalen / id est, Galli occidentales, comparatione aliorum, qui Ostualen / id est, Galli Orientales in regione Monasteriensi dicebantur, accepti. Habebat- que Franci ab oriente Saxones, Theutones, Germanos, & Marcomannos: ad meridiem, Coloniës et Gallos: ad occidentem, Tungros et Morinos, qui maritima incolebat: ad aquilonem vero, Scotos, Orchadas, Dacos, simul et mare. Nannenus ergo et Quintinus, vbi cum exercitu Treuiorum applicuissent ad loca, in quibus reliqua Francorum remanerant, sociorum reditum expectantes, aciem instruex- runt, & perìécuti fugientes vsque ad Carbonariam syluam, retrocedere compulerunt, nō paucis eorum trucidatis. Hinc ortum est odium Francorum in Treuiros, propter quod postea Rheno transmisso, in regione Treuiorum hyemare coeperunt, & omnia deua- stare. His autem peractis, Quintino vtile vifum est, si exercitum omnem Treuiorum tradu- cerent in Franciam, imparatosque subita irruptione praeoccuparent. Sed Nanneno con- silium Quintini non placuit, qui Francos in solo proprio ad refidendum esse non dubita- bat audentiores. Quapropter Nannenus à Quintino recedens cum suis, ad Moguntiam 40 reueritur. Quintinus autem in suo consilens proposito, circa Musium castellum', Rheno trans- misso, produxit exercitum, & Francos primo delere incursu meditabatur', animo excelso et maiore, quam viribus ad vincendum. Sed Franci non segnes, Gallos virili exceperit oc- cursu, initoque praelio, multa Treuiorum millia interierunt, paucis fuga saluatis. Cecidit in eo congresu Heracleus, legionis Romanae tribunus, & pene omnes, qui militibus prae- rant, iaculis et gladio Francorum cum co perierunt. Paucis namque exceptis, quibus nox atra salutem, & nemora latendi praebuere facultatem, totus Quintini exercitus gladio,ar- cu, & palude interrijt. Franci, morte Valentiniani Caesaris audita, Rhenum transire, Galliamque inuader decreuerit. Annals of Trithemius.

... held office for twelve years. Clodoucus begot Gosvertus, who held office for twenty-six years. In his sixth year Conon, pope of Rome, ordained Saint Kilian, a Scottish monk, as bishop and sent him to the Eastern Franks to preach the faith of Christ. Gosbert begot the younger Gosbert, who held office for nineteen years. The younger Gosbert begot Hetan, who held office for twenty years. When, with him, the male line had died out, in the year of the Lord's nativity 740, in the eighth Roman indiction, the duchy of Eastern Francia remained without a duke for twelve years, under the authority of Pippin, mayor of the palace and afterwards king of the Franks, who entrusted it to his son Charles the Great.

Thus there were in Eastern Francia twenty-one dukes, succeeding one another over 414 years; they make up the sacred sevenfold number tripled in order, and not foreign to mystery. In the year of the Lord's nativity 752, in the fifth Roman indiction, Pippin, raised from mayor of the palace to king of the Franks, as was said above, handed over the often-mentioned duchy of Eastern Francia to Saint Burchard, first bishop of the church of Wurzburg, and to his successors, as perpetual property.

From that time, apart from the bishops of the church of Wurzburg, down to the present day no one by right has been able to claim for himself the duchy of the aforesaid Francia, although by the rashness, not the right, of certain kings and emperors rebellious against the Roman Church and excommunicated, as if in vengeance for themselves, the contrary was sometimes attempted. Among these Conrad, the third of that name, afterwards emperor, since he was Swabian by nation, violently usurped for himself the duchy of Eastern Francia by royal permission; nevertheless, after he had been made Caesar, he restored it to the church with manifold satisfaction.

Let these things, briefly touched upon in a necessary historical digression concerning the origin, genealogy, and succession of the dukes of the people of Eastern Francia, suffice. Let us now return to the order of the kings of the Franks, from which we departed. Clodomir, king of the Franks, after many deeds bravely performed, at last died in the eighteenth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord 337, in the tenth Roman indiction.

The Thirty-Seventh.

Richimer, the elder son of King Clodomir, succeeding his father, reigned for thirteen years. Throughout all the days of his reign he was always in contention with the Romans and Gauls; with the aid of his uncle Genebald, that is, the duke of Eastern Francia, residing at the city [unclear], and of the other princes of the Franks, as well as the Thuringians, Saxons, and fierce German allies, he fought against them many times as victor and afflicted them with great slaughter.

In the fourth year of his reign, having gathered the support of his allies with a very great multitude of fighters, he entered Gaul and laid everything waste with fire and sword. Against him Tiberianus, prefect of the Romans, also moved a great army of his men to war; when their forces were joined for battle, they fought for a long time with doubtful fortune, and many fell slain on both sides. At last, however, the Gauls were defeated and compelled to seek safety in flight.

In the sixth year of King Richimer, in the fourth indiction, the Romans, gathering in troops into one body with the Gauls, under Constantine the Great, Caesar, declared war on the Franks. King Richimer, since he was a high-souled, strong, and bold prince, was in no way terrified; as usual he summoned as allies the Teutons, Germans, Saxons, and Thuringians. When these had been united with the Franks, he set against the Romans and Gauls an army of almost two hundred thousand, with whom he fought vigorously. In the first engagement the Romans were victorious; in the second, defeated and overcome, they fled with loss among their men.

In the last year of his reign, Richimer, king of the Franks, when he was [unclear] about to fight again with the Romans, was killed in battle, namely in the thirteenth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord's nativity 350, in the eighth Roman indiction.

The Thirty-Eighth.

Theodomir, son of the aforementioned King Richimer, reigned after the death of his father for ten years. Throughout all the days of his reign he lived in contention with the Romans and fought many battles against them with varying outcome. His mother, named Hafila, was the daughter of the king of the Saxons. At that time the kings of the Franks lived in the territories of the Tungri, across the river Meuse, in the fortress which antiquity called Dispargum. From the boundary of the Franks as far as the river Loire the Gauls dwelt under the rule of the Romans; beyond the Loire were the Goths, intermixed with peoples of various nations.

Theodomir reigned ten years.

The seat of the kings of the Franks was among the Tungri at Dispargum.

The duchy of Eastern Francia was vacant for twelve years.

There were twenty-one dukes at [Wurzburg?].

These prelates and dukes of the Eastern Franks Trithemius enumerates in order down to his own age in the Compendium on the Origin of the Franks, published at Basel, vol. I of German Histories, folio 322.

The duchy of Eastern Francia belongs solely to the aforesaid church of Wurzburg.

Conrad [I?], not duke of [unclear], but [unclear].

Richimer reigned thirteen years.

War is joined between the Franks and the Romans.

The Romans again declared war on the Franks.

The Romans are defeated by the Franks in battle.

Theodomir reigned ten years.

The seat of the kings of the Franks was among the Tungri at Dispargum.

Saint Kilian is made bishop.

COMPENDIVM LIB. I. 34 Alarico, deliberatione cum suis praehabita, Gallias alioqui furore mutarum gentium agitatas, Gothis inhabitandas conceffit. Wandali autem, qui remanerant in Gallijs, audientes Gothorum adventum, quamuis ex una essent natione Scanziana procreati, nihilominus timore perterriti, Galliam defuerunt, & cum Alanis, Suetijs, Hispaniarum partem occuparunt, ubi annis ferme triga commorati, postea in Africam navigauerunt, & Hipponam vrbem destruxerunt. Alaricus vero, permiffione Honorij Caefaris, Galliam periturus, cum suis Italia digreditur: super quem comes Stilicon, Romani ductor exercitus, in fefto Dominica Resurrectionis nihil mali fufpicientem non iufius irruit, eumque ad pugnam inuitum prouocauit. Et primo quidem impetu victor exstitit, in feco congreflu victus, falutem fuga quere compulfsit. Alaricus rex, qui hoc factum Honorij subornatione creditit, mox foedus, quod cum eo fecerat, rupt, itinereque mutato, in Italiam reuertitur, & omnia circumquaque Honorij partium depopulatur. Honorius vero Caefar intelligens comitem Stiliconem tantorum effe caufam malorum, eum cepit, & cum Euchario filio capite thuncavit. Alaricus autem rex vrbem Romam cepit, edificia multa subuertit, & civis in rebus grauiter laefit. A fanguine tamet et hominum cade temperaui, & fugientibus ad fan et torum Basilicas pepercit. Die tertia difceffit sua fponre à Roma, nauigaturusque in Siciliam, naufragium pertulit. & non multo post infirmatus grauiter, fubito vitam cum morte commutavit. Dum haecagerentur in Italia per Gothos, Franci tempus adfeffere rati, quo fibi Galliam subijcerent vniverfam, contraftis copijs, magnum adunauerunt exercitum, & subduci bus Faramundo, Marcomiro, Sunnone, Priamo, & Antenore, fines Gallicanos ingreffi, primo cum Wandalis congregendiuntur, qui Gallias denuo incurfabant, quorum regem Godgifith (quem nonnulli Godogifilum nuncupant) cum viginti millibus occiderunt. Et nifi Respendial rex Alanoru, Wandalis ex Hispania, ubi tune regnabat, tempeftue veniflet in auxilium, omnes fuiffent à Francis occifi. Anno domini cccc. xix. obijt Genebaldus, inter rex Francorum, filius Dagoberti, & nepos Marcomiri regis, anno principatus sui xxi, poft cuius mortem Franci (vt dicemus) denuo reges habuerunt. Eodem nanque anno, statim poft obitum Genebaldi, conuenientes in vnum proceres et maiores natu Francorum, confilium habuerunt inter fe maturum, vtile iudicantes, vt more veterum, fibi regem confiituerent exducibus vnum. Et bonus eft viuis fermo in oculis omnium, conuenereuntque in caufa huius negotij ad aliam diaetam duces subscripti: Pharamundus videlicet dux Francorum Orientalium: Marcomir dux, & Sunno dux, fraetres Pharamundi, Orientalis: Clodius dux, filius Pharamundi: Dagobertus dux, filius Marcomiri: Nicanor dux, Pharabert9 dux, Richimer dux, Antenor dux Menipolitarũ, Priamus dux frater eius, Bertheri dux Gallicanus, Heribert dux Insulanus, Sunno dux, & Richer dux, filij Genebaldi ducis et interregis Francoru defuncti, Diocles dux, & Meroueus dux, Ade- rant etiam ex facerdotibus et fapientibus Francoru: Salegafthald fummus pontifex Iouis, Gafthald, Herhald magifer epiftolarum, Wifogafthald pontifex Diana, Rutvivicus, A- delhardus, Richeri, & alij complures tam explebeis quam ex proceribus. Hi omnes communicato inter fe matura deliberationis confilio, tandem de vnanimi confenfui Pharamundum ducem Francia Orientalis apud Wirciburg, in regem Francorum eliguerunt, qui filius fuerat Marcomiri ducis, anno Domini (vt fupra diximus) quadrifentimo quarto defuncti: qui Marcomirus fuit Clodij, qui fuit Dagoberti, qui fuit Genebaldi primi ducis Francorum Orientalium, & fraeris Marcomiri regis, quorum pa- ter fuit Clogio rex Francorum, qui (vt fupra diximus) obijt anno domini, ccc. lxxviii. QUADRAGESIMVS TERTIVS. Pharamundus fuit rex Francorum 43. Marcomir dux cum regno ann. 43. ducatum vero Francia Orientalis eodem moxanno commendauit Marcomiro fra- tri fuo gubernandum, quoeille strenue rexit annis decé et octo: cuius genus et fuccelfores in ducatu fecundũ ordinem continuando, vtque ad vltimu duce Heranũ, & Carolũ filium Pippini Magnu, defcriptifimus fupra, quando genealogiam primi ducis praenotauimus. Compendium, Book I.

The Franks [unclear]. The Eastern Franks cross the Rhine. The city of Trier is destroyed by the Franks.

The boundaries of the kingdom of the Franks at this time were greatly enlarged beyond the Meuse; they had occupied a great part of Gaul, though the Romans were unwilling. Nor did they desist from what they had begun, until at length, reckoning from this point onward, within about seventy years they subjected all Gaul to their rule.

In the times of the aforesaid king Theodomirus, Dagobert, son of Genebald, the first duke of the Eastern Franks, and successor to his father in the principate, gathered a multitude of fighters, crossed the Rhine, and, after carrying off booty, laid waste Cisrhenian Gaul with fire and sword. He plundered and burned the very ancient city of Trier, built in the times of Abraham, prince of the Jews.

But King Theodomirus was at length captured by the Romans inhabiting Gaul, together with his mother Hastila, was beheaded, and died in the tenth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 460, in the third Roman indiction.

The Thirty-Ninth.

The reign of Clogio: 18 years. Saint Anthony dies. Julian the apostate fights with the Alemanni. The Franks take the city of Cambrai. The Franks hold Gaul as far as the Saone. The legions of the Romans in Germany. War of the Romans with the Saxons.

Clogio, son of King Theodomirus, succeeding his father, reigned over the Franks for eighteen years, a spirited, strong prince, and of singular prudence. He fought many battles with the Romans and Gauls, and harshly avenged the death of both his father and his mother in the blood of very many enemies. In his first year, Saint Anthony, abbot and hermit, departed to the Lord on the seventeenth day of the month of January, in the 105th year of his age.

At the same time also the Alemanni had a war with the Romans, not far from the Rhine, in the territories of the people of Strasbourg. In that battle many fell on both sides; yet more of the Alemanni were killed than of the Romans, whose army’s commander was Julian Caesar, despiser of God and apostate.

Clogio, king of the Franks, wishing to avenge his father’s death, gathered a huge army, entered Gaul in force, and stormed the city of Cambrai, where he killed without pity many Romans whom he found there.

Advancing from there, he subjected Gaul to his kingdom as far as the river Saone. Against him the Romans, fighting more with treacheries than with strength, could do nothing.

In the thirteenth year of Clogio, king of the Franks, while the leaders with their armies were laying waste the Gallic provinces, Valentinian, Caesar of the Romans, having secretly and swiftly led legions through Sarmatia into the territories of the Germans, waged war with the Saxons in the territories of the Franks, this side of the Oder, not far from the sea. In it many on both sides fell, killed by the sword. Yet victory at last passed to the Romans, and the defeated Saxons took flight.

But King Clogio died in the eighteenth year of his reign, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 378, in the sixth Roman indiction, leaving three sons by the queen: Marcomirus, who succeeded his father in the kingdom; Dagobert, who after the death of the brother just named held the kingdom under the name of duke, as we say below in its own place; and Hector, surnamed Degenbart, from whom Pippin and Charles, afterward emperor, the Great, derived their lineage, as we have said in the second volume.

The Fortieth.

Marcomirus, Clogio’s elder son, succeeding his father in the aforesaid year in the kingdom of the Franks, reigned for fifteen years, a magnanimous, strong, and bold prince, who fought many battles with the Romans.

Indeed, in the first year of his reign the Romans, aided by the forces of the Gauls, stirred up war against him. He met them with the Franks and Saxons in a fearless encounter, fought bravely not far from the city of Cologne, struck down many thousands of the enemy, and divided the spoils among his helpers and friends. This war lasted four years.

But the Franks, spirited with their inborn ferocity, met the Romans for battle, just as a lion is accustomed to tear apart a little dog with extended claws, as men to be handed over at once to death and without pity. At length, after four years had passed, the Romans, considering that they could not tame the Franks and subject them to themselves, recalled by [edict?] the remnants of the legions that had survived, and sent them to other places. Yet the Franks, not ceasing on that account from harassing the Gauls, continued what they had begun.

In the ninth year of Marcomirus, king of the Franks, in the fifteenth Roman indiction, Maximus, king of Britain, sprung from the lineage of the Caesars, received the name and diadem of the Roman Empire from the soldiers stationed in England.

A few years earlier Octavius, king of Britain, lacking a son, had called him from Rome into Britain with the consent of the nobles; for he was a Briton on his mother’s side, but a Roman on his father’s; and he gave him his daughter

COMPENDIVM LIB. I. manis perpetuum contraxerant foedus, quod vsque ad obitum regis Marcomiri per annos ferme cccc. xxx. inuiolabiliter foeratum est ab omnibus. Marcomiro autem rege Francorum a Valentiniano Caaeare (vt prius est dictum) anno domini cccc. xciii. occido, Doringi, & Saxones, cum Germanis et Theutonibus a societate Francorum receperunt, rebus non satis prouide sub ducibus actis. Huius occasione dissidij, rex Clodius Doringam potenter intruit, regem vicit et gentem, eolque tributum Francis dare annuum, & Vincentium deinceps obedere mandatis coartavit, vt qui liberorum sub iure foederis antiqui socii manere contemplerant, corum serui, subditi et tributarij esse cogerentur. Simile Germanis postea contigit atque Saxonibus, qui rupto societatis foedere, deinceps Francos non amplius (vt prius) fenerunt amicos, sed reges et dominos. Exinde rex Clodius Rheno simul et Moae transmissis, expeditionem mouit in Galliam, omnemque regionem Tungrorum deuauit, & potenter obnens, Francorum regno subiugavit, atque pro confirmatione nouae possessionis olim amisse tunc vero recepta, ibidem aliquandiu confedit, inde vique ad tabulam procedens omnia recepit. Post haec anno undecimo, indictione Romanorum quinta, Clodius rex Francorum considerans Romanorum potestatem haud parum defecisse, misit exploratores in ulteriorem Galliam, vt situm terra, fortitudinem gentis, vrbiumque, ac munitionum custodiam diligentiter explorarent, sibique renunciare studerent quantorius. Eo tempore Burgundiones habitabant in provincia Lugdunensi, & Gothi in Aquitania, qui cum Hispanis et Gallis terram occupabant. Reuersti exploratores ad Clodium, retulerunt regiones esse optimas, fructiferam penitus terram, situm quoque amoenissimum, gentem inermem, pauidam, inualidamque, & Romanorum in vrbibus paruae esse custodiam. Quibus auditis, rex Clodius, cui nihil plus animo fuit quam nomen, gloriamque Francorum dilatare et regnum, magnum fuorum contraxit exercitum, & mouens ultra flumen, quod Tabula nominatur, versus mare, in Galliam, vrbem Cameracensem obfedit, & cepit, Romanis, quos in ea reperit, cunctis militibus occisis. Inde mouens per Carbonarium nemus ad Tornacensem viber, iter festinans direxit, qua civitas Romanorum fuit praëdio munita. Romanis vero milites, qui erant in praëdio, cum audissent Francorum aduentum, contra eos extra vrbem processerunt ad bellum, in quo vsque ad vnum omnes a Francis fuerunt occisi, vt nec vnius quidem remanserit ex cunctis, qui ceterorum interitus nuncium detulisset Romanis. Vrbem vero Tornacensem cum omni regione sibi subiecerunt. Deinde progresi vterius Franci, Morinos, Tarauanos, & quicquid reliquae fuerit Galliarum, vsque ad mare, in suam receperunt omnimodam potestatem, possidentque universa vsque in praesentem diem, qua Romanis deinceps nec recuperauerunt, imo nec recuperare poterunt, in sempiternum. Aruit enim, qua dudum floruit. Clodius vero insignis Francorum rex, posteaquam regni terminos magnifice dilatauit, omnemque terram Galliarum, qua fuit inter Rhenum, ab oriente: & mare Morinum, ab occidente: Britannicum, ab Aquilone: vsque ad Sequanam, versus meridiem, hoc est, Batauos, Maenapios, Tungros, Tarauanos, Morinos, Ambiones, Cameracenses, Tornacenses, Atrebatenae, Beluacenses, & quicquid his regionibus interiaecat, vltraque Sequanam vsque ad Ligerim, Francorum regno potenter fecisset subiectum. Moritur anno regnisui viceclivi: Dominica vero natiuitatis, cccc. xlvi. indictione xiii. QUADRAGESIMVSQVINTVS. Meroveus Clodij memorati regis maior nati filius, patri succedens, regnauit super Francos annis duodecim: princeps potentia, fortitudine, magnitudineque rerum gestarum nulli praecedentium regum inferior, qui Romanum contruit imperium, & patris vestigia gloriosa imitatione fecutus, regnum Francorum id paucis, quibus regnauerat 50 annis, non mediocriter augmentauit. Omnes enim Galliarum fines, quos pater Francorum adiunxerat regno, cunctis regni sui diebus non solum sub ditione sua cotinuit, sed etiam Romanis vbliber inuentus, vel occisis, vel fugatis, terminos acquisita possessionis longelaterque mirum in modum dilatauit. Anno regni sui octavo, terramotus pene fuerunt affidui, & signa in coelo plura, & metuenda sunt ostensa. Nam adueesperante quadam die coelum rubens vrgnis ab Aquilone apparuit, intermissis per igneum ruborem lineis quibusdam clarioribus, in hastae similitudinem deformatis, Eclipsin luna patitur, cometes horrendae magnitudinis apparuit,

ANNAL TRITHEMII. 29 suam vxorem, cum qua, Octauio mortuo, totius insulae regnum obtinuit. Venerat au- tem vocatus in Britanniam cum exercitu militiae Romanorum, & maior pars militum cum eo remansit, paucioribus numero in Italiã teuersis. Deinde post mortem Va- lentiniani Valentis Caesarũ, anno regni sui Britannici quinto, in superbiam elatus mente, quietis impatiens, Caesarem se constitui Romanorum fecit ab his, qui cum eo remanterant militibus, contra Gratianum, quem sibi Romani pręfecerant. Mox ita- que vt Caesar à militibus salutatus est, Britâniae regnum vicario procurandum commisit, omnemque nobilitatem iuuentutem militia totius insulae Brittannia (quae nunc An- glia dicitur) in vnum convocans, cum eis in Galliam nauigauit, talem habens intentio- 10 nem animi, vt deuictis Galliis, Romam proficisceretur, sibique imperium subijceret. Anno igitur Marcomiri regis Francorum nono; dominice vero natiuitatis CCCCLXXXVII. indictione Romanorum quintadecima, Maximus Britannie rex, cum ingenti multitudine suorum nauigio intrauit Gallias, omnia per circuitum re- gionis hostiliter vastauit. Et primo quidem applicuit cum nauibus ad littus terrae Ar- moricae, quae ab illo tempore deinceps Britania noua, siue minor dicta est, vsque in pręsentem diem, quam tunc inhabitabant Franci, sub moderamine ducis Iubalchi, quem reges Francorum vicarium regni illis in locis constituerant. Dux autem Iubalchus in- troitu tantae multitudinis gentium haud mediocriter turbatus, copias vt potuit suorum contraxit, procedensque obuiam venientibus, cum eis bellum commisit, in quo ipse cum 20 quindecim Francorum millibus fuit occisus, caeteris surgâ salutem q̃arentibus. Denique vt nominis sui terrorem cunctis perygnum incuteret, magna crudelitate vsus est: quippe qui mulieres, virgines, senes iuuenes, paruulos infantes, quot- quot reperit, sine misericordia trucidauit. Erant autem Franci reges, duces, nobiles, milites, populus omnis, idolorum vana supersitione adhuc obeecati atque polluti. Maximus vero, etsi Tyrannus, tamen cum omni militia, populo suo fuit Christianus. Hac de Iubalcho Francis obtenta victoria, Maximus principatum illum Armoricum contulit duci Conano, qui fuit ex fratre nepos Octauii regis Britannie supradicti, relicta- 30 que cum ea bona parte exercitus Britannorum ad custodiam, ipse cum reliqua multitu- dine copiarum discedens inde, per yniuersamq̃ Galliam discurrrens, contradi- centes suo imperio non minus crudeliter quam potenter bello armis fecit obe- dientes. Interea Gratianus Romae Caesar, intelligens Maximum sibi nomen diadema Romani vfurpasse imperii, egressũmque magno cum exercitu de Britannia vastare coepisse Gallias, contractis ipse co piis, contra eum mouit in Galliam, vrbem Pari- siensem cum exercitu intrauir. Congreissũ postea cum Maximo, proditione Mero- baldi magistri militum superatus est, fugâ lapsus, venit Lugdunum: vbi postea fuit occifus. Conanus autem, quem Maximus regem in Armorica regione constituerat, fre- 40 qnter occurrens, viriliter cum dimicabat, multisq̃ corum peremptis, reliquos in fugam conuertit. Consecutus postremo pacem, quietam Armoricici regni poffef- tionem, cum nobilibus suis cõpit habere consiliũ, quomodo vxores liberos, quos in Britannia dimiferant ad se quantotius facerent cum omni suppellectili perduci dome- fica, ne generis propago deficeret. Militum vero numerus, qui de Britannia venerant cum Conano in Armoricam, 50 fuit triginta millium pugnatorum; Plebanorum vero agricolarum (vt Galfredus est auctor) fuerunt centum millia, qui omnes iussionẽ de Britannia in Armorican nauigauerant. Ex his multi non habebant vxores: caeteri vero qui habebant, eas in Britan- nia dimiferant cum paruulis, quando Maximum sequi cogebantur. Conanus autem o- mnis populus eius, cum essent Christiani, filias Paganorum muta colentium vxores ducere, nulla ratione consenserunt. Quae etiam si fuissent Christianae, cum Gallis tamen commistionis nuptialis nullum eis placuit habere commertium. Fuit in diebus illis subregulus quidam in Britannia (quae nunc Anglia vocatur) no- mine Dionotus, qui mortuo Caradoco fratre suo, Cornubiae tenebat principatum, cui 60 Maximus rex profecturus in Galliam, vt viro prudentiffimo, commendauerat regnum. his wife, with whom, after Octavius had died, he obtained the kingdom of the whole island. He had come, however, when summoned into Britain, with an army of Roman soldiers, and the greater part of the soldiers remained with him, a smaller number returning to Italy. Then, after the death of Valentinian and Valens, the Caesars, in the fifth year of his British reign, lifted up in mind into pride and impatient of peace, he had himself made Caesar of the Romans by those soldiers who had remained with him, against Gratian, whom the Romans had set over them. Therefore, as soon as he was hailed as Caesar by the soldiers, he entrusted the kingdom of Britain to be governed by a deputy, and, summoning into one body all the nobility and the military youth of the whole island of Britain, which is now called England, he sailed with them into Gaul, having this intention in mind: that, once the Gauls had been conquered, he would set out for Rome and subject the empire to himself.

Accordingly, in the ninth year of Marcomir, king of the Franks, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 487, in the fifteenth Roman indiction, Maximus, king of Britain, entered Gaul by ship with a great multitude of his men and laid waste everything round about the region in hostile fashion. And first indeed he landed with his ships on the shore of the land of Armorica, which from that time thereafter has been called New Britain, or Lesser Britain, down to the present day. The Franks then inhabited it, under the governance of Duke Iubalchus, whom the kings of the Franks had appointed deputy of the kingdom in those places. Duke Iubalchus, not a little disturbed by the entry of so great a multitude of peoples, drew together the forces of his men as best he could, and, advancing to meet those who were coming, joined battle with them. In that battle he himself was killed with fifteen thousand Franks, while the rest sought safety in flight.

Then, in order to strike terror of his name into all throughout the kingdom, he used great cruelty: for he slaughtered without mercy women, virgins, old men, young men, and little children, as many as he found. The kings, dukes, nobles, soldiers, and all the people of the Franks were still blinded and polluted by the empty superstition of idols. Maximus, however, although a tyrant, was nevertheless, with all his soldiery and his people, Christian. After this victory over Iubalchus had been won from the Franks, Maximus bestowed that Armorican principality on Duke Conan, who was the nephew by his brother of Octavius, the aforesaid king of Britain; and, leaving with him a good part of the army of the Britons for protection, he himself departed from there with the remaining multitude of troops and, ranging through all Gaul, made those who resisted his rule obedient by war and arms, no less cruelly than powerfully.

Meanwhile Gratian Caesar at Rome, learning that Maximus had usurped for himself the name and diadem of the Roman empire and, having gone out from Britain with a great army, had begun to lay waste Gaul, himself gathered troops and moved against him into Gaul, entering the city of Paris with his army. Afterwards, engaging with Maximus, he was overcome through the treachery of Merobaudes, master of the soldiers; slipping away in flight, he came to Lyons, where later he was killed.

Conan, however, whom Maximus had established as king in the Armorican region, frequently met [unclear], fought manfully with [unclear], and, after many of them had been killed, turned the rest to flight. Having at last obtained peace and quiet possession of the Armorican kingdom, he began to take counsel with his nobles as to how they might as quickly as possible have their wives and children, whom they had left in Britain, brought to them with all their household equipment, lest the offspring of their race should fail.

The number of soldiers who had come from Britain with Conan into Armorica was thirty thousand fighting men; of commoners and farmers, however, as Geoffrey is the authority, there were one hundred thousand, all of whom had sailed by command from Britain into Armorica. Of these many did not have wives; but the others who did have them had left them in Britain with their little children when they were compelled to follow Maximus. Conan, however, and all his people, since they were Christians, by no reasoning consented to take as wives the daughters of pagans who worshipped mute things. Even if they had been Christians, nevertheless it did not please them to have any matrimonial commerce of mingling with the Gauls.

There was in those days a certain petty king in Britain, which is now called England, named Dionotus, who, after the death of his brother Caradocus, held the principality of Cornwall; to him King Maximus, when about to set out for Gaul, had entrusted the kingdom, as to a most prudent man. He had an only daughter named Ursula, in the judgment of all the most beautiful among all the maidens of Britain, and very devoted to Christ. COMPENDIVM LIB. I. Regnum Francorum maxum omnibus regis totius Europae. Regnum Francorum maxum omnibus regis totius Europae. Hinc manifeste constat, quoniam sic sunt Franci, qui remanerant cum Germanis, & lingua, & moribus vtuntur Germanorum, ita etiam qui Gallias cum regibus intrant cum Gallis manerunt, & mores, & loquendi vium cum fedibus mutauerunt: & quos natura Germanos ab exordio natiuitatis constituit, cos locorum mutatio in medio Gallorum loquela et moribus similiter Gallos fecit. Enimvero cum essent in Troia, mores et sermones frequentabant etiam Troianos: inter Scythas quoque Scythicos: in Germania, Germanos: & in Gallia didicere ac tenuere Gallicanos. Sic et Aeneas ex Troianis veniens in Italiam cum sua gente, sermonis paulatim oblitus patrii, moribus et lingua vii coepit Romanuentis. Post haec Meroueus rex Francorum, a gratitudine corruptus, in paganismo idolorum, sic ut omnes progenitores sui, moritur anno regni sui duodecimo: dominica autem natiuitatis, cccc. LVIII. indictione Romanorum, vndecima. QUADRAGESIMVS SEXTVS. Hildericus Merouei regis filius, patri succedens in regno Francorum, varia mutatione rerum bis regnauit. Primo enim post patre regnauit anno duntaxat vno: deinde propter insolentiam suam et luxuriam (sicuti dicemus) regno deicetus, fugit in Doringiam. Post quem Franci super se constituerunt Aegidium quendam Romanum, quo post triennium fugato, Hildericus de Doringia reuocatus in Franciam, regnauit annis viginti duobus. Et factum est omne tempus regni eius a prima institutione eius post partem vique ad mortem annorum sex et viginti, quorum ramen nò regnauit nisi xxiii. regnum Aegidio (sicut diximus) occupante annis tribus, ipso in Doringia exulante apud Basinum regem. Anno quidem vno duntaxat in regno exacto, conspirantes in eum proceres regni, volebant eum interficere, propter eaque nimis insolentem et luxuriosè viuens, filias et vxores corum atque nobilium sua turpitudine plures vitiasset. Quod vbi comperit, cum paucis fugit in Doringiam, mansitque apud Basinum regem Doringorum, cognatum suum annis tribus, recessit autem deicetus à Francis, anno domini cccc LIX. indictione xii. Post cuivis a regno discessum, codem mox anno Francorum principes regem super se constituerunt Aegidium quendam Romanorum apud Sueffionenses praefectum, qui annis tribus, Hilderico exulante, regnum Francorum occupauit. Is continue sequiens in principes optimatesque regni corum, plures trucidavit, praeter vanam suspicionem, nullam habens rationabilem causam. Vnde reliqui metuentes sibi quandoque imminere similia, in tyrannum conspirationem vnanimes ordinarunt, tolerabilius fore iudicantes eum regno pati praesidere, qui natis vxoribusque abuteretur subditorum, quam illum sustinere diutius, qui nihil fitiret amplius quam sanguinem principum. Anno igitur dominice natiuitatis cccc LXXII. indictione Romanorum quintadecima, Hildericus industria et fide Wimbaldi amici sui, qui fuit vnis ex potentioribus regni principibus, ex Doringia reuocatus in regnum Francorum, omnium fauore procerum et gentis in regnum paternum restituitur, & Aegidius cum tis odiosus inde fugatur. Et regnauit deinceps Hildericus modestissime adhuc annis viginti duobus. Cumque audisset Basina, vxor Bañani regis Doringorum, quod Hildericus esset à Francis restitutus in regnum, dimisso viro suo secura est eum in Galliam, nimio eius amore concitata, quem ex diuturna familiaritate cohabitandi apud Doringos contraxerat. Hildericus veniente hilari vultu admittes, libi vt notam desumplit vxorem Basina regis à quo triennio benigne fuerat hospitio receptus, male humanitatem hanc remunerans. Instante autem prima nuptiarum nocte, Basina monuit Hildericum paulisper differre concubitum, foresque cubiculi obseruare, & quae tertio viderit in atrio portenta renunciare vaticinantì sibi per omnia fideliter. Mulieri credulus rex vt mandauit obsequitur, obseruatque tertio axibus, ad eam reuerfus est, dicens primo fe vidisse in atrio palati Rhinocerotas, id est, Vnicornes, leones quoque et leopardos. Secundo lupos et vrfos furentes, seque mutuo infectantes. Tertio vidi, ait, canes plures, sed exiguos, qui fece mutuo dente lacera- bant, & mordebant infesto, sed quid significant tu dicio.

30 Compendium, Book I ... knew her very well, but also loved her greatly. Therefore, having sent messengers and letters to him, he asked that she be sent to him as his wife. Secondly he asked that, when the husbands went out by Maximus’s command, they should put on ships the wives and children of the soldiers and common people left in Britain, together with their household goods, and send them to him into the Armorican kingdom. Thirdly he commanded that, according to the number which he had expressed in his letter, virgins should be sent: noble women, for the soldiers of noble lineage; and likewise common women for the commoners, whom each man who then had no wife might take as wives for themselves.

Dionotus, seeing Conanus’s messenger and wishing to satisfy his desire, gathered from the various provinces of Britain eleven thousand daughters of nobles, and from the rest, of lower rank, sixty thousand virgins and women, all of whom he ordered to assemble on a fixed day within the walls of London. He also ordered ships to be brought from all the shores of Britain, sufficient for the transport of so great a multitude. Although this had pleased many in so great an assembly, nevertheless it displeased many also, who loved their parents and fatherland with greater affection. Nor were there perhaps lacking some who, preferring chastity to marriage, would have rather lost their life in any land than be married.

At last, when the things necessary for the transport had been prepared, the women entered the [appointed?] ships and, by the river Thames, passed into the seas. Finally, when they turned their sails toward the Armoricans, that is, from north to south, suddenly a great storm arose at sea, and, the fleet being divided, the ships were separated from one another. Great danger pressed upon all, and the greater part of the ships was scattered into the depth of the sea and was submerged with the women. Those who escaped so great a danger were driven to barbarous nations and islands of the sea, and by an unknown people were either slaughtered or consigned to perpetual slavery. For they had fallen upon the army of the impious princes Wanius and Melga, who, hired for pay by Caesar Gratian, were devastating Britain first, and then the maritime nations and the surrounding islands, out of hatred for Maximus; by them they cruelly perished for the love of chastity.

Wanius, moreover, was king of the Huns, or, if you prefer, Gnauius in the manner of the Gauls; Melga was king of the Picts. The emperor Gratian had hired them for pay and sent them into the borders of Germany and Gaul together, so that they might afflict those who followed the party of Maximus. Around [unclear] regions they encountered [the women] cast there by the wind; and since they were both beautiful and Christian, they solicited them to intercourse with themselves. But when the women, faithful in Christ, refused to consent to the shamefulness of the wicked men, they were miserably slain by the impious.

This lamentable history of the holy seventy-one thousand virgins and women, besides infants and little children, Hunibald does not relate; but the aforesaid author Geoffrey of Monmouth records it at the end of the fourth book, on the origin of the people and the deeds of the kings of the island of Britain, which was first called the Island of Giants; then from Brutus the first king it was called Britain; afterward it was named Albion; and finally, having obtained the name of England, it retains it to this day.

But Marcomirus, the above-mentioned king of the Franks, because he was a prudent man, so governed the reins of his principality that he followed neither the party of Maximus nor that of Gratian, because the former had taken Armorica away from the Franks, after many of them had been cruelly and without reason killed; and they cruelly slew an innumerable multitude of the people. When this had been reported to King Maximus, who at that time was staying at Trier, he sent a certain Gratian, a citizen, with two legions into Britain, to drive the enemies from there. With the Huns and Picts, however, were Scots and Norwegians, all of whom Gratian, after an engagement had been made, put to flight into Ireland.

In these times Maximus, king of the Britons and usurper of the Roman empire, after all Gaul had already been conquered and Caesar Gratian had been killed at Lyon, established the seat of his kingdom in the city of Trier; there he also called a synod of bishops, at which Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, appeared in person and shone forth with many signs and miracles. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, was also present, and Ausonius, bishop of Bordeaux,

COMPENDIVM LIB. I. poribus Hilderici regis memorati Francorum, post Odoacari à Rugijs discessum, Longobardi Rugium inuadunt: quibus co tempore quintus rex nomine Gudeoch principabatur, & in eo regno aliquandiu habitarunt. Hildericus autem rex Francorum, posteaquam plura fortiter gessisset, anno regni sui consumati xxiii. interrupti vero, xxvi. dominica autem nativitatis, cccc. lxxxiii. moritur, indictione Romanorum septima. QUADRAGESIMVS SEPTIMVS. Clodoveus Hilderici regis ex Basina filius, cum esset annorum vnius et viginti etatis, patri succedit, & regnauit annis triginta: quoru quindecim paganus, ficit omnes ante eum reges Francorum, in vanitate consumpsit, & reliquos quindecim in fide Christi renatus fideliter exegit. Erat autem princeps forma egregius, & animi virtute praeclarus, qui mox in principio regni sui filium ducis quondam Romani Aegidij, nomine Siagrium, Suectionis principantem, fugavit, & urbem regno Francorum adiecit. Inde progressus civitatem Remorum (cuius ecclesiae tum praefuit sanctus Remigius praeful doctissimus) cepit, ecclesias tam ibi, quam alibi omnes spoliavit, plurefque incendit, & praedam iuxta legem militibus divisit. Quicquid in tota Gallia fuit iuris Romanorum, Clodoveus breui totum dominio Francorum subiecit: sicut et manet vsque in praesentem diem. Hic duxit vxorem Clotildem, filiam Hilderici regis Burgundionum, quem Gunde baldus rex eius frater peremerat, vxoremque eius matrem scilicet Clotildis, ligato ad coluim eius saxo, praecipitauit in aquam. Erat autem Clotildis Christiana fidelis, qua regem sedulo monebat in dominum Iesum credere, & vanam idolorum culturam abnegare. Quod et si contemneret à principio, exactis tamè in regno annis quindecim, victoria obtenta de Alemannis (vt dicemus suo loco) postea creditit Christo. Anno regni sui nono, Clodoveus rex bellum mouit in Doringiam, propterea quod et tributum olim eis impositum soluere contemnerent, & eius matrem Basinam nò folum de adulterio, sed etiam de furto calumniarentur manifeste. Veniens itaque in regionem Doringorum, omnia ferro deuastauit et igne, regem vicit, & ad solutionem tributorum coegit. Anno regni sui undecimo, rex Clodoveus contra his copijs, aduerlus Alaricum regem Occidentalium Gothorum duxit exercitum, quem decimo lapide ab urbe Pietavorum sibi congregauit, cum pluribus occidit: cuius et thesauros omnes, & civitatem ipsum suo regno adiecit. Anni regni sui quintodecimo, qui fuit dominica nativitatis cccc. xcix, indictione Romanorum septima, cum Alemanni rursus in superbiam erécti, Franci nec subiacere vellent, nec amplius dare tributum, Clodoveus ingentem fuorum conuocauit exercitum, & mouit contra Alemannos fortem expeditionem ad praelium. Initio certamine acriter ancipitique martie diu fuit pugnatum, & plures vtrobique ceciderunt. Postremo divina ordinante providentia pugnantibus fortiter Alemannis, Franci paulatim coepertunt deficere: cumque iam prope videretur, vt fugeret, rex perfusus lachrymis, apud se tacitus oratui, dicens: Domine Iesu Christe, quaem vxor mea filium predicat esse Dei, & omnia posse datur in te fideliter credentibus, si dederis mihi victoriam de his inimicis meis hodie, credam in te, et in nomine tuo baptizari me faciam, & ero nomini tuo fidelis servus atque deo-tus, quam dixi vixero. Cumque sic orans, manibus et oculis in coelum eleuatis, subgemisceret, Christi affuit repente auxilium: quo praesente, in fugam conuertuntur Alemanni, & qui prius vt murus pugnabant immobiles, subito nunc fugiunt, quemadmodum solèr pauentiffima mulieres. Cecidit in eo praelio rex Alemannorum cum multis. Verum cum Franci Alemannos fugientes instantius persequi non cessarent, ad regem Clodoucum illi clamabant: Ne persequaris nos amplius, ô rex victoriosissime, quia tui iam sumus, tibi nos perpetuos servituros nunc dein ceps pollicemur. At ille his morus precibus, interdixit peraecutionem, suceptosque in dedicationem Alemannos, in Galliam reuerfus est. Cumque venisset in palatium, consilio Clotildis reginae vocauit ad se Remigium, ecclesiae Remensis sanctissimum episcopum: à quo plenius de fide Christiana instructus, in consilio publico, audientibus Francorum proceribus cunctis, sefec cum summa reuerentia et humilitate ad sacri baptismatis mysterium preparauit. Qui cum lauandus iam baptisteriù intraret, Sanctus ad eum Remigius praeful sacudifissimus ait, Mitis, depone colla Sicaber. Adora qu'incendisti: Incende qu'adorasti. Ex quo manifestu est, Fraecos aliquando prius dictos fuisse Sicam.

Nec diu postea etiam filius eius Victor, in gratiam fauorem Theodosij, gladio perijt. 10 Post Maximi autem interitum, Marcomirus rex Francorum cõtractis copijs, magnum suorum exercitum transmisit in Galliam sub ducibus Sunnone, Genebaldo, Priamo, & Antenore, quatinus non solum recuperarent amissa, sed omnem quoque Galliam Francis redderent subiectam. Et breui quidem tempore multa recupérantes, quae Maximus abstulerat, etiam Galliae partem non modicam regno Francorum addiderunt. Verunta- men Armoricarum regnum, quod Britones inhabitabant (vt diximus) sub Conano, illa vice obtinere non poterant, quod tamen postea receperunt. Interim vero quod hî duces bello intendunt Gallicano, Romani Francorum regnum, duce Valentiniano Caesare, qui cum Theodosio imperabat, exercitum grandem misertũt in Germaniam, Francos (vt sperabant) penitus deleturi. Contra quos Marcomir rex Fran- 20 corum, cum Germanis atque Saxonibus processit ad bellum, facta congressione ab ho- stibus peremptus cecidit cum multis, alijs fuga labenti bus, anno regni sui xv. Dominiciae vero natiuitatis CCC. XCIII. indictione Romanorum sexta. Valentinianus autem vlte- rius progredi volens, omne regnum Francorum, quod in partibus erat Cifrhenanis, suo cupiens subiugare imperio, propter Longobardorum incursionem, in Italiam retrocede- re compulsus fuit. Sed astu necessitatem occultans retro abeundi, nuncios misit ad eos qui remanserant in regno, francos, per quos mandauit, vt denuo aut bellum eligerent, aut Romanis penderent tributum. At Franci iam rege destituti, roboreque militiae cum ducibus in Gallia consultito, cum Imperatoris necessitatem recessius nescirent, atque ni- hil aliud quam bellum immunere putarent, viribus impares se viderent esse, Romanis 30 promisere tributum, quod tamen nec promittere sine principum consensu voluntate, tunc (sicut diximus) procul absentium potuerunt, nec soluere. His Valentinianus impe- rator cum Francis, vt voluit peractis, in Lombardos profectus est. Interea ducibus Francorum, Dagoberto, Sunnoni, Genebaldo, Priamo, Antenori, & caeteris natu maioribus, qui bella gentis tractabãt in regione Gallorũ, nunciantur omnia, quae Romani, duce Valentiniano, egiissent cum Francis, quomodo regem morti, gẽ- tem addixissent tributo, quae semper fuit libera, nulli ab origine Troiana fuisset subie- cta. Irati sint, commoti sint, turbati sint valde, multiq́ue deliberauere consultationi- bus, quemadmodum hanc prudenter vindicarent iniuriam. Post multam igitur diuturnam eorum consultationem, postremo in vnam conue- 40 nere sententiam, vt magis patriam in libertate conseruare deberent auita quam rebus vr- gere Gallicanis. Annals of Trithemius

[Burdigalensis?], who wrote a metrical work on the praises of his homeland and of the city of Trier, which he entitled Mosella, from the river flowing past. Jerome also, the priest of Bethlehem, at the same time copied out at Trier the book of blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, On the Synods.

Maximus, moving from Trier with a very great army, appointed his infant son Victor king of the Gauls, and deputed Quintinus and Nanneus, princes of the city of Trier, as his guardians. Then he himself set out with the army into Italy and was killed by Theodosius, in the thirteenth year of Marcomir, king of the Franks. Not long afterward his son Victor also perished by the sword, to win the favor and goodwill of Theodosius.

After the death of Maximus, Marcomir king of the Franks assembled forces and sent a great army of his men into Gaul under the leaders Sunno, Genebald, Priam, and Antenor, so that they might not only recover what had been lost but also make all Gaul subject to the Franks. In a short time, recovering many things which Maximus had taken away, they also added no small part of Gaul to the kingdom of the Franks. Yet the kingdom of the Armoricans, which the Britons inhabited, as we have said, under Conan, they could not obtain on that occasion; nevertheless they afterward recovered it.

Meanwhile, while these leaders were intent on the Gallic war, the Romans, under Valentinian Caesar, who ruled with Theodosius, sent a great army into Germany, hoping to destroy the Franks utterly. Marcomir, king of the Franks, advanced against them to battle with Germans and Saxons; when the engagement was fought, he fell, slain by the enemy with many others, while others slipped away in flight, in the fifteenth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 393, the sixth Roman indiction. Valentinian, wishing to advance farther and desiring to subjugate to his rule the whole kingdom of the Franks that was in the Cisrhenane regions, was compelled to withdraw into Italy because of an incursion of the Lombards. But, craftily concealing the necessity of going back, he sent messengers to those Franks who had remained in the kingdom, through whom he commanded that they either choose war anew or pay tribute to the Romans. But the Franks, now deprived of their king, and with the strength of their soldiery [unclear] with the leaders in Gaul, since they did not know the emperor’s necessity for withdrawal and thought nothing other than war was threatening, saw that they were unequal in strength and promised tribute to the Romans. Yet they could neither promise it without the consent and will of the princes, then, as we have said, far absent, nor pay it. When Valentinian the emperor had carried out these matters with the Franks as he wished, he set out against the Lombards.

Meanwhile all the things that the Romans, under Valentinian, had done with the Franks were reported to the leaders of the Franks, Dagobert, Sunno, Genebald, Priam, Antenor, and the other elders who were directing the wars of the people in the region of the Gauls: how they had condemned the king to death and bound to tribute a people which had always been free and had been subject to no one since its Trojan origin. They were angry, they were moved, they were greatly disturbed, and many deliberated in councils as to how they might prudently avenge this injury.

After much and long consultation, therefore, they finally came to one opinion: that they ought rather to preserve their ancestral fatherland in liberty than to press on with Gallic affairs. Therefore, leaving Duke Priam in the Gallic territories with a sufficient [unclear], [unclear] was ruler of the kingdom for almost five years, as Hunibald indicates, a magnanimous and warlike man. In his time Marcomir, son of Clodius, held the duchy among the Eastern Franks for sixteen years. Dagobert took up the government of the kingdom under the name of duke in the year of the Lord’s nativity 393, the sixth indiction.

Dagobert, brother of Marcomir king of the Franks, who was killed by Valentinian, son of the aforesaid king Clogio, after the death of his brother was, by the consent of the Franks, interim king or governor of the kingdom for almost five years, as Hunibald indicates; he too was magnanimous and warlike. In his time Marcomir, son of Clodius, held the duchy among the Eastern Franks for sixteen years. Dagobert took up the government of the kingdom under the name of duke in the year of the Lord’s nativity 393, the sixth indiction.

In the second year of Duke Dagobert, Valentinian Caesar, after sending messengers to the people of the Franks in Germany, demanded the tribute imposed in the preceding year. To him the leaders and people of the kingdom sent back word through the same messengers as follows: The everlasting liberty of the Franks is accustomed to impose tribute on other nations, not to pay it. But you, who fought with an unarmed few when the strength of the Franks was absent, conquered by war, not by courage. If you trust that you have the right to exact tribute from the Franks, come whenever you wish; by the sword we shall show [unclear] that we are, and have always been, utterly free. We make this known to you, so that you do not send anything unarmed to us on this matter, since we contend to give up life rather than lose liberty.

Valentinian demands tribute from the Franks. The Franks neglect tribute.

ANNAL. TRITHERMII. Sicambros, non apud Scythas, sed inter Germanos. Clodoveus itaque primus omnium regum Francorum fidem Christi suscepit, & per Sanctum Remigium baptizatus est anno aetatis suae XXXVI. regni autem, XV. dominica vero nativitatis, CCC. XCIX. indictione Romanorum septima. Eodem die post regem fuerunt baptizati ex principibus aulicis, atque nobilibus Francorum tria millia. Et reliquum populum diebus postea sequentibus vinuerunt. pontifices et sacerdotes domini cum ingenti laetitia baptizabant, gratias omnipotentis Dei miserationibus agentes, qui per suam gratiam, ut pacem daret ecclesia, gentem ferocissimam iugo fidei subiecit. Magna deinceps pro Christi honore facta sunt non solum per Clodoveum, sed multo magis per succelfores eius Francorum reges, ecclesiae costruenda, fundata feruntur Deo plura per Germaniam, Italia, & Gallia coenobia, divinique cultus ministerii cum tempore multipliciter sunt augmentatum. Clodoveus autem rex, et si homo fuerit in subditos pientissimus, in suis tamem conlangueos nimium legitur extitifle crudelis, quippe qui plures nobilissimos de antiqua regum Francorum propagine ortos, reges, duces et principes crudeliter et insidiosi fecit occidi, ut regnum solus haberet. Verum ut paucos ex multis posteritati commendemus, amor nos impellit historiae veritatis. Regnabat eo tempore apud Coloniam Agrippinam homo senex, de regum Francorum semine procreatus, nomine Sigebertus, quem Clodovei pater Hildericus, post acquisitam Coloniam, illi vicarium regni posuerat. Is filium habebat nomine Ludovicum, cui rex Clodoveus in astutia et dolo sic scripsit: Pater tuus iam senex est, & regno inutilis, qui si moreretur, tibi cum amicitia nostra regnum illius proueniret, & non alteri. Iuuenis regni cupiditate seductus, patrem deliberavit occidere. Cum autem rex Sigebertus die quadam nihil mali fulsipactus de Colonia egresseretur, & Rheno transmigso, per Buroniam sylvam venationem ageret cum paucis, claro meridie dormientem in tentorio, immisit super eum percuttoribus, patrem filius, tanquam eius regnum possessorus iuxta Clodovei promissum, fecit occidi. Caede,imo parricidio, nequissime peracto, Ludovicus regi scripsit Clodoveo: Pater meus est mortuus, & ego thesauros eius penes me teneo cum regno. Mitte ergo viros, & quicquid tibi ex thesauro patris meti placerit, bona tibi voluntate transmittam. Cui rex Clodoveus refcripsit: Gratias ago boni voluntati tue, & rogo ut venientibus nostris patefacias cuneta, tu regnum patris cum amicitia nostra solus de cetero iam possessorus. Venientibus autem legaris Clodovei regis, Ludovicus patris thesauros ostendit: qui dum varia conficerent atque diversa, iuuenis ait, In hane pater meus thecam nummos aureos consueuit repnere. Immitte, vnus affantium inquit, manum tuam vsque ad fundum, ut probes si omnia sint aurum. Quod cum fecisset, & esser valde declivius, vnus ille qui iuuerat, eleuata manu securim in eius cerebrum vibravit, & statim in eodem loco mortuus est. His nequiter peractis, rex Clodoveus venit Coloniam, quasi neficius scelerum, & convocato vniverso civitatis populo, dixit: Audite ciues optimi, nefandum quod breui contigit malum, Ludovicus filius parentis mei Sigeberti, patrem suum falsis circumuenit sermonibus: quod ego in sidiarei eius vitae: Cumque ille per Buroniam sylvam fugeret, immisit super eum latrunculis, genitorem suum interfecit. Ipse quoque dum thesauros incubaret, a quo nefici percutitus interigit. Sed in his ego nequiquam sum conscius. Nec enim possim sanguinem parentum meorum effundere, cum sit nefas. Sed quia sic ista contigerunt, do vobis consilium: si videtur acceptum, convertimini ad me, vt sub mea sitis defensione. Atilli manibus et vocibus plaudentes, cum more gentis erectum elypeco, regem super se constituerunt. Et sic regnum Sigeberti cum omnibus thesauris eius in suam acceptit potestatem. Prosternebat enim Deus quotidiae hostes sub manibus ipsius, & augebat regnum illius valde, co quod ambularet recto corde in via mandatorum Dei. Regem etiam Cararicum, & filium eius dolo cepit: quos primo tondens, alterum prebyterum, alterum vero diaconum ordinavit: quorum thesauros cum regno sibi subiiciens, ambobus postea fecit amputari capita. Riuacharium quoque regem apud Cameracũ Francis imperantem, & nimis petulanter luxurioseque viuentẽ, vna cum Richario fratre eius proditorie captos, à bello fugientes propria manuscuri percutiens occidit. Lingomirum etiam fratrem corum apud Coenomanniam regnantem, simili crudelitate fecit occidi. Quibus mortuis, regna eorum cum thesauris sibi usurpavit. Interfectit et alios reges

Anno autem sequente Valentinianus deceptus consilio suorum denuo misit ad Fran- cos Sisinnium comitem aulicum, vt eos bonis induceret persuasionibus ad solutionem tributi, firmissimamque amicitiam Romanorum. Sed Franci non immemores eorum, quae prius Valentiniano remandauerãt, necemque Marcomiri regis sui amantissimi vin- dicare cupientes, missum ad se comitem cum tota societate quam adduxerat, gladio per- emerunt; in contemptum Valentiniani, omnium Romanorum. Post haec Franci maximo suorum in vnum adunato exercitu, sub ducibus Sunnone Genebaldo (quem Galli Gundebaudum nuncuparunt) cum impetu Rheno transmisso in fines Romanorum irrumpentes, omnia depopulantes, etiam Coloniẽsibus metum incusserunt. Omnia enim quae fuerũt inter Rhenum, Mosam, Tabulam, fluīos, suo cõ- tendebāt subiungere dominio. Verum posteaquam excursus Francorum innotuit apud Treuiros, Nannenus Quintinus principes Treuirorūm (qui, sicut Colonieses, Roma- norum partes sequebantur) collecto exercitu impetus in eos facere constituerũt. Nam interea Franci regione Gallorum vastata, multisque illorum peremptis, ad sedes patrias cum exercitus parte spolia transmisserunt vlterius procedentes. Cum Nannenus Quintinus Treuirorūs prędicta eadem exercitu venissent, Fran- ci (vt diximus ) in bono numero iam praeda onusti Rhenum transissent; intentionem habentes reuertendi ad socios, quod reliquum erat Gallis intactum pro viribus desolã- di, secuta est Francos confusio magna propter inconsultam minus cautam partitio- nem exercitus. Erant enim primae Francorum sedes (quod sepe diximus) circa fines o- stia Rheni, vbi nunc est Hollandia, Selandia, populi Traieđesẽs, Gelrenses, Frisij, quo- rum pars nomen postea Westasen/ id est, Galli occidentales, comparatione aliorum, qui Ostualen/ id est, Galles Orientales regione Monasteriensi dicebantur, accepit. Habebat̃- que Franci ab oriente Saxones, Theutones, Germanos, Marcomannos: ad meridiem, Colonienses Gallos: ad occidentem, Tungros Morinos, qui maritima incolebāt; ad aquilonem vero, Scotos, Orechadas, Dacos, simul mare. Nannenus ergo Quintinus, vbi cum exercitu Treuirorūm applicuissent ad loca,in quibus reliquia Francorum remanerant, sociorum reditum expectantes, aeciem instruxe- runt, perfeccuti fugientes vsque ad Carbonariam syluam, retrocedere compulerunt, nõ Paucis eorum trucidatis. Hinc ortum est odium Francorum in Treuiros, propter quod postea Rheno transmisso, in regione Treuirorūs hyemare coeperunt, omnia deua- stare. His autem pręctis, Quintino vtile visum est, si exercitum omnem Treuirorūm tradu- cerent in Franciam, imparatosque subita irruptione praeoccuparent. Sed Nanneno con- silium Quintini non placuit, qui Francos in solo proprio ad resistendum esse non dubita- bat audentiore. Quapropter Nannenus à Quintino recedens cum suis, ad Moguntiam 40 reuertitur. Quintinus autem in suo consistens proposito, circa Musium castellum', Rheno trans- misso, produxit exercitu, Francos primo delere incursu meditarabatur', animo excelso malore, quam viribus ad vincendum. Sed Franci non segnes, Gallos virili excep̃rũt oc- cursu, initoque pręcio, multa Treuirorūs millia interierunt, paucis fuga saluatis. Cecidit in eo congregēsu Heracleus, legionis Romanae tribunus, pene omnes, qui militibus prae- rant, iaculis gladio Francorum cum eo perierunt. Paucis namque exceptis, quibus nox atra salutem, nemora latendi prębuere facultatem, totus Quintini exercitus gladio, ar- cu, palude interijt. Anno dominicae natiuitatis CCC.XCIII.indictione septima, Valentinianus imperator 50 apud Viennam Galliae vrbem dolo, austeritate Arbogasti magistri militum, laquozo in- terijt, Eugenius quidam Romanus, eiusdem Arbogasti machinatione regnum Gallia- rum artipuit, triennio regnauit: postea bello cum Theodosio imperatore commisso, ab eo peremptus est. Franci morte Valentiniani Coesaris audita, Rhenum transire, Galliamque inuadere decreuerũt. Quotum cõsilium Arbogastus intelligens, praeuenit, qui apud Coloniam A- grippinam, rigente hyeme, ac Rheno congelato, traduxit exercitu, Francos Rheno proximos, hostili coepit incursione vastare. Compendium of Book I

When Valentinian received this news, he wondered at the constancy of the Franks, and said to those standing around: “Frank, Frank, you are a hard people, to be named rather from ferocity than from liberty.” And the matter rested in the current year, because at that time the Roman commonwealth was suffering many and varied hostile incursions from different nations.

But in the following year Valentinian, misled by the counsel of his own men, again sent Sisinnius, a count of the court, to the Franks, so that by good persuasions he might induce them to the payment of tribute and to the very firm friendship of the Romans. But the Franks, not forgetful of what they had previously sent back to Valentinian, and desiring to avenge the death of Marcomir, their most beloved king, killed with the sword the count sent to them, together with the whole company that he had brought, in contempt of Valentinian and of all the Romans.

After this the Franks, having united a very great army of their men into one force, under the leaders Sunno and Genebald, whom the Gauls called Gundebaud, crossed the Rhine with violence and, breaking into the territories of the Romans, devastated everything, and even struck fear into the people of Cologne. For they were striving to subject to their own rule all that lay between the rivers Rhine, Meuse, and Tabula. But after the incursion of the Franks became known among the Treveri, Nannenus and Quintinus, leaders of the Treveri, who, like the people of Cologne, followed the Roman side, gathered an army and resolved to make attacks upon them. For meanwhile the Franks, after laying waste the region of the Gauls and killing many of them, sent the spoils on to their ancestral seats with part of the army, while they themselves proceeded farther.

When Nannenus and Quintinus of the Treveri had come with the aforesaid army to that same place, the Franks, as we have said, already laden with plunder in good number, had crossed the Rhine, intending to return to their companions, to lay waste with all their strength whatever remained untouched among the Gauls. Great confusion followed the Franks because of the ill-considered and insufficiently cautious division of the army. For the first seats of the Franks, as we have often said, were around the borders and mouths of the Rhine, where now are Holland, Zealand, the peoples of Utrecht, Gelderland, and the Frisians. Part of these later received the name Westasen, that is, western Gauls, by comparison with the others, who in the region of Münster were called Ostualen, that is, eastern Gauls. And the Franks had to the east the Saxons, Teutons, Germans, and Marcomanni; to the south, the Gauls of Cologne; to the west, the Tungri and Morini, who inhabited the seacoast; but to the north, the Scots, the Orkneys, the Danes, and likewise the sea.

Therefore, when Nannenus and Quintinus had arrived with the army of the Treveri at the places where the remainder of the Franks had stayed, awaiting the return of their companions, they drew up a battle line and pursued them as they fled as far as the Carbonarian Forest, forcing them to retreat, after slaughtering not a few of them. From this arose the hatred of the Franks toward the Treveri, because of which they later crossed the Rhine and began to winter in the region of the Treveri and to devastate everything.

After these things had been done, it seemed useful to Quintinus that they should lead the whole army of the Treveri across into Francia and, by a sudden incursion, seize the Franks while they were unprepared. But Quintinus’s counsel did not please Nannenus, who did not doubt that the Franks would be bolder in resisting on their own soil. Therefore Nannenus withdrew from Quintinus with his men and returned to Mainz.

But Quintinus, persisting in his purpose, crossed the Rhine near the fortress of Musium and led out the army. He was planning to destroy the Franks at the first attack, with a spirit prouder than his strength for victory. But the Franks, not sluggish, met the Gauls with a manly encounter; and when battle had been joined, many thousands of the Treveri perished, with few saved by flight. In that encounter fell Heracleus, tribune of the Roman legion; almost all who were in command of the soldiers perished with him by the missiles and sword of the Franks. For, with a few exceptions, to whom the black night gave safety and the woods afforded the opportunity of hiding, the whole army of Quintinus perished by sword, bow, and marsh.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 393, in the seventh indiction, the emperor Valentinian perished at Vienne, a city of Gaul, by trickery and by the severity of Arbogast, master of the soldiers, by a noose. A certain Roman, Eugenius, by the machination of the same Arbogast, seized the kingdom of the Gauls and reigned for three years; afterward, when war was joined with the emperor Theodosius, he was killed by him.

When the Franks heard of the death of Caesar Valentinian, they resolved to cross the Rhine and invade Gaul. Arbogast, understanding their plan, anticipated it; at Cologne Agrippina, in the harsh winter, when the Rhine was frozen, he led an army across and began to devastate, by hostile incursion, the Franks nearest to the Rhine.

14 COMPENDIVM LIB. I. Alarico, deliberatione cum suis praehabita, Gallias alioqui furore mutarum gentium agitatas, Gothis inhabitandas concessit. Wandali autem, qui remanferant in Gallijs, audientes Gothorum aduentum, quamuis ex vna essent natione Scanziana procreati, nihilominus timore perterriti, Galliam defuerunt; & cum Alanis, Suetijs, Hispaniarum partem occuparunt, vbi annis ferme triginta commorati, postea in Africam nauigauerunt, & Hipponam vrbe m destruxerunt. Alaricus vero, permissione Honorij Caefaris, Galliam petiturus, cum suis Italia digreditur: super quem comes Stilicon, Romani ductor exercitus, in festo Dominice Refurrectionis nihil mali suspicantem non iuslus irruit, eumque ad pugnam inuitum prouocaretur. Et primo quidem impetu victor extitit, in secundo congressu vistus, salutem fuga querere compulsus fuit. Alaricus rex, qui hoc factum Honorij subornatione credidit, mox foedus, quod eum eo fecerat, rupit, itinereque mutato, in Italiam reuertitur, & omnia circa truncauit. Stilico comes ab Hispania interficiatur. Roma capitur; & subieritur ab Alarico rego Gothorum. Alaricus autem rex vrbem Romam cepit, aedificia multa subuerit, & ciues in rebus grauiiter laesit. A sanguine tamen et hominum caede temperauit, & fugientibus ad sanctorum Basilicas pepercit. Die tertia discessit sua sponte à Roma, nauigaturusque in Siciliam, nanguardum pertulit: & non multo post infirmatus grauiter, subito vitam cum morte commutauit. Dum haecagerentur in Italia per Gothis, Franci tempus adesse rati, quo sibi Galliam subiicerent vniuersam, contractis copijs, magnum adunauerunt exercitum, & subduci bus Faramundo, Marcomiro, Sunnone, Priamo, & Antenore, fines Gallicanos ingressi, primo cum Wandalis congregiuntur, qui Gallias denuo incursabant, quorum regem Godgisith (quem nonnulli Godogisilium nuncupant) eum viginti millibus occiderunt. Et nisi Respendial rex Alanorũ, Wandalis ex Hispania, vbi tune regnabat, tempestiue venisset in auxilium, omnes fuissent à Francis occidi. Anno domini cccc.xix.obijt Genebaldus, interrex Francorum, filius Dagoberti, & nepos Marcomiri regis, anno principatus suꝑxxi.post cuius mortem Franci (vt dicemus) denuo reges habuerunt. Eodem nanque anno, statim post obitum Genebaldi, conuenientes in vnum proceres et maiores natu Francorum, consilium habuerunt inter se maturum, vile iudicantes, vt more veterum, sibi regem constituerent ex ducibus vnum.
