On the Origin of the Franks.

Recovering the booty for their own men who had been despoiled, they returned. But the spoils of the enemy, which were many, they divided among their allied friends.

Meanwhile, when the Gauls who were living beyond the Rhine as far as the British Sea, the Morini, Ambiani, Tungri, and their friends who were in those regions, had heard that Diocles had left the kingdom with a great army of his people, they gathered in a great multitude and resolved utterly to destroy the Sicambri, who were on that side between the Meuse and the Rhine. When the leaders of the Sicambri learned this through scouts, they divided the army into three parts, arranging two in separate battle-lines against the enemy, while they placed the third in ambush. As the Gauls approached with only one line, when they saw that the Sicambri had two lines, they were thrown into confusion; but there was no time to arrange the lines otherwise, since the Sicambri at once directed their first line straight against the Gauls. The second line, breaking in from the side, shattered the order of the Gauls. And when the battle was fiercely fought, and the strength of the Gauls was giving way into flight, the Sicambri came upon them from ambush. Enclosed by the Sicambri, the Gauls were slaughtered like cattle, so that out of 88,000 scarcely 10,000 remained. For many were drowned in the river as they fled.

Exulting in this victory, the Sicambri sacrificed to their gods Jupiter and Venus not only animals, but also children and as many of the Gallic enemy as they had led away captive, offering the males to Jupiter and the females to Venus. From that time the Sicambri, enriched by the spoils of their enemies and by the deeds they had accomplished among the neighboring peoples, became feared throughout the surrounding region. Diocles, through all the days of his reign, had war with the Gauls, and there was scarcely a year in which he did not at least once move his army against them.

He died in the thirty-ninth year of his reign, 297 years before the birth of Christ. He left four sons, whose names were these: Helenus, Priamus, Nicanor, and Basanus, who themselves also left many sons after them.

Helenus, the eldest son of Diocles, reigned after his father for fourteen years, a wanton and idle man, in whose time the Gauls, often making raids, inflicted many losses on the Sicambri. Against them his brothers, with the princes of the kingdom, frequently led the army and fought with varying fortune, sometimes defeated and sometimes also victorious. But the king remained at home, idle and given over to lust.

In the thirteenth year of his reign, the Sicambri, assembled at Neopagus, by the common judgment of all deposed Helenus, an idle and useless king, from the kingdom and compelled him to return to private life, in the year 283 before the birth of Christ our Savior. In his place they elected his younger brother.

Basanus, the younger son of the late Diocles, after his brother Helenus had been deprived of rule, was appointed king by the common will and election of the Sicambri, and reigned for [unclear] years: a man wise in his generation, high-minded, warlike, and not inferior to his father in fortune. The Sicambri made him both king and pontiff of the sacred rites. Because of his wisdom and his wonderfully performed deeds they commonly called him great Basan, in the vernacular die groten Basan. For the Sicambri held him in such reverence and honor that they venerated him no differently than a true god. Under penalty of certain death, no one was permitted to contradict his command, even in the least matter. Wherever he went, he ordered a rope or cord to be carried before him, and a sword as a sign of justice, which he observed so firmly that he spared neither son nor brother, neither princes nor dukes, indeed no one, who had committed even a small offense against the law. By law he marked robbery, theft, adultery, deceit, fraud, and every injury or insult among the Sicambri as subject to the penalty of death, and he punished without any mercy all who offended even a little in these matters against the legal sanctions.

He had a young son named Sedanus. This man, led astray by youthful desire, had committed with the wife of a certain man of humble condition what he knew to be forbidden by law, and [unclear]. His father the king, learning of this matter, ordered him to be arrested and beheaded with a sword. Because of this, the mother of the young man and the king’s wife, who was the daughter of the king of the Orcades, was moved by very bitter sorrow, and, driven by womanly lack of restraint, cried out against the king: “O cruel tyrant, not king, you who practice cruelty under the title of law, how will you spare others, when you have slain your own son?” To her the king said before all the people: “Woman, it is yours to obey your husband, not to reproach the king. I swear to you by my god, Saturnian Jupiter, that if I were not moved by anger, I would kill you this very hour, you who have always been most dear to me.”

After eight days the king, by the judgment of the princes and nobles of the kingdom, repudiated the woman, although she was very beautiful and uniquely beloved by him above all the rest, and sent her back to her father, the king of the Orcades. From that time the Sicambri began to fear Basanus their king so greatly that no one among [unclear].

The Gauls, in the absence of their king, attempt to lay waste the Sicambri.

The Sicambri sacrificed to Jupiter and Venus.

Helenus reigned after his father for 14 years.

King Helenus is deposed.

Basanus, a great king and pontiff, reigns for 36 years.

The king, out of love for the law, beheads his own adulterous son.

King Basan repudiates his wife, who is angry over the killing of her son.

DE ORIGINE FRANCORVM. ti negotio, bonis verbis protractos apud se diutius retinuit, & prudenter cauens ne ru- mori eorum quae ipse mente conceperat, in illorum noticiam deueniret; iussit suis vt eos in omnibus copiose prouiderent, latos cum illis peragerent dies. Interim Clodomēr missis occulte ad reges Thoringiae, Saxoniae nuntiis, eos vocauit in auxilium, cum fuis ad unato magno pugnatorum exercitu bellum in Gallos mente conceptit. Or- dinatis rebus nuntios honorifice dimisit, ne in via quicquam de praemissis exerciti- bus ad notitiam eorum venire posset de suis, comites illis quasi pro conductu tuti itineris vsque in Galliam cum literis adiunxit. Tenor literarum haec continebat: Clodomer Rex Magnus. Miramur de vobis Galli, 10 quod terram à nobis queritis recipere, quam progenitores nostrri olim à vestris ire belli, sicut ab iniimi- cis suis, à quibus multas acceperant iniurias; iusta vietistudine obtinuerunt. Cogitate vires vestras nostris impares, cessate ab hac temeritate vestra. Quod sciōtra vos venire vultis, statuitius vobis nó- fracti animis occurrere, defensare gladio, quod gladio maiores nostri acquisinerunt. His Galli re- cognitis magnum contraxerunt exercitum, vt ponte super Mosa flumen fabricato exer- citum contra Sicambros traduxerunt, custodiam relinquentes circa pontem ne abad- uersarijs occuparetur. Diffimulauit haec omnia rex Clodomerus quasi nesciret, ordinatisque militibus, exercitum in quatuor partes diuisit, habens in vna qualibet plusquam triginta sex millia pugnatorum. Duas partes in totidem acies ordinauit. Tertiam locauit in infidijs. Quar- 20 tam dimisit à latere per grym vt pontem occisis eustodibus praeoccuparent. Venientes agitut Galli habentes ipsi acies duas; cum Sicambris habuere congressum, non longe à Mosae flumine prope castellum Delon. At vero Sicambi fugientibus similes paulatim retrocesserunt; donec Gallos longius à flumine protraxerunt vsque ad locum insidiarum. Ibi sane bellum atroxcom missum est. Steterunt enim fortiter Sicambri cum Gallis dimi- cantes. Interim quartus Clodomeri exercitus circumgyrando pontem occupauit, cuius rei accepto signo, hi qui latebant de insidijs protumpunt, Gallos inuadunt atrociter cō- pugnantes. Postremo Galli fugam ineuntes cum pontem nescirent praeoccupatum à Si- cambris retrocedere festinaretur. Cū ecce subito se vident in medio hostiũ esse conclusos, cessi sunt pene omnes miserabiliter trucidati paucis equorū velocitate ad nemora lapsis. 30 Reliqua fortiter à Clodomiro rege facta Hunibald satis diffuse conscripsit. Moritur autem Rex Clodomer anno regni sui xviii. Ante Christi natiuitatem anno ccxxiiij, fi- lios relinquens tres, Nicanorem, Helianum Helenum. Nicanor primogenitus regis Clodomiri succedens patri, regnavit annis xxvi. Eius tēpore iterum Gothi Sclavi fines Saxonū inuaferunt, cōtra quos rogatus à rege Saxonicè processit ad bellū, rediit victor multis ditatus spolijs. Cū rege Archadum praeliū gessit in fauorē regis Britannię soceri sui, cuius filiā habuit vxorē nomine Constantiā, de qua suce- pit quinque filios, Marcomerū, Anthenorē, Priamū, Helenū Clodiū. Primogenitus patri successit in regno, Secūdus maritima rexit, Tertius obijt in Anglia, Quartꝰ ducatū gessit in Germania Cisrhenaņa, intér̄ Saxoniā, Rhenū Moguntiacū. Quintꝰ dux fuit inter Mosā 40 Rhenū fluuios. Nicanor Rex obiit anno regni sui xxvi. Ante Christi natiuitatē cxcvj. Marcomer filius Nicanoris maior natu patri succedens regnavit annis xviii. prin- ceps singularis prudentiae ac modestiae, in subditos pius in hostes seuerus. Hic enim à facerdotibus facatorum Iouis in omni sapientia veterum excellenter edoctus in vatici- nijs, praeditionibus, in somniijs, augurijs, similem apud Germanos non habuit. Ma- iorum suorū fortia gesta corā se in templo in palatio frequenter fecit recitari, in car- minibus patrijs decantari. Multa praelia gessit, victor cum Romanis, Gallis, Gotthis, di- uersis gentibus, quorum seriem Hunibald historiographus Francorum diligenter con- scripsit. Moritur anno regni sui xxiij. ante Christi natiuitatem clviii. Clodius primogenitus regis Marcomeri filius patri succedens regnatit annis xi. 50 Huius tempore Galli cum auxilio Romanorum excursum facientes vltra Mosam Sicam- bros valde contrinerunt. Anno regni sui vltimo contracto tam suorum quam Saxonum exercitu maximo iterum pugnavit cū Gallis, à quibus non satis caute se habens in agmine fuit occisus. Sicambri autem nō obstante Regis morte bellum profequuntur Gallos vi- cerunt. Occisus fuit Clodius rex anno ante Christi natiuitatē clvi. regni vero sui xi. Anthenor filius Clodij maior natu post patrē regnauit annis xvj. Hic inducias fecit cū Gallis ad decē annos placuit Romanis. Erat autem Anthenor rex plus amator pacis q̄ belli. Patris necē libenter vindicasset, fed illo tēpore nō potuit. Iste rex prohibuit filios ho- sium dijs immolari. Moritur anno ante Christi natiutatē cxxi. Regni vero sui anno xvj. On the Origin of the Franks.

... in the matter, having drawn them out with fair words, he kept them with him for a rather long time; and, prudently taking care that no rumor of the things he had conceived in his mind should come to their knowledge, he ordered his men to provide for them abundantly in all things and to spend pleasant days with them. Meanwhile Clodomer, secretly sending messengers to the kings of Thuringia and Saxony, called them to his aid; with his own men, once a great army of fighters had been assembled, he conceived war in his mind against the Gauls. When matters had been arranged, he honorably dismissed the messengers; and lest anything concerning the armies already sent ahead could come to their knowledge on the road, he added companions from among his own men, as if for the conduct of a safe journey as far as Gaul, with letters.

The tenor of the letters contained this: “Clodomer the Great King. We marvel at you, Gauls, that you seek to receive from us the land which our forefathers once obtained from yours by the law of war, as from their enemies, from whom they had received many wrongs, by just vicissitude. Consider that your strength is unequal to ours; cease from this rashness of yours. Since I know that you wish to come against us, we have resolved to meet you with spirits unbroken, and to defend with the sword what our ancestors acquired with the sword.” When the Gauls learned these things, they assembled a great army and, after a bridge had been built over the river Meuse, led the army across against the Sicambri, leaving a guard around the bridge lest it be occupied by their adversaries.

King Clodomer dissembled all these things as though he did not know them; and, having drawn up his soldiers, he divided the army into four parts, having in each one more than thirty-six thousand fighters. He arranged two parts into as many battle-lines. The third he placed in ambush. The fourth he sent around from the flank so that, after killing the guards, they might seize the bridge first. Therefore the Gauls came, themselves having two battle-lines; they engaged with the Sicambri not far from the river Meuse, near the fortress of Delon. But the Sicambri, like men in flight, gradually withdrew, until they had drawn the Gauls farther from the river, as far as the place of the ambush. There indeed a fierce battle was joined. For the Sicambri stood firm, fighting bravely with the Gauls. Meanwhile Clodomer’s fourth army, wheeling around, occupied the bridge. When the signal of this event had been received, those who were lying hidden burst out from the ambush and attack the Gauls, fighting fiercely. At last the Gauls took flight; since they did not know that the bridge had been occupied beforehand by the Sicambri, they hastened to retreat. And behold, suddenly they saw that they were shut in among the enemy, and almost all were miserably cut down and slaughtered, a few escaping to the woods by the speed of their horses. Hunibald wrote at sufficient length the rest of the brave deeds done by King Clodomer. King Clodomer died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the year 224 before the birth of Christ, leaving three sons: Nicanor, Helianus, and Helenus.

Nicanor, the firstborn of King Clodomer, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-six years. In his time the Goths and Slavs again invaded the borders of the Saxons; against them, when asked by the king of Saxony, he went forth to war and returned victorious, enriched with many spoils. He waged battle with the king of the Arcadians in favor of the king of Britain, his father-in-law, whose daughter, named Constantia, he had as wife. By her he had five sons: Marcomer, Anthenor, Priam, Helenus, and Clodius. The firstborn succeeded his father in the kingdom. The second ruled the maritime regions. The third died in England. The fourth held the duchy in Germany on this side of the Rhine, between Saxony, the Rhine, and Mainz. The fifth was duke between the rivers Meuse and Rhine. King Nicanor died in the twenty-sixth year of his reign, in the year 196 before the birth of Christ.

Marcomer, the elder son of Nicanor, succeeding his father, reigned eighteen years: a prince of singular prudence and moderation, dutiful toward his subjects, severe toward enemies. For he, excellently taught by the priests of the sacrifices of Jove in all the wisdom of the ancients, in prophecies, predictions, dreams, and auguries, had no equal among the Germans. He frequently had the brave deeds of his ancestors recited before him in the temple in the palace and sung in his native songs. He waged many battles, victorious against the Romans, Gauls, Goths, and various peoples; Hunibald, the historiographer of the Franks, diligently wrote their sequence. He died in the twenty-third year of his reign, in the year 158 before the birth of Christ.

Clodius, the firstborn son of King Marcomer, succeeding his father, reigned eleven years. In his time the Gauls, with the aid of the Romans, making an incursion beyond the Meuse, greatly crushed the Sicambri. In the last year of his reign, after assembling a very great army both of his own men and of Saxons, he again fought with the Gauls, by whom, since he did not keep himself sufficiently cautiously in the column, he was killed. The Sicambri, however, notwithstanding the king’s death, pursued the war and defeated the Gauls. King Clodius was killed in the year 156 before the birth of Christ, and in the eleventh year of his reign.

Anthenor, the elder son of Clodius, reigned after his father for sixteen years. He made a truce with the Gauls for ten years; it pleased the Romans. King Anthenor was more a lover of peace than of war. He would gladly have avenged his father’s murder, but at that time he could not. This king forbade the sons of enemies to be sacrificed to the gods. He died in the year 121 before the birth of Christ, and in the sixteenth year of his reign.

Anthenor the Sicambrian reigned sixteen years.

68 IOANNES TRITHEMIVS Clodomerus rex regnauit anno 20. Clodomerus filius Anthenoris post patrem regnauit annis xx. Anno eius primo Romani Numantinos per Scipionem subuerterunt, & in suam potestatem compuletunt. Anno eius sexto Galli finitis inducijs quas cum patre eius rege Anthenore fecerunt ante decem annos, exercitu magno collecto Mosam transeunt, quibus Clodomero occurrente, bellum grauissimum commissum est, & multi ab vtraque parte ceciderunt, Galli autē qui remanierant retrocesserunt, & quam diu rex Clodomerus vixit, amplius Mosam non transierunt. Moritur autem rex Clodomerus anno antenatiuitatem Domini cxxi. Regni autem accepti Sicambrorum anno x x. Merodactus rex regnauit anno .xx. Merodach primogenitus filius Clodomeri postpatrē regnauit annis XXVIII. prineceps strenuus, audacissimus, & nimium bellicosus, qui multa bella contra Romanos, Gallos, Moguntinos, Treurenfes, & Colonienfes gessit. Nam auxiliarijs Saxonibus atque Germanis exercitum ccxx. milliū pugnatorū cōtra Romanos produxit in Italiā, & deuaftans regionem, cum copijs ad Rauennam vsque peruenit, ditatusque spoliis multis, victor ad propria remeauit. Multas tamen in reditu Romanorum Colonias grauiter afflixit, & magna cis damna intulit. Vnde postmultas tam victorias quam praelia, Romani tandem coniunctis sibi Gallis contra eum prooesserunt ad bellum in finibus Sicambrorum, inter Mosam et Rheum. Et ne Saxones more suo Sicambris fierent auxilio, Romani prius subduxerunt Sclauos et Gothos, qui fines Saxoniae orientalis incursarent. Rex ergo Merodacus Cimbrorum regem aquilonarem cum centum millibus pugnatorum et exinsula- nis habuit adjutorem. De suis vero ducenta habuit millia. Anno itaque regni sui XXII. Marius Romanorum princeps, legiones Romanas cum Gallis duce Theodomeno vltra Mosam destinauit contra Sicambros, & simul acriter punauerunt, & multa millia ex vtraque parte ceciderunt mortui et fugerunt Sicambri. Nā ex eorum parte occisi sunt xx. millia et plures capti. Posthac Merodachus instaurato exercitu Gallos iterum et iuvasit et superauit. Moritur ante Christi nativitatē anno XCIII. Regni sui anno XXVIII. Cassander patri succedens in regno annis x XI. regnauit, cuius tempore Galli auxiliaryario Romanorum milite fines Sicambrorum Mosano flumine traiecto saepius infesta-runt, quibus fortiter contra pugnauit Borbista Gothorum rex cum maxima pugnatorū cum rege Saxonum venit, bellum atrox committitur. Borbista rex Gothorum fugit multis fuortum amissis. Iterum postea Pugnatus regionem deuaftauit, spoliauit Saxones vsque ad Vistulam fluuium, & retrofugit. Contra Gallos faepe pugnauit, faepe victor, nec minus aliquando spretus fortuna. Moritur anno antenatiuitatem Christi LXXII. Regni sui anno XXI. Antharius filius Gassandri regis primogenitus regnauit anni XXXV. De quo scribit Hunibaldus quod Moguntinos Romanorum colonos miserabili clade attriuit. Cum innumerabilis exercitu Galliam intrauit, vicos incendit, praedam et spolia infinita reportauit. Verum cum senuiffet anno regni sui ultimo, irrumpentibus iterum in Batauiam Gal- lis cum exercitu occurrat et cum viginti millibus fiurum occiditur. Galli magnam contra Sicambros stragem fecerunt. Occifus est anno ante Christi nativitate MXXXVIII. Anno regnantis XXXV. Francꝭ Antharij regis maior natu filius patri succedens regnauit XXVI. annis, àquo Sicambri deinceps nomen Francorum assecuti vsque in praefentem retinent diem. Fuit enim homo ferox, bellicosus, & gentis firme defensor acerrimus: multageffit cum ex- teris nationibus bella, semper victor, & gloriosus triumphantor. Cuius anno tertio iterum Gothi cum Scandianis populis Saxoniae fines depopulati sunt, & per decem annos ibide confederunt. Sed cum successiue semper plus et magis irrumperent in Saxoniam, compulfis metu eorum Saxones Francum regem Sicambrorum cum Thoringis in auxilium vocauerunt, & in multitudine ccxxx. milliū pugnatorũ contra Gothis prooesserunt in bellum, Sicambri autem ceteris audacius, dimicantes et quasinumen quoddam interpel-lantes frequenter regis sui inter pugnandum nomen inclamabant vociferantes: Hie Franck/ hie Franck. Abeo tempore gens illa nomen mutauit, & paulatim non folum apud se, sed etiam ab alijs nationibus Franci sunt dicti quam Sicambi, quoque tandem in toto nomen illud obtinuit, Franci dicerentur et non amplius vel raro Sicambri, vt Salagastald teftatur. Nam et gens ipsa nominis nouitate vsque adeo delectabatur, vt regem postulerent, & principes qđ thesueretuo sancirent edicto, se non amplius Sicambros vocari, sed Francos. Johannes Trithemius

King Clodomer reigned 20 years. Clodomer, son of Anthenor, reigned after his father for twenty years. In his first year the Romans overthrew the Numantines through Scipio and brought them under their power. In his sixth year the Gauls, after the truce which they had made with his father, King Anthenor, ten years before had ended, gathered a great army and crossed the Meuse. Clodomer met them, and a very severe battle was joined, and many fell on both sides. But the Gauls who remained withdrew, and as long as King Clodomer lived they crossed the Meuse no more. King Clodomer died in the 121st year before the birth of the Lord, and in the twentieth year after receiving the kingdom of the Sicambri.

King Merodactus reigned twenty-eight years. Merodach, the first-born son of Clodomer, reigned after his father for twenty-eight years, a vigorous, very bold, and exceedingly warlike prince, who waged many wars against the Romans, the Gauls, the Mainz people, the Trier people, and the Cologne people. For, with Saxons and Germans as auxiliaries, he led an army of 220,000 fighters against the Romans into Italy; and, devastating the region, he reached as far as Ravenna with his forces, and, enriched with much spoil, returned victorious to his own lands. Yet on his return he grievously afflicted many colonies of the Romans and inflicted great losses upon them. Hence, after many victories as well as battles, the Romans at last, joining the Gauls to themselves, advanced to war against him in the borders of the Sicambri, between the Meuse and the Rhine. And lest the Saxons, according to their custom, should come to the aid of the Sicambri, the Romans first drew away the Slavs and Goths, who were to make incursions into the borders of eastern Saxony. King Merodach therefore had as his helper the northern king of the Cimbri with one hundred thousand fighters and islanders. Of his own men, however, he had two hundred thousand.

And so in the twenty-second year of his reign Marius, prince of the Romans, sent the Roman legions together with the Gauls, under the leadership of Theodomenus, beyond the Meuse against the Sicambri, and at the same time they fought fiercely; and many thousands on both sides fell dead, and the Sicambri fled. For on their side twenty thousand were killed and more were captured.

After this Merodach, renewing his army, again both invaded and overcame the Gauls. He died in the ninety-third year before the birth of Christ, in the twenty-eighth year of his reign.

Cassander, succeeding his father in the kingdom, reigned for twenty-one years. In his time the Gauls, with auxiliary Roman soldiery, crossed the river Meuse and often harried the borders of the Sicambri. Borbista, king of the Goths, fought bravely against them, and came with a very great number of fighters together with the king of the Saxons; a fierce battle was joined. Borbista, king of the Goths, fled, having lost many of his own. Afterwards [Pugnatus?] again devastated the region, plundered the Saxons as far as the river Vistula, and fled back. He often fought against the Gauls, often victorious, and no less at times scorned by fortune. He died in the seventy-second year before the birth of Christ, in the twenty-first year of his reign.

Antharius, the first-born son of King Cassander, reigned thirty-five years. Of him Hunibald writes that he crushed the Mainz people, Roman colonists, with a pitiable slaughter. With an innumerable army he entered Gaul, burned villages, and carried back endless booty and spoils. But when he had grown old, in the last year of his reign, the Gauls again burst into Batavia; he met them with an army and was killed with twenty thousand of his men. The Gauls made a great slaughter against the Sicambri. He was killed in the thirty-eighth year before the birth of Christ, in the thirty-fifth year of his reign.

Francus, the elder son of King Antharius, succeeding his father, reigned twenty-six years. From him the Sicambri thereafter obtained the name of Franks, which they retain down to the present day. For he was a fierce man, warlike, and the most keen defender of his people; he waged many wars with foreign nations, always victorious, and a glorious triumphator. In his third year the Goths again, together with the Scandinavian peoples, laid waste the borders of Saxony and settled there for ten years. But when, successively, they were always bursting into Saxony more and more, the Saxons, compelled by fear of them, called Francus, king of the Sicambri, together with the Thuringians, to their aid; and with a multitude of 230,000 fighters they advanced to war against the Goths. The Sicambri, however, fighting more boldly than the rest and frequently invoking the name of their king in battle as if it were some divine power, cried out, shouting: “Here, Frank! Here, Frank!” From that time that people changed its name, and little by little not only among themselves but also by other nations they were called Franks rather than Sicambri, until at last that name prevailed everywhere, so that they were called Franks and no longer, or only rarely, Sicambri, as Salagastald testifies. For the people itself took such delight in the novelty of the name that they asked the king and princes to sanction by perpetual edict that they should no longer be called Sicambri, but Franks. This request pleased the king, as one who desired the immortality of his name--

On the Origin of the Franks

…to attain immortality, and for the nation to be distinguished by his own name. He decreed that henceforth they should no longer be called Sicambri, but Franks, that is, noble, free, or warlike, and to be feared by the other nations. Yet the name Sicambrian was brought into oblivion not suddenly, but over much time and by degrees, as is found among the writers of those times, who sometimes called them Sicambri, sometimes Franks.

Remigius also, bishop of Rheims, when he was about to baptize Clovis, king of the Franks, who was the first of the Frankish kings to become Christian, after the Alemanni had been overcome, in the presence of a multitude of nobles, said to him as he laid aside the royal ornaments and humbled himself at the font, with all of us hearing, in another intelligible voice: “Meekly bow your neck, Sicamber; adore what you burned; burn what you adored,” that is, adore Christ, whose churches you burned as a pagan; burn the idols which you then adored.

This King Francus, after the Goths had been driven from the borders of the Saxons, on his return with his army met a messenger saying that the Gauls had crossed the Meuse, had laid waste the region, and had withdrawn with a great booty of spoils. Immediately King Francus, having accepted eighty thousand Saxons as auxiliaries, joined with his own an army of [unclear] thousand fighters, crossed the Rhine, and came as far as the Meuse. Seeing the desolation of the region which the Gauls had made, he was moved in spirit and swore, saying: “See, my fellow-soldiers, what these treaty-breaking Gauls have done. I swear by the head of my father Antharius that I will give no rest to my head until I have avenged myself on them.” And all praised his purpose.

Thus, when the Meuse had been crossed, he stationed forty thousand to guard the bridge; with the rest of the army he advanced into Gaul and made such slaughter as none of the Sicambri before him either could or dared to imagine. For, advancing as far as the river Tabul toward the sea, from the north he consumed the Tarubani, the Tongri, the Legii, and whatever lies between or beside them, with fire and sword so cruelly that he spared neither infants nor women. He routed the Gauls who engaged him with such fierceness that he seemed to be some divine power, not a man. Hence all the nations round about, greatly terrified, called them Franks, that is, fierce men. More than two hundred thousand Gauls fell by the sword of the Franks, with men, women, boys, and infants.

Moved by this, the Senate and People of Rome sent legions of soldiers against the Germans, with Marcus Lollius as commander; for they could not safely attack the Franks unless they had first overcome the Saxons. At first the Romans were victorious and killed eighteen thousand Germans. But when King Francus heard of the slaughter the Romans had made, he sent his son Chlogio as commander, with a great army of fighters, against the Romans; after many of them had been killed, they compelled the rest to flee, in the twenty-fourth year of King Francus.

Francus, king of the Franks, after many deeds bravely done, died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, but in the ninth year before the birth of Christ. His wars, customs, institutions, and laws were written by Clodomer, the supreme pontiff, in verse, and by Hunibald in prose.

Chlogio, the elder son of King Francus, succeeded his father and reigned thirty years: a most cunning man, an augur, seer, and wondrous magician. His mother Lothildis, daughter of the king of the Thuringians, was high priestess of the temple of Pallas; by her arts she drove mad all the enemies whom she wished against her son and the Franks. Clodomer, counsellor of the Franks, writes great things about these matters in Hunibald, things which exceed belief.

In the tenth year of his reign, King Chlogio, at the insistence of his mother, appointed his second-born son, named Phrisus, prince and duke of that region which afterward from his name has been called Phrisia down to the present day, against the incursions of the Cimbri and the Orchades. After ten years, with King Chlogio and all the Franks permitting, Phrisus was raised to kingship, yet on this condition, that he should pay tribute to the Franks each year: three hundred sixty oxen, twenty talents of pure butter, and three thousand royal cheeses. And thus Phrisia became a most powerful kingdom.

In the tenth year of the aforesaid Chlogio, king of the Franks, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was born in Bethlehem, a city of the tribe of Judah among the Jews in the province of Palestine. Before this, in the fourth year of Chlogio, the Romans laid waste Germany in hostile fashion, sometimes defeated and sometimes also victorious. Concerning the other deeds of Chlogio, his wars, prophecies, oracles, truces, and actions done with the Romans, see Hunibald. He died in the year of the Lord 20, but in the thirtieth year of his reign, after many deeds magnificently performed.

Herimer, the second-born son of King Chlogio, reigned after his father for twelve years, a man exceedingly warlike and bold. In the third year of his reign the Gauls, leading an army as far as the Meuse, in an unexpected hostile incursion [unclear] everything which seemed to belong to the Franks, or to consent to them [unclear].

Johannes Trithemius

They laid waste [unclear], and, after gathering booty, withdrew. When this became known to Herimer, he summoned to himself the leaders beyond the Meuse, deposed them, and, after fining [unclear] with the goods of the Franks, reduced them to private life. For he had prescribed this: a man placed in authority under the king of the Franks [unclear]. For he had prescribed this: a man established in authority under the king of the Franks [unclear] is reduced to private life. For this was the chief provision: if through [his?] negligence enemies invade and injure the land of our people, he shall pay half of his honors into the common purse of the king, and shall no longer be prince. If he willingly permitted this, he shall be punished with death, and his wives, with his children and goods, shall belong to the king.

After this he himself crossed the Meuse, fought many wars with the Gauls, and withdrew and fled, sometimes victorious and sometimes also defeated. At last, however, when the Romans were bringing aid to the Gauls in the war, he was killed in the twelfth year of his reign, and in the thirty-second year of the Lord’s nativity, while Christ himself was preaching salvation to the human race in Judea.

Marcomerus reigned eighteen years.

Marcomerus, brother of Herimer, succeeding to the kingdom of the Franks, reigned eighteen years. In his second year Jesus, the Son of God, suffered and died in Judea according to the flesh, and, rising from death on the third day, lives forever. In his fourteenth year Claudius Caesar of the Romans made Britain and the Orkney islands tributary to the Romans. By crossing between the Meuse and the Rhine he grievously afflicted the Franks, and with the aid of the Gauls forced them to retreat as far as the islands of the Rhine. King Marcomerus died in the fiftieth year of the Lord, and the eighteenth of his reign.

Clodomarus reigned twelve years.

Clodomerus, son of Marcomerus, succeeding his father in the kingdom, reigned twelve years. Crossing the Rhine with the army of his own people and of the Saxons, he compelled the Gauls to retreat beyond the Meuse, and recovered everything that had been lost. With the aid of the Germans he waged war against the Romans not far from Mainz and laid waste the fields of the Treveri. He died in the twelfth year of his reign, and in the sixty-second year of Christ.

Anthenor reigned six years.

Anthenor, son of Clodomarus, succeeding his father, reigned six years. Throughout all the time he reigned he waged war with the Gauls, and for this cause he died miserably. For in the last year of his reign he led an army over the river Meuse after a bridge had been built, and, laden with much plunder, returned without waiting for the Gauls. When part of the army of the Franks had crossed the river and the king with others was remaining last on the bank, suddenly the bridge, overloaded by the multitude of horsemen, broke and fell, and many were killed. The king, stunned and dismayed in spirit, was taking counsel with those who had remained with him about recovering the bridge, when it was announced to him that the Gauls were present with a great army and ready to fight. But since they were few, it did not seem safe to him to await the presence of the Gauls; and yet he could not flee otherwise than through the river. Therefore, throwing away his arms and whatever could weigh him down, keeping his belt over his tunic and his sword, he mounted his horse and tried to cross the river. The other foot-soldiers did likewise, having nowhere to flee, and entrusted themselves to the waters. Some of these reached the bank by swimming; the rest were submerged by the force of the waves, among them King Anthenor. With him perished nine most noble dukes of the Franks, all born of royal stock, namely: Duke Priamus, Duke Clodius, Duke Richimer, Duke Anthenor, Duke Marcomet, Duke Walther, Duke Clogio, Duke Herimer, and Duke [Luthvicie?], with sixty-three other nobles. And so Anthenor perished in the sixth year of his reign, the sixty-eighth year of the Lord’s nativity.

Ratherius, after the death of his father, reigned twenty-one years. In his second year Nero Caesar of the Romans began the first persecution against the Christians, in the fourteenth year of his rule, and committed other dreadful crimes. King Ratherius, however, was in conflict with the Gauls and Romans on all the days of his reign, and fought several battles with them. He died in the twenty-first year of his reign, in the eighty-ninth year of the Lord’s nativity.

Richimer, succeeding his father, reigned thirty-three years. He waged war with the Goths and came out victorious. For in the eleventh year of his reign the Goths were again laying waste the territories of the Saxons and Germans by a hostile incursion. Therefore Windekind, king of the Saxons, Richimerus, king of the Franks, and Hermanfrid, king of the Thuringians, engaging the Goths with a very great army of their peoples, killed twenty thousand of them and put the rest to flight. There is a town beside the river Oder named Franckenfurt, which the Franks are said to have founded at that time, after obtaining victory over the Goths. There King Richimerus appointed his second-born son duke, and left with him a great part of the army. The king [unclear] the wives, children, and all their household goods back into [Cisthenan?] Francia to them.

The name of the duke, the king’s son, was Suimo. His son Clodomer succeeded him in the dukedom, and the successor and son of that man was Suimo the Second, who in the year of the Lord 146 founded a city at the outlet of the river Spre-[Sui?], not far from the Germanic Sea, and from his own name called it Suimonia. They remained in that land for a long time, retaining the name of Franks, until at last they were called Marcomeri from a certain duke Marcomerus, whose son Brand built the city of Brandenburg.

On the Origin of the Franks

In the fifth year of King Richimer, Domitian Caesar of the Romans, the younger brother of Titus, after Nero stirred up the second persecution against the Christians; he also, first of all the Caesars, in his sixth year, ordered himself to be called Lord and God.

King Richimer, in the eleventh year of his reign, waged war with the Roman Gauls not far from the city of Basana, which is now called Aachen. At the same time the legions of Roman soldiers at Cologne, after a war with the Franks had been engaged not very successfully, on receiving news of the death of Caesar Cocceius Nerva, made Ulpius Trajanus Crinitus, a Spaniard by nation, emperor. He stirred up the third persecution against the Christians. Later, having been instructed, he ordered that Christians should not be sought out, but that only those who presented themselves voluntarily ought to be killed. Afterwards, however, changed again, he raised a fourth persecution against them. Richimer, king of the Franks, died in the year of the Lord 113, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign.

Odemar, the first-born son of Richimer, king of the Franks, reigned after his father for thirteen years, a prince very beloved by the people of the Franks. He abstained from wars as far as could be done. He made truces, that is, truces or assurances, with the Gauls and Romans, and showed himself so much a friend of both that all lamented his death. Therefore, having peace with everyone, he devoted all his zeal to the dignity and adornment of the nation, renewing laws and establishing new cities and fortifications. Among many cities he founded one in his own name, in the land that was called Tuendia, which lies between the Saxons and the Franks, bordering near the little river Vecht; he ordered it to be called Odemarshesin, in the fourth year of his reign, and in the 117th year of the Lord’s nativity. King Odemar died in the fourteenth year of his reign, and in the year of the Lord 128.

Marcomer, son of Odemar, reigned after his father for twenty-one years. He had as wife the daughter of the king of Britain, named Athildis, by whom he begot seven sons, whose names are these: Clodomer, who succeeded his father in the kingdom; Marcomer, who was duke among the Nitriones and founded a city of his own name, called Marcoburg; Clogio, who perished in Britain; Franc, who was duke among the Hogian peoples from Coblenz as far as the Main, toward the east between the people of Mainz and the Saxons, who, restoring the old city Helenopolis beside the bank of the Main, ordered it to be called Frankfurt; Merodac, who died when struck by a boar in the hunt; Nicanor, who was duke of the island of Holland; and Odemar, whom his father appointed pontiff of sacred rites. At that time Doracus, counsellor and philosopher of the Franks, flourished, a man eminently learned in all the sciences of the world, who presided over songs and annals. The Franks had peace all the days in which Marcomer reigned, and under him they greatly increased in wealth and power, augmented in number and dignity. Doracus writes in the annals, as Hunibald reports, that the Romans always regarded the Franks with suspicion both in war and in peace, as though [unclear] by name Hasildis, by whom he begot three sons, Farabert, Nicanor. The elder by birth succeeded his father. The second was king of Phrista. The third, Rorich, was drowned in a river, from whom the name Rora has remained for the river down to the present day, between the castle Neocum [unclear] for the most part happened under Paramund and his followers. King Marcomer died in the twenty-first year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 148.

But in the year of the Lord 165.

Clodomer, the first-born son of King Marcomer, reigned after his father for seventeen years. He was a prudent, modest, and active man. He had as wife the daughter of the duke of the Rugii, named Hasildis, by whom he begot three sons: Farabert; the third, Rorich, was drowned in a river, from whom the name Rora remained for the river down to the present day between the castle Neocum. The elder succeeded his father. The second was king of Phrista. The third, Rorich, was drowned, from whom the river Rora [unclear] down to the present day between the castle Neocum. For the most part it happened under Paramund and his followers. King Marcomer died in the twentieth year of his reign, but in the year of the Lord 175.

But in the year of the Lord 185.

Farabert, son of Clodomer, the elder by birth, reigned after his father for twenty years. Of his [unclear]

Suimo reigned eighteen years and fought many battles with the Gauls and Romans. For in his time Severus Caesar of the Romans brought Britain, which is now England, back again into subjection to the Romans, which did not please Suimo and his princes. Therefore, when Severus had died in Britain, Suimo laid waste Gaul in the penultimate year of his reign and returned victorious. He died in the 148th year of his reign, and in the 223rd year of the Lord’s nativity.

Suimo reigned 28 years.

Johannes Trithemius. Hilderic reigned 40 years.

Hilderic, the elder son of Suimo, succeeding his father, reigned forty years, a man powerful in arms and of great prudence. On an island of the Rhine he built a very strong castle, not far from Neoco, which he called Hildeburg from his own name. In his time flourished Hildegast, the wisest philosopher of the Franks, counsellor and seer, or prophet, born of royal seed, who succeeded Odemar in the highest pontificate. For forty-six years he was of such opinion and reputation among the Franks that he was heard by all as though he were some divine power, and gave commands both to kings and dukes and to the whole people of the Franks as if he were God and Lord.

The prophecy of Hildegast concerning [arvosa Friderum], that is, the lion and the serpent.

On the birthday of King Hilderic, standing in the temple of Jove at Neopagus before the image of that very god, after prayers poured forth for prophecy, he began to rave, as is the custom with those prophesying; and with head shaken and hands curved back, he prophesied thus: “Victory comes to the Franks from the western god, whom the ancient Dardanian fathers worshipped. Whatever the Gaul possesses, whatever all Germany possesses, all will yield to your right, warlike Sicambrian. When he has given you the first king from the name, whom the princes and dukes without a king shall establish, while he reigns the Frank will reign without end.” Concerning the Romans too he added these words: “Behold, the great god will give the Frank the brothel-camps, and the lion will break the eagle, the serpent [unclear].”

For they had been more accustomed to live in fields than in cities or in beautiful or elaborate dwellings. Often, indeed, by command of their kings they were compelled to change their seats and homes, and therefore they did not care for beautiful buildings. But Hildegast taught them more cultivated speech and manners, and to build houses divided into different apartments. For whatever they had constructed before, through excessive simplicity, was contemptible. Hence the Germans, taking up a proverb, when they see anything made or painted with ancient simplicity, are accustomed to say down to this day: “This is an old work of the Franks.” Das ist ein alt Fränckisch Werck. The rest concerning Hilderic is in Hunibald. He died in the fortieth year of his reign, and in the 253rd year of the Lord’s birth.

Bertherius, son of King Hilderic, reigned after his father for seventeen years. In his time the Romans, who were staying in legions in Gaul on this side of the Rhine, waged war with the Suevic Alemanni, leading their army to Augusta, the city of the Raetians, which is now in Swabia, in the seventh year of Berther, king of the Franks, where Valerian was created Augustus by the soldiers in the army, and Gallienus was called Caesar by the senate at Rome, Gallus and Volusianus having been killed by Aemilianus.

The Franks devastated Italy, Gaul, and Spain.

In Berther’s tenth year, Germans, with the aid of the Franks and Saxons, entered the territories of the Romans as enemies, and, devastating everything, came as far as Ravenna.

Clodius reigned 27 years.

In Berther’s eleventh year, the Alemanni crossed the Rhine, entered Gaul with a great army, and, coming as far as Trier, cruelly devastated everything with fire and sword. Proceeding from there, they reached as far as Italy and inflicted many losses on the Romans. In the following year the Franks, having the Germans and Saxons as allies, by order of King Berther, under the dukes Anther, his son, and Luther, son of the king of the Saxons, ranged through Gaul with a great army and devastated it, beginning from the region of the Tungri, through the [Belucaci?] as far as the Seine, and farther, devastating everything, they reached as far as Spain and overthrew the city of Tarragona. King Berther died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 261.

The Franks went again into Gaul.

Clodius reigned 27 years.

In Berther’s eleventh year, the Alemanni crossed the Rhine, entered Gaul with a great army, and, coming as far as Trier, cruelly devastated everything with fire and sword. As they proceeded from there, they reached as far as Italy and inflicted many losses on the Romans. In the following year the Franks, having the German Saxons as allies, by order of King Berther, under the dukes Anther, his son, and Luther, son of the king of the Saxons, ranged through Gaul with a great army and devastated it, beginning from the region of the Tungri, through [Belucae?] as far as the Seine, and farther, devastating everything, they reached as far as Spain and overthrew the city of Tarragona. King Berther died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 351.

In Berther’s eleventh year, the Alemanni crossed the Rhine, entered Gaul with a great army, and, coming as far as Trier, cruelly devastated everything with fire and sword. As they proceeded from there, they reached as far as Italy, having the German Saxons by order of King Berther under the dukes Anther, his son, and Luther, son of the king of the Saxons; with a great army they ranged through Gaul and devastated it, beginning from the region of the Tungri, through [Belucae?] as far as the Seine, and farther, devastating everything, they reached as far as Spain and overthrew the city of Tarragona. King Berther died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 361.

Clodius, son of Berther, reigned after his father for twenty-eight years. In his eighth year the Romans expelled the Franks from the territories of Spain and inner Gaul, many being slain on both sides. For the Franks withdrew as far as their old seats on the Meuse.

Thereafter, in the twelfth year of his reign, King Clodius, desiring to avenge himself on the Romans, again invaded Gaul through his dukes, and many thousands of the Romans were killed by the Franks. And so

The Franks held a great part of inner Gaul for seven years.

In the nineteenth year of King Clodius, the Romans came again under the commander Probus, and again expelled the Franks from Gaul, with not a few of their own men killed and destroyed in war on both sides.

Caesarum, anno suo sexto, Dominum et Deum appellari praecepit. Rex autem Richimer anno regni sui xi. bellum cum Romanis Gallis, non longe à ciuitate Basana, que nunc ad Thermas Grani nuncupatur. Eodem tempore mili- tum legiones Romanorum apud Agrippinam Coloniam post bellum cum Francis non fatis foeliciter commißum, accepto nuncio de morte Caesaris Coccei Neruae, Vlpiniũ Traianum Crinitum natione Hispanum Imperatorem fecerunt, qui tertiam perfecutio- nem mouit in Christianos: Postea informatus praecepit Christianos non inquiri, sed spon- 10 te se ingerentes tantum debere occidi. Postemo tamen iterum mutatus quartam eis per- fecutionem suscitauit. Richimerus autem rex Francorum obijt, Anno Domini cxiii. Re- gni sui xxiiii. Odemarus Richimeri regis Francorum primogenitus filius post patrem regnauit annis xiii. princeps populo Francorum valde amabilis, qui temperauit à bellis quo ad fie- ri portuit. Inducias, id est, treugas siue confidentias fecit cum Gallis atque Romanis, &; se- tam vtriusq́ue exhibuit amicum, vt omnes mortem eius deplorarent. Vnde pacem ha- bentis cum omnibus, totum suum studium impendit pro decore &; ornatu gentis, reno- vando leges, &; constituendo nouas ciuitates &; munitiones. Inter multas autem ciuita- tes vnam suo nomine fundauit, in terra que Tuendia nominabatur, quae est inter Saxo- 20 nes &; Francoes, conterminans iuxta alueolum Vechtanum, quam nominari praecepit Odemarshesin / anno regni sui quarto, Dominica autem natiuitatis centefimo scepti- modecimo. Clogio qui perijt in Britania, Franc qui fuit dux apud Hogios populos à Confluenti vsque ad Moenum, versus Orientem inter Mo- gintiacos &; Saxones, qui veterem vrbem Helenopolim iuxta Moeni littus inflaurans, 30 Franckenfurt nominari praecepit. Pacem habuerunt Franci eundis diebus quibus Marcomerus regnauit, &; multum sub eo diui- tijs &; potentia creuerunt, aucti numero &; dignitate. Doracus in annalibus scribit, vt re- 40 fert Hunibald, quod Romani Francoes &; bello &; pace semper habuerunt suspectos, quasi rum nomine Hasildam, de qua genuit tres filios Farabertum, Nicanorem. Secundus fuit rex Phrista, Tertiõs Roricħ in flumine submersus est, à quo nomen fluuio mansit Rora vsque in praesentem diem inter Neocum castellum magna ex parte contigit sub Paramundo, &; eius sequacibus. Cuius an- 60 Suimo re- gnoauit ani- xviii. &; multa praeliages- fit cum Gallis atque Romanis. On the Origin of the Franks.

...suffered no small loss from the Franks, Germans, Suebi, that is, Alemanni, and Saxons. But in the eleventh year of King Clodius, Claudius Caesar led the Roman army against the Suebi; the Suebi, meeting him not far from Lake Benacus with thirty thousand men, fought fiercely. At length the victory fell to the Romans, and more than twelve thousand of the Suebi fell, the rest seeking safety in flight.

King Clodius died in the seventeenth year of his reign, and in the year 288 of the Lord’s Nativity.

Walther, son of King Clodius, reigned after his father for eight years. In his first year Diocletian began at Rome and ruled for nearly twenty years; he was of such arrogance and pride that he ordered himself to be publicly worshipped as God.

In the first, second, third, and fourth years of King Walther there were great disturbances in Britain, which is now England. For, after Lucius, king of the Britons, had died some years before, he who first had received the Christian faith from Pope Eleutherius in the time of Suimon, son of Pharabert, king of the Franks, in the year of Christ 188, the Romans appointed Severus, a senator, in his place and sent him into Britain with two legions; when he landed, the Britons received him at the shore with war.

After he was at length slain at York, Carausius, born in Britain of the lowest rank, was declared king with the consent of the Romans and exercised much tyranny. When he at last had been killed, in the times of Walther, king of the Franks, the Romans sent Alexius in his place with three legions of soldiers. But the Britons, unable to bear the rule of the Romans any longer, themselves appointed Asclepiodotus as their king, and killed Alexius with two legions of Romans. But they besieged Gallus the prefect with the third legion at London; when he saw that he could not resist, after receiving permission to depart, he surrendered the city. Asclepiodotus began in the eighth year of Walther and reigned ten years.

The Romans were powerful in these times and ruled many nations. The Franks, however, were afflicted by the utmost hatred of the Romans; nevertheless they remained quiet, silently awaiting the prophecy of their prophets, which had not yet arrived. King Walther died in the eighth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 296.

Dagobert, son of King Walther, reigned after his father for eleven years. He was very gentle toward his subjects; hence it came about that great and small revered him as a father, each pursuing him with great reverence and honor.

In the fourth year of Dagobert, king of the Franks, Coel, duke of Gloucester, rising against his lord Asclepiodotus, king of the Britons, induced by the promises of the Romans, killed him in war. Rejoicing at this news, the Romans sent Constantius, a senator, who had previously subdued Spain for them, a man no less prudent than bold. When Coel heard that he had landed on the shore, he sent messengers, sought peace, and promised tribute to the Romans, provided only that he might have the kingdom. Constantius agreed. These terms having been settled, Coel died within forty days; soon afterward Constantius took his daughter, named Helena, to whom no maiden in the land was equal in beauty, knowledge of the liberal arts, and skill with musical instruments. [unclear] afterward succeeded in the kingdom, and prevailed not only over the Britons but also against Maxentius for the empire of the Romans.

For Constantius, having been made emperor, made Constantine Caesar and entrusted Gaul to him. At that time the Alemanni occupied Gaul in great power; Caesar Constantine waged war with them in the fourth year of the aforesaid Dagobert, king of the Franks, at the city of Langres in Gaul, and killed sixty thousand of them. Dagobert, king of the Franks, died in the eleventh year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 307.

Clogio, son of Dagobert, succeeding his dead father, reigned only two years. For in the second year of his reign the Romans fiercely invaded the kingdom of the Franks around the Meuse and the Rhine, namely in that year in which Constantius, dying at York in Britain, commended the kingdom and empire to his son Constantine with his mother.

When therefore Clogio, king of the Franks, fought rather incautiously, he was intercepted by the Romans and killed, leaving two sons, of whom the elder by birth was then in his thirtieth year, while the younger by birth, Richimer, was eighteen. But by the law of the Franks it was forbidden for anyone to be advanced as king unless he had completed the twenty-fourth year of his age. Hence it came about that neither of Clogio’s sons could come to the kingdom, but their paternal uncle, by election of the princes, was crowned king. King Clogio was slain in the second year of his reign, and in the year of Christ 309.

The Alemanni, that is, the Suebi, are cut down by the Romans.

Clodomerus frater Clogionis post eum regnauit annis XVIII. cuius anno secundo Alemanni, qui &; Sueui, grauiter à Romanis afflicti, Francos, Thuringos, &; Saxones in auxilium vocauerunt, monentes &; orantes, ne tardarent eis citius in adiutorium subue-nire, attento, quoniam si Romani, vt animis conceperant, superassent, iam Franci, Saxo-nes, &; Thuringi ab eis sine dubio peterentur. Hac Germani victoria potiti cum spolia in castris confueto more diuiderent, orta 10 est inter duos milites, quorum alter vero Thuringus erat, quaedam turbatio, quae in tantum crevit, quod periculosa seditio fuit subsecuta. Johannes Trithemius

Clodomer reigns for 18 years. Genebald, duke of the Franks, fights against the Romans.

Clodomer, the brother of Clogio, reigned after him for eighteen years. In his second year the Alemanni, who are also Suebi, having been severely afflicted by the Romans, called the Franks, Thuringians, and Saxons to their aid, warning and entreating them not to delay in coming swiftly to help them, considering that, if the Romans, as they had conceived in their minds, should prevail, the Franks, Saxons, and Thuringians would without doubt soon be attacked by them. When these matters had been recognized, King Clodomer appointed his brother Genebald commander of the army, and placed under him eighty thousand men. The other kings also did likewise; having been called to their aid, they joined auxiliary soldiers to the Alemanni and formed a great army, and, assembling against the Romans, fought fiercely and killed more than forty-six thousand of them; the rest sought safety in flight.

When the Germans had obtained this victory and were dividing the spoils in the camp according to their accustomed manner, there arose between two soldiers, one of whom was a Thuringian, a certain disturbance, which grew so great that a dangerous sedition followed. For each had many men of his own people adhering to him. Nevertheless, through the intervention of the authority of the dukes and princes, they ceased from tumult on that occasion. The cause of the disturbance was that the Suebian soldier, named Adelbert, had said that a Thuringian named Gunther had secretly taken away something from the booty common to all. But when the Thuringian denied the theft, the Suebian offered to prove his statement by duel. When the princes allowed this, the combat of single battle was undertaken, and the Thuringian was killed by the Alemannian in the second encounter. When his body had been stripped of its arms and clothing, the theft too of which he had been accused was found in his possession. At this shame the Thuringians were stirred in mind beyond measure. Yet, concealing their anger, one hundred and twenty men afterward held counsel apart as to how they might avenge Gunther, who had been slain, upon Adelbert the Suebian, and ordered everything to be kept most secret.

Therefore, on the following night they rushed upon the tent in which they suspected Adelbert the Suebian to be, and cried out, “Hand over to us the murderer, that he may die.” What more? They run to arms. The Suebi determined to defend their innocent soldier, or to die with him, and, rushing against those one hundred and twenty Thuringians, almost all were slaughtered. When this was announced in the camp of the Thuringians, at once driven to fury, at daybreak they rushed upon the Suebi, shouting in madness, “Ogyverrederß hoeß vwichi.” But the Suebi, not sluggish, seized their arms and defended themselves bravely. A fierce battle was joined between friends, in which more than twelve thousand Thuringians were killed by the Suebi; the rest, slipping away in flight, came to the camp of the Franks, who were distant from them by about two leagues. For the matter had become known neither to the Franks nor to the Saxons until it had been carried out, because they had pitched camp not in the same place, but far from one another.

After this, the princes and dukes of the Franks and Saxons labored with great efforts for peace and concord between the Alemanni and the Thuringians; but since both sides complained that they had been gravely injured, they could not restore full peace. They did, however, obtain truces for three years, during which the parties were to abstain from war, until in the meantime, as the disturbance of the commotion cooled, it should be allayed. From that time down to our age there remains a perpetual hidden discord between the Suebi and the Thuringians, although many do not know the cause, and they pursue one another mutually.

In the sixth year of Clodomer, king of the Franks, when the truces or agreements between the aforesaid peoples had ended, the Alemanni declared war on the Thuringians. But the Thuringians, distrusting their own resources, sent noble and distinguished messengers to King Clodomer and the nobles of the Franks, asking with great urgency that, as friends, they would deign to send forces to their aid against the Alemanni. At that time there were great movements of peoples in Britain and in all the surrounding islands. The king of the Franks, because the settlements of his people were not far distant from Britain, was in great anxiety, fearing the treacheries of the Romans, lest perhaps they should make an incursion by land and harass the borders of the Franks, as indeed they had often done before.

Therefore, after taking counsel with his men, he answered the envoys of the Thuringians in a public assembly of the magnates, saying: “Through Duke Genebald, my very dear brother, I have long understood what was the cause, friends Thuringians, of the discord between you and the Alemanni, and of those disturbances which today are at the gates. But you yourselves know very well that the Romans with the Gauls press upon us daily and observe most diligently whether by any occasion they might be able to destroy our kingdom. Therefore I do not judge it prudent for us in these perilous times to divide the people and, with our own affairs neglected, to guard those of others. If we could do this without danger to ourselves, as we have often done before, we would do it now also with friendly service. For the distance of the places is too great for us to fight against the Alemanni, since they hold the beginning and source of the Rhine, while we hold its farthest mouths.”

When these things had been heard from the king of the Franks, the envoys of the king of Thuringia answered: “Lord king of Francia, and you nobles of the Franks, listen. We have a broad, fertile, and pleasant land; wherefore, if it pleases you, it is

DE ORIGINE FRANCORVM. 75 plus est Rex nõster cum vniuersa gente Thuringorum dare populo vestro terram optimam, que est ad Maenri pĩs, & inter Alemanos: vt nobis in murum, & Alemani suis in exterminium. Ad petitio- nem Thuringorum Franci dederunt consensum, & oblata susceperunt. Anno igitur Dominicae nativitatis cccxvi. qui fuit septimus annus Clodomeri re- gis Francorum, in mense Aprili nonodecimo die mensis exiuerunt viri armati, triginta millia, agricultores, & variarum rerum artifices, duo millia sexcenta octoginta sex, cum vxoribus, liberis, & rebus suis de Francis Cismarina, vbi nunc est, Traiectum, Hollandia, Geldria, Selandia, pars Phrifiae, & Westhaliae; simul et Brabantia cum adiacentibus terris multis selecti, & iusti à rege ascendere in terram, quam promiserant se Thoringi Francis daturos:quam etiam cum magna laetitia susceperunt. Ducem Rex super populum missum, & exercitum omnem constituit fratrem suum Genebaldum, qui annis prioribus cum Alemanos dimicauerat, fuitque vir magnae prudentiae, audax et bellicosus, qui terminos sibi et populo suo donatos non solum bene exit, sed etiam in breui multum ampliauit. Cumque exiussent patrios lares Franci, dux Genebaldus cum viginti millibus pagnatorum processit, ad locum sibi à Thuringis destinatum, reliqua vero decem vtilia pro tutela populi subsequentis cum filio suo Marcomero in itinere post se dimisit. Cum autem percepissent Alemani quod Franci nouas à Thuringis fedes accepif- fent iuxta Moeni littora inter medium eorum, valde timuerant et missis ad Genebaldum ducem legatis pacem orant, & omnem causam litis Thuringiã et Saxoniam. In eorum au- tem introitu omnes Thuringi regis lui Heroli mandato retrocesserunt in Thuringiã, & dispositas sibi mansiones receperunt, alimenta Francis ad integrum annum sufficientia iustu regis dimitrẽtes. Franci aũt noui aduenae in terra iam sua consederunt, primo in eo mittunt. Similiter etiam Thuringi fecerunt. Et sic magnum inter illos dissidium Gene- baldi prudentia fuit extinctum. Eodem anno in mense Septembri Marcomer dux Genebaldi filius cum reliquo Francorum populo venit in meridianalem Thuringiam, & fedes promissas acceperunt circa Moenum fluuium, ab oriente habentes Bohemiã, à meridie Alemaniam, ab occi- dente Rhenum et Moguntiam, ab aquilone vero Thuringiã et Saxoniam. In eorum an- tem introitu omnes Thurgini regis lui Herolĩ mandato retrocesset in Thuringiã, & dispositas sibi mansione receperunt, alimen̄ta Franci ad integrum annuum sufficiētiā tis impatiētess et ad bella promptissimos. Nec tamẽ poterat eos prohibere propter multa iustus dimittētes. Franci prouincijs plus consueto fuerunt nimium oc- cupati. Dux Genebaldus autẽ Dux genuit Clodomero rege Francorum, qui regnauit in Fran- cia occidentali circa mare, Mosam et Rhenum fcedus iniijt, cum Alemanis et Thuringis, quo fortior esset, ad impugnam Romanos, & Gallos, qui finibus Franciae; ab alia Rhe- ni parte imminebant apud Moguntiam, & Argentinam, contra quos Rheno transmisso sapius dimicauit, & plures corum occidit. Genebaldus autẽ Dux genuit Dagobertum, qui presuit genti annis xxi. Clodius aũt genuit Marcomerum, autem genuit Clodium, qui praefuit annis xxiii. Clodius aũt genuit Faramundum, qui anno ducatus sui secũdo, in regem Francorum fuit electus, vt ordine suo inferius est scriptum. Praedicti quatuor ordues Frãcorum orientalium per annos 94. populo praesidentes terminos accepta post- essions, vsque ad Rheni flumen dilatarunt, & magnum Gallis atque Romanis damnum fecerunt. Sed iam nunc quae restant de regum Francorum sucessione continuanda sint. Rex autem Clodomir obijt anno regni sui xviii. Domini cccxxviii. Richimerus Clodomeri filius posti patrem regnauit annis xiiii. & cunctis regni sui diebus cũ Romanis, & Gallis in consētione fuit, & multa cũ eis praelia com̄isit. Hic etiam reꝑore patriis sui cum Casare Constantio patre Constantini dimicauerat, anno videl. Do- mini ccxviij. Constantius enim Britanniam Romanorum iustu ingressurus, Francorum gentẽ in finibus Rheni ad Mare et Mosam commorantem hostiliter invuasit, & retroce- dere compulit, multis eorum in bello peremptis. Quo tandem in Britannia mortuo G 2 runt, vbi none est Francia Orientalis. On the Origin of the Franks.

[unclear] our king, with the whole people of the Thuringians, [is ready?] to give to your people an excellent land, which is by the banks of the Main and among the Alemanni, so that it may be a wall for us and the destruction of the Alemanni. At the petition of the Thuringians, the Franks gave their consent and accepted what was offered.

Therefore in the year of the Lord’s nativity 316, which was the seventh year of Clodomir, king of the Franks, on the nineteenth day of April, there went out from Cismarine Francia, where now are Utrecht, Holland, Guelders, Zeeland, part of Frisia and Westphalia, and also Brabant with many adjacent lands, thirty thousand armed men and two thousand six hundred eighty-six farmers and craftsmen of various trades, with their wives, children, and possessions, chosen and approved by the king to go up into the land which the Thuringians had promised to give to the Franks; and they received it with great joy.

The king appointed as duke over the people sent out and the whole army his brother Genebald, who in earlier years had fought with the Alemanni. He was a man of great prudence, bold and warlike, who not only held well the borders given to him and his people, but in a short time greatly enlarged them. And when the Franks had left their ancestral hearths, Duke Genebald advanced with twenty thousand fighters to the place assigned to him by the Thuringians; the remaining ten thousand, for the protection of the people following behind, he left on the road after him with his son Marcomer.

When the Alemanni learned that the Franks had received new settlements from the Thuringians beside the banks of the Main, in their midst, they were greatly afraid, and, sending envoys to Duke Genebald, they begged for peace, and [unclear] every cause of quarrel [with?] Thuringia and Saxony. At their entry all the Thuringians, by command of their king Herol, withdrew into Thuringia and received the dwellings assigned to them, leaving, by order of the king, provisions sufficient for the Franks for a whole year. But the Franks, newly arrived, settled in the land now their own; first in that [unclear] they send. The Thuringians did likewise. And so the great discord between them was extinguished by Genebald’s prudence.

In the same year, in the month of September, Marcomer, the son of Duke Genebald, came with the remaining people of the Franks into southern Thuringia, and they received the promised settlements around the river Main, having Bohemia on the east, Alemannia on the south, the Rhine and Mainz on the west, and Thuringia and Saxony on the north. At their entry all the Thuringians, by command of their king Herol, withdrew into Thuringia and received the dwellings assigned to them, leaving, by just command, provisions sufficient for the Franks for a whole year. The Franks, impatient [unclear] and very ready for wars. Yet he could not restrain them because they were more than usually occupied in many provinces.

Duke Genebald, however, [unclear] with Clodomir, king of the Franks, who reigned in western Francia around the sea, the Meuse, and the Rhine, entered into an alliance with the Alemanni and Thuringians, so that he might be stronger to attack the Romans and Gauls, who threatened the borders of Francia on the other side of the Rhine at Mainz and Strasbourg. Against them he often fought after crossing the Rhine, and killed many of them.

Duke Genebald begot Dagobert, who ruled the people for twenty-one years. Clodius, however, begot Marcomer, and he begot Clodius, who ruled for twenty-three years. Clodius begot Faramund, who in the second year of his dukedom was elected king of the Franks, as is written below in its proper order. The aforesaid four leaders of the eastern Franks, presiding over the people for ninety-four years, extended the borders of the possessions they had received as far as the river Rhine, and did great damage to the Gauls and Romans. But now what remains concerning the succession of the kings of the Franks must be continued. King Clodomir died in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the year of the Lord 328.

Richimer, son of Clodomir, reigned after his father for fourteen years, and throughout all the days of his reign was in conflict with the Romans and Gauls, and joined many battles with them. He had also in his father’s lifetime fought with Caesar Constantius, the father of Constantine, namely in the year of the Lord 218. For Constantius, about to enter Britain by command of the Romans, made a hostile attack on the people of the Franks dwelling along the borders of the Rhine by the sea and the Meuse, and compelled them to retreat, many of them being slain in battle. When he at last died in Britain [unclear].

Clodomerus frater Clogionis post eum regnauit annis XVIII. cuius anno secundo Alemanni, qui &; Sueui, grauiter à Romanis afflicti, Francos, Thuringos, &; Saxones in auxilium vocauerunt, monentes &; orantes, ne tardarent eis citius in adiutorium subue-nire, attento, quoniam si Romani, vt animis conceperant, superassent, iam Franci, Saxo-nes, &; Thuringi ab eis sine dubio peterentur. Quibus recognitis Rex Clodo mer Gene-baldum fratrem suum exercitus constituit, cui octoginta virorum millia subiecit. Simili-ter fecerunt &; caeteri Reges, in auxilium vocati, coniuncti Alemannis subsidiarii milites magnum statuerunt exercitum, congregssique Romanis acriter pugnauerunt, &; plus quā quadraginta sex millia eorum perimerunt, caeteri salutem fuga quaesiuierunt. Hac Germani victoria potiti cum spolia in castris confueto more diuiderent, orta 10 est inter duos milites, quorum alter vero Thuringus erat, quaedam turbatio, quae in tantum crevit, quod periculosa seditio fuit subsecuta. Vterque enim de sua gente plures habuit sibi adhaerentes. Ducum tamen &; principum auctoritate interueniente ces-fauerunt illa vice à tumultuatione. Caussa turbationis fuit, quod miles ille Sueuus nomi-ne Adelbert dixerat: Thuringum nomine Gunther nescio quid furtiue de preda commu-ni omnium subtraxiffe. Verum vbi Thoringus furtum negaret, obtulit se Sueuus ad pro-bandum dictum suum duello, qđ cum admitterent principes, monomachiae bellum cō-mittitur, &; Thoringus ab Alemanno, in secundo congressu peremptus est. Cuius cada-uer, cum armis &; vestimentis fuisset nudatum, etiam furtum de quo fuerat accusatus pe-nes eum inuentum est. Qua confusione accepta Thuriꝰ vitra modū animis sc̄iuēt. 20 tamen dissimulantés iram, consilium postea seorsum habuerunt viri centum vigintique modo Guntherum de Adelberto Sueuo vindicarent occisum, omnia secretissime mane-reiubent. Nocte īguitur infęquente super tētorum, in quo supicabantur esse Adelbertum Sueuum irritunt, &; clamantes trade nobis homicidam vt moriatur. Quid plura? Ad arma concurrunt. Sueui fuū defendere militẽ innocentem, vel cum eo mōri flatuunt, istruen-tesque in illos centum viginti Thoringos omnes pene trucidantur. Quod cum nunciatum fuisset in castris Thoringorum, mox in furorem cōcitati, mane diluculo, in Sueuos pro-filiunt, cum infania vociferantes, Ogyverrederß hoeß vwichi. At Sueui non segnes arma cor-ripientes fortiter se defenꝑdunt. Atrox inter amicos pugna committitur, in qua plus quam duodecim millia Thoringorũ à Sueuis perempta funt, caeteri fuga lapsi, ad castra Fran-coruṁ, qui ad duarum fere leuarum distantiam, ab his aberant, peruenerunt. Nec enim Francis, nec Saxonibus innotuerat res, donec perpetrata fuerat, quia non in eodem loco, 30 sed procul ab inuicem castra posuerant. Post hęc principes, &;duces Francorum, Saxonumque propace, &; concordia inter Alemannos, &; Thuringos magnis laborauē conatribus, sed cum ambę partes grauiter se laefas quererentur, plenam reformare pacem non potuerunt. Inducias tamen impetra-uerunt ad tres annos, in quibus à bello partes deberent abstinere, donec medio tempore deferuescente commotionis turbatio ledaretur. Ab illo tempore vsque ad nostram aetatẽ perpetua manet inter Sueuos, &; Thuringos occulta diffenꝑio, cum plures caussam igno-rent, &; se mutuo infecquuntur. Anno Clodomeri Francorum regis sexto treugis, siue inducijs inter praescriptas gẽ-tes finitis, Alemani bellum Thuringis indixerunt. Sed Thuriꝰ rebus suis disfidentes, nuncios miserunt nobiles, &; insignes ad Clodomerum regem, &; Francorum proceres, magna cum instantia rogantes vt eis in auxilium copias mittere contra Alemanos, vt a-mici dignarentur. Erant eo tempore magni gentium motus, in Britannia, &; in cunctis Insulis circumiacentibus. Rex autem Francorum quia nō longe distabant fedes suae gen-tis à Britanniā in magna follicitudine fuit, metuens Romanorum infidias ne forte per terram excurrerent, &; fines Francorum infestarent, sicut &; antea sapius fecerunt. Vnde cũ suis habito cōsilio Thuringorum legatis respondit, in concione magnato-50 tum publica dice̓ns: Duce Genebaldo fratre meo chariffimo dudū intellexi que fuerit inter vos ami-ci Thoringi, &; Alemanos causa diffidiꝰ &; earũ que hodie funt in foribus turbationū. Sed vos ipsi optime scitis qđ Romani cum Gallis quotidis nobis imminēt, ac diligentissime obseruant, si qualibet occasio-ne regnum nostrũ possent destruere. Vnde cautũ nobis non iudico his periculosis tẽporibus populũ diuide-re, &; neglectis propriis aliena tutari. Quod sipossemus sine periculo nostro, sicut ante hac sapius feci-mus, &; nunc amica feruitute faceremus.
