DE ORIGINE FRANCORVM. 97 Anno sequenti Carolus rex congregato iterum Wormatiae principum generali conuentu, communi omnium consensu bellum Saxonibus indixit. Contracto non paruo Francorum exercitu, Saxoniam intrauit, & cuncta ferro, & igne depopulatus est. Eref purg castrum quoddam cum obtinuisset, idolum Saxonica lingua Ermenful nuncupa-tum destruxit. Inde discedens ad Westaram fluuium processit, vbi conuenientes Saxones gratiam regis postularunt fidem promittentes. At rex acceptis XII. obsidibus pacem concessit. Prima regis Caroli M. expeditio in Saxones. Anno Domini DCCLXXXIII. cum Adrianus Papa insolentiam Desiderij regis Longobardorum, & oppressionem ecclesiae diutiùs ferre non posset, missa legatione ad Caro-lum, eius opem implorauit. Qui collecto exercitu Longobardiam intrauit, ac Desiderium in Ticinensi vrbe, quae nunc est Papia obsedit. Longa tandem obsidione ciuitatem, ad de-ditionem compulit, quam relique ciuitates secutae regis Caroli se potestati subdiderunt. Rex itaque subacta, & prout tempus admifit ordinata Italia in Franciam reuertitur, Defide-rium regem secum ducens captiuum, Adelgisus vero Desiderij filius in Graeciam fugit, ad Constantinum Imperatorem, ibique vitam finiuit. 10 Carelui rex in fauorem ecclesie Ro-mana vin-cit Longo-bardos. Interim verò quod rex Carolus erat bello implicatus in Longobardia, Saxones na-cta de absentia eius occasione contiguos sibi Hassiorum terminos deuastare coeperunt. Venientesque in locum, qui Fritislaria nominatur, ecclesiam quam sanctus archiepisco-pus Bonifacius quandam consecrauit, incendere moliti sunt. Erant enim Saxones adhuc 20 eo tempore cultores idolorum. Cumque multa vi eam incendere conarentur, apparue-runt quibusdam tam ex paganis quam ex Christianis, duo iuuenes, in albis vestimentis o-mne incendium prohibentes, quorum praesentia Saxones territi, omnes in fugam con-uertsi sunt nullo perfequente. Anno Domini DCCLXXIIII. Carolus de Lombardia domum regressus, priusquam cum Saxones venisse sentirent, tripartitum in eorum terram misit exercitum, qui dire-cptionibus, & incendijs cuncta vasantes, compluribufque eorum qui resistere conati sunt interfectis, cum ingenti praeda reuersi sunt. Et haec secunda fuit expeditio Caroli regis in Saxoniam. 30 Anno Domini DCCLXXV. Carolus rex Magnus decrevit Saxoniam ingredi, & tam diu in ea perseuerare, donec aut fidem Christi susciperent, aut omnes exterminarentur. Toto igitur Francorum impetu Saxonie petens, primo incursu Sigeburgum munitiffi-mum castellum, quod ex opposito Rheni duobus à Bunna distat miliaribus, in quo Saxo-num erat praesidium cepit, Eresburgum à Saxonibus destructum restituens muniuit, in eoque Francorum praefidium posuit, multaque strage facta obsides ab eis et à Westphalis acceptis pacem dedit potentibus et recessit. Anno Domini DCCLXXVII. Carolus rex Magnus habito principum regni Franco-rum consilio in loco Padelbrunna, in finibus Saxonie vbi nunc est ciuitas epifcopalis, ite-rium iam quarto exercitum duxit in Saxoniam omnefque sibi fallaciter deuotos inuenit. Cuncti enim ad eum venerint praeter Witikindum vnnum ex primoribus Westhaliorum, 40 qui multorum sibi conscius facinorum regem timuit, & cum paucis ad Sigefridum regē Danorum profugit, Caeteri autem qui conuererant in tantum se regis potestati submis-e-runt, vt ea conditione veniam tunc mererentur, quatenus, si eius statuta vlterius violaret patria et libertate priuarentur. Multi ad instantiam regis baptizati sunt, quorum tamen pau-ci veri Christiani extiterunt. Anno Domini DCCLXXXVIII. rex Carolus mouit in Hispaniam, & vrbes quas suae di-tioni subegit atque à Saracenis obsides accepit. Interea Saxones comperto quod rex longe abesset sumptis armis, vsaque ad Rhenum profesti sunt. Sed cum amnem transire non pos-sent, quicquid à Tuitio villa, quae est in opposito Coloniae, vsque ad Confluentiam, vbi Mosella influit Rheum, vicorum, villarumque fuit, igni et ferro depopulati sunt, nullũ 50 sexus vel aetatis discrimen facientes, sed infantes, vna cum matribus occiderunt. Quod cum rex Altfiodoro positus audisset, orientales Francos, & Alemannos, ad propufandos eos continuo misit. Quorum aduentum Saxones audientes confestim re-ceserunt. Sed isti è vestigio illos insecuti, repererunt eos in partibus Hassiorum iuxta flu-uium Adernam, statimque in ipso fluminis vado adorti, fanta caede strauerunt, vt pau-cissimi remanserint. Anno sequenti qui fuit Dominicae natiuitatis DCCXXXIX. Carolus iam quinto ex-peditionem mouit in Saxoniam in eo loco traducens exercitum vbi Lippia influit Rhe-num haud procul à vico, qui Wesel nuncupatur. Cui eum Saxones occurrerent armati, 1 Carolus M. quinto mo-net in Saxo- niam. Saxones de-uastât par-tes Franco-rum. Quarta Ca-roli regis expeditio in Saxones. Tertia Caroli regis expedi-tio facta in Sa-xonen. Saxones de-vastāt par-tes Franco-rum. Saxones de-uostät par-tes Franco-rum. FÜRSTL. HOFBIBLIOTHEK SPYER * * * SPYER

On the Origin of the Franks.

In the following year King Charles, having again assembled at Worms a general council of the princes, with the common consent of all declared war on the Saxons. Having gathered a considerable army of Franks, he entered Saxony and laid everything waste with sword and fire. When he had taken a certain fortress, Eresburg, he destroyed the idol called in the Saxon language Ermensul. Departing thence he advanced to the river Weser, where the Saxons, coming together, sought the king’s favor and promised fidelity. But the king, after receiving twelve hostages, granted peace.

The first expedition of King Charles the Great against the Saxons.

In the year of the Lord 773, when Pope Adrian could no longer endure the insolence of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, and the oppression of the Church, he sent an embassy to Charles and implored his aid. Charles, having gathered an army, entered Lombardy and besieged Desiderius in the city of Ticinum, which is now Pavia. At length, after a long siege, he compelled the city to surrender; the remaining cities followed it and subjected themselves to King Charles’s power. Therefore the king, after Italy had been subdued and set in order as time permitted, returned to Francia, bringing King Desiderius with him as a captive. Adelgisus, however, Desiderius’s son, fled to Greece, to the emperor Constantine, and there ended his life.

King Charles, in favor of the Roman Church, defeats the Lombards.

Meanwhile, because King Charles was engaged in war in Lombardy, the Saxons, taking opportunity from his absence, began to devastate the neighboring territories of the Hessians. And coming to the place called Fritzlar, they attempted to burn the church which the holy archbishop Boniface had once consecrated. For the Saxons at that time were still worshippers of idols. And when they were trying with great force to burn it, there appeared to certain persons, both pagans and Christians, two young men in white garments preventing the whole fire; terrified by their presence, the Saxons all turned to flight, though no one pursued them.

In the year of the Lord 774, Charles, having returned home from Lombardy, before the Saxons perceived that he had come, sent a three-part army into their land; devastating everything with plundering and fires, and killing very many of those who attempted to resist, they returned with immense booty. And this was the second expedition of King Charles into Saxony.

In the year of the Lord 775, King Charles the Great resolved to enter Saxony and to remain in it so long until either they should receive the faith of Christ or all be exterminated. Therefore, making for Saxony with the whole force of the Franks, in the first assault he took Sigiburg, a very strongly fortified castle opposite the Rhine, two miles from Bonn, in which there was a Saxon garrison; restoring Eresburg, which had been destroyed by the Saxons, he fortified it and placed a Frankish garrison in it. After causing great slaughter, and after receiving hostages from them and from the Westphalians, he granted peace to those capable of giving it and withdrew.

The third expedition of King Charles made against the Saxons.

In the year of the Lord 777, King Charles the Great, after holding council with the princes of the kingdom of the Franks at the place Paderborn, on the borders of Saxony, where there is now an episcopal city, now for the fourth time led an army into Saxony and found all of them deceitfully devoted to him. For all came to him except Widukind, one of the foremost men of the Westphalians, who, conscious of many crimes, feared the king and fled with a few men to Sigefrid, king of the Danes. The rest, however, who had assembled submitted themselves so far to the king’s power that they then merited pardon on this condition: that if they should hereafter violate his statutes, they would be deprived of homeland and liberty. Many were baptized at the king’s insistence, yet few of them proved true Christians.

The fourth expedition of King Charles against the Saxons.

In the year of the Lord 778, King Charles moved into Spain, and the cities which he brought under his authority, and received hostages from the Saracens. Meanwhile the Saxons, discovering that the king was far away, took up arms and advanced as far as the Rhine. But since they could not cross the river, whatever there was of hamlets and estates from the village of Deutz, which is opposite Cologne, as far as Koblenz, where the Moselle flows into the Rhine, they laid waste with fire and sword, making no distinction of sex or age, but killed infants together with their mothers.

Saxons devastate parts of the Franks.

When the king, stationed at [Altfiodoro], heard this, he immediately sent the eastern Franks and the Alemanni to drive them back. Hearing of their arrival, the Saxons at once withdrew. But those men, following them on their trail, found them in the regions of the Hessians beside the river Eder, and immediately attacked them in the very ford of the river and laid them low with such slaughter that very few remained.

The Saxons devastate parts of the Franks.

In the following year, which was the 779th from the Lord’s nativity, Charles now for the fifth time moved an expedition into Saxony, leading the army across at that place where the Lippe flows into the Rhine, not far from the village called Wesel. When the Saxons met him armed,

Charles the Great moves for the fifth time into Saxony.

170
98 IOANNES TRITHEMIVS Bucholtz. apud Bucholdz victi sunt et multieorum occisi, caeteri salutem fuga quaesiuerunt. Rex aurem Carolus Westphalorum regionem ingressus eos omnes in deditionem accepit. Inde mouens ad Wesfaram castra locauit. ibi Angrarij, & Ostphali obsides dederunt, & sacramenta iurauerunt, quibus peractis rex Wormaciam reuersus est. Anno Domini DCCCLXXX. Carolus rexiam sexto mouit in Saxoniam, cui venienti omnes orientalium partium Saxones occurrerunt, multisque de populo baptizati sunt. Veniens inde ad locum vbi Hora, & Albis confluunt, ordinauit rex tam Saxones, quam Selauos, reuersusque in Franciam, & habito consilio, Romam causã orationis cum Hildegarde vxore liberisque profectus est, ac natale anni Papiae celebravit DCCCX. Hoc anno Dominicae natiuitatis indictione nona Carolus rex Francorum Pippini regis filius, postquam regnasset annis XXXIII. Anno aetatis suae LIX. factus est Imperator Romanorum, & imperauitannis XIII. Cum enim Romae esset propter calumniam Leoni Papae tertio nimis iniuriose factam, & natale Domini ibidem celebraret, in ipsa die sacratissima ad missarum solennia veniens, dum ante confessionem beati Petri Apostoli, ab oratione, nihil minus cogitanti, ne dicam speranti, quam Imperium, Leo Papalibus infulis ornatus capiti eius coronam imposuit, & Imperatorem Romanum pronunciauit. A cuncto mox populo Romano conclamaturn est: Carolo Augusto à Deo coronato Magno, & pacifico Imperatori Romanorum, vita et victoria. Post quas laudes vnctus ab Apostolica manu, & more antiquorum principum adoratus à Papa et ablato patritij nomine, quo antea 20 fuerat insignitus, Imperator et Augustus appellatus est multarum fauore gentium. Anno Domini DCCCLI. Carolus Imperator Aquisgrani hyemauit. Estate autem ducto exercitu in Saxoniam, omnes qui trans Albin flumen habitabant Saxones in Franciam transtulit, & pagos transalbianos ab O driatis populis inhabitandos, & colendos sub tributò annuo concessit. Anno Domini decev. Imperator misit filium suum Carolum, cum exercitu in Bohemia regno Franccorum subsecitur. hemiam, qui depopulatis omnibus ducem terrae illius nomine Lechonem occidit, & eius ducatum regno Francorum fecit subiectum. Anno Domini octingentesimo vndecimo, Imperatoris Caroli maior natu filius, & ipse nomine paterno dictus Carolus, pridie nonarum Decembris obijt. Anno Domini otingentesimo decimotertio, Carolus Imperator habito generali conuentu principum Aquisgrani, filium suum Ludouicum regem Aquitanie ad se vocavit, eique imponens coronam imperialis nominis sibi confortem fecit. Bernhardum verò nepotem suum, filium Pippini filii sui regem Italiae constituit. Eodem anno pons Rheni apud Moguntiam, quem Imperator per decem annos ingenti labore, & opere mirabili, de ligno ita construxit, vt perenniter durare posse videtur, in mense Maio; ita tribus horis fortuito incendio conflagrauit, vt praeter hoc quodaqua tegebatur, nec vna quidem hastula ex eo remaneret. Multa Episcoporum consilia edem anno iussu Imperoris facta sunt. Anno Dominicae natiuitatis DCCXV. indictione Romanorum octaua, mensis la- nuarij, die vicefima octaua, Carolus cognomine Magnus rex Francorum, & Imperator Romanorum semper Augustus Aquisgrani moritur, & ibidem in Ecclesia beatae Mariae semper virginis, quam ipse construxerat, honorifice sepelitur, anno aetatis suae XII. regni fui Francorum XLVI. Imperij autem XIII. qui regno Francorum non minus prouinciarum adiunxit quam prius habuit. Ludouicus rex et imperator fi. filii Caroli annis 26. Ludouicus consuetudine Sicambrorum L. in V. mutantium, comes in Francia Orientali consensu S. Burghardi Wirtzburgensis epifcopi, monasterium Svartzachenfe, haud procul à Moenolium, opitulante Innua vxore eius construxit, cuius Ecclesiam sub honore Domini nostrî Iesû Christi, in memoriam quoque lanctae Dei geniticris, sanctorumque Sebastiani, & felicitatis martyrum consecrari fecit, & Monachos ordinis diui patris nenedicti ibidem collocauit. Anno Domini DCCXVII. Ludouicus Imperator Aquisgrani conuentum celebravit principum in quo Lotharium primogenitum suum nominis, & Imperij confortem sibi con-

98 Johannes Trithemius

Bucholtz.

at Bucholtz they were defeated and many of them slain; the rest sought safety in flight. But King Charles entered the region of the Westphalians and received them all in surrender. Moving from there to Wesfaram he pitched camp. There the Angrarians and Eastphalians gave hostages and swore oaths; when these things had been done, the king returned to Worms.

In the year of the Lord 780, King Charles now for the sixth time moved into Saxony. As he came, all the Saxons of the eastern parts met him, and many of the people were baptized. Coming from there to the place where the Ohre and the Elbe flow together, the king set in order both the Saxons and the Slavs; and, having returned into Francia and held counsel, he set out for Rome for the sake of prayer with his wife Hildegard and his children, and celebrated the Nativity of the year at Pavia. 800.

In this year of the Lord’s Nativity, in the ninth indiction, Charles, king of the Franks, son of King Pippin, after he had reigned thirty-three years, in the fifty-ninth year of his age, was made emperor of the Romans and ruled as emperor for thirteen years. For when he was at Rome because of the charge made too wrongfully against Pope Leo III, and was celebrating the Lord’s Nativity there, on that most sacred day itself, coming to the solemnities of the Mass, while before the confession of the blessed Apostle Peter, after prayer, he was thinking of, not to say hoping for, nothing less than the empire, Leo, adorned with the papal insignia, placed a crown upon his head and proclaimed him emperor of the Romans.

At once it was shouted by the whole Roman people: “To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peace-bringing emperor of the Romans, life and victory.” After these acclamations, he was anointed by the apostolic hand and, in the manner of the ancient princes, adored by the pope; and, the title of patrician, with which he had previously been distinguished, having been removed, he was called Emperor and Augustus by the favor of many nations.

In the year of the Lord 804, Emperor Charles wintered at Aachen. But in summer, having led an army into Saxony, he transferred into Francia all the Saxons who lived beyond the river Elbe, and granted the districts beyond the Elbe to be inhabited and cultivated by the Obodrite peoples under an annual tribute.

In the year of the Lord 805, the emperor sent his son Charles with an army into Bohemia; after laying everything waste, he killed the duke of that land, named Lecho, and made his duchy subject to the kingdom of the Franks.

In the year of the Lord 811, the elder son of Emperor Charles, himself also called by his father’s name Charles, died on the day before the Nones of December.

In the year of the Lord 813, Emperor Charles, after holding a general assembly of the princes at Aachen, called to himself his son Louis, king of Aquitaine, and, placing the crown upon him, made him his partner in the imperial name. But Bernard, his grandson, the son of his son Pippin, he appointed king of Italy.

In the same year the bridge over the Rhine at Mainz, which the emperor had constructed of wood over ten years with immense labor and marvelous workmanship, so that it seemed able to last forever, in the month of May was so consumed in three hours by an accidental fire that, apart from what was covered by the water, not even one little splinter of it remained. Many councils of bishops were held in the same year by order of the emperor.

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 814, in the eighth indiction of the Romans, on the twenty-eighth day of the month of January, Charles, surnamed the Great, king of the Franks and ever-august emperor of the Romans, died at Aachen, and there in the church of blessed Mary ever virgin, which he himself had built, was honorably buried, in the seventy-second year of his age, the forty-sixth of his reign over the Franks, and the thirteenth of his empire; he added no fewer provinces to the kingdom of the Franks than it had had before.

Louis king and emperor, son of Charles, 26 years.

Louis, according to the custom of the Sicambrians, who change L into V, a count in East Francia, with the consent of Saint Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, built the monastery of Schwarzach, not far from the Main, with the help of his wife Imma; he caused its church to be consecrated in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also in memory of the holy Mother of God and of the holy martyrs Sebastian and Felicity, and established monks of the order of the divine father Benedict there.

In the year of the Lord 817, Emperor Louis held an assembly of the princes at Aachen, in which he [unclear] Lothar, his firstborn, as his partner in the name and empire

On the Origin of the Franks.

there he appointed, the others being called kings; he set one over Aquitaine, another over Bavaria, [unclear], retaining for himself the kingdom of the Franks together with the empire.

In the year of the Lord 840, in the third indiction of the Romans, Louis, king of the Franks and emperor of the Romans, died and was buried in the church at Metz. After his death Lothar, under the name of emperor, held Italy; Pippin obtained Aquitaine; Charles, Gaul; and Louis, Germany.

The division of the kingdom of the Franks into two kingdoms, the German and the Gallican.

In the year of the Lord's nativity 861, from the entry of the Sicambri, or Franks, into the kingdom in Germany and the seats accepted at the mouths of the Rhine, the year 1280, in the fourth indiction of the Romans; in the 2030th year from the destruction of Troy, the three sons of King and Emperor Louis divided among themselves the very broad kingdom of the Franks, together with the empire of the Romans. In this division Lothar, as has been said, obtained Italy with the title of the Empire; Louis obtained Germany; Charles, Gaul; and Pippin their nephew, Aquitaine.

From that time the division of the kingdom of the Franks, begun as a twofold division, has remained, now for 673 years down to the present day, and will remain henceforth perpetual. This division, confirmed by the writings and law of the ancestors, made from one kingdom of the Franks two kingdoms, of which one is that of Germany, the other only of Celtica and Aquitaine. For the greater part of Belgic Gaul, in the later division, was adjudged to the kingdom of Germany; in that kingdom are these provinces, with their cities.

All Alemannia, or Swabia, with its cities: Constance, Basel, [Biriensibus?], the Helvetians, Lausanne, the people of Sion, who are also the Valaisians; also the Burgundy of Besancon; Lotharingia, Metz, Liege, Cambrai, Arras, Flanders, Holland, Zeeland, Brabant, Utrecht, Cologne, Trier, with the Mosellans, Mainz, Worms, and Speyer, with the [Cynonoti?] and [Westrasi?] and the Vosges people, Strasbourg with Alsace, and all the rest adjacent to these, belong to the kingdom of Germany, and are called cities of the German kingdom, not of the Roman Empire.

Next, all Germany is subject to this kingdom, in which are: the Frisians, Saxons, Hessians, Westphalians, [Hogij?], who are also the Wetterau people, Thuringians, Meisseners, the margraves of Brandenburg, Pomeranians, Rugi, people of Stettin, Holsteiners, Danes, Swedes, Norwegians, Prussians, Poles, Silesians, Sorbs, who also are the Bohemians of old and are called Slavs, Austrians, Carinthians, [Siturij?], Tyroleans, Bavarians, Rhaetians, and whatever lies among these. But it is also clear that all Italy, apart from the goods of the Church, by ancient right belonged to the kingdom of the Franks of Germany, under the rule of Charles the Great.

Therefore the king of Germany, whoever he may be for the time, has two things: the kingdom and the empire. To the kingdom he is elected by the princes and needs confirmation by no one; but to the empire, which is joined to the kingdom by right, he must be confirmed and anointed by the Roman pontiff. The kingdom is to be called by the name of the Germans, but the empire by the name of the Romans. Those who call Maximilian king of the Romans speak confusedly, since they ought rather to have said king of the Germans. Likewise those who say that Cologne, Trier, Liege, Metz, or other cities of Germany are imperial cities do not speak correctly, since they are royal cities. For if it should ever happen that the empire were taken away from the Germans, the kingdom of Germany would nevertheless remain, free as it now is, having subject to itself all the provinces and cities throughout all the places written above, as it has them subject today.

Louis, therefore, brother of the emperor, son of the elder Louis and grandson of Charles the Great, having obtained the kingdom of Germany in the division, reigned thirty years. After him his son, named Charles the Younger, was king of Germany and emperor of the Romans for eleven years; under him the kingdom was divided among his brothers. For he himself, with Germany, had the empire; Louis had East Francia; Charles, Alemannia; and Carloman, Bavaria, with his son Arnulf afterward obtaining the monarchy of the whole German kingdom and also of the empire. From this point the name of the Franks remained with Gaul to the kings of Gaul, and gradually began to depart from the Germans. We are German Franks; they, however, are Gauls.

1514.

End of the Compendium of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James at Wurzburg, on the origin of the people of the Franks, and also on their kingdom, name, and kings.

Boamun- dus. Ingramus. THEODO Rex Bauariae, post Adelgerum supra dictum ducem super Bauaros regna- vit, cuius geosta passim habentur dispersa. Theodo. Hie genuit Theobertum filium. 50 Tassilo dux Sclauos deuicit, construxit monasterium Laurisham, &amp; alia multa : O- thilo vero pater eiꝰ, inter alia etiam fundauit monasteriorum Altaha, ordinis sancti Benedicti in Bauaria, quod adhuc hodie exstat. Paul. Diac. 4.cap.2. Desiderio rege Lōgobard

Chronicle of the Succession of the Dukes of Bavaria and of the Counts Palatine, by Johannes Trithemius, Abbot: to Philip, Count Palatine, Prince-Elector.

Bavaria, as certain writers say, took its name and origin from a certain Duke Boiarus, whom they report to have come from Armenia into this region before the Trojan War with a great people. After the inhabitants had been driven out, being very rude and living like beasts on acorns, he committed the excellent land to cultivation by oxen.

Boiarus, the first duke of Bavaria, from whom the people and the region received their name, reigned in Bavaria for many years, and after him his sons down to the destruction of Troy; their names and deeds, because of their excessive antiquity, we do not know.

Norix, king of Bavaria, son of the most valiant Hercules, from whom Bavaria was afterward called Norica, built a notable city upon the Danube, which today is called Regensburg, and which Tiberius Caesar, a long time afterward, called Tiberina. Many dukes succeeded this Duke Norix in Bavaria at intervals of time down to Tiberius Caesar; their names and deeds antiquity has brought into oblivion.

Boamundus, duke of Bavaria, a noble prince, driven from Armenia by Tiberius Caesar, came into Bavaria with Ingramus, a man equally noble, and there reigned over the Bavarians for many years.

Adelgerus, duke of Bavaria, a brave and vigorous man, after Boamundus and Ingramus ruled the Bavarians for many years.

Theodo, king of Bavaria, after the aforesaid Duke Adelgerus, reigned over the Bavarians; his deeds are found scattered here and there.

Gerobaldus, king of Bavaria, in the time of the Emperor Maurice, was a most Christian man. Among other children he had a most devout daughter named Theodelinda, whom he gave as wife to Otharius, king of the Lombards; through her many good things were done in the Church of God. To this holy queen blessed Gregory wrote the four books of the Dialogues and many letters, in the year of the Lord 600.

Gondoaldus, king of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid Gerobaldus and brother of Queen Theodelinda, reigned after his father in Bavaria in the time of Childebert, king of the Franks, having under him Bavaria and Austria and the province of Noricum.

When Otharius, king of the Lombards, had died, Agilulf was elected king after him; he married his widow Theodelinda. Blessed Gregory asked her by letter to induce her husband to accept peace with the Romans, and she did so.

Childebert, king of the Franks, being at war with the Lombards, expelled Gondoaldus, the queen’s brother, from Bavaria, because he was bringing aid to the Lombards, and gave his duchy to Tassilo, son of Othilo, king of Bavaria. For Bavaria, being extensive, was at times subject to several princes.

Othilo, king of Bavaria, and afterward duke, was the father of Tassilo. He had as wife Hiltrud, sister of King Pippin, that is, the father of Charlemagne; by her he begot this same Tassilo.

Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, son of King Othilo, after his kinsman Gondoaldus had been expelled by Childebert, received his duchy from this same Childebert, king of the Franks. He had as wife Luitburg, daughter of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards, who bore him a son Theodo, whom Saint Rupert, bishop of Worms, baptized at Regensburg in the year of the Lord 561. This man begot a son Theobert.

Duke Tassilo defeated the Slavs, built the monastery of Lorsch, and many other things. Othilo, his father, among other things also founded the monastery of Altaha, of the Order of Saint Benedict in Bavaria, which still exists today.

CHRONICVM DVCVM BAVARIAe. 101 eo tandem perduxit, vt confoederatis sibi Hunnis in vindictam patris, Carolum magnum nepotem suum bello aggrederetur. Adrianus Papa, missis legatis ad Tassilonẽ ducem Bauariae, monuit eũ vt se Carolo subiiceret, qui precib. legatorum persuasus, venit Wormaciam ad imperatorem, legatis se comitantibus, ibique in fidem Caroli iurauit, sed non permansit in fide. Vnde ab Adria- no Papa fuit cum omnibus sibi adhaerentibus excommunicatus. Carolus à Roma post coronationem suam reuersus Wormatiam, Tassilonem ex principū consilio ad terminum vocauit, obedientiam &; fidelitatem ab eo exigit, sed Tas- filo nec ad conuentum principum venit, nec Imperatori volvit obedire. 10 Commotus Imperator, Bauariam ac Tassilonem bello aggressus, tribꝰ cinxit exer- citibus: Ipse cum vno exercitu castra posuit iuxta Augustam, &; inter Bauariam et Alema- niam, in loco qui dicitur Leche. Pipinus filius eius aduenit cum Italis in valle Tridentina, & Saxones eum Francis ad Danubium venientes, Bauariam triplici agmine circumdede- runt. Tandem dux Tassilio videns se imparem tantis exercitibus, veniam petit, cam- que impetrat dato filio suo Theodone cum aliis duodecim pro obsidibus in manus Im- peratoris. Carolus Pascha in Ingelheym celebrat, ibi iubet adesse ducem Tassilonem, qui cum venisset grauiter à Bauaris &; alijs fuit de infidelitate regi exhibita accusatus. Vnde cũ iudi- cio principum capitalem deberet subiire sententiam, indulgentia regis cuius consangui- 20 neus erat, ad poenitentiam cū Theodone filio in monasterium Laurisham detrufus, mul- ta postea sanctitate vixit. Hic Tassilo plurima monasteria in Bauaria fundauit, videlicet Wessenbron, Trem- munster, Laurishã, Weltenburg, &; Pfaffenmunster. Muros ciuitatis Patauiensis renoua- uit, &; sedem Episcopalem tunc transtulit ex Lauriaco. Sunt qui dicunt eum à Carolo Imperatore magno in carcere excaecatum, obiectu continuo duarum laminum ignitarum. Quomodoque uid sit, constat eum in Mona- sterio suo Laurisham, quod antea in Straramontensi non longeà Wormacia construxe- rat, magnis sumptibus, vitam sub regula diui Benedicti finisse, &; ibidem nō sine opinione sanctitatis sepultum ferunt. 30 Tassilone à ducatu deposito, &; Monasterium ingresso, Imperator ducatum Baua- riae, Geroldo comiti commisit, qui ab Hunnis (qui sunt Vngari) interfectus est, Anno do- mini, mccxcix. vt patet in Chronica Coloniensi. Eo tempore, quo sanctus Bonifacius Moguntinam regebat ecclesiam, Occarius et Albertus fratres &; clarissimi duces Noricum, viri fortes, nobiles ac deuotissimij amore videndi Romam adierunt. Quibus Zacharias Papa narrabat calamitatem quam ab infi- delibus patiebatur: vnde moti Christianissimi duces zelo fidei vna cum Romanis se armis praecingunt hostes fortiter inuadunt, spolia diripiunt, &; eos exire finibus ecclesiae com- pellunt: Spolia vero Romanis dimittunt, quoniam non pro bonis corporalibus, sed pro Dei honore se venisse &; pugnasse testabantur. Quibus Papa inter multas reliquias, quas 40 dedit, etiam corpus sancti Quitrini concessit. Hi duo sanctissimi duces in Norica prouincia multa fundarunt templa. NAYNVs dux Bauarie, tempore Caroli Imperatoris magni multa contra infide- les fortiter gessit à quibus tandem interfectus est, vir omnino zelo Christianae fidei ex- cellentissimus, vide caetera q̃ gessit in xxv. libro Vincentii capitulo xxi. Speculi. Eodem ferme tempore Lanfridus, Wairamus, & Hellandus principes Bauariae chri- stianissimi, multa bona ecclesie Dei exhibuerunt, pugnantes bella Domini cum magno feriore pietatis. Construxerunt inter alia quatuor monasteria, videlicet Burtochlarum, Schlechodorf, Scheplarum. Sciendum est, quod pater supra dictorum duorum fratrum, ducum Noricorum 50 Alberti &; Occarii fuit Burgundus, cuius vxor, mater corundem fuit Bauara. E quibus Occarius morabatur in Burgundia in principatu paterno: Albertus vero iunior annis xii. comitatus habebat in Bauaria. Hi duo apud Pippinum regẽ patrem Carolũ Mar- tellum, Gernoldum et Diogenẽ. Porto Carolus Martellus genuit Pippinum regẽ, patrem KAROLI Mag.n. Inu. per Morte orige. Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria

he finally brought it to the point that, with the Huns allied to him, in vengeance for his father he attacked Charlemagne, his kinsman, in war.

Pope Adrian, having sent legates to Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, warned him to submit himself to Charles. Persuaded by the entreaties of the legates, he came to Worms to the emperor, with the legates accompanying him, and there swore fealty to Charles; but he did not remain in fealty. Therefore he was excommunicated by Pope Adrian, together with all who adhered to him.

Charles, having returned from Rome to Worms after his coronation, summoned Tassilo, on the counsel of the princes, to an appointed day, and demanded obedience and fidelity from him; but Tassilo neither came to the assembly of the princes nor wished to obey the emperor.

The emperor, moved to anger, attacked Bavaria and Tassilo in war and surrounded them with three armies. He himself, with one army, set up camp near Augsburg, and between Bavaria and Alemannia, in the place called the Lech. Pepin his son arrived with the Italians in the valley of Trent, and the Saxons, coming with the Franks to the Danube, surrounded Bavaria with a threefold battle-line. At last Duke Tassilo, seeing that he was unequal to such great armies, sought pardon, and obtained it, giving his son Theodo, with twelve others, as hostages into the hands of the emperor.

Charles celebrated Easter at Ingelheim; there he ordered Duke Tassilo to be present. When he had come, he was gravely accused by the Bavarians and others of infidelity shown to the king. Therefore, although by the judgment of the princes he ought to have undergone a capital sentence, by the indulgence of the king, whose kinsman he was, he was thrust into the monastery of Lorsch for penance together with Theodo his son, and afterwards lived in great holiness.

This Tassilo founded very many monasteries in Bavaria, namely Wessobrunn, Kremsmünster, Lorsch, Weltenburg, and Pfaffenmünster. He renewed the walls of the city of Passau, and at that time transferred the episcopal see from Lauriacum.

There are those who say that he was blinded in prison by Charles the great emperor, by the continuous application of two heated plates. However that may be, it is agreed that in his own monastery of Lorsch, which he had previously built in [Straramontensi], not far from Worms, at great expense, he ended his life under the rule of Saint Benedict; and they say that he was buried there not without a reputation for holiness.

After Tassilo had been deposed from the duchy and had entered the monastery, the emperor entrusted the duchy of Bavaria to Count Gerold, who was killed by the Huns, who are the Hungarians, in the year of the Lord 1299, as is clear in the Cologne Chronicle.

At the time when Saint Boniface governed the church of Mainz, Occarius and Albertus, brothers and most illustrious dukes of Noricum, strong, noble, and most devout men, went out of love to see Rome. Pope Zacharias told them of the calamity that he was suffering from the unbelievers; wherefore the most Christian dukes, moved by zeal for the faith, armed themselves together with the Romans, bravely attacked the enemies, seized the spoils, and compelled them to leave the boundaries of the Church. But they left the spoils to the Romans, since they declared that they had come and fought not for bodily goods, but for the honor of God. Among the many relics which he gave them, the pope also granted them the body of Saint Quirinus. These two most holy dukes founded many churches in the province of Noricum.

Naynus, duke of Bavaria, in the time of the emperor Charles the Great, did many brave deeds against the unbelievers, by whom at last he was killed, a man altogether most excellent in zeal for the Christian faith. See the rest of what he did in the twenty-fifth book of Vincentius, chapter twenty-one, of the Speculum.

At almost the same time Lanfridus, Wairamus, and Hellandus, most Christian princes of Bavaria, bestowed many benefits on the church of God, fighting the wars of the Lord with a great fervor of piety. Among other things they built four monasteries, namely Burtochlarum, Schlechdorf, and Scheyern.

It should be known that the father of the two brothers named above, the dukes of Noricum Albertus and Occarius, was Burgundian, whose wife, their mother, was Bavarian. Of these, Occarius remained in Burgundy, in his paternal principality; but Albertus, younger by twelve years, held counties in Bavaria. These two, in the time of King Pepin, father of Charles Martel, [Gernoldum] and [Diogenem]. Further, Charles Martel begot King Pepin, father of Charles [unclear].

102 IOANNIS TRITHEMII Caroli magni, Carolomannum et Grifonem ducem Bauariae, ex Schuanahilde vxore, quae fuit filia ducis Bauarie. Griffo. GRIFFO iste Bauariam, ingressus, ducatum sibi iure haereditario vēdicare cupiens, Tassilonem ducem eiecit: Sed Pippinus rex, frater, ducatum Tassiloni restituit, &amp; Griffo-nem in Franciā duxit, dans ei duodecim ciuitates more Comitū. Qui minime contentus, multa in fratres bella cōmouit: vnde parum fortunatus quinto post anno interficitur. Expulso itaque Griffone de Bauaria per Pippinum fratrem, Tassilo ducatum obti-nuit, quem tandem Carolus magnus filius Pippini (vt dictum est) deposuit, &amp; prouinciā comitibus siue praefectis commisit. PIPPINVS itaque frater Griffonis genuit Carolum magnum. Qui post deditionē 10 Tassilonis ducis, Bauariam aliquanto tempore non per duces, sed per Comites fecit gu-bernari. Carolus autem genuit Ludouicum cognomento Pium, qui ei successit in Impe-rio, cuius secunda vxor fuit Iudith filia Welfi comitis Bauarie: vnde et amp; ducem eum seu re-gem Bauarie exactis comilibus constituit. Genuit et amp; Carolum, quem regem Alemaniae constituit, &amp; Pippinum, quem fecit regem Aquitanie et amp; Hispanie. Carolo magno Im-pe-ratore mortuo, &amp; Aquisgrani sepulto, Ludouicus dux Bauarie filius eius successorit. LVDOVIVS cognomento Pius, filius Caroli magni, &amp; postea Romanus Im-perator, habuit vxorem nomine Margaretham, ex qua tres filios suscepit: Lotharium, Pip-pinum, &amp; Ludouicum. Quorum primum Lotharium Bauarie praefecit, qui eriam post eū Imperator fuit. Mortua vxore Margaretha, aliam duxit nomine Iudith, filia Welfi co-mes Bauar. 20 gem Bauariae. exactis comilibus constituuit. Genuit et amp;amp; Carolum, quem regem Alemanniae constituit, &amp;amp; Pippinum, quomodocumque fecit regem Aquitaniae et Hispaniae. Carolum magnum imperatorem mortuo, &amp;amp; Aquisgraniorum sepulcro invenitur, Ludouicus dux Baiuariae filius eius successit. LVDOVICVS PRVST cognomento Pius Imperator, post multa egregie facta obijt, Metis sepultus, cui Lo-tharius filius eius rex Baiuariae successorit, contra quem fratres eius grauisissimum apud Altif-siodortum bellum moverunt, in quo multa millia hominum cecidisse antiquitas testatur. LOTHARIVS Istè Imperator, vxorem habuit Egillam filiam regis Angliae, qua pe-perit ei duos filios, Lotharium, &amp;amp; Ludouicum, qui ei in imperio succersit. Ab hoc Lotha-rio Lotharingiam appellatum esse ferunt LVDovicvs filius Ludouisci Pij Imperatoris, sublimato in imperium Lothario 30 fratre suo, ipse regnum Baiuariae et amp;amp; Alemaniae obtinuit, qui habuit tres filios: Carolum postea huius nominis terrium Imperatorem, Ludouicum regem Francorum, Carolo-mannum vltimum regem Baiuariae. Carolomanno rege Baiuariae mortuo, &amp;amp; in Etingem sepulcro, frater eius Ludouicus rex Francoxim Orientalium, sibi Bauariam subiugat, Arnolpho fratris filio dedit duca-tum Carinthie et amp;amp; Mosburgum. Et sic cessauerunt reges in Baiaria. LVDOVICVS frater Carolomanni, rex Francoxim Orientalium, habitò bello cũ Nordmannis, Francofordiae ad Moenum moritur, &amp;amp; in Monasterio Laurissam sepelitur, &amp;amp; Arnulphus ad ducatum Baiuariae redijt. Anno Domini DECCXLVI. Lotharius Imperator imperium deseruit, cū iam imperas-set annis XV. &amp;amp; assumpto peregrino habitu Monachus factus est in Monasterio Prumiensi, 40 ordinis sancti Benedicti. Cui Ludouisci filius in Imperio successit annis XXI. LVDovicvs huius nominis secundus, filius Lotharij Imperatoris, patri in imperio suc-cedens imperauit annis XLI. Cuius pater Lotharius ante imperiũ rex Baiuariae fuit Theodeberga filia Caroli calui patrui sui, quae peperit ei vnũ filium Carolũ nomine, &amp;amp; filiam vnam nomine Gillam, quam dedit Bosoni cuidam nobili, &amp;amp; fecit eum ducem Burgundiae. Postea dimi-sit imperium filio suo Carolo caluo, &amp;amp; monasteriorum ingressus obijt. CAROLVS CALVVS filius Ludouisci Pii Imperatoris, &amp;amp; Iudith filia Vulpi comitis Ba-uariae post Ludouicũ nepotē suum imperauit annis ferme quatuor, vxorē habuit Adeldru-dē sororem Bosonis ducis burgundiae, qua peperit ei filium Vnum Ludouicum nomine et amp;amp; duas filias Theobergam, quam dedit Ludouico regi nepoti suo vxorem, &amp;amp; Iudith vxo-rem Baldeuini comitis Flandrie. Istè Carolus multa Monasteria constructxit. CAROLO CALVO Imperatore mortuo, Carolus huius nominis tertius, frater Ca-duodecim, vxorē habuit Adelburgam filiā regis Granarie. Hic tandem horribili visione inferni territus, multos cognatorium suorum ob malā administrationem populi regnique, poenis grauisissimis torqueri iussit, imperioque dimisso, peregre profectus esse dicitur. Hic nō reliquit heredem, &amp;amp; cognomen eius erat Carolus grassisus. C A R O L O

Johannes Trithemius of Charlemagne, Carloman and Grifo, duke of Bavaria, by his wife Swanahild, who was the daughter of the duke of Bavaria.

Grifo. This Grifo, entering Bavaria, wishing to claim the duchy for himself by hereditary right, drove out Duke Tassilo. But King Pippin, his brother, restored the duchy to Tassilo and led Grifo into Francia, giving him twelve cities in the manner of counts. He, by no means content, stirred up many wars against his brothers; hence, with little fortune, he was killed in the fifth year thereafter.

Therefore, after Grifo had been expelled from Bavaria by his brother Pippin, Tassilo obtained the duchy; him at last Charlemagne, son of Pippin, as has been said, deposed, and entrusted the province to counts or prefects.

Pippin, therefore, the brother of Grifo, begot Charlemagne. After the surrender of Duke Tassilo, he caused Bavaria for some time to be governed not by dukes but by counts. Charlemagne begot Louis, surnamed the Pious, who succeeded him in the empire; his second wife was Judith, daughter of Welf, count of Bavaria; hence also he established him as duke or king of Bavaria after the counts had been driven out. He also begot Charles, whom he established as king of Germany, and Pippin, whom he made king of Aquitaine and Spain. When the emperor Charlemagne had died and been buried at Aachen, Louis, duke of Bavaria, his son, succeeded him.

Louis, surnamed the Pious, son of Charlemagne and afterward Roman emperor, had a wife named Margaret, by whom he received three sons: Lothar, Pippin, and Louis. The first of these, Lothar, he placed over Bavaria, and he also was emperor after him. When his wife Margaret had died, he married another, named Judith, daughter of Welf, count of Bavaria. [unclear] king of Bavaria, after the counts had been driven out. He begot also Charles, whom he established as king of Germany, and Pippin, whom in some way he made king of Aquitaine and Spain. When the emperor Charlemagne had died, and is found in the tomb at Aachen, Louis duke of Bavaria, his son, succeeded him.

Louis Prust, surnamed the Pious, emperor, after many distinguished deeds, died and was buried at Metz; Lothar his son, king of Bavaria, succeeded him. Against him his brothers waged a very grave war near Auxerre, in which antiquity testifies that many thousands of men fell.

Lothar. This emperor had as wife Egilla, daughter of the king of England; she bore him two sons, Lothar and Louis, who succeeded him in the empire. They say that from this Lothar Lotharingia was so named.

Louis, son of the emperor Louis the Pious: when his brother Lothar had been raised to the empire, he himself obtained the kingdom of Bavaria and Germany. He had three sons: Charles, afterward the third emperor of this name; Louis, king of the Franks; and Carloman, the last king of Bavaria.

When Carloman, king of Bavaria, had died and been buried at Ötting, his brother Louis, king of the eastern Franks, subjected Bavaria to himself and gave to Arnulf, his brother's son, the duchy of Carinthia and Moosburg. And thus kings ceased in Bavaria.

Louis, brother of Carloman, king of the eastern Franks, after a war had been fought with the Northmen, died at Frankfurt on the Main and was buried in the monastery of Lorsch; and Arnulf returned to the duchy of Bavaria.

In the year of the Lord 855, Lothar the emperor abandoned the empire, when he had already ruled for fifteen years, and, having assumed the garb of a pilgrim, became a monk in the monastery of Prum, of the order of Saint Benedict. Louis's son succeeded him in the empire for twenty-one years.

Louis, the second of this name, son of the emperor Lothar, succeeding his father in the empire, ruled for forty-one years. His father Lothar, before the empire, was king of Bavaria. Theutberga, daughter of Charles the Bald, his father's brother, bore him one son, named Charles, and one daughter, named Gilla, whom he gave to a certain nobleman Boso, and made him duke of Burgundy. Afterward he gave up the empire to his son Charles the Bald, and, entering monasteries, died.

Charles the Bald, son of the emperor Louis the Pious and of Judith, daughter of Welf, count of Bavaria, after Louis his nephew, ruled for almost four years. He had as wife Adeltrude, sister of Boso, duke of Burgundy; she bore him one son named Louis and two daughters, Theoberga, whom he gave as wife to King Louis, his nephew, and Judith, wife of Baldwin, count of Flanders. This Charles built many monasteries.

When the emperor Charles the Bald had died, Charles, the third of this name, brother of Ca[unclear], [unclear] twelve, had as wife Adelburga, daughter of the king of Granaria. He at last, terrified by a horrible vision of hell, ordered many of his relatives, because of their bad administration of the people and the kingdom, to be tormented with very severe punishments; and, having given up the empire, he is said to have set out abroad. He left no heir, and his surname was Charles the Fat.

Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria.

... Rudolf, duke of Bavaria, having been reduced to a count, he himself took up the duchy of Bavaria. And thus the duchy of Bavaria remained with the Saxons until Henry the Third, emperor; under him, when the stock of this Henry failed, the duchy reverted to the nephews of the aforesaid count Rudolf, as we shall say in its place. This duke Henry had as wife Lucardis, daughter of Arnold, duke of Bavaria, sister of the aforesaid count Rudolf; she bore him two sons, Bruno, margrave of Saxony, and Henry, later duke of Bavaria, and one daughter named Gerburg, abbess in Gandersheim.

And since we have said that all the modern dukes of Bavaria descended from the stock of Charlemagne, we must continue the line of descent from Count Rudolf, though the dukes of the Saxons were interposed for some years, until the duchy of Bavaria returned to the nephews of that Rudolf, so that the truth of what has been said may shine more clearly for all.

Rudolf, from duke become count of Bavaria, together with his brothers, pursued Duke Henry, the husband of his sister, as an invader of his paternal inheritance; he besieged and took Regensburg, and drove out Henry’s wife with her sons. Note that, when Arnold, duke of Bavaria, had died, Emperor Otto I had entrusted it to Berthold, his brother; and when he too had died, he appointed his own brother Henry duke, as has been said.

Welf, count of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid count Rudolf, had as wife Adelaide, daughter of the count of lower Baden; she bore him a son named Conrad, whose son Welf again obtained the duchy of Bavaria, as we shall say later.

Henry. Henry, duke of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid Duke Henry the Saxon, brother of Otto I, succeeding his father in the duchy of Bavaria, had as wife Bertha, daughter of the duke of Lotharingia; she bore him three sons and two daughters: two Henrys, of whom the elder was later emperor; Bruno, bishop of Augsburg; Gisela, wife of Saint Stephen, king of Hungary, who was converted to the faith of Christ; and Hedwig, whom Lothar, burgrave of Magdeburg, took as wife.

Conrad. Conrad, count of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid count Welf, had as wife a woman named Atza, daughter of the margrave of Mount Calym; she bore him three sons: Welf, who [unclear] the duchy.

Saint Henry, emperor and duke of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid Henry, duke of Bavaria, after Otto III had died without children, was made emperor of the Romans by election of the princes: a vigorous, devout, and most holy man, who did many good things in the commonwealth. He had as wife Cunegund, daughter of Sigfrid, count palatine of the Rhine, most holy in conduct and life; both remained in holiness until death through love of Christ, and both were also enrolled in the catalogue of the saints.

Note: the counties of Bavaria at this time were several, namely Trubensis, Valaisiensis, [unclear], Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt, Simon, archbishop of Bremen.

Henry, emperor and duke of Bavaria, son of the aforesaid Henry, duke of Bavaria, after Otto III had died without children, was made emperor of the Romans by election of the princes: a vigorous, devout, and most holy man, who did many good things in the commonwealth. He had as wife Cunegund, daughter of Sigfrid, count palatine of the Rhine, most holy in conduct and life; and both remained in holiness until death through love of Christ, and both were also enrolled in the catalogue of the saints.

Note: the counties of Bavaria at this time were several, namely Trubensis, Valaisiensis, Burchard, bishop of Hall, Simon, archbishop of Bremen.

Trube. Valey. When at length all the counts of Trube-Valey had died, their county [unclear]. Dachau, Andechs, Wittelsbach, Bogen, Kastl, Amertal, Scheyern. In the course of succession there were many counts in these places; to recount them all by name would be too lengthy and difficult.

When the count of Dachau had died, those three counties devolved upon the counts of Scheyern. The counts palatine of Wittelsbach were few; and when they too at length failed, the county in Wittelsbach also devolved upon Scheyern.

Henry, emperor from duke of Bavaria, among the many good things that he did, established the bishopric of Hamburg, and constructed the monastery of Monks’ Mountain of the Order of Saint Benedict [unclear]; Saint Cunegund, his most chaste wife, with help from her own patrimony, [unclear] with an army returns to her father.

In the year of the Lord 1005, Henry, the Bavarian emperor, entered Italy; in the siege of a certain castle he was captured, but, with the Lord’s help, was freed, lowering himself down through the wall.

Since the region of Bavaria is very broad, it was subject, at intervals of time, to different dukes at different times: sometimes to one, sometimes to two, and at times even to several.

Ernest. Ernest, duke of Bavaria, coming from the Maeotic Marshes into Bavaria, in the times of O[unclear].

Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria

After Charles III had been deposed from the empire, Arnulph, duke of Bavaria, son of Carloman, the last king of Bavaria, was made emperor by the consent of all. He ruled for twelve years, a powerful, wealthy, and fortunate man, who accomplished many outstanding things in the commonwealth. He had as wife Agnes, daughter of the emperor of the Greeks, by whom he had two sons, Arnold and Bernher. Arnold married Agnes, daughter of the king of Hungary; and his brother Bernher married her sister, likewise a daughter of the king of Hungary, named Beatrice. These two sisters, daughters of the king of Hungary, were baptized in the castle which the emperor Arnolph built in Bavaria, a very strong one, named Scheyern. Arnold obtained the duchy of the Noricans, and his brother Bernher received the county of Scheyern and the county of the Palatine of the Rhine. Arnold himself gave his daughter, named Adelheid, as wife to Otto, duke of Saxony; she bore a son named Henry, whom Arnold made duke of Bavaria, against the will of Bernhert, his count of Scheyern. And thus the duchy of Bavaria came for some time to the Saxons; but afterward it was again restored to the Bavarians.

When the empress Agnes, mother of the aforesaid Arnold and Bernher, had died, Arnolph took another wife, Lucard, daughter of Vulp, duke of Bavaria, by whom he had two sons: Louis, who succeeded him in the empire, and Conrad, father of Conrad, the first emperor, who was made duke of Lotharingia; and one daughter, named Lucard, whom the duke of the Saxons took as wife. He also had a son by a concubine, named Rindebald, whom his father afterward made king of Lotharingia, in the year of the Lord 896.

And so Arnold, son of the emperor Arnolph, duke of the Noricans, begot his daughter Adelheid for Otto, duke of the Saxons; she bore Henry, the above-named duke, and a daughter Adelheid, who later became abbess in Quedlinburg, a virgin of holy conduct.

Bernhard, his brother, count in Scheyern, begot by his wife Beatrice, daughter of the king of Hungary, Otto of Wittelsbach, count Palatine of the Rhine, and Echard, later count of Scheyern in Bavaria. Echard begot Arnold, Otto, and Conrad. Further, Arnold begot Conrad, called the Monk of Scheyern; and this Arnold was lord in Dachau, his brother Otto in Scheyern, and Conrad in Valley. From these three brothers, sons of Count Echard, many counts and princes of Scheyern took their beginning, so that at one time in a certain court of Vulp, duke of Bavaria, at a tournament, there were thirty-four counts, all descended from Scheyern, although not all of them dwelt there; for each one was established in his own lordship. And thus the castle of Scheyern, deprived of inhabitants and at length ruinous from age, was changed into a monastery in the year of the Lord 1304, as we shall say later. But all those thirty-four died within three years afterward, except two, Arnold of Dachau and Otto of Scheyern. This Arnold, lord of Dachau, begot Conrad; Conrad begot Arnold and Conrad; Arnold begot Conrad, duke of the Ruthenians, who was killed near Milan and buried in Scheyern.

The emperor Arnulph, powerful and an outstanding defender of the Christian faith, overcame the Normans in a fierce war, killed innumerable numbers of them, and drove them from the territories of the Christians after they had afflicted Germany for forty years. In the same war he killed Sigifrid, king of the Normans, and Gotfrid, king of the Danes. Returning from Gaul to Bavaria after the slaughter of the Normans, the emperor brought with him the body of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, which he placed at Regensburg in the monastery of Saint Hemeranus the martyr, where it is still honorably preserved today.

Conrad, by Lucard, the second wife of the emperor Arnulph, duke of Lotharingia, begot two sons, Eberhard, who was killed, and Conrad, afterward emperor of the Romans; Arnold, the aforesaid brother of his father, opposed him, as we shall say more fully later in its time.

After the capture of Rome, the defeat of the Northmen, and many other glorious deeds, the emperor Arnulph died. There are those who write that he was consumed by lice, which, growing from the excessively frequent eating of garlic, no one could ward off by any skill.

Louis, son of Arnulph, was a Bavarian emperor. After the emperor Arnulph had died,

Louis III, emperor:

Louis his son, the third of this name in the empire, succeeded him, born of Lucard, daughter of Vulp, duke of Bavaria; and thus by both parents he was Bavarian. He was the brother of Arnold, duke of the Noricans, and Bernher, count of Scheyern. He had as wife Lucard, daughter of Ludolph, duke of Saxony, sister of Otto, and died without children.

The Bavarians fight with the Hungarians and are defeated; to them Bavaria and Franconia

Johannes Trithemius

...while they were attacking fiercely, the Bavarians again make ready for battle, and, when the army of the emperor Louis comes up, they kill many of the Hungarians and turn the rest to flight. Conrad, duke of Lotharingia, brother of this Louis and son of Arnolph, a Bavarian by birth, was killed by the treachery of Adalbert, margrave of Bamberg.

Louis III, emperor of the Romans, son of the Bavarian emperor Arnolph, dies without children in the year of the Lord 813; after him Conrad, the son of his brother, is elected.

Conrad the emperor, born of a Bavarian father, the duke: when the emperor Louis, son of Arnolph, had died, Conrad, son of his brother Conrad, duke of Lotharingia, whom Adalbert, margrave of Bamberg, had killed, from the line of Charlemagne, was made the last emperor in the empire. He did not have a wife. Eberhard, of whom we shall speak later, [unclear].

Arnolph, duke of Bavaria, brother of Conrad, father of this Conrad, duke of the Romans, that is, son of the emperor Arnolph, opposed this emperor Conrad; defeated at length by him, he fled with his wife and children into Hungary, until the death of the aforesaid Conrad.

King Conrad, after Duke Arnolph had been driven out of Bavaria, planned in like manner to attack Henry, duke of the Saxons, and so he besieged Merseburg. There on the king’s side fell Eberhard his brother and Hatto, archbishop of Mainz, and he himself scarcely escaped. Thereafter Henry, duke of the Saxons, devastated all the king’s land. When King Conrad was about to die, he sent the crown of the kingdom to the above-mentioned Henry, duke of the Saxons, who reigned after him; and he died in Eastern Francia, buried at Würzburg.

Arnolph, duke of Bavaria, having heard of the death of King Conrad, returns from Hungary to Bavaria and is received by all with great honor, all asking that he deign to take up the kingdom of the Romans. Since Henry, duke of the Saxons, was succeeding in the kingdom, and all the princes except the aforesaid Arnolph, duke of Bavaria, obeyed him, Henry gathered his army and advanced against him in war, and besieged Regensburg. And Duke Arnolph, seeing that he could not resist so great a multitude, opened the gates, sought favor, and obtained it. Accordingly a very firm peace is made between them under these conditions: that the king confer upon Duke Arnolph the full fief or lordship over all the bishoprics in Bavaria, leave him to possess his duchy peacefully, and hold him chief among his friends; and so it was done. And so Henry remained in the kingdom. When he died, Otto I, his son, succeeded; after him Otto II, son of the first; then Otto III, son of the second, who died without children. And Henry, duke of Bavaria, succeeded the aforesaid in the empire by election, as we shall say later in its place.

Under Otto I the emperor there was a very grave war between the Christians and the Hungarians. At that time they were still unbelievers at Augsburg, where the emperor himself triumphed with the Christians. There fell Conrad, duke of Bavaria, and Count Theobald, brother of Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg.

The cause of the war [unclear] just: Count Bernher was claiming the duchy of Bavaria as the legitimate heir; the sons of his brother, one of whom was emperor, opposed him. Moved by this, he summoned the Hungarians, asking for aid. After Count Bernher of Scheyern was killed by the Hungarians, Eberhard and Bernher, his sons, succeeding in the place of their father, were claiming the duchy of Bavaria, which Eberhard at last [unclear], as we shall say.

Arnolph, duke of the Noricans, dies, leaving, among other children, Duke Rudolph after him, and a daughter named Lucarda, whom Henry, duke of Saxony and later also of Bavaria, son of Henry I the emperor and brother of Otto I, took as wife, as we shall say later.

Rudolph, duke of Bavaria after the death of the aforesaid Henry I, rebels against Emperor Otto, his son; hence from duke of Bavaria he was made count in Scheyern.

Henry the Saxon, duke of Bavaria, son of Henry I the emperor, and brother of Otto I, and

ERNESTVS iunior dux Noricorum,filius supradicti ducis Ernesti mortuo patre , mini- sterio se dedit magistrorum,vt sermonẽ Latinum, Graecum, Italicum disceret, qui post- ca miranda fecit. HENRICVS comes Palatinus Rheni,amicus Othonis Imperatoris,huncducem Erne- stum odio habens, apud Imperatorem vitricum grauiter solebat (licet iniuste) accusare, quasi vitae imperij ipsius infidiatorem,quod Ernestum minime latebat: vnde cum Im- perator quadã die in ciuitate Spirensi cõfilio comitis Henricii,cIausis ianuis secreto vtere- tur,Ernestus comitate se Wetzlo comite inpatruo,irompensianuas confregit,Henricũ Palatinũ in latereImperatis sedẽtem interfecit,assumptaque deinde cruce,cũ Wetzelino patruo multis alijs, ad terrã sanctã perrexit.Sed mora in mari tempestate.omnes praeter ipsum multa egregia facta,terra marique in multis regionibus longinquis patrauit, quae habentur in scriptis.Reuersus deinde cum Wetzelino comite in patriam , plures attulit homines diuersarum nationum formarum.Imperator autem comperta eius innocen- tia,ad gratiam suam filium recepit,constituens eum dominatorem principem totius curiaeimperialis. Anno domini,MVIII. sanctus Henricus Imperator dux Bauariae,comitem Flandriae Baldevvinum sibi rebellem vicit,sibique subdidit, Gandauum cepit,Bolislaumque du- cem Poloniae Saxones crebro depraedantem,facta congressione superauit, ad fidẽ Chri- sti cum gente sua conuertit,habens in exercitu sanctum Stephanum regem Vngariae soro- ris suae virum. Henricus sanctus Imperator obijt anno domini MXXV.Bamberga in maiori Ecclesia quam ipse construxerat sepultus,cuius gesta in scriptis habentur.Conradus dux Franco- niaein imperium sucessit,post quem Henricus tertius, post illum quartus Imperator. HENRICVS dux Bauarie,frater Conradi ducis Sueuiae,post sanctum Henricum ex duce Imperatorem,Ducatum Bauariae obtinuit.Hic construxit monasterium in Osterhofen, in Patauiensi dioecesi:regnum Bernhardus Ecchardus tandem (vt supra diximus) obti- nuerunt. CVNO,dux Noricorum,filius Eechardi ducis supradicti,Ducatum Bauariae quem pater obtinuit,post mortem eius assumpsit.Hie foedus inijt cum Vngaris, quos en auxilium cõ- tra Henricum Imperatore tertium inuocauit,anno Domini MLIIII. CVNO dux Noricorum,tandem ab Henrico Imperatore de Bauaria pulsus,fugit ad Vn- garos.Anno Domini MLV.Ibique quam diu vixit,in exilio permansit.Imperator fratri suo Conrado Ducatum eius donauit,qvi paulo post obijt. CONRADVS dux Bauarie,frate Imperatoris Henrici quarti,expulso Cunone,ducatum eius ab Imperatore suscepit, qui non longe postea mortuus est , anno videlicet Domini MLVI. AGNES imperatrix,mater Henrici quarti,pof mortem Conradi supradicti, ducatum Bauariae à filio suscepit,quem post aliquot annos Othoni cuidam nobili degente Saxo- nũ donauit,de quo postea dicemus.Anno Domini M LXI.Agnes imperatrix,mater Hen- rici Imperatoris quarti,ducatum Bauariae Othoni comiti de Northeym contulit, ipsa in Italiam perrexit. OTHO dux Bauaria,genere Saxo,comes in Northeym, ducatum Bauariae ab impera- trice vt dictum est accepit,vir nobilis,strenuus,iustus,in Aula regis Henrici potens acce- ptiffimus.Ortho dux Bauarie praedictus,monasterium praedicti ordinis sancti Benedicti in Northeym fundauit,donans illi plura praedia, dona comitatus sui.Otho iste dux Bua- ria,cum clarus esset in aula regis Henrici, acquireret sibi authoritatem publicam,inui- dia quorundam impiorum hominum , per quendam subordinatum iniuste accusatus, quod

Johannes Trithemius

... of Emperor Otto I, obtained the duchy of the Norici. The same Emperor Otto gave him a part of the forest in the province of the Norici, namely in that place where the Castellense monastery of the order of Saint Benedict now stands; after rooting out the woods, he made the land fit for ploughs. From this duke Ernest many notable lords of Bavaria descended in the Norican province, especially the counts of Castello-Sultzbach.

This Ernest, duke of the Norici, had as wife Adelheid, daughter of the duke of Burgundy, who bore him a son named Ernest, of whom marvelous things are told. When Duke Ernest the elder died, Emperor Otto I joined his wife Adelheid, mother of the younger Ernest, to himself in marriage; she bore him Otto II, emperor, and a daughter Mechthild, who was abbess in Quedlinburg.

Ernest the younger, duke of the Norici, son of the aforesaid Duke Ernest, after his father’s death, gave himself to the service of masters, so that he might learn Latin, Greek, and Italian speech; afterwards he did marvelous things.

Henry, count palatine of the Rhine, a friend of Emperor Otto, hating this duke Ernest, was accustomed to accuse him gravely before the emperor his stepfather, though unjustly, as if he were plotting against the life of the empire itself; this was by no means hidden from Ernest. Hence, when the emperor one day in the city of Speyer was secretly engaged with the son of Count Henry, with the doors closed, Ernest, with Count Wetzel his uncle accompanying him, burst in, broke down the doors, killed Henry the palatine as he was sitting at the emperor’s side, and then, having taken up the cross, went with Wetzel his uncle and many others to the Holy Land. But after a delay at sea in a storm, all except himself [unclear]; he accomplished many outstanding deeds, on land and sea, in many distant regions, which are preserved in writings. Then, returning with Count Wetzel to his homeland, he brought back several men of diverse nations and forms. The emperor, when he had learned of his innocence, received his son back into his favor, appointing him ruling prince of the whole imperial court.

In the year of the Lord 1008, Saint Henry the emperor, duke of Bavaria, defeated Baldwin, count of Flanders, who was rebelling against him, and subjected him to himself; he took Ghent, and, after an engagement, overcame Boleslaus, duke of Poland, who was repeatedly plundering the Saxons, and converted him with his people to the faith of Christ, having in his army Saint Stephen, king of Hungary, his sister’s husband.

Saint Henry the emperor died in the year of the Lord 1025, and was buried at Bamberg in the greater church which he himself had built; his deeds are preserved in writings. Conrad, duke of Franconia, succeeded to the empire; after him Henry III, and after him the fourth emperor.

Henry, duke of Bavaria, brother of Conrad, duke of Swabia, after Saint Henry, from duke became emperor and obtained the duchy of Bavaria. He built a monastery in Osterhofen, in the diocese of Passau; Bernard and Eckhard at length obtained the kingdom, as we said above.

Cuno, duke of the Norici, son of the aforesaid Duke Eckhard, took up the duchy of Bavaria, which his father had held, after his death. He entered into a treaty with the Hungarians, whom he called to his aid against Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1054.

Cuno, duke of the Norici, at length driven out of Bavaria by Emperor Henry, fled to the Hungarians in the year of the Lord 1055. There, as long as he lived, he remained in exile. The emperor gave his duchy to his brother Conrad, who died a little later.

Conrad, duke of Bavaria, brother of Emperor Henry IV, after Cuno had been expelled, received his duchy from the emperor; he died not long afterward, namely in the year of the Lord 1056.

Agnes the empress, mother of Henry IV, after the death of the aforesaid Conrad, received the duchy of Bavaria from her son; after some years she gave it to a certain noble Otto, living among the Saxons, of whom we shall speak later. In the year of the Lord 1061, Agnes the empress, mother of Emperor Henry IV, conferred the duchy of Bavaria on Otto, count of Northeim; she herself went into Italy.

Otto, duke of Bavaria, a Saxon by race, count in Northeim, received the duchy of Bavaria from the empress, as has been said: a noble, vigorous, and just man, powerful and very acceptable in the court of King Henry. The aforesaid Otto, duke of Bavaria, founded in Northeim a monastery of the aforesaid order of Saint Benedict, giving it many estates, gifts from his county. This Otto, duke of Bavaria, since he was distinguished in the court of King Henry and was acquiring public authority for himself, was unjustly accused, through a certain subordinate, by the envy of certain impious men, that

180
CHRONICON DVCVM BAVARIAe. 107 quod in necem regis cõspirasset, primum à curia, deinde etiam à ducatu pulsus, cum prin- cipibus Saxoniae et Thuringię bellum contra Imperatorem gerit. Ducatum Bauariae Vul- pi seu Welff obtinuit. VULPI qui et Weilff. dux Bauariae, filius Conradi comitis Bauariae, ducatum Baua- riae, quem proauigenitoris fui ante possiderunt, post Orthonem ab Imperatore vt legiti- mus haeres recepit. Nam proauicus eius Rudolphus, filius Arnolphi ducis Baiuariae dux fuit, qui rebellans Otthoni Imperatori primo, & victus ab eo, ex duce comes de Scheyern fa- ctus fuit, sicut supra dictum est. Restituto itaque ducatu Bauariae ad lineam Arnolphi Imperatoris, seriem genera- tioneis ducatum ex Carolo Magno descendentium inceptam prosequamur. Nec sum nescius, quofdam inter scriptores hunc ducem Weiff natione Sueuum, nonnullos vero Italiam filium cuiuidam Marchionis fuisse aufos contendere. Constat autem filium e- um fuiffe Contradi comitis Baiuariae, filij Arnolphi ducis et Imperatoris Romano- rum. Nee refert vbi natus sit, modo generationis series, Baiuariae ducibus legitimis constet descendisse. Itaque dux iste Welff desponsauit sibi vxorem Ethelinam filiam ducis Otthonis co- mitis Northeymensis supradicti: Sed pulfo à ducatu Orthone, filiam ei remisit, veritus Henricum regem à quo ducatum acceperat, qui inimicus erat Otthonis, quam Herman- nus comes Postea duxit in vxorem relictam vi- duam regis Angliae, quae peperit ei tres filios, & vnam filiam, Henricum cognomento Ni- grum, qui dux Baiuariae post eum fuit, Vulpi, qui in Italiam perrexit, Sigeberturn, & Adel- heydam, quam Conradus Burggrauius Medeburgensis duxit vxorem. OTTHO quondam dux Bauariae et comes in Northeym, contra Imperatorem in Saxonia multa praelia habuit, in quorum vno Ernestus Marchio Baiuariae, filius Ernesti du- cis tenoris (qui laepe victor in Vngaria et diuerfis alijs regionibus extiterat) occubuit, an- no Domini MLXXV. Caetera, quae Ottho praefatus cum Saxonibus contra Imperatorẽ fecit, & ab eo passus fuit, & quomodo tandem ad gratiam eius receptus est, scripta copiofissime per Lamper- tam Monachum Hirsfeldensem * in geffis ipsius Henrici Imperatoris habentur, quae ni- mis taedofum eft hic exprimere. WELFF, dux Baiuariae cognito quod iniufe Saxones à rege Henrico premerentur, noluit ei contra cosdem auxiliũ praebere, vnde et hostis reipublicae iudicatus, etiam ab eo ducatu priuatus eft: fed iterum in gratiam ab Imperatore receptus, non folum ducatum recipere meruit, fed etiam filium suum in ducem Baiuariae confirmari. Deinde cruce fi- gnatus tempore Vrbani Papae secundi, anno Domini MCVI. ad terram sanctam profe- ctus eft, & Cypro mortuus, & sui pene omnes, cum multis alijs Christianis, infidijs Alexij Imperatoris Graeorum perpetui et capti fuht. Iste dux Welff inter alia quae fecit, construxit Monasteria, videlicet Steyngarden, Altorff, Vvingarten, Altenmunfter, & Nietenbach. Quo mortuo, & in monasterio Artes- heym sepulto, Henricus cognomento Niger, ei in ducatu Baiuariae successit. Sunt qui scri- bunt hunc ducum Welff post mortem luttae vxoris suae, matrem Henrici quarti Impera- toris, Agnetam duxisle vxorem. ECCHARDVS dux Bauariae, frate Wrernheri de Scheyren, qui prò recuperando patris ducatu Vngaros tertio contra Imperatorem eduxit, de quo supra dictum eft, tempore Vr- bani Papae secundi; cum Gotfrido duce Lotharingia cruce signatus, ad terram sanctam profectus eft, & Hierufalem à Christianis recuperata fuit. Fuit etiam his temporibus Ot- thonis Episcopi Bambergensis, & Fridericum comitem in Ammerthal, qui monasterio Castellensi iacet sepultus. Hic habuit filiam nomine Sophiam, quam dedit vxorem Otho dux Baiuariae in Ammerthal, filius (vt quibusdam placet) Ernesti, qui in monasterio Castelleni multa bona fecit, ibidemque sepultus eft. HENRICVS dux Bauariae cognomento Niger, filius Welff ducis supradicti, ha- buit vxorem Wolffhildem filiam Magni ducis Luneburgensis: qua peperit ei duos filios, & quatuor filias. Henricum, Weilff, Sophiam, quam dedit Bertholdo duci Thu- ringiae, quo occifo, Marchionem Steyredensem Lupoldum secundũ accepit maritum. Se- cunda filia vocabatur Vvolff hildis, quã dedit Rudolpho comiti Praegnicenfi. Tertiã no-

Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria.

because he had conspired for the murder of the king, he was driven first from the court and then also from the duchy, and waged war against the emperor with the princes of Saxony and Thuringia. Welf, or Welff, obtained the duchy of Bavaria.

Welf, also called Welff, duke of Bavaria, son of Conrad, count of Bavaria, received from the emperor, as the legitimate heir, the duchy of Bavaria after Otto; his forefathers had possessed it before. For his great-grandfather Rudolph, son of Arnolph, duke of Bavaria, had been duke; rebelling against Otto, the first emperor of that name, and defeated by him, he was made count of Scheyern from duke, as was said above.

Thus, after the duchy of Bavaria had been restored to the line of the emperor Arnolph, let us continue the sequence of generations of the dukes descending from Charlemagne, begun earlier. I am not unaware that some among the writers have dared to maintain that this duke Welf was a Swabian by nation, while others say that he was an Italian, the son of a certain marquis. But it is established that he was the son of Conrad, count of Bavaria, son of Arnolph, duke and emperor of the Romans. Nor does it matter where he was born, provided that the sequence of descent is established to have come down to the lawful dukes of Bavaria.

Therefore this duke Welff betrothed to himself as wife Ethelina, daughter of the aforesaid duke Otto, count of Northeim. But when Otto was driven from the duchy, he sent the daughter back to him, fearing King Henry, from whom he had received the duchy and who was Otto's enemy. Count Hermann afterward took her as his wife, left as a widow by the king of England. She bore him three sons and one daughter: Henry, surnamed the Black, who was duke of Bavaria after him; Welf, who went into Italy; Sigebert; and Adelheid, whom Conrad, burgrave of Magdeburg, took as wife.

Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria and count in Northeim, had many battles against the emperor in Saxony; in one of them Ernest, marquis of Bavaria, son of Duke Ernest [unclear], who had often been victorious in Hungary and in various other regions, fell, in the year of the Lord 1075.

The other things that the aforesaid Otto did with the Saxons against the emperor, and suffered from him, and how at last he was received back into his favor, are written very fully by Lampert, the monk of Hersfeld, in the deeds of that Emperor Henry; it would be too tedious to set them out here.

Welf, duke of Bavaria, learning that the Saxons were being unjustly oppressed by King Henry, refused to give him aid against them; whence he too was judged an enemy of the commonwealth and was also deprived by him of the duchy. But afterward, received again into the emperor's favor, he deserved not only to recover the duchy but also to have his son confirmed as duke of Bavaria. Then, having taken the cross in the time of Pope Urban II, in the year of the Lord 1106 he set out for the Holy Land, and died in Cyprus; and almost all his men, with many other Christians, were destroyed and captured through the treachery of Alexius, emperor of the Greeks.

This duke Welff, among other things that he did, built monasteries, namely Steingaden, Altdorf, Weingarten, Altenmunster, and Nietenbach. When he died and was buried in the monastery of [Artesheym?], Henry, surnamed the Black, succeeded him in the duchy of Bavaria. Some write that this duke Welff, after the death of his wife Jutta, took as wife Agnes, the mother of Emperor Henry IV.

Ecchard, duke of Bavaria, brother of Werner of Scheyern, who for the recovery of his father's duchy brought the Hungarians out for the third time against the emperor, of whom mention was made above, in the time of Pope Urban II, took the cross with Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, and set out for the Holy Land, and Jerusalem was recovered by the Christians. There was also in these times Otto, bishop of Bamberg, and Frederick, count in Ammerthal, who lies buried in the monastery of Kastl. He had a daughter named Sophia, whom Otto, duke of Bavaria in Ammerthal, son, as some think, of Ernest, took as wife; he did many good things for the monastery of Kastl and was buried there.

Henry, duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Black, son of the aforesaid duke Welff, had as wife Wulfhild, daughter of Magnus, duke of Luneburg. She bore him two sons and four daughters: Henry, Welf, Sophia, whom he gave to Berthold, duke of Thuringia; after he was killed, she took Leopold II, marquis of Steyr, as husband. The second daughter was called Wulfhild, whom he gave to Rudolph, count of [Praegnicen?]. The third

HENRICVS enim dux Bauariae et Saxoniae, gener Lotharij, qui genuit ex Gertrade vxore sua Henricum cognomento Leonem, de quo vulgus miranda refert. 20 quod cum Griffonibus pugnauerit, Leonem abduxerit, de maris periculo, per Grif-fonem insutus corio equino portatus fuerit.
