Catharina vero tali nomine digniffima, Diuae sibi cognominis exemplum imitata, spretis ca- 120 IOAN. TRIT. CHRON. DVCVM BAVARIAe. ducarum rerum illecebris, sponsum sibi Christum quaesiuit. Tanta prosapia Palatinorum! tot Episcopii vbi quis tantum recensendis nominibus defatigaretur: tot ex illa progenie Bohemiae, Dania, Vngariae, ac Romanorum Reges prodierunt, vt si opinione ma- iorum niti oporteat, non fit Germaniaꝫ progenies, cui plus de- beat nobilitas. Haec Irenicus lib. 3. Exeges. Ger- man. cap. 50. CATALO'

Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria

son, and brother of Louis and Frederick: what he suffered, and how, and by whose treachery he was captured, even boys in the streets, so to speak, know; on this occasion there is no need to set it out in writing.

Now let us pursue the sequence of the Counts Palatine of the Rhine and Dukes of Bavaria, descended indeed from Rudolf, but divided into another line, after King Rupert and his son Stephen, with John and Otto of Mosbach.

Christopher, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of John, son of Rupert, king of the Romans, after the death of Erik, king of Dacia, Norway, and Sweden, took as wife the daughter of John, Margrave of Brandenburg. When he had had her for three years, [unclear] without children. He was buried at Helmensberg.

Frederick, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Stephen of Zweibruecken, [unclear] son, [took as wife] Margaret, daughter of the Duke of Guelders, who bore him John, heir of the paternal possession; Stephen, dean of the church of Cologne; Frederick, canon and cantor of the church of Mainz; Rupert, bishop of Regensburg; and William, canon of Trier, who died as a young man in Trier. This Frederick, a just and pious prince, died in the year of the Lord 1480, and was buried in the choir of the monastery of the regulars at Ravengiersburg.

Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Stephen of Zweibruecken, son of Rupert, king of the Romans, took as wife Margaret, daughter of the Duke of Guelders, who bore him Caspar, Alexander, and John. The wars that took place between him and Frederick, Count Palatine of the Rhine, prince and guardian of our Philip, and how great were the losses he suffered from them, are known to all round about.

Rupert, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Stephen, son of Rupert, king of the Romans, was bishop in the church of Strasbourg.

Stephen, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Stephen, son of Rupert, king of the Romans, was bishop in the church of Cologne.

John, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Stephen, son of Rupert, king of the Romans, a learned man and most renowned for integrity of morals, was first bishop of Muenster and afterward archbishop of Magdeburg. Many heralds of praise concerning him present themselves to me, which at present are not to be entrusted to the service of the pen. In the year of the Lord 1475 he died, not without suspicion of poison.

Otto, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of the elder Otto of Mosbach, [unclear] of Rupert the king, and brother of the above-mentioned younger Otto, is bishop of Strasbourg. See [Wimphelingius?]. [unclear] wrote, and many letters; we have only these few things from Irenicus. We shall append them.

Frederick was succeeded by Philip, whom Rudolf Agricola, Jerome Aleander, and Jakob Wimpheling, men of the greatest weight, testify to have surpassed so many mortals in piety, magnanimity, clemency, and in every measure of virtue. He was most handsome both in the strength of his limbs, in the endowments of marriage, and in the habit of his body; and he would have been most fortunate, had the German wars raged less against him. Eight sons survived him, so great a hope of descendants. Dying, he handed over the Palatinate to the elder Louis; Bavaria to the sons of the deceased Rupert, over whom he placed Frederick, a most accomplished duke. Three others act as prelates; the remaining two are very great provosts. Among the daughters, Elizabeth, the eldest by birth, as Alexander says, was given in marriage to Philip, Margrave of Baden; Amelia to the Duke of Pomerania; Helena to the man of Mecklenburg: three heroines to as many heroes and to the greatest princes in Germany. Catherine, however, most worthy of such a name, imitating the example of the saint who shared her name, despised the enticements of perishable things and sought Christ as her bridegroom. So great was the lineage of the Palatines! So many bishoprics, that one would be wearied merely by recounting the names; so many kings of Bohemia, Denmark, Hungary, and of the Romans came forth from that stock, that if one must rely on the opinion of the ancestors, there is no family in Germany to which the nobility owes more.

This is Irenicus, book 3 of the Exegesis of Germany, chapter 50.

12I CATALGVS ILLVSTRIVM VIORVM GERMANIAM SVIS INGE- NIIS ET LVCVRATIONIBVS OMNIFARIAM EXORNAN- TIVM DOMINI IOHANNIS TRITHEII ABBATIS SPANHEMENSIS ordinis sancti Benedictiti: ad Iacobum Wimpfelingum Sletstatinum Theologum. EPISTOLA MAGISTRI MATTHEI HERBENI TRAIECTENSIS, AD INSIGNEM VIRVM IODOCVM BEYSELIVM, PATRICIVM AQVENSEM. CVM nuper è solo paterno ad vteriores Germanie partes profeclurus discedens, ad Aquasgrani peruenissem, teque Iodoc amicorum obferuandissime pro vete- ri iam prope nostra coniunctione at que amicitia salutandi gratia domi conue- nissim. accepi in mandatis vt in ea peregrinatione doctissimos quosdant viros (Germanos quidem) gratia et benevolentia tibi obstrictos, aqus in partibus Rheni haberes adirem, & ex tuo nomine salutarem. Postiquam igitur eo loci navigio applicuissem vbi Nahus apud Pingiones Rheno influens, iter per Crui zennachum euntibus monstat ad Spanhem: mox enolo ē naui, ad Trisbe- mium abbatem ciuis coenobij me accingo: saluto primum deinde literas tuas trado. Prouinde ita abeo amplector, vt neque lautijs neque elementius à magno prelato excepti postuissem. Vbi autem occasio deambulandi concessa est (quod plerique post primorum amicorum congreguss, atq́ue refecliones fùt) circumfert me, atq́ue illico in admirandam bibliothecā suam introducit: vbi plurima tum Hebrae- ium Graeca volumina intucor. Nam latinorum in omni arte, scientia et facultate ingens copia e- rat. Demiror itaq́; vnius hominis in tam varijs monumentis consequendis constituendisq́ue exa- dam diligentiam, atq́ue vehementer obstupesco, enim in tota Germania non existimauerim tantum peregrinorum voluminium extitisse. Nam quinque linguarum (sermone et caractere a se longe di- stantium) libros in codicibus perantiquis illie repeeri: quos Trithemiꝰ vigilans sinduum non sine multo sudore comportauit. Hoc igitur modo (Iodoce doctissime) fulciram inuenti Spanhemensem biblio- thecam. Nequeeam solum verum etiam et parietes totius domus abbatialis (quae ampla est) & testu- dines camerarum, Grecis, Hebracis, Latinis verbis characteribusq́ue decentissime ornatas apsexi. Quamobrem ego quoque ita mecum reputo, si in Germania nostra Hebreae academia fit ea Spanhemense eanobium est: vbi plus eruditionis concipere possib; ex parietibus, quam multorum aliorum puluerulentis atque, librorum inanibus bibliothecis. Quiequid enim antiquitatis et eruditionis Germania in librjs habere potest: monasterium Spanhemensj Trithemio abbate procurante possidet. Mansi autem apud abbatem nostrum dies vndecim non sine exacta memoria tui: vbi cum quadam die inter loquendum in eius libro sermonem, qui de scriptoribus ecclesiasticis est editus incideremus: intuli mirari me tam preciaros scriptores, quos in eo libro cognoueram Germaniam nostram habusse, & etiā bodierna die habere meminisseq́; à qnodam doctissimo philosopho Italico audisse, neminē se vnqua̓do- ctum Germanum praeter vnnum Albertū Magnum legendo vsquam comperisse. Tum vero abbas subri- dens, eo inquit magis igitur credendū est Italos germanorū laudes in scriptis suis ex professo praeteriisse: quoque aliorū praeteritione suoriꝰ gloria maior videretur. Possium quidē tibi palam facere multo plures vetustissimos atque, celeberrimos Germanos scriptores extitisse qua̓ in libro meo de scriptoribus eccleßia- sticis agnouisti. Et producens ex biblio: heca illa sua ingentē librū, nihil nisi Germanie doctissimos scri- ptores et sanctissime memorie viros comprahendentē ostendit: quē vt inspexi, acipi iustantiffime orare atque obsecrare (quod te et quemlibet doctum virum fecisse non ambigo) efficeret ne tantā gloria ma- torum nostroru̇ Germania nostra deinceps orbę degert: curaretq́; primo quoque die officine impressorie mandaretur. Effecturus enim quo excusus lectione aque imitatione plures sanclos viros et bonarum artium studiosos essemus habituri. Exoraui itaque abbatem qui se aliquin facilem praebet amicis: ipsum- que volumen ad laudem Germaniae nostre obtinui imprimendum. Hac sunt Iodoce suauissime, que apud dominum abbatem Spanhemensem agnout: vidi, effeci: que longioris more impatiens ade re scribere institui. Vale. Excoenobio Spanhemensi xxx. calend. septembrijs. Anno virginē partius millefi- mo ccccxcv. L

Catalogue of Illustrious Men Who Adorn Germany in Every Way by Their Talents and Lucubrations, by Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, to Jakob Wimpfeling of Sélestat, Theologian.

Letter of Master Matthaeus Herbenus of Maastricht to the Distinguished Man Jodocus Beyselius, Patrician of Aachen.

[unclear]

When recently I was leaving my paternal soil to set out for the further parts of Germany, and had come to Aachen, and had met you at home, Jodocus, most worthy of regard among friends, for the sake of greeting you, in view of our now almost long-standing association and friendship, I received instructions that on that journey I should visit certain very learned men, Germans indeed, bound to you by favor and goodwill, whom you had in the regions of the Rhine, and greet them in your name.

After therefore I had landed by boat at the place where the Nahe, flowing into the Rhine near Bingen, shows the road through Kreuznach to those going to Spanheim, soon, having left the boat, I make my way to Trithemius, abbot of that monastery. First I greet him, and then hand over your letters. Accordingly he embraces me so that I could not have been received more splendidly or more graciously by a great prelate.

But when an opportunity for walking about was granted, which for most people comes after the gatherings and refreshments of first friends, he leads me around, and immediately introduces me into his admirable library, where I behold very many Hebrew and Greek volumes. For of Latin books in every art, science, and faculty there was an immense abundance. And so I marvel at the exact diligence of one man in acquiring and arranging such varied monuments, and I am vehemently astonished; for I would not have thought that in all Germany there existed so great a number of foreign volumes. For I found there books of five languages, widely differing from one another in speech and character, in very ancient codices, which Trithemius, wakeful and assiduous, had brought together not without much toil.

In this way, therefore, most learned Jodocus, I found the library of Spanheim furnished. Nor that alone, but I also saw the walls of the whole abbatial house, which is spacious, and the vaults of the rooms most fittingly adorned with Greek, Hebrew, and Latin words and characters. Wherefore I too reckon thus with myself: if there is a Hebrew academy in our Germany, it is that monastery of Spanheim, where one can take in more learning from the walls than from the dusty and empty libraries of books belonging to many others. For whatever antiquity and learning Germany can possess in books, the monastery of Spanheim possesses, through the care of Abbot Trithemius.

I stayed with our abbot eleven days, not without exact remembrance of you. There, when one day in conversation we fell upon discussion of his book, which has been published on ecclesiastical writers, I said that I marveled that our Germany had had such distinguished writers, whom I had come to know in that book, and still had them at the present day; and I recalled that I had heard from a certain most learned Italian philosopher that he had never anywhere, in his reading, found any learned German except the one Albertus Magnus.

Then the abbot, smiling, said: “Therefore all the more is it to be believed that the Italians have deliberately passed over the praises of Germans in their writings, so that by passing over others their own glory might appear greater. I can indeed openly make known to you that there have existed far more very ancient and very celebrated German writers than you recognized in my book on ecclesiastical writers.” And bringing forth from that library of his a huge book, containing nothing except Germany’s most learned writers and men of most holy memory, he showed it to me. When I had looked at it, I began most urgently to beg and entreat him, as I do not doubt that you and any learned man would have done, that he should bring it about that our Germany should not henceforth go deprived of so great a glory of our ancestors, and that he should see to it that it be entrusted at the first possible day to the printer’s workshop. For when printed, through reading and imitation, it would bring it about that we would have more holy men and students of the good arts.

And so I prevailed upon the abbot, who in any case shows himself obliging to friends, and obtained that volume to be printed for the praise of our Germany. These are the things, most pleasant Jodocus, which I learned, saw, and accomplished with the lord abbot of Spanheim, and which, impatient of a longer delay, I resolved to write to you. Farewell. From the monastery of Spanheim, the thirtieth day before the Kalends of September. In the year of the Virgin’s giving birth 1495.

Si quid vir- tutis, si quid eruditionis, si quid laudis, de nostris apud veteres auctores inuenerint ne ad multorum noticiã perueniat, aut citius abradunt, aut sua publicantes nostra omittũt. Sic denique Plinium de Germanorũ bellis perisse fama est: sic multae ac variae de rebus geslis nostratium antiquitus conscriptae feruntur amissae historie. Sebastianum quoque Murrho- nem Colmariensem, virum vndecunꝫ: doctissimũ, triumque linguarũ principaliũ non me- diocriter peritũ, tuis cohortationibus eousque perduxisti: vt de laudibus germanorũ epito- ma perpulchrum ediderit: in quo res fortiter gestas nostrorum principũ, pro fide catholi- ca, pro republica, pro sancta Romana ecclesia, luculentò sermone digessit: & nationis 20 nostrae clarissima ingenia, opera, & inuenta breui compendio recensuit. Sed nec his quidem contentus, animum tuum sempet ad maiora nostrorum laudum praeconia elenas: & quã- to plura laudibus nostris condigna inueneritis, tanto ampliora concupiscis. Vnde et ne- quoque crebris epistolis et precibus exhortaris, quatenus de laudibꝰ Germano um aliuid debeam scribere: & illustrium virorum huius nationis, qui eruditione ingenioque prae- stantes varia conscripserunt catalogum ordinare. Diu fateor distuli, partim rei familiaris sollicitudine detentus: partim altioris studij sudore occupatus. Sed nunc tandem ni- mia importunitate tua victus sum: & fateor me superatum. Suscipe itaque mi lacobe ca- talogum, quem tantopere postulasti: cumque lima vire castigationis et eruditionis corri- ge: & sic demum ad aliorum examen venire concede. Nec omnes qui Germaniam no- stram fuis ingenijs et opusculis illustrem reddiderunt comportasse me putauers: sed eo- rum duntaxat memoriam habuisse: quorum scripta pre occupationibus meis ad manum 30 potui reperire. Paucos recensui è pluribus, quatenus detractor inuidus per istos sentiat, quanti nobis adhuc defint quos iste catalogus minime portar. Neque enim mihi caeteros perquirendi dabatur ocium: neque impense per alios comportandi. Denique in fine post- eaquam vita defunctorum seriem contexui: quosdam adhuc in carne viuentes adjunx: ne sia nobis iam praetermissi fuerint, ad noticiam posteritatis minimę pertingeret. E- nimuero qui nobis iam notissimi sunt, citõ in obliuionem deuenient, siliteris et scriptis non fuerint cõmendati. Non minor mihi cura est viros eruditos qui aliuid pro vtilitate legentium scripserunt in noticiam posteritatẽ deducere, quam veterum opuscula in bi- bliothecã mei coenobij comportare. Scio tamen quibusdã non satis placere quod ingeniae 40 viuentiũ commendare literis volui, qui hoc nõ ad vtilitatẽ posteritatis, sed ad vanã lauda- tionẽ humanae conditionis factum arbitrantur. His ego paucis respondendum existimo, quoniam ad alia festino: Et si laudare hominem ante mortem in his quae meritoria sunt. non debeo, ingenium quod naturale est et bonis malisque commune literis mandare non prohibeor. quod Hieronymum prosperum, Gennadium, lsidorum, Honorium, Si- geber tum et alios multos fecisse intucor. Denique multi sunt his temporibꝰ eruditissimi viri, quorum memoriam posteris commendare pietatis est, & nõ minoris vtilitatis. Of Johannes Trithemius

Letter of Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Master Jacob Wimpfeling of Sélestat.

Since there are some, my very dear Jacob Wimpfeling, who, blindly treading upon the histories of the times, despise our Germany as though it were barren and devoid of the liberal arts; who contend that in it outstanding men of intellect and writers on ecclesiastical discipline have flourished only few and rare. For they have become such shameless praisers of their own nation that they believe they can become more famous by disparaging others. They extol the slight deeds of their own people and the small talents in their own men with painted colors of eloquence, and, blinded by envy, utterly conceal the great virtues of the Germans, their brave deeds, their most brilliant talents, their faith, fervor, and devotion. If they find among ancient authors anything of virtue, anything of learning, anything of praise concerning our people, lest it come to the knowledge of many, they either scrape it away at once, or, publishing their own things, omit ours. Thus, indeed, Pliny on the wars of the Germans is said by report to have perished; thus many and various histories, written in antiquity concerning the deeds of our people, are said to have been lost.

But you, most learned man, stirred by this rashness of rivals, have appeared as a true lover and defender of our fatherland, since you do not cease to write various things in praise of the Germans, and to urge others by words and examples to do the same. You have won over to yourself Lupold of Bebenburg on the fervor, zeal, and constancy of the ancient German princes in the Christian religion; and you have brought many volumes of ancient authors on these very matters into your library. Sebastian Murrho of Colmar also, a man most learned from every quarter and not moderately skilled in the three principal languages, you have brought by your exhortations to the point that he has published a very fine epitome on the praises of the Germans, in which he set in order, in lucid speech, the brave deeds of our princes on behalf of the Catholic faith, the commonwealth, and the holy Roman Church; and he reviewed in brief compendium the most brilliant talents, works, and inventions of our nation.

But not even content with these things, you always raise your mind to greater proclamations of our praises; and the more things worthy of our praises you find, the greater things you desire. Hence you also exhort me by frequent letters and entreaties that I ought to write something on the praises of the Germans, and to arrange a catalogue of the illustrious men of this nation who, outstanding in learning and intellect, wrote various works. I confess I put it off for a long time, partly detained by concern for domestic affairs, partly occupied by the sweat of higher study. But now at last I have been overcome by your excessive persistence, and I confess myself defeated.

Receive therefore, my Jacob, the catalogue which you have so greatly requested; correct it with the file of your chastening and learning, and then at last allow it to come to the examination of others. Nor should you think that I have gathered together all who made our Germany illustrious by their talents and little works, but only that I have kept the memory of those whose writings, amid my preoccupations, I could find ready to hand. I have reviewed a few out of many, so that by these the envious detractor may perceive how many are still lacking to us whom this catalogue by no means contains. For neither was leisure given me to seek out the rest, nor expense to gather them through others.

Finally, at the end, after I have woven together the sequence of those who have departed life, I have added certain men still living in the flesh, lest, if they should now be passed over by us, they would by no means reach the knowledge of posterity. For indeed those who are now very well known to us will quickly fall into oblivion if they have not been commended by letters and writings. I have no less concern to bring to the knowledge of posterity learned men who have written something for the benefit of readers than to bring the little works of the ancients into the library of my monastery.

Yet I know that it does not sufficiently please certain people that I wished to commend in writing the talents of the living, who think that this was done not for the benefit of posterity but for the vain praise of the human condition. I think these men must be answered briefly, since I hasten to other matters. And if I ought not to praise a man before death in those things which are meritorious, I am not forbidden to commit to writing talent, which is natural and common to good and bad alike; I observe that Jerome, Prosper, Gennadius, Isidore, Honorius, Sigebert, and many others did this. Indeed, what the most holy fathers laudably did for the benefit of posterity, no wise man should forbid me, who desire to do the same with the same intention. Finally, there are many most learned men in these times whose memory it is pious, and of no less benefit, to commend to posterity. Unless antiquity had done this with equal piety, not all the most famous ancient writers would long since have come down to our memory

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

[unclear]. There are also those who think that in this age there are either no illustrious writers in the humanities, or only a few; and I trust that I have done something pleasant and welcome for them, if I have brought even a few out of many to their knowledge. For although I could not mention all men outstanding in talent, nevertheless I have provided an occasion for our studious Germans, so that henceforth they too may be able to add others to these and enlarge our work by their own diligence. Farewell. From Spanheim, on the sixth day before the Ides of February, in the year of the Lord MCCCCXCI.

Preface of Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, to the Book on the Illustrious Men of the German Nation, to Jacobus V. [Sletslatinus?].

Germany, which, because of its fertility in all good things, could rightly be called Germania, if Caesar did not think the contrary, from the beginning of its conversion to the Christian faith has always shone with famous teachers; through their talent and most holy morals it deserved to be illuminated more abundantly than other nations. Of these, many have been inserted into the catalogue of saints; many preceded this custom of canonizing saints in time.

This is proved by the very ancient books composed by them; miracles prove it. Nevertheless, at the request of friends, I have resolved to gather the works of certain talents into this catalogue, intending to provide an opportunity for posterity, so that, where they know that we have stopped, they themselves may by their own zeal complete the praises of the Germans. For I, situated in a corner of Germany, have not had the opportunity to search out the others who are lacking from our catalogue; but those whom I had at hand I offer to our Germans, asking that each one add to ours the writers who come his way, and thus finally learn, in rivalry with us, that they have been and are learned. Nor should it escape anyone that I have placed among the Germans all illustrious writers whom I found to have been Teutons. For the Mosellans and Treverans, although they inhabit a great part of Belgic Gaul, are nevertheless German in customs and language, and for that reason they have not undeservedly been numbered among our Germans. Concerning the other Teutons round about, too, a similar opinion should be held. But let this much about these matters suffice; now, God granting it, let us take up the beginning of writing according to the proposed subject.

Book of Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, on the Luminaries, or on the Illustrious Men of Germany, who, outstanding in talent, wrote various works.

Maximus, the seventh bishop of the church of Mainz, a man most holy in life and conduct, nobly learned both in secular letters and in the divine scriptures, was ready in talent, distinguished in speech, and outstanding in action. Since he was an eloquent and celebrated preacher of the divine word, he converted many to the faith of Christ by word and example, not only throughout his own diocese but also through neighboring and more distant regions, sowing the word of faith. He is said to have written many letters to various persons and to have committed many homilies to writing; but antiquity has not allowed any of these to come into our hands. Finally, against the Arians, who in his time did many evils in the Church of God, he composed some excellent works. He flourished at Mainz in the times of the emperors Constantius and Constans, under Pope Liberius, in the year of the Lord CCCLX.

Paulinus, the twenty-eighth archbishop of Trier, by nation indeed an Aquitanian, but in life and conduct for the most part dwelling among the Treverans, disciple of the blessed Maximinus, archbishop of Trier, and his son in baptism, a learned and most holy man, was banished into exile by the Arian heretics for the faith of Christ; in Phrygia he triumphed by a glorious suffering. He wrote many elegant letters in matters of the Catholic faith, in which he appeared no less learned than holy. But he also wrote some other works for the faith against here-

CAROLVS Imperator Magnus Pippini ducis secundi regis filius natione Alema-nus ex imperiali castro Ingelnhem ( vbi vsque hodie camera natiuitatis eius in capellam consecrata ostenditur) vir vita conuersatione Christianissimus sanctorum nume-60 rum

Of Johannes Trithemius [unclear] he published. He died in Phrygia under Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, in the year of the Lord 357, in the fifteenth indiction.

Boniface, also called Winfrid, first archbishop of the church of Mainz, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, English by nation but German in his way of life and dignity: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, upright and most holy in life and morals. By his learned preaching he converted many to the Christian faith, so that he was deservedly held to be the teacher and apostle of the Germans. He wrote several distinguished little works, of which I have seen the following: To Pope Gregory II, On the Faith of the Holy Trinity, one book; The Life of Saint Lebuin, one book; Letters to Various Persons, one book; On Various Deeds of the Saints, one book; and certain other things. At last, while preaching the word of God in Frisia, he was crowned with martyrdom under Pippin, king of the Franks, in the year of the Lord 755, in the eighth indiction, in the thirty-seventh year of his episcopate, on the Nones of June. He was buried in the monastery of Fulda, which he himself built.

Walafrid, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and remarkably learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, excelling in verse and prose, a monarch of regular discipline, father of many monks, wrote, among other little works of his talent: The Life of Saint Gall in prose, one book; the same afterwards in verse, one book; On the Divine Offices also, one book; and various letters to various persons, and certain other things. He flourished about the times of the emperor Tiberius, in the year of the Lord 700.

Willibald, priest of Saint Boniface, a monk of the divine father Benedict, brother of Saint Walpurga, virgin abbess of Heidenheim, and afterwards bishop of Eichstatt, a learned and most holy man, ready in intellect and sweet in speech, wrote, at the command of Saint Lullus of Mainz, archbishop after Boniface, The Life of the same most holy martyr Boniface, two books, and, as is reported, certain letters to devout servants of God. He flourished under Pippin, father of the emperor Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 760.

Ryggandus, bishop of Metz, grandson of King Pippin by his sister, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters as well, venerable no less in life and conduct than in dignity. Among other monuments of his talent he wrote The Rule of the Canons of the Church of Metz, one book, and various letters to various persons. He transferred from Rome the bodies of the holy martyrs Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius; of these, he deposited the body of Saint Nazarius in the monastery of Lorsch, then of our order in Germany, in the diocese of Worms. He flourished in the times of Pippin, his uncle, king of Charlemagne, in the year of the Lord 870.

Haymo, third bishop of the church of Halberstadt in Saxony, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none in his time in secular letters, acute in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout in life and conduct, was of most celebrated industry in delivering homilies to the people; from him he became most learned in every discipline of the good arts. Then, as his merits advanced, he was appointed third abbot of the monastery of Hersfeld. Finally, likewise, he was chosen third bishop of Halberstadt. He wrote many, almost innumerable volumes, of which the following are extant: On the Five Books of Moses, five books; On Joshua, one book; On Tobit, one book; On Ezra and Nehemiah, three books; On the Book of Judith, one book; On Esther also, one book; On Job, one book; On the Song of Songs, one book; On the Proverbs of Solomon, one book; On Ecclesiastes, one book; On Isaiah the Prophet, four books; On Jeremiah the Prophet, one book; On Ezekiel also, four books; On Daniel, one book; On the Twelve Minor Prophets, twelve books; On the Psalms, one book; On the Gospels, homilies through the cycle of the year, two large volumes, two books; On All the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books; On the Canonical Epistles, seven books; On the Apocalypse of John, one book; On the Holy Trinity, one book; On the Memory of Christian Things, ten books; On the Variety of Books, four books; On the Acts of the Apostles, one book. He composed sermons, homilies, letters, and various other treatises, but they have not yet come into our hands. He died under Louis, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 934, in the twelfth indiction, in the thirteenth year of his episcopate, and was buried in the church of Saint Stephen at Halberstadt.

Charles the Great, emperor, son of Pippin the second duke and king, German by nation, from the imperial castle of Ingelheim, where to this day the chamber of his birth, consecrated as a chapel, is shown, a man most Christian in life and conduct,

197
CATALOGVS ILLVSTRIVM VIRORVM. 125 rum non immerito relatus, in scripturis diuinis studiosissimus, &amp; in secularibus literis e- gregie doctus, ingenio subtilis, eloquio clarus et amp; difertus, &amp; multarum linguarum cogni- tione infignis, graecae, latinae et amp; hebraicae peritus, nequaquam à catalogo illustriū virorum germaniae reijciendus. Enim uero artes liberales studiosissime coluit, earumque doctores plurimum veneratus magnis afficiēbat honoribus. In discenda grammatica Petrum Pisa- num diaconum senem audiuit, in ceteris disciplinis Albinū cognosmento Aleui num mo- nachum ordinis sancti Benedicti et amp; diaconum quondam discipulum de Britannia Saxo- nici generis hominem, virum vndecunq́ue doctissimum praeceptorē habuit: apud quem et amp;rhetoricae et amp; dialecticae praecipue tamen astronomiae addiscendae plurimum et amp; temporis 10 laboris impartiuit. Discebat artem computandi, &amp; intentione sagaci syderum cursum curiosissime rimabatur. Religionem Christianam qua ab infantia erat imbutus, sanctissi- me et amp; cum summa pietate coluit, &amp; multa pro eius honore disposuit. Ecclesiam et amp; ma- ne et amp; vespere, item nocturnis horis et amp; sacrificij tempore quo ad eum valetudo permiserat impigre et amp; cum magna deuotione frequentabat. Bibliothecam in palatio suo Aquensi preciosissimam et amp; maxima librorum copia repletam comportauit: quam moriens vendi et amp; in eleemosynam pauperum distribui fecit. Edidit inter cetera ingenij sui opera multas et amp; varias additiones legum et amp; iurium omniū nationum quae sub suo regno et amp; impetrio de- gebant in multis voluminibus. Item iura Saxonum composuit, item leges Alemanorum, item leges Franccorũ, item multa et amp; varia carmina de gestis veterū edidit. Inchoauit etiam 20 grammaticam patrij sermonis videlicet theutonici siue Alemanicicquã alijs occupatus finire non potuit. Huius grammaticae fragmenta vidi et amp; etiam quaedam volumina se- cundum eiusdem regulas composita, de quibus in sequentibus mentio fiet, cum ad Otfri- dum Wissenburgensis coenobij monachum peruenerimus. Multa quoque ad eius iussio- nem volumina per diuersos edita sunt: quae suis auctoribus relinquimus. Felix respu- blica cuius princeps tam gloriosus philosophus erat. Moritur tandem post multa san- ctissima exercitia in Basilica beatae Dei genitricis, quam ipse sumptuosissime construxerat, apud Aquastriari sepultus. Anno Domini DCCC.XIIII. indictione VII.V. cal. Februarij. anno aetatis sua LXXII.Regni XLVII. 30 EINHARDVS praedicti Caroli Imperatoris Magni quondam cancellarius, &amp; post ca monachus ordinis diui patris Benedicti, &amp; primus abbas monasterij Selgenstatensis Moguntinae diocēsis supra Mogonum, vir in secularibus literis eruditissimus, &amp; diuina- rum scripturarum non ignarus, ingenio acutus, eloquio difertus, vita et amp; conuersatione praecipuis graece ac latine peritus, &amp; tam metto quam profã excellens: inter cetera in- genij sui opufcula Psalterium Gallicanum abbreuiauit excerpens de illo omnes versus o- rationis verba habentes. Scripsit etiam tam ex persona sui quam Imperatoris multas elegantes et amp; vtiles epistolas ad diuersos in varijs negocijs et amp; causis. Gesta quoque Caro- li imperatoris lib.I. Notabilem infuper historiam temporum de gestis Germanorum et Francorum lib.II. Et quaedam alia quead nos minime veniunt. Claruit sub Carolo Im- 40 peratore magno et amp; Ludouico filio eius, anno Domini DCCC.XX. FRECVLPHVS Episcopus Lexouiensis, monachus quondam Fuldensis, or- dinis diui patris Benedicti Albini disciplinus, ad quem Rabanus abbas Fuldensis multis voluminibus exercitauit ingenium, vir in diuinis scripturis studiosissimus et amp; valde eru- ditus, atque in docenda plebe satis idoneus: nec minus conuersatione quam scientia infignis: fertur quaedam praeclara scripsisse opnscula. De quibus extant septem volu- mina ad Helisacharum ab exordio mundi viq́ue ad natiuitatem saluatoris rerum gesta- rum tam gentilium quam ludaeorum continentia historiam. In quo etiam operē mul- tas diuniarum scripturarum difficiles quaesiones subtiliter enodauit. Scripsit infuper ad diuersos et amp; elegantes et amp; varias epistolas, quarum ad Rabanum aliquas legisse me memi- 50 ni. Sed et amp; alia nonnulla edidit, quae nos latent. Claruit sub imperio Ludouici primi, filij Ca- roli magni anno Domini DCCC.XL. HAMVLARIVS Fortunatus tertius et amp; sexagesimus à sancto Euchario Tre- uerorum archiepiscopus, &amp; sacrosancta Romanae ecclesiae (vt ferunt) cardinalis, vir in diuinis scripturis eruditissimum, &amp; in secularibꝰ literis egregie doctus, graecae ac latinae peritus, scripsit non spernendae lectionis opuscula. De quibus feruntur sub- iecta: De diuinis officijs, lib.I. Ad Ludouiicum Imperatorem de eadem re, lib.VII.De mysterijs sacris lib.I. Variae quoque ad diuerfos epistolae. Hic per Carolum Imperato- rem ad Constantinopolim missus ad Michaelem Imperatorem Graecorum: sua mira- L 3

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

[of men?] not undeservedly included, most devoted to the divine Scriptures and excellently learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect, clear and eloquent in speech, distinguished by knowledge of many languages, skilled in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew, by no means to be rejected from the catalogue of the illustrious men of Germany. Indeed, he most zealously cultivated the liberal arts, and, greatly venerating their teachers, honored them with great distinctions. In learning grammar he heard Peter of Pisa, an aged deacon; in the other disciplines he had as teacher Albinus, surnamed Alcuin, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict and formerly a deacon, a disciple from Britain, a man of Saxon stock, most learned in every respect. With him he spent very much time and labor in learning rhetoric and dialectic, but especially astronomy. He learned the art of computation, and with keen attention most carefully investigated the course of the stars. The Christian religion, with which he had been imbued from infancy, he cultivated most devoutly and with the greatest piety, and he made many arrangements for its honor. He attended church zealously and with great devotion in the morning and evening, likewise in the night hours and at the time of the sacrifice, so far as his health allowed him. In his palace at Aachen he assembled a most precious library, filled with a very great abundance of books; when he died, he had it sold and distributed as alms to the poor. Among the other works of his intellect he published many and various additions of the laws and rights of all the nations that lived under his kingdom and empire, in many volumes. Likewise he composed the laws of the Saxons; likewise the laws of the Alemanni; likewise the laws of the Franks; likewise he published many and various songs concerning the deeds of the ancients. He also began a grammar of his native tongue, namely Teutonic or Alemannic, which, occupied with other matters, he could not finish. I have seen fragments of this grammar, and also certain volumes composed according to its rules; mention of these will be made below, when we come to Otfried, monk of the monastery of Weissenburg. Many volumes also were published by various men at his command; these we leave to their own authors. Happy is the commonwealth whose prince was so glorious a philosopher. At length, after many most holy exercises, he died in the basilica of the blessed Mother of God, which he himself had built at very great expense, and was buried at Aachen, in the year of the Lord 814, in the seventh indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventy-second year of his age and the forty-seventh of his reign.

Einhard, once chancellor of the aforesaid Emperor Charles the Great, and afterward a monk of the order of the divine father Benedict, and first abbot of the monastery of Seligenstadt in the diocese of Mainz above the Main, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, acute in intellect, eloquent in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, skilled especially in Greek and Latin, and excellent both in meter and in prose: among the other little works of his intellect, he abbreviated the Gallican Psalter, extracting from it all the verses containing words of prayer. He also wrote, both in his own person and in that of the emperor, many elegant and useful letters to various persons on various affairs and cases. Also The Deeds of Emperor Charles, one book. Moreover, a notable history of the times concerning the deeds of the Germans and Franks, two books. And certain other things which have by no means come down to us. He flourished under Emperor Charles the Great and his son Louis, in the year of the Lord 820.

Freculph, bishop of Lisieux, once a monk of Fulda, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a disciple of Albinus, to whom Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, exercised his talent in many volumes, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, and sufficiently fit for teaching the people; no less distinguished in conduct than in knowledge: he is said to have written certain excellent little works. Of these there are extant seven volumes addressed to Helisachar, containing a history of events from the beginning of the world down to the birth of the Savior, both of the gentiles and of the Jews. In this work he also subtly untangled many difficult questions of the divine Scriptures. He wrote, moreover, elegant and varied letters to various persons; I remember having read some of these to Rabanus. But he also published several other things which are unknown to us. He flourished under the rule of Louis the First, son of Charles the Great, in the year of the Lord 840.

Hamularius Fortunatus, the sixty-third archbishop of Trier from Saint Eucharius, and, as they say, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently taught in secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin, wrote little works of reading not to be despised. Of these the following are reported: On the Divine Offices, one book. To Emperor Louis on the same matter, seven books. On the Sacred Mysteries, one book. Various letters also to various persons. Sent by Emperor Charles to Constantinople, to Michael, emperor of the Greeks, he, by his wondrous

Anno Domini DCCC.X. Rabanus Maurus archeiscopus Magnanisenis. RABANVS MAVRVS Maguentius post sanctum Bonifacium sextus archiepiscopus Maguntinensis patria Thoringus ex ciuitate Fuldensi oriundus: Albani disciplusus primum monachus Fuldensis coenobij factus, cum adhuc puer esset decem annorum : omne deinceps studium ad scientiam conuertit scripturarum: in omniteruditione tam secularium quam diuinarum scripturarum longe doctissimus euafit: philofophus clarus poetae insignis, rhetor facundus, astronomus computista celeberrimus, graece latina hebraicae peritus: cui similem suo tempore non habuit ecclesia. De inde succrescentibus meritis anno aetatis sue quinto tricesimo omnium fratrum suffragio eiuidem coenobij abbas electus est: praesidens regiminiannis quatuor viginti, multa pene infinita composit volumina. Demum post mortem Orgarij Moguntinensis archiepiscopi ciuidem ecclesiae Pontifex confecratus est, annis noueminpraesulatu sedens multa bona fecit ecclesię. STRABVS monachus Fuldensis Rabani supradicti abbas quondam discipluse notarius,vir certeiipse doctissimus,tamindiuinis scripturis quam in secularibus literisad plenum instructus,theologus, philofophus, poetae celeberrimus: ingenio promptuselarum eloquio:scripfit nonnulla in factis voluminibus opuscula:quibus memoriam sui posteritati commendauit.Sed pauca eorum ad noticiam meam peruenerunt.Ferunturautem pręcipue commentariorum in Genesim lib.I.in Exodum quoque lib.I.in Leuiticum lib.I alia multa.Iste Strabus vir studiosissimus glossamquam magistralem siueordinariam vocant super totam Bibliam primus comportauit ex dictis sanctorum patrum:quam alij postmodum adiunctis quibusdam ampliarunt.Claruit subLudouico Lothario Imperatoribus,anno Domini DCCC.LX. LV PV S Seruatus presbyter (ad quem sanctus Rabanus abbas Fuldensis octo libros in epistolam Pauliad Romanos scripfisse legititur) vir indiuinis scripturis studiosus59 eruditus. in secularibus literisque doctus, scripfit inter cetera ingenij sui opusculalibrum de tribus quaetionibus,id est de libero arbitrio, depreadestinatione, defanguine Christi quadam superflua taxatione vel redemptione vsque adsalutem impiorum.Nam super hacre orta fuit quedam turbatio fidei in ecclesia anno DominiDCCC.XLIIX.Alia infuer nonnulla edidit:sed ad noticiam meam none-runt.Claruit cum Rabano subLothario imperatore,anno Domini DCCCL.NOTGE-

126 Of Johannes Trithemius by [unclear] wisdom and diligence he established and confirmed true and perpetual peace and friendship between them. He flourished under the emperors Charlemagne and Louis his son, in the year of the Lord 810.

Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz.

Rabanus Maurus of Mainz, after Saint Boniface the sixth archbishop of Mainz, a Thuringian by nationality, sprung from the city of Fulda, a disciple of Alcuin, was first made a monk of the monastery of Fulda when he was still a boy of ten years. Thereafter he turned all his study to the knowledge of the Scriptures. In all learning, both of secular and of divine writings, he became by far most learned: a distinguished philosopher, an eminent poet, an eloquent rhetorician, a most celebrated astronomer and computist, skilled in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew; in his time the Church had no one like him. Then, as his merits increased, in the thirty-fifth year of his age he was elected abbot of the same monastery by the vote of all the brethren. Presiding over its government for twenty-four years, he composed many, almost countless, volumes. At last, after the death of Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, he was consecrated bishop of the same church; sitting for nine years in the episcopate, he did many good things for the Church. Of his little works the following are reported: To Bishop Freculph, On Genesis, four books; On Numbers, four books; On Leviticus, four books; On Deuteronomy, four books; On Joshua, two books; On Judges, two books; On the Book of Ruth, one book; On Kings, to Hildewin, abbot of Saint-Denis, four books; also On Paralipomenon, four books; On Ezra and Nehemiah, three books; On Tobit, one book; On the Book of Judith, seven books; On [unclear], one book; On the Psalms, one book; On the Proverbs of Solomon, one book; On Ecclesiastes, one book; On the Song of Songs, one book; On the Book of Wisdom, three books; On Ecclesiasticus, ten books; On Isaiah the Prophet, eight books; On Jeremiah the Prophet, twenty books; also On Ezekiel the Prophet, twenty books; On Daniel the Prophet, three books; On the Twelve Minor Prophets, twelve books; On the Books of Maccabees, three books; On the Gospel of Matthew, eight books; On the Gospel of Luke, three books; On the Gospel of Mark, four books; On the Gospel of John, two books; On all the Epistles of Paul, twenty-one books; On the Catholic Epistles, seven books; On the Acts of the Apostles, one book; On the Apocalypse of John, one book; On the Faith of the Most Holy Trinity, one book; also On the Praise of the Holy Cross, a work of wondrous genius, two books; To Bishop Haymo, On the Universe, or Etymologies, twenty-one books; also On Universal Nature, one book; to Bishop Haistulf, On the Instruction of Clerics, three books; On the Divine Offices, one book; On the Ecclesiastical Computus, two books; To Emperor Louis, one book; On Questions of the Canons, one book; To Bishop Regenbald, one book; On the Blessings of the Patriarchs, one book; a Homiliary of the ceremonies of the whole year, two books; also Letters to various persons, one book. But he composed various epigrams and many treatises in humane letters which have not yet come into our hands. He died under Emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 855, in the third indiction, in the sixty-eighth year of his age, when the ninth year of his episcopate had been completed. He was buried in the monastery of the holy martyr Alban near Mainz, then of the order of Saint Benedict.

Strabus, a monk of Fulda, once the disciple and notary of the aforesaid Abbot Rabanus, was certainly himself a most learned man, fully instructed both in divine Scripture and in secular letters, a theologian, philosopher, and most celebrated poet, quick in talent and clear in speech. He wrote several little works in sacred volumes, by which he commended his memory to posterity. But few of them have come to my knowledge. Chiefly there are reported commentaries On Genesis, one book; also On Exodus, one book; On Leviticus, one book; and many others. This Strabus, a most studious man, was the first to compile over the whole Bible the gloss which they call the master gloss or ordinary gloss, from the sayings of the holy fathers; others afterwards enlarged it by adding certain things. He flourished under the emperors Louis and Lothar, in the year of the Lord 860.

Lupus Servatus, priest, to whom Saint Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, is read to have written eight books on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, was a man studious and learned in divine Scripture, and learned also in secular letters. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote a book On Three Questions, that is, on free will, on predestination, and on the blood of Christ, concerning a certain superfluous assessment or redemption extending to the salvation of the impious. For over this matter there arose a certain disturbance of faith in the Church in the year of the Lord 848. Besides these he published several other works, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished with Rabanus under Emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 850. Notge-

199
CATALOGVS ILLVSTRIVM. 127 NOTGERVS episcopus Leodiensis ex abbate monasterij sancti Galli, Rabani quō- dam familiarissimus, vir in diuinis Scripturis eruditissimus, & in secularium literarum dis- ciplinis omnium sui temporis facile doctissimus, philolophus, poeta, musicus,astrono- mus theologus celeberimus,nec minùs conuersatione quam scientia venerabilis, scrip̄t multa praeclara necessaria opuscula,quibus nomē suum ad multorum notitiam transmisit. Equibus pauca in noticiam nostrae lectionis peruenetunt. Vidi opus ori- ginale prosarum sue sequentiarum per circulum anni de festis, quod scripsit ad Lutuar- dum episcopum Vercellensem magni Imperatoris archicapellanum lib.I. ad Sa- lononem poftea Constantiensis ecclesiae pontificem de praecipuis sacrae Scripturae ex- positoribus lib.I.de musica symphoniarum modis lib.I. epistolarum ad diuerfos lib.I. fermones omelias varias composuit. Et quosdam sacrae Scripturae libros eleganter exposuit:aliquae multa scripsit. Huius Notgeriadhuc monachi apud sanctum Gallium Nicolaus papa primùs sequentias confirmauit: in missa decantari concessit. Scripsit moltos varios hymnos , cantus, antiphonas responsoria quae vsque hodie in eccle- fia Dei frequentantur laudibus. Claruit in episcopatu sub Lothario Imperatore Anno Domini DCCCL. SALOMON episcopus Constantiensis ex monacho coenobij sancti Gallii, ordi- nis diui patris Benedicti, supra nominati Notgeri quondam auditor atque discipulus, vir in diuinis Scripturus studiosus eruditus, atque in secularibus literis egregie do- ctus : metro exercitus prosa, ingenio subtilis difertus eloquio, nec minus con- uersatione quam sciencia venerandus. Scripsit de septem artibus quas liberales vocant librum vnum.Vocabularium quoquenon spernendum librum vnum.Epistolarum ad diuerfos librum I. fermones quoque multos , variosque tractatus condidisse dicitur, qui ad manus nostras non venerunt. Claruit sub Lothario imperatore Anno Domini,DCCCLX. WANDELBERTVS diaconus monachus Prumiensis coenobij ordinis san- cti Benedicti,in diocesi Treurensi, vir tam in diuinis Scripturis quam in secularibus li- teris eruditissimus ingeniꝰ acutus, dilertus eloquio, philosophus, rhetor, poeta do- ctissimus, scripsit inter alia ingenij sui opuscula , ad Marquardum abbatem, vitam san- cti Goaris presbyteri, librum vnū.De miraculis eiusdē sanctissimi viri librum vnum.Mar- tyrologium metrice perpulchrum composuit.Alia quoque plura edidit, quae ad manus nostras non venerunt.Claruit temporibus Lotharij Ludouici Imperatorum,Anno Domini,DCCCXLX. CHRISTIANVS qui Druthmarus monachus presbyter monasterij Corbe- liensis(natione quidem Aquitanicus) sed conuersationegermanus,vir certe vndecun- de doctissimus,grecae latinae peritus, scripsit intér alia ingenii sui monumenta ad gelistas scripturum, quod fecisse dicitur, quamquam nihil eorum ad notitiā lectio- nibus Matthaei.lib.I.fermones quoque multos omelias varias librum vnum, alia mul- ta q;non vidi.In prologo expositionis Marthaei promittit se in alijs quoque euan- geliorum postulat sermones, quod scripsit multa praeclara volumina:quibus scripsit metro prosa multa praeclara volumine: quibus Ofridus menachus coenobij W.steinbur- gensis. OTFRIDVS monachus Wissenburgensis coenobij ordinis sancti Benedicti Spi- rensis diocesis,Rabani Mauri abbatis Fuldensis quondam auditor atque dicipulus,vir in diuinis Scripturis eruditissimus , in secularibus literas egregie doctus, philosophus, rhetor,astronomus,poeta,theologus,nulli suo tempore secundus, ingenio excel- lens difertus eloquuo : scripsit metro prosa multa praeclara volumina: quibus nomen suum ingenium ad pofteros transmisit.Ex eo volumine quo Carolus Im- perator quondam magnus barbariem theutonicae nostrae linguae materna secundū eafdem regulas cō- ducere grāmaticales edoctus,multa miranda lingua sermo ille regulatas a nostro plus differat, tunccumque sermonis nostri peritus:quippe cum sermo illè regulatus à nostro plus compo- fuit metro seu carmine,quae nemo facile nostra aetate legere intelligere potest,quan- quam Efrucius à latino.Mirabile tamen est lectione dignum quicquid vir iste com̄po- suit dum in theutonico sermone regulas posuit, quasi in versibus pedes numeros cu- stodivit. Ex cuius opusculis extant libiecta.Ad Luitbertum octauum Moguntinae ecclesiae archiepiscopum,in quatuor euangelia secundùm praedictas regulas metricum L4

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

NOTGER, bishop of Liège, formerly abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, once very close to Rabanus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and easily the most learned of all men of his time in the disciplines of secular letters, a philosopher, poet, musician, astronomer, and very celebrated theologian, venerable no less for his way of life than for his knowledge, wrote many excellent and necessary little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of many. Of these, a few have come to the notice of my reading. I have seen the original work of proses or sequences for the cycle of the year concerning the feasts, which he wrote to Lutward, bishop of Vercelli, archchaplain of the great emperor, book I; to Salomon, afterward bishop of the church of Constance, On the Principal Expositors of Sacred Scripture, book I; On Music, the Modes of Harmonies, book I; Letters to Various Persons, book I. He composed sermons and various homilies. And he elegantly expounded certain books of Sacred Scripture; he wrote many other things. While this Notger was still a monk at Saint Gall, Pope Nicholas I confirmed the sequences and allowed them to be sung in the Mass. He wrote many various hymns, chants, antiphons, and responsories, which down to the present day are used frequently in the Church of God in praises. He flourished in the episcopate under Emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 850.

SALOMON, bishop of Constance, formerly a monk of the monastery of Saint Gall, of the order of the divine father Benedict, once hearer and disciple of the above-named Notger, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and exceptionally taught in secular letters; practiced in verse and prose, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, and venerable no less for his way of life than for his knowledge. He wrote one book On the Seven Arts which they call liberal. Also one book, a Vocabulary, not to be despised. One book of Letters to Various Persons. He is also said to have composed many sermons and various treatises, which have not come into my hands. He flourished under Emperor Lothar in the year of the Lord 860.

WANDELBERT, deacon and monk of the monastery of Prüm, of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, sharp in talent, eloquent in speech, a philosopher, rhetorician, and most learned poet, wrote, among other little works of his talent, to Abbot Marquard, the Life of Saint Goar the priest, one book; On the Miracles of the same most holy man, one book. He composed a very beautiful Martyrology in verse. He also published several other works, which have not come into my hands. He flourished in the times of the emperors Lothar and Louis, in the year of the Lord 849.

CHRISTIAN, who is Druthmar, monk and priest of the monastery of Corbie, Aquitanian indeed by nation but German by way of life, certainly a man most learned in every respect, skilled in Greek and Latin, wrote, among other monuments of his talent, [unclear] which he is said to have made, although none of these has come to the notice of my reading; On Matthew, book I; also many sermons and various homilies, one book, and many other things which I have not seen. In the prologue to the exposition of Matthew he promises that he would also write on the other evangelists, because [unclear] requested sermons, [unclear] he wrote many excellent volumes; by which [unclear] he wrote many excellent volumes in verse and prose; by which [unclear]

Ofrid, monk of the monastery of Wissenburg.

OTFRID, monk of the monastery of Weissenburg, of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Speyer, once hearer and disciple of Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, exceptionally taught in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, astronomer, poet, theologian, second to none in his time, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote many excellent volumes in verse and prose, by which he transmitted his name and talent to posterity. From that volume in which Emperor Charles, once the Great, [unclear] the barbarism of our German mother tongue according to the same grammatical rules, many wonderful things [unclear] that language and speech regulated [unclear] differs more from ours, and then anyone skilled in our speech; indeed since that speech, regulated, differs more from ours [unclear] he composed in meter or verse, which no one in our age can easily read and understand, although [unclear] from Latin. Yet whatever this man composed is wonderful and worthy of reading, since in German speech he set rules, as if in verses he preserved feet and numbers. Of his little works there are extant [unclear]. To Luitbert, eighth archbishop of the church of Mainz, On the Four Gospels according to the aforesaid metrical rules

200
128 IOANNIS TRITHEMII opus magnum et admirandum, quod praenotauit, gratiam theotisce, libro 5. ad Ludo- uicum regem lib. 1 ad Salomonem Constantiensem episcopum lib. 1. ad monachos sancti Galli lib. 1. in p̄falterium tria magna volumina eodem genere sermonis. Item de extremo iudicio lib. 1. De gaudijs quoque regni caelestis lib. 1. Sermones: & omelias tam de tempore quam de sanctis edidit lib. 2. epiftolarum ad diuerfos lib. 1. epigrammata multa in vtraque lingua vario genere metri lib. 2. alia quoque multa edidit quae priorum negligentia perdita, & ignorantia monachorum abbatumque defidia rasa et lacerata in manus nostras non venerunt. Claruit temporibus Ludouici et Lotharij imperatorum Anno domini, DCCCLXX. FRANCO episcopus Leodiensis, vir in diuinis Scripturis eruditissimus et in studio secularium literarum egregie doctus, philofophus, rhetor, poeta, & musicus excellens, ingenio acutus, sermone difertus, vita et conuerfatione deuotus atque sanctissimus, pluri- bus annis publicae scholae praefuit: & multos in omni scientia discipulos doctiflimos enu- triuit. Scripfit inter alia ingenij fui opufcula, sermones et multos et valde vtiles pro aedi- ficatione fideliũ lib. 1. ad Hermannum quoque Coloniensem archiepiscopum de qua- dratura circuli lib. 1. de computo ecclesiaftico lib. 1. epiftolarum quoque ad diuersos lib. 1. cantus denique multos, antiphonas, legendas et responforia in honorẽ sanctorum dulci et regulari melodia composuit. Alia quoque nonnulla scripfisse dicitur: quae ad notitiam nostrae lectionis non venerunt. WERENBERTVS monachus apud sanctum Gallum ordinis diui patris Benedic- ti Rabani Mauri Fuldensis, quondam auditor atque difcipulus, vir in diuinis Scripturus eru- ditus, arque in secularibus literis egregie doctus, philosophus clarus, poeta infignis, graeci sermonis non ignarus, scripsit pro Aedificatione tegentium multa praeclara volumina, quibus talentum fibi commiffum à domino cum ingenti lucro reportauit. Sermones et multos et elegantes compositū lib. 1. epistolarum quoque ad diuerfos lib. i. epigramma- ton diuersi generis metri lib. 1. in euangelijs quoque lib. 4. Hymnos etiam et cantus in ho- nore domini nostrj lefu Christi et sanctorum varios composuit. Caetera quae scripfisse di- citur (etsi multa sunt) ad noticiam meam minime venerunt. Claruit sub Ludouico im- peratore secundo. Anno Domini, DCCCLXX. HARTMVDVS monachus eiusdem monasterij sancti Galli ordinis beati patris nostri Benedicti Rabani Mauri quondam auditor arque difcipulus, (ad quem Otfridus Wissenburgensis monachus multis epistolis exercitauit ingenium) vir vndecunque do- ctus, ingenio subtilis, eloquio difertus, vita et conuersione deuotus, graecae, latinae et hebraicae peritus, adde et arabice non ignarus: scripsit tam metro quam profa multa praecla- ra opufcula, fed nihil eorum ad noticiam nostrae lectionis memini peruennisse. Feruntur autem super quibusdam Bibliorum libris commentarij eius non abĳciendi, item epifto- larum ad diuersos lib. i. sermones quoque, cantus, hymni, & varij in scripturis sanctis tra- ētatus, quos studiosus quisque inquirat. Claruit temporibus Lotharij et Ludouici filij ejus imperatorum, Anno Domini DCCCLXX. STEPHANVS episcopus Leodienfis poft Franconem, vir in diuinis Scripturar do- ctus et in secularium litterarum disciplinis magnifice peritus ingenio promptus, sermone compositus, vita et conuersatione deuotus. Scripfit non spernendae lectionis quaedam repperi: Vitam sancti Lamperti pontificis et martyris lib. 1. ad episcopum quoque Meten- sem lib. 1. sermones etiam multos et elegantes compoluit, & plures ad diuersos epistolas. Officium quod de sancta Trinitate in octaujs Pentecostes annue cantamus, ex volumine Albini Stephanus iste composuit, & dulci melodia regulauit. Sed et defancta cruce, de sancto Lamperto martyre aliisque multis pulchra venustate ordinauit. RATBODVS ecclesie Traiectensis episcopus quartus decimus, vir in diuinis Scri- pturis valde eruditus, & secularium literaru non ignarus, ingenio subtilis eloquio clarus, vita et conuenfatione sanctissimus, multis et viuus et defunctus miraculis corrufcauit. Hunc in bonis literis Nanno philofophus doctiffimus instituit: à quo in omni scientia e- greffius est, & poftremo praefatae vrbs episcopus ordinatus, subgraui perfequutione Da- norum annis decem et septem praefuit. Scripfit autem in laudibus sanctorum nonnulla praeclara opufcula, de quibus ego tantum repperi fubiecta: Laudes sancti Martini episcopi Thuronensis lib. 1. laudes sanctj Bonifacij Moguntini archiepiscopi et martyris lib. i. laues sanctae Amalbergae virginis lib. i. sermones et tomos

Johannes Trithemius

a great and admirable work, which he entitled, in German, Grace, in five books; to King Louis, one book; to Solomon, bishop of Constance, one book; to the monks of Saint Gall, one book; on the Psalter, three great volumes in the same kind of speech. Likewise, On the Last Judgment, one book; also On the Joys of the Heavenly Kingdom, one book. He published sermons and homilies, both for the season and for the saints, in two books; letters to various persons, one book; many epigrams in both languages, in various kinds of meter, two books. He also published many other things which, lost through the negligence of earlier men and scraped away and torn by the ignorance and sloth of monks and abbots, have not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the emperors Louis and Lothair, in the year of the Lord 870.

Franco, bishop of Liege, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in the study of secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, poet, and excellent musician, keen in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout and most holy in life and conduct, presided for many years over the public school and trained many very learned pupils in every branch of knowledge. Among other little works of his talent he wrote many very useful sermons for the edification of the faithful, one book; also to Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, On the Squaring of the Circle, one book; On the Ecclesiastical Computus, one book; also letters to various persons, one book. Finally, he composed many chants, antiphons, legends, and responsories in honor of the saints, in sweet and regular melody. He is also said to have written some other things, which have not come to the knowledge of our reading.

Werenbert, a monk at Saint Gall of the order of the holy father Benedict, formerly a hearer and pupil of Hrabanus Maurus of Fulda, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher, an outstanding poet, not ignorant of the Greek language, wrote for the edification of readers many splendid volumes, by which he brought back with great profit the talent entrusted to him by the Lord. He composed many elegant sermons, one book; also letters to various persons, one book; epigrams in different kinds of meter, one book; also on the Gospels, four books. He also composed various hymns and chants in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the saints. The rest which he is said to have written, although they are many, have by no means come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Louis II, in the year of the Lord 870.

Hartmud, a monk of the same monastery of Saint Gall, of the order of our blessed father Benedict, formerly a hearer and pupil of Hrabanus Maurus, to whom Otfrid, the monk of Weissenburg, exercised his talent in many letters, a man learned on every side, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout in life and conduct, skilled in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew, and furthermore not ignorant of Arabic, wrote many splendid little works both in meter and in prose; but I do not remember that any of them has come to the knowledge of our reading. There are said to exist commentaries of his, not to be rejected, on certain books of the Bible; likewise letters to various persons, one book; also sermons, chants, hymns, and various treatises on the sacred Scriptures, which every studious person should seek out. He flourished in the times of the emperors Lothair and Louis his son, in the year of the Lord 870.

Stephen, bishop of Liege after Franco, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and magnificently skilled in the disciplines of secular letters, prompt in intellect, orderly in speech, devout in life and conduct. I have found certain things of no contemptible reading that he wrote: The Life of Saint Lambert, bishop and martyr, one book; also to the bishop of Metz, one book. He also composed many elegant sermons, and several letters to various persons. The office concerning the Holy Trinity, which we sing every year on the octave of Pentecost, this Stephen composed from the volume of Albinus and set to sweet melody. But he also arranged, with beautiful grace, works on the Holy Cross, on Saint Lambert the martyr, and on many others.

Ratbod, the fourteenth bishop of the church of Utrecht, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, most holy in life and conduct, shone forth with many miracles both while alive and after death. Nanno, a very learned philosopher, instructed him in good letters; from him he advanced in every branch of knowledge, and finally, ordained bishop of the aforesaid city, he presided for seventeen years under the grave persecution of the Danes. He wrote certain splendid little works in praise of the saints, of which I have found only the following: Praises of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, one book; Praises of Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz and martyr, one book; Praises of Saint Amalberga the Virgin, one book; sermons and tomes

Hic celebrata synodo in monasterio Selgenstatensi cum epifcoꝑis et amp; Abbatibus suis,Anno Domini M.xxxii.indictione 6.multa bona et amp; vti-lia constituit, quae in scripturis auctenticis habentur.Huic synodo Burckhardus Wor-maciensis epifcoꝑus vir doctissimus (cuius statim mentio fiet) personaliter interfuit.Ad hunc Aribonem Archiepiscopum eo qod effet amator literarum, &amp; doctorum multi vitj celebres sua ingenia exercitanjs varia opufcula perfriperunt.Moritur sub Conrado Imperatore, Anno Domini M.xxxi.indictione 14.episcopatus vero sui Anno xij.BURCKHARDVS ex monacho ordinis sancti Benedicti Wormaciensis seu Wan-20 gionum episcopis Alberti Gemblacenfis abbatis viri doctissimi quondam auditor atque discipulus(cuius Gratianus jn decretis meminit LXXIII.dif.In nomine Domini)vir certe-tam jn diuinjs scriptris quam in secularibus literis eruditissimos,ingenio subtilis et amp; clarus eloqujo.Scripsit ad aedificationem ecclesiae quoad praeclara volumina:quibus nomen suuim et amp; praesentibus et amp; pofteris commendaujt.Ex his vidi volumen illud magnum,&amp;in-figne opus decretorum jn vigintj libris diftinctum: quo ante compilationem Gratiʒni-monachi iuristarum vtetabatur induftria.Scripsit etiam ad diuerjos multas elegantes epi-ftolas.Caetera quae composuit,jad me non venerunt.Claujt temporibus Henrici primj Anno Domjnt M.xx.BERNO abbas Augiensis coenobij, ordinis sanctj Benedictj Constantienfis dice-30 cesis,vir jn diuinas Scripturis studiosus et amp; eruditjs,atque in secularibuj literis egregie do-c-tus,philosophus,rhetor et amp; musicus celeberrima opinjonis,nec minus vita quam erudi-tione praeclarus.Scripsit non spernenda lectionis plura opufcula:de quibus subiecta fe-runtur.Ad Piligrimum archiepiscopum Colonjensem egregium volumen de musica,cuius originale apud nos est lib.j.de inftrumentis quoque musicae lib.1.ad Aribonem su-pradiectum archiepiscopum Moguntinum,de aduentu Domini lib.i.de officio Misse lib.j.De ieiunjo quatuor temporum lib.j.de ieiunio fabbati lib.j.de mensura monochordi-lib.j.epistolarum ad diuerfos lib.j.Sermones quoquead fratres.Et alia complura.Claujt tempoꝛibus sanctj Henricj Imperatoris primj sed regjs secundj.Anno Domjnt M.xx.ADELBOLDVS epifcoꝑus Traictentfis ex monacho ordinis diuj patris Benedictj 40 (sub cuius nomine Herigerus abbas Lobienfis dialogum de aduentu domini composuit) vir jn diuinjs scripturus studiosus et amp; cruditus atque in secularibug literis egregje doctus,in-genio subtilis,eIoqujo difertus,vita et amp; conuersatione praecipuis,&amp; ob eas virtutes in curia sanctj Henricj Imperatoris,magno jn precio habitus.Scripsit nonnulla haud conte-m-nendae lectionis opufcula,quibus nomen suum pofteris notificaujt.E quibus extat,vira et amp;gesta eiusdem sanctj Imperatoris Henrici lib.j.de laudibus sancta crucis lib.t.de laudi-bus quoque sanctae Mariae lib.i.varios etiam fermones jn laude sanctorum edidit. Et alia multa tam metro quam prosa quae ad notitiam meam non venerunt.Moritur sub Cond-rado Imperatore secundo.Anno Domini M.xxvij.indictione x.epifcoꝑatus sui anno xviii.s.Cal.Decembris.BRUNO epifcoꝑus Herb-50 bipoletenfis.Herbipolenfis studiosus et amp; eruditjs,&amp; secularium litteraruj non ignarus, ingenio prae-vius et amp; defunctus,miraculis corrufcauit.Scripsit et amp; comportaujt ex dictis antiquorum patrum non spernendum opus super toto Psalterio,textumq̃ in multis antea vitiatum mirabili scientia correxit.Siquid amplius scripsit,jad me non peruenit.Moritur sub Hen-rico Imperatore secundo Anno Domjnt M.xlv.indictione XIII.Sexto Cal.Iunij,&amp;jn sanctorum numero relatus est.ADEL

Of Johannes Trithemius 130

of the [unclear] diocese, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and a philosopher, rhetorician, poet, and distinguished theologian most learned in all the letters of secular studies, skilled in Greek and Latin, subtle in talent, profound in knowledge, sweet, ornate, and eloquent in speech, most excellent in expounding the divine Scriptures. Among the other works of his talent he wrote: On Leviticus, a very celebrated and highly useful work, 20 books; On the Epistles of the Apostle Paul, 14 books; also a History of the Kings and Princes of the Franks, 1 book; also a Chronicle of His Own Times, 1 book; Letters to Various Persons, 1 book; Various Sermons, 1 book; and many poems of diverse kinds. He is read to have made very elegant commentaries on many books of the Bible, and also to have written several other treatises, which have by no means come down to us.

Aribo, the nineteenth archbishop of the church of Mainz, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, renowned in talent and pleasing in speech, wrote, among other monuments of his talent, a very beautiful work on the fifteen Gradual Psalms, 1 book, and various letters to different persons. Having celebrated a synod in the monastery of Seligenstadt with his bishops and abbots, in the year of the Lord 1032, indiction 6, he established many good and useful measures, which are contained in authentic writings. Burckhard, bishop of Worms, a most learned man, of whom mention will be made immediately, was personally present at this synod. To this Archbishop Aribo, because he was a lover of letters, many famous men, exercising their talents, wrote various little works. He died under Emperor Conrad, in the year of the Lord 1031, indiction 14, in the twelfth year of his episcopate.

Burckhard, formerly a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, bishop of Worms, or of the Vangiones, once the hearer and disciple of Albert, abbot of Gembloux, a most learned man (whom Gratian mentions in the Decrees, distinction 73, “In the name of the Lord”), a man certainly most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in talent and renowned in speech. He wrote for the edification of the church several distinguished volumes, by which he commended his name both to the present and to posterity. Of these I have seen that large volume and notable work of decrees, divided into twenty books, which the diligence of jurists used before the compilation of the monk Gratian. He also wrote many elegant letters to various persons. The rest that he composed have not come down to me. He flourished in the times of Henry I, in the year of the Lord 1020.

Berno, abbot of the monastery of Reichenau, of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Constance, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, and musician of very celebrated reputation, no less distinguished in life than in learning. He wrote several little works of reading not to be despised, concerning which the following are reported: to Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne, an excellent volume On Music, of which the original is with us, 1 book; also On Musical Instruments, 1 book; to the aforesaid Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, On the Advent of the Lord, 1 book; On the Office of the Mass, 1 book; On the Fast of the Four Times, 1 book; On the Fast of Saturday, 1 book; On the Measure of the Monochord, 1 book; Letters to Various Persons, 1 book; also Sermons to the Brothers. And many other things. He flourished in the times of Saint Henry, emperor first, but king second, in the year of the Lord 1020.

Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht, formerly a monk of the order of the divine father Benedict (under whose name Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, composed a dialogue On the Advent of the Lord), a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, and on account of those virtues held in great esteem in the court of Saint Henry the Emperor. He wrote some little works of reading by no means to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these there is extant the Life and Deeds of that same Saint Emperor Henry, 1 book; On the Praises of the Holy Cross, 1 book; also On the Praises of Saint Mary, 1 book. He also published various sermons in praise of the saints. And many other things, both in verse and prose, which have not come to my knowledge. He died under Conrad II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1027, indiction 10, in the eighteenth year of his episcopate, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December.

Bruno, bishop of Würzburg. [Würzburg] devoted to and learned, and not ignorant of secular letters, [unclear] in talent and deceased, shone with miracles. He wrote and compiled from the sayings of the ancient fathers a work not to be despised on the whole Psalter, and with wondrous knowledge corrected the text, previously corrupt in many places. If he wrote anything further, it has not come down to me. He died under Emperor Henry II, in the year of the Lord 1045, indiction 13, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, and was numbered among the saints.

Adel
