CATALOGVS ILLVSTRIVM VIRORVM. 129 tomos varios elegantissimos lib. 1. epistolas etiam exhortatorias scripsit ad diuerfos. Of- ficium quoque de translatione sancti Martini dulci modulatione composuit: varios cantus in honorẽ sanctorum, quaedam alia quae nos latent. Moritur sub Conrado Im- peratore Anno Domini DCCCXVII. indictione V. tertio Cal. Decembris, episcopatus fui Anno XVIII. Dauantriae sepultus. REGINO abbas monasterij Prumiensis ordinis diui patris Benedicti, in dioecesi Regino ab- bas Prumi- ensis. Treuerorum, vir in diuinis Scripturis eruditissimus, in secularibus literis egregie do- ctus, ingenio subtilis, eloquio clarus, vita conuersatione deuotus, facile inter docto- res sui temporis obtinuit principatum. Scripsit ad Adelberonem Metensem episcopum 10 historiam de gestis Francorum Theutonicorum à natiuitate Christi vsque ad sua tem- pora lib. 10. lubente Ratbodo archiepiscopo Treuerorum comportavit ex decretis sen- tentijs patrum generalium consiliorum opus canonicꝰ insigne, quod praenotauit, de ecclesiastica disciplina religione Christiana in duobus voluminibus lib. 2. sermones quoque multos elegantes composuit libr. 1. epistolas quoque ad diuerfos, libr. 1. alia complura quae ad notitiam nostrae lectionis adhuc minime venerunt. Claruit tempori- bus Arnoldi Imperatoris. Anno Domini DCCCCX. WINDICHINVS monachus Corbeiẽsis in Saxonia ordinis sancti Benedicti, vir in diuinis Scripturis doctus, in teunlaribus literis eruditissimus ingenio promptus cla- rus eloquio, metro excellens prosa, scripsit vtroque stylo multa praeclara volumina, 10 quibus nomen suum posteritati consecrauit. E quibus ego tantum repperi subiecta. Ad Mechtildam filiam Ottonis primi de gestis Saxonum, lib. 3: ad eandem gesta Ottonis pri- mi lib. 1. sermones ad fratres lib. 1. epiftolarum ad diuersos lib. 1. vitã diui Pauli primi Here- mitae profaice metricę li. 2. passionem quoque Teclae virginis similiter metricę lib. 1. epi- grammaton lib. 1. alia insuper multa scripsisse dicitur: quae ad notitiam meam non vene- runt. Claruit temporibus Ottonis Imperatoris primi, Anno Domini DCCCL. ROSVIDA monasterij Gandeshemensis in Saxonia sanctimonialis virgo, nobi- lis ordinis diui patris Benedicti, in diuinis Scripturis studiosa erudita, secularium que literarum disciplinis probe imbuta, ingenio praestans clara eloquio, nec minus con- uersatione quam eraditione insignis, scripsit tam metro quam prosa multa praeclara opuscula, quibus (sexum ingenio superans) nomen suum cum ingenti gloria transmi- fit ad posteros. Ex his ego legi subiecta : Ad Gerbergam abbatissam heroico carmine de vita conuerfatione intemeratae Dei genetricis virginis Mariae librum vnum. de passione domini eodem carmine lib. 1. item de sancto Gangolfo lib. 1. de passione sancti Pelagii martyris his temporibus in Corduba passi lib. 1. de lapsu Theophili vicedomini eius poenitentia lib. 1. de laspu cuiusdam iuuenis per sanctum Basilium conuentui, lib. 1. de passione sancti Dionysij epifcopi martyris, lib. 1. de paflone sancx Agnetis virginis lib. 1. omnia praedicta elegantiꝰ carmine composuit. Scripsit praterea sex comoedias stylo imi- tata Terentium, quorum prima inscribitur conuensio Gallicani principis: passionem in- cludens Iohannis Pauli martyrum. Secunda est de passione Agapis. Chioniae Hirenae 40 virgûm. Tertia de resuscitatione Calymachi Drusianae per sanctũ Iohanẽm. Quar- ta de lapsu conuerfatione Mariae neptis Abrahae Heremitae. Quinta inserbitur conuensio Thayde meretricis. Sexta vero passionem recitat sanctarum virgûm, Fidei, Spei, Cha- natris. Scripsit etiam metricę gesta Ottonis Imperatoris primj, lib. 1. epigrammatum di- uerforum lib. 1. quasdam non inelegantes epistolas. Caetera quae composuit ad notitiam nostrae lectionis non venerunt. Claruit temporibus Otthonis primi secundi clarissimo- rum Imperatorum, Anno Domini DCCCCLXX. SMARAGDVS Abbas monasterij sancti Michaelis in Saxonia ordinis diui patris Benedicti, vir in diuinis Scripturus valde eruditus, secularium literatum non ignarus, ingenio acutus, sermone compositus, vita conuerfatione deuotus, regularis difci- lo plina moderator celeberrimus, in exponendis Scripturis sanctis nomen suum longe lateque innoutit, magnam eraditionis famam obtinuit. Scripsit enim multa praecla- ra volumina, de quibus extant subiecta. In regulam sanctiffimi patris nostri Benedicti lib. 1. in totum Pfalterium lib. 1. in epistolas Euangelia per circulum anni libr. 2. sermo- nes ad fratres alios lib. 1. opus quoque insigne de virtutibus: quod prenotauit Diade- ma monachorum lib. 1. super Donato maiore commentum fecit non abiiciendum. Alia quoque multa tam in diuinis quam in secularibus scripturis volumina scripsisse dicitūr, quae ad manus nostras non venerunt. RADVLPHVS monachus coenobij Fuldensis ordinis diui patris Benedicti Herbi- Radulphus menachius Fuldensis. Rudolphus menachius Fuldensis. Smaragdus abbas S. Michaeles in Saxonia. /

various very elegant volumes, 1 book. He also wrote exhortatory letters to various persons. He also composed, in sweet melody, an Office on the translation of Saint Martin, various chants in honor of the saints, and certain other works that are unknown to us. He died under Emperor Conrad in the year of the Lord 817, in the fifth indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the eighteenth year of his episcopate. He was buried at Deventer.

REGINO, abbot of the monastery of Prum, of the order of the holy father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, exceptionally instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in speech, devout in life and conduct, easily held the first place among the teachers of his time. He wrote for Adelbero, bishop of Metz, a history of the deeds of the Frankish Germans from the birth of Christ down to his own times, 10 books. At the command of Ratbod, archbishop of Trier, he compiled from the decrees and decisions of the fathers and of general councils a distinguished canonical work, which he entitled On Ecclesiastical Discipline and the Christian Religion, in two volumes, 2 books. He also composed many elegant sermons, 1 book; also letters to various persons, 1 book; and many other things which have not yet come at all to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished in the times of Emperor Arnulf, in the year of the Lord 910.

WIDUKIND, a monk of Corvey in Saxony, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, ready in intellect, distinguished in speech, excellent in verse and prose, wrote in both styles many excellent volumes, by which he consecrated his name to posterity. Of these I have found only the following: to Mechtild, daughter of Otto I, On the Deeds of the Saxons, 3 books; to the same, The Deeds of Otto I, 1 book; sermons to the brothers, 1 book; letters to various persons, 1 book; the life of Saint Paul the First Hermit, in prose and verse, 2 books; also the passion of the virgin Thecla, likewise in verse, 1 book; epigrams, 1 book. He is said besides to have written many other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Otto I, in the year of the Lord 950.

ROSWITHA, a consecrated virgin of the monastery of Gandersheim in Saxony, noble, of the order of the holy father Benedict, devotedly learned in the divine Scriptures, and well imbued with the disciplines of secular letters, outstanding in intellect, distinguished in speech, and no less notable for conduct than for learning, wrote, both in verse and in prose, many excellent little works, by which, surpassing her sex in talent, she transmitted her name to posterity with great glory. Of these I have read the following: to the abbess Gerberga, in heroic verse, on the life and conduct of the unstained Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, 1 book; on the Passion of the Lord, in the same verse, 1 book; likewise on Saint Gangolf, 1 book; on the passion of Saint Pelagius, martyr, who suffered in these times at Cordoba, 1 book; on the fall of Theophilus the vicedominus and his repentance, 1 book; on the fall of a certain young man, converted through Saint Basil, 1 book; on the passion of Saint Dionysius, bishop and martyr, 1 book; on the passion of Saint Agnes, virgin, 1 book. She composed all the aforesaid in very elegant verse. She wrote besides six comedies, imitating Terence in style, of which the first is entitled The Conversion of the Prince Gallicanus, including the passion of the martyrs John and Paul. The second is on the passion of Agape, Chionia, and Irene, virgins. The third is on the resurrection of Calimachus and Drusiana through Saint John. The fourth is on the fall and conversion of Mary, niece of Abraham the Hermit. The fifth is entitled The Conversion of Thais the Prostitute. The sixth recounts the passion of the holy virgins Faith, Hope, and [Charity?]. She also wrote in verse the deeds of Emperor Otto I, 1 book; epigrams of various kinds, 1 book; and certain letters not without elegance. The rest that she composed have not come to the knowledge of our reading. She flourished in the times of Otto I and II, most illustrious emperors, in the year of the Lord 970.

SMARAGDUS, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael in Saxony, of the order of the holy father Benedict, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, acute in intellect, composed in speech, devout in life and conduct, a very celebrated guide of regular discipline, made his name known far and wide in expounding the holy Scriptures and obtained a great reputation for learning. For he wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are extant: on the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, 1 book; on the whole Psalter, 1 book; on the Epistles and Gospels through the cycle of the year, 2 books; sermons to the brothers and others, 1 book; also a distinguished work on the virtues, which he entitled The Diadem of Monks, 1 book. He made a commentary on the greater Donatus that is not to be rejected. He is said also to have written many other volumes, both on divine and on secular writings, which have not come into our hands.

RADULPHUS, a monk of the monastery of Fulda, of the order of the holy father Benedict,

Catalogue of Illustrious Men

Adelmann the grammarian, formerly a cleric of the church of Liege, bishop of Brixen, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, not moderately learned in secular letters, a philosopher, poet, and dialectician famous in his time, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote, in a twofold style, certain little works not to be despised, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these there survives a not unpleasant little book on the body and blood of the Lord, addressed to Berengar of Tours, at one time his fellow pupil under Fulbert of Chartres, who was already then beginning to teach errors on this matter; in it he strives against him with many testimonies of the Scriptures. On the same matter he issued a letter to Paulinus, primicerius of Metz. He wrote many letters to various persons, and certain other things. He flourished under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1040.

Ratbertus Paschasius, abbot of Corbie of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, a distinguished translator of Greek and Latin discourse, venerable no less for his life than for his knowledge. He wrote to a certain Placidus, an abbot of our order, a notable work on the sacrament of the altar, one book; also the life of Saint Adalhard the bishop, one book; on the Lamentations of Jeremiah the prophet, one book; and several other works unknown to me. He translated some things from Greek into the Latin tongue. He flourished in the time of the ruler Charles the Fat, in the year of the Lord 880.

Theoderic, monk of the monastery of Saint Matthias the Apostle near Trier, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence. Among other monuments of his study he wrote on the discovery of Saint Celsus, one book; on the miracles of the same saint, one book; many sermons in honor of the saints, one book. He also published some other works which have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished under the emperor Otto III, in the year of the Lord 1000.

Theoderic, archbishop of Trier, the seventy-second after Saint Eucharius, formerly provost of the greater church of Mainz, a zealous and learned man, of outstanding industry in conducting ecclesiastical business. He wrote On the Praises of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, one book; also the life of Saint Liuttrudis, one book; and certain other things. Under the pontificate of this Theoderic, the canons of the greater church of Trier ceased to be regulars. He flourished in the times of the emperors Otto II and III, in the year of the Lord 967. He was buried at Mainz in the church of Saint Gangolf, which he himself had built and endowed for twelve brethren.

Remigius, monk and abbot of the monastery of Saint Luthwin at Mettlach, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, a man most zealous and very learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout in life and conduct, a philosopher, poet, and musician by far the most distinguished of all in his time. He was of such knowledge and learning that from all Germany and Gaul he had most distinguished pupils placed under his instruction to be taught; of these many are read to have been taken up into ecclesiastical rule in diverse regions of the world, some consecrated as abbots, others as bishops. He wrote many excellent little works, by which his name is made known to posterity: on the five books of Moses; not careless commentaries on the Gospel; also Rules on the Apostle; On the Vision of Habakkuk, one book; also an Excerpt from Priscian, one book; a commentary on Donatus, one book. At the command of Eckebert, archbishop of Trier, [unclear] by all of which he shows himself a most learned man. But he published many other things which [unclear].

Goldscherus, monk of the monastery of Saint Matthias near Trier.

Alia denique nonnulla cõ- posuit, quae ad noticiam nostrae lectionis non venerunt. HERMANNVS qui dicebatur Contractus, monachus coenobii sancti Galli, ordi- nis diui patris nostri Benedicti, filius Comitis de Veringen apud Sueuos, vir in diuinis Scripturis eruditissimus, & in secularibus literis omnium doctorum sui temporis doctis- simus, philosophus, rhetor, astronominus, poeta, musicus, & theologus celeberrimus, trium linguarum, Graecae, latinae et Arabicae peritissimus, atque Hebraicae non ignarus, metro ex- cellens et prosa, vita quoque et conuerfatione deuotissimus. Scripsit multa praeclara vo- lumina, quibus memoriam sui posteris commendauit. De quibus subiecta feruntur: De 10 musica lib.I. de monochordo lib.I. de sexaetatibus mundi lib.I. de astronomia lib.II. de cõ- positione astrolabij lib.III. de ecclipsibus solis et lunae lib.I. de computo lib.I. de quadratura circuli lib.I. de conflictu Rythmimachiae lib.I. de physio- nomia quoque lib.I. vitas plurium sanctorum patrum elegantissimo stylo composuit. Epistolas quoque multas ad diuerfos libr.I. diuersi generis edidit pene infinita carmina. Hymnos quoque et cantus in honorem sanctorum dulcissima modulatione multos cõposuit. Equib.est illa de beata Dei genetrice Antiphona, falue regina. Et illa: Alma re- demptoris, cum multis alijs. Transtulit etiam nonnulla Graecorum et Arabum volum- na in latinum, sicut per se fatetur in praefatione quadam Aristotelis. Cuius meriti Her- mannus iste coram Deo fuerit, & quantam ei beatissima virgo Maria gratiam praefiterit, in secundo libro illustrium virorum ordinis nostri me iam ex parte memini descripsisse 20 licet paucis et breuibus. Claruit tẽporibus Henrici Imperatoris tertij. Anno Dominii M.XL. HELPERIVS monachus eiusdem coenobij sancti Galli ordinis diui patris Bene- dicti, vir et ipse in diuinis Scripturis multum eruditus, atque in secularibus literis doctifi- mus, philosophus , astronominus, & poeta celeberrimus ingenio subtilis et disertus elo- quio, nec minus vita quam eruditione infignis. Scripsit tam metro quam prosa multa praeclara opufacula, sed pauca eorum ad manus nostras peruenerunt. Vidi enim duntaxat et legi librum clarissimum quem de computo Ecclesiastico edidit. Et alium de musica praenotatum. Sed et quãdam carmina. Caetera quae composũt ad manus nostras non 30 venerunt. Claruit eodem tempore quo Hermannus Contractus. Anno Domini M.X.L. ROGERVS monachus in Saxonia Corbeienfis coenobij, ordinis sancti Benedicti, vir in diuinis Scripturis studiosis et eruditus, & secularium literarum non ignarus, inge- nio et eloquio clarus. Scripsit vitam et gesta Brunonis Archiepiscopi Colonjenfis fra- tris Ottonis primi Imperatoris lib.I. alia quoque nonnulla edidit, quae ad notitiam meam non venerunt. ALGERS ex scholastico monachus Corbienfis coenobii, ordinis diui patris no- stri Benedicti, vir in sanctis Scripturis iugi studio exercitatus, veterum quoque lectione di- ues, atque in secularibùs litteris magnifice doctus, ingenio cautus disertus eloquio, car- mine valens prosa. Scripsit inter alia ingenij sui opufacula, volumen infigne de Sacra- mento altaris lib.I. de eadem re contra Berengarium lib.I. de gratia quoque Dei libero 40 hominis arbitrio lib.I. alia insuper nonnulla scripsisse dicitur , sed ad noticiam nostrae le- ctionis minime venerunt. ECKEBERTVS clericus Leodienfis ecclesiae,in diuinis Scripturis stuiosus et eru- ditus, atquein secularibus literarum disciplinis egregie doctus, ingenio subtilis clarus eloquio, metro excellens non minus quam prosa. Scripsit vtroque stylo non spernenda opufacula, quibus memoriam sũi posteris commendauit, equibus extat volumen eleganti carmine compositum quod praenotauit:De Aenigmatibus rusticanis lib.I.Et poftea scri- psit de eadem realium maiusculum.Caetera quae composuit,ad noticiam meam non ve- nerunt. Hermannus, who was called Contractus, a monk of the monastery of Saint Gall, of the order of our holy father Benedict, son of the Count of Veringen among the Swabians, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, the most learned of all the doctors of his time; a most celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, astronomer, poet, musician, and theologian; most skilled in three languages, Greek, Latin, and Arabic, and not ignorant of Hebrew; excelling in verse and prose, and also most devout in life and conduct. He wrote many splendid volumes, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among these the following are given: On Music, one book; On the Monochord, one book; On the Six Ages of the World, one book; On Astronomy, two books; On the Construction of the Astrolabe, three books; On the Eclipses of the Sun and Moon, one book; On Computation, one book; On the Squaring of the Circle, one book; On the Contest of Rithmomachy, one book; also On Physiognomy, one book. He composed lives of several holy fathers in a most elegant style. He also published many letters to various persons, one book, and almost countless poems of different kinds. He also composed many hymns and chants in honor of the saints with very sweet melody. Among them is that antiphon concerning the blessed Mother of God, “Salve Regina,” and that one, “Alma Redemptoris,” with many others. He also translated some volumes of Greeks and Arabs into Latin, as he himself acknowledges in a certain preface to Aristotle. Of what merit this Hermannus was before God, and how great a grace the most blessed Virgin Mary bestowed on him, I remember that I have already described in part, though in few and brief words, in the second book of the illustrious men of our order. He flourished in the times of the emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1040.

Helperius, a monk of the same monastery of Saint Gall, of the order of the holy father Benedict, himself also a man much learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters; a most celebrated philosopher, astronomer, and poet, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, no less notable for his life than for his learning. He wrote many splendid little works, both in verse and in prose, but few of them have come into our hands. For I have only seen and read the very famous book which he published On Ecclesiastical Computation, and another entitled On Music, as well as certain poems. The rest which he composed have not come into our hands. He flourished at the same time as Hermannus Contractus, in the year of the Lord 1040.

Rogerus, a monk in Saxony of the monastery of Corvey, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, distinguished in intellect and speech. He wrote the Life and Deeds of Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, brother of the emperor Otto I, one book. He also published certain other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Otto III, in the year of the Lord 1000.

Algerus, from scholasticus a monk of the monastery of Corvey, of the order of our holy father Benedict, a man exercised by constant study in the holy Scriptures, rich also in the reading of the ancients, and magnificently learned in secular letters; prudent in intellect, eloquent in speech, strong in verse and prose. Among other little works of his intellect, he wrote a notable volume On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book; On the Same Matter against Berengarius, one book; also On the Grace of God and the Free Will of Man, one book. He is said to have written certain other works besides, but they have by no means come to the knowledge of my reading.

Eckebertus, a cleric of the church of Liege, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and exceptionally learned in the disciplines of secular letters; subtle in intellect, distinguished in speech, excelling in verse no less than in prose. He wrote, in both styles, little works not to be despised, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among these there is extant a volume composed in elegant verse, which he entitled On Rustic Riddles, one book. And afterwards he wrote a somewhat larger work on the same subject. The rest which he composed have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Leo, the ninth pope, previously called Bruno, bishop of the city of the Leuci, which is called Toul, under the archbishop of Trier, by country an Alsatian, from the counts of Egesheim, sat in the chair of Peter after Damasus for seven years. He was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally learned in the disciplines of secular letters, venerable no less in conduct than in knowledge. He wrote to Constantine [Monomachus?], emperor of the Greeks, On Extirpating Heresies, one book; to the bishops of Africa and Egypt, one book; also letters to various persons, one book; and certain other works unknown to us. He died under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1054, in the seventh indiction, and is reported to have been distinguished by many miracles. Hum

CATALOGVS ILLVSTRIVM VIRORVM. 133 H V M B E R T V S monachus Tullensis, ordinis sancti Benedicti, Leonispapae noni H U m b e r t u s compatriota, vir vndecunque doctissimus, quem Leo praefatus pontifex de Lotharingia, Tullensi videlicet monasterio, Romam traduxit, & ad praedicandum Siculis verbum Dei epifcopum ordinauit. Postea vero sancta Romana Ecclesia praefulem sibi Cardina-lem constituit, homo religiosis et sanctissimus. Scripsit inter caetera ingenij sui monu-menta contra errores Berengarij multa Syntagmata. Missus per Leonem papam ad Con-stantinopolim pro haeresibus extirpandis, sua mirabili scientia et facundia vsque adeo Nicetam Pectoratum monachum, Heresiarcham in praesentia Constantini monachi Imperatoris et Michaelis patriarchae disputando confutauit et deuicit, vt librum suum 20 quem aduersus Romanam Ecclesiam ediderat, mox anathematizaret, eumque propria manu exurendum flammis injiceret. Scripsit ergo eandem disputationem suam per mo-dum dialogi sub nomine Romani et Constantinopolitani interloquentium lib.1. & vari-as ad diuersos epiftolas, & quaedam alia quaead notitiam nostram non venerunt. Huius Humberti, viri doctissimi meminit Lanfrancus in libro suo aduersus Berengarium 25 Nunc tempore Leonis papae noni, Anno Domini Mille-simol. B E R N O L D V S presbyter Ecclesiae Constantiensis in Suevia, vir deuotus, studiosius Bernoldus presbyter constan-tiensis. & eruditus ingenio promptus et clarus eloquio, fertur quaedam non spernendae lectionis etudisse opufcula, quibus nomen et memoriam sui posteris commendauit: sed nulli co-rum ad manus nostras memini peruennisse. Romanum ordinem scripsit et correxit ad vti-litatem ecclesiae. Claruit sub Henrico quatro, Anno Domini m.LX. L A M P E R T U S de Legia monachus coenobij Eucharij et Matthiae Apo-stoli, extra moenia Treuerorum, ordinis diui patris Benedicti, vir vndecunque doctassi-mus philosophus, Rhetor, musicus et poetae clarissimus, ingenio subtilis et comptus elo-quio. Hie amore celebristis patriae natale solum deferes peregrinus venit in Germaniam, & pri-mum quidem in monasterio sancti Martini Coloniae monachus factus est, & duobus multas ad diuerfos, carmina diuersi generis elegantissima et multa et varia cõposuit, & alia complura nobis incognita. Catalogue of Illustrious Men

Humbert, a monk of Toul, of the Order of Saint Benedict, fellow-countryman of Pope Leo IX, a man most learned in every respect, whom the aforesaid pontiff Leo brought from Lotharingia, namely from the monastery of Toul, to Rome, and ordained bishop to preach the word of God to the Sicilians. Afterwards the holy Roman Church appointed him a cardinal prelate for itself, a most religious and most holy man. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote many treatises against the errors of Berengar. Sent by Pope Leo to Constantinople for the extirpation of heresies, by his wonderful learning and eloquence he so far refuted and defeated in disputation Nicetas Pectoratus, a monk and heresiarch, in the presence of Constantine Monomachus the emperor and Michael the patriarch, that Nicetas at once anathematized the book which he had published against the Roman Church, and with his own hand threw it into the flames to be burned. He therefore wrote that same disputation of his in the form of a dialogue, under the names of a Roman and a Constantinopolitan speaking with one another, one book; and various letters to various persons, and certain other things which have not come to our knowledge. Lanfranc mentions this Humbert, a most learned man, in his book against Berengar. He flourished in the time of Pope Leo IX, in the year of the Lord 1050.

Bernold, priest of the church of Constance in Swabia, a devout man, studious and learned, ready in talent and distinguished in eloquence, is said to have put forth certain little works of reading not to be despised, by which he commended his name and memory to posterity; but I do not recall that any of them has come into our hands. He wrote and corrected the Roman Order for the use of the church. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Lambert, monk of the monastery of Saint Laurence at Liege, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, formerly hearer and disciple of Adelmann the Grammarian, bishop of Brescia, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and remarkably instructed in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, and most celebrated poet, distinguished in talent and eloquent in speech, whom the aforesaid excellent pontiff Adelmann commends in notable verses, wrote many splendid volumes both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his name to posterity. But of these I have been worthy to see only a few: the Life of Saint Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, one book; On the Miracles of the Same, one book; also Hymns in varied kinds of verse, one book; Epigrams, one book; letters to various persons, one book. He also composed an office for Saint Heribert and for many other saints, and arranged it with sweet melody. The rest that he wrote have by no means come into our hands. He flourished in the times of Emperor Henry III and Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Lambert of Liege, monk of the monastery of Eucharius and Matthias the Apostle outside the walls of Trier, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, rhetorician, musician, and very distinguished poet, subtle in talent and elegant in speech. He wrote certain splendid little works both in verse and in prose; of these I have found only the following: On the Miracles of Saint Matthias the Apostle, a great work composed in verse, [unclear] books; also on Saint Agricius, one book; to Lambert his abbot he published the Life of Saint Matthias the Apostle, one book; also various sermons in honor of the saints, one book; very many letters to various persons; very elegant poems of different kinds, many and varied; and several other things unknown to us. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080.

Marianus Scotus, monk of Fulda, of the Order of our divine father Benedict, a man [unclear]. Here, from love of his most celebrated homeland, leaving his native soil, he came as a pilgrim into Germany, and first indeed became a monk in the monastery of Saint Martin at Cologne, and [unclear] for two [unclear]; summoned to Mainz by the archbishop because of his holiness and learning, he lived enclosed at Saint Martin for seventeen years and persevered for others until death. He was, moreover, a very great computist and a most diligent assessor of past time, as the very distinguished monuments which he published prove. Of these the following are extant: a notable volume of Chronicles from the beginning of the world down to his own times, [unclear] books; On the Harmony of the Evangelists, one book; also On Computation, one book; various sermons; and several letters to various persons. He died under Henry, the third emperor but the fourth king, in the year of the Lord 1086, in the ninth indiction, in the fifty-eighth year of his age, and was buried in the church of Saint Martin at Mainz, not without a great reputation for sanctity.

134 Of Johannes Trithemius

Of Theodoric, of the monastery of St Alban at Mainz.

THEODORIC, a monk of the monastery of Saint Alban the Martyr at Mainz, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, outstandingly instructed in secular letters, a philosopher and most distinguished poet, subtle in talent and renowned in eloquence, is said to have written certain excellent little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these the following are extant: To Richard, abbot of Fulda, On the Life and Miracles of Our Most Holy Father Benedict, one book; also On His Translation into Gaul, to the same man, one book; Letters to Various Persons, one book. He also published many varied poems. But there are several others which have not yet come into our hands. He flourished under Emperor Henry II, but the third king of this name, in the year of the Lord 1040.

WENERIC, formerly a cleric of the church of Trier, bishop of Vercelli, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, ready in talent and renowned in eloquence, wrote some little works of exercise, by which he proved his learning. In that discord which existed between Hildebrand, Pope Gregory VII, and Emperor Henry IV, he wrote, in the person of Theodoric, bishop of Verdun, while he himself was still a cleric at Trier, to the same Pope Gregory, a volume furnished with divine Scriptures: for he did not rebuke him, but, as an elder, entreated him as a father, with friendly affection, as though grieving, suggesting to him all the things which talkative rumor had spread abroad that he had done or said against right, divine law, and equity. It is entitled On the Discord of Priesthood and Empire, one book. He also composed many other things, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080.

ERHARD, a monk of Corvey in Saxony, of the Benedictine order, a man most zealous in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in talent and ready in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in delivering homilies to the people, wrote, among the other little works of his talent, a notable work On the Pentateuch, five books; also Homilies, one book. He is also said to have written many other things, and to have expounded the sacred Scriptures in many volumes; these have not come to my knowledge.

WILLERAM, abbot of the monastery of Mersburg, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man learned in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular literature, skilled in verse and prose, shone forth no less renowned in life than in learning. After he had for some time devoted his labor to the letters of philosophy in the school of Paris, he returned to his homeland, that is, eastern Francia, which is called Franconia. Made scholasticus of the church of Bamberg because of the eminence of his learning, he did not abandon the sweet fellowship of letters. At length, considering that the vain glory of the world passes away with time, scorning the age and despising worldly things for the love of God, he put on the monastic habit in the monastery of Fulda. As his merits increased, he was finally elected abbot at Mersburg. He wrote a work mixed of meter and prose on the Song of Songs, which he entitled On the Nuptials of Christ and the Church, two books; also various sermons to the brothers; and, as they say, several letters to various persons. He also composed many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080[?].

BERNARD, a monk of the monastery of Saint Vitus of Corvey in Saxony, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine writings and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent, renowned in eloquence, skilled in verse and prose, wrote some little works of his talent, by which he made his name known to posterity. To Hartwig, archbishop of Magdeburg, he published a volume, indeed in lucid but bitter speech, against Henry IV, king but the third emperor, in which it is clearly evident how grievous and hateful the same Henry was to the Saxons. He wrote besides many varied letters, and several other things unknown to us. He flourished in the times of the same Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080[?]. He composed various things.

WILLIAM, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Speyer, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, musician, computist, and most celebrated theologian, devout and most holy in life and conduct, who was renowned for many miracles in life and death, magnificently restored by word and example the monastic discipline among the Germans, which had almost collapsed. He wrote, in lucid speech, little works not to be despised, of which the following are extant: Constitutions of His New Reform, one book; also On Music, one book; also On the Clock, one book; he made a correction of the Psalter, one book; he published various letters to various persons, among which many are said to have been to Anselm II, archbishop of Canterbury, with whom he was most familiar. Some letters of this Anselm to this William are also extant. He also published some other things, which have not come to me. He died under Emperor Henry III, but King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1091, in the fourteenth indiction, on the fourth Nones of July. He was buried in the middle of his church.

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

Wolfhelm, abbot of the monastery of Brauweiler, which is nearly two miles distant from Cologne, born in the district of Ribuarien in the same diocese of Cologne, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular letters, devout and most holy in life and conduct, renowned for the performance of many miracles, subtle in intellect, polished in speech, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote some distinguished volumes, but few of them have come to my knowledge. Against Berengar of Tours, On the Sacrament of the Altar, he published a small but necessary work addressed to Abbot Meginhard, one book; also many sermons to the brothers, various letters to different persons; likewise many elegant poems, composed in various kinds of meter; he arranged epigrams over all the volumes of his library. He is also said to have written several other works, which have by no means come to the notice of our reading. He was first a monk in the monastery of Saint Maximin at Trier, then at Saint Pantaleon in Cologne; afterward he was made abbot at Gladbach; finally he was transferred as abbot to the aforesaid monastery of Brauweiler, where he presided as the third in order. He died under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1091, in the fourteenth indiction, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

Theoderic, abbot of the monastery of Saint Trudo of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, composed in speech, also practiced in verse and prose. He wrote many distinguished little works in both kinds, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of many. Among these the following are reported: Life of Saint Trudo, one book; Life of Saint Bavo, one book; Life of Saint Remold, one book; various sermons to the brothers, one book; also several letters to different persons, one book; certain other works as yet unknown to us. He is said to have flourished in the time of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Conrad, monk of the monastery of Brauweiler, of the order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Cologne, once a hearer and disciple of the most holy abbot Wolfhelm, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters. For the edification of the faithful he wrote volumes not to be despised, with which he usefully occupied his talent; of these the following are extant. The Life of the same Saint Wolfhelm, abbot, addressed to Eberhard of Brauweiler and Herman, abbots of Saint Pantaleon, one book; On the Miracles of the same blessed Wolfhelm, one book; sermons in honor of the saints; several other works unknown to us. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Stephen, also called Herrand, the fourteenth bishop of Halberstadt, formerly abbot of the monastery of Ilsenburg in Saxony, of the order of our most holy father Benedict, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, venerable no less for holiness than for knowledge, wrote, in the person of Count Louis, faithful to the Church, a most elegant letter in the form of a little book, in defense of obedience to the Roman Church, against Henry IV, rebel against the Roman Church, to Waltram, bishop of Naumburg, who stubbornly defended the party of Henry IV against obedience to the supreme pontiff. He also composed other letters in the same cause concerning various ecclesiastical affairs, and various treatises, but they have by no means come into our hands. He died under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1107, in the fifteenth indiction.

Rupert, abbot of Deutz near Cologne, formerly a monk of the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liege, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man in the divine Scriptures, with the Holy Spirit enlightening him, the most learned of all the learned men of his time, not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect, sweet and composed in speech, shone forth renowned no less for holiness than for knowledge. While he was placed in the aforesaid monastery at Liege, when he was still a young man, he applied the greatest zeal to divine letters; but since, because of the slightness of his ability, he made little progress, he turned himself with tears from infancy to prayer, and, the most blessed Mother of God manifestly appearing to him and promising grace, he obtained such knowledge in all Scripture that he had no equal in his time. And lest you think it a fable, he himself confesses these things about himself in many places of his works. Thereafter he had such love for sacred readings that not even while sleeping did he seem to rest from divine conversations, while his tongue and lips were moved as if he were reading something. He wrote almost infinite volumes, of which I have found the following. To Cuno, abbot of Siegburg, afterward bishop of Regensburg, On the Victory of the Word of God, a most beautiful work, thirteen books; On Genesis, nine books; On the Song of Songs, a work to be commended with every praise, seven books; On the Book of Genesis, Job, ten books; On the Books of Kings, On Saint David, fifteen books; On the Old Testament, the great work of Saint Job, twelve books; On the Divine Offices, twelve books; On the Twelve Minor Prophets, thirty books; On the Gospels, twelve books; On the Divine Offices, twelve books; On the Twelve Minor Prophets, thirty books; On the Gospels

136 Of Johannes Trithemius ... on the Gospel of Matthew, 8 books; on the Gospel of John, 1 book; Meditations, 3 books, taking as the material to be followed the miraculous fire of the monastery of Tuitium; also on the Rule of Saint Benedict, 1 book; an Apology for the same work, 1 book; on the four most difficult questions, 1 book; also many and various sermons, 1 book; letters to various persons, 1 book. He is also said to have written many other things, but they have not yet come to the notice of our reading. He flourished, shining with much sanctity and learning and with miracles, under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120. And he died under Lothar III.

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Lympurg, of the order of the holy father Benedict, in the diocese of Speyer, a man excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, devout in life and conduct. He applied himself to philosophy for not a few years in the gymnasium of Paris, while he was still a secular man, and became learned in every scholastic science. At length, having returned to his homeland, namely to the city of the Vangiones, whence he had drawn the origin of his life, he despised philosophy, useless to the soul, together with the things of the world, for the love of God, and put on the habit of holy conversion in the aforesaid monastery; and finally, as his merits increased, by the consent of all the brethren he was elected abbot. There he established, by word and example, the greatest observance of regular discipline, and he deserved often to be refreshed by divine revelations. At the command, seen in a vision, of the most holy Mother of God, he wrote a very beautiful work in praise of the same Virgin: on the Song of Songs, 1 book; on the contempt and vanity of this world, 2 books; on Saint John the Baptist, 1 book; also of his own revelations, 1 book. He also composed many sermons in honor of the saints whose relics or patronages are held in his monastery, and letters to various persons, and various treatises on the holy Scriptures. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord [1120?].

Rudolf, abbot of the monastery of Saint Trudo, of the order of the holy father Benedict, in the diocese of Liege, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and skilled through long practice, and sufficiently learned in the knowledge of secular letters, distinguished in talent and life, excellent also in verse and prose. He wrote little works not to be despised in reading, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among these there is an excellent work against the Simoniacs, 7 books; also a chronicle of deeds of past time, 1 book. He also published many poems of different kinds. He also composed chants in praise of the saints with sweet and regular modulation. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1125.

Franco, second abbot of the monastery of Hasligem, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and well instructed in the knowledge of secular literature, strong in talent and distinguished in speech. He wrote certain commendable little works, both in meter and in prose, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. While he was still a monk, at the command of Fulgentius his abbot, he began an excellent work on the grace of God, which afterwards, when made abbot, he completed. He also wrote metrically on the state of future glory, 1 book; also letters to various persons and various sermons; and certain other things. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1110.

Eckhard, first abbot of the monastery of Saint Lawrence the Martyr, which is called Vraugia, near the Hercynian forest in the diocese of Wurzburg, of the order of the holy father Benedict, a man devoted to and very learned in the divine Scriptures, and not moderately learned in secular letters, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote little works not to be despised in reading, in which he magnificently exercised his talent; among them the following are reported. In imitation of Boethius he wrote, in both kinds, that is, in an alternating style, an excellent volume which he entitled The Lantern of Monks, 1 book; also various and many sermons to the brethren; also many poems and epigrams of different kinds; and certain other things. He flourished under the Emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 1130.

Engelbert, abbot of the monastery of Admont, of the order of Saint Benedict, a man distinguished for learning in the Scriptures and venerable no less for integrity of morals than for knowledge, made his name known by writing and expounding various things, and both by word and example did the lowest things for the edification of his brethren. Among the other works of his talent he wrote: on vices and virtues, 1 book; also many useful sermons to the brethren, 1 book; also several letters. But he also published many other things which have not come into our hands.

Johannes Trithemius

under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1165, indiction 14, in the thirty-sixth year of her age, the twenty-third of her conversion, and the thirteenth of the visitation of the heavenly light, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July. She was buried in the church of the monks of Saint Florinus the martyr, in the middle of the choir, not without the very greatest reputation for sanctity.

Hildegard, a nun, abbess of the monastery of Saint Rupert the Confessor opposite the town of Bingen, on the other side of the river Nahe, in the diocese of Mainz, of the order of our lord father Benedict, born in the county of Sponheim, once a disciple of the blessed virgin Jutta, sister of Megenhard, count of Sponheim, our founder, a virgin of most holy way of life and from her childhood enlightened by divine revelations, was renowned in her life for many miracles, and spread the odor of sanctity into distant regions, so that Eugenius III, Anastasius IV, Adrian IV, and Alexander III, Roman pontiffs, often visiting her by their writings, commended both themselves and the Roman Church to her prayers. Eugenius III also, in a council held at Trier, with Saint Bernard and many cardinals, bishops, abbots, and clerics present, approved the books of this virgin, read publicly before all, as divinely inspired and consonant with the Catholic faith, and admonished her by apostolic letters to persevere in the undertaking she had begun.

She wrote many little works from angelic revelation, of which the following are extant: a brief explanation on the Rule of Saint Benedict, one book; to Wibert the monk, on thirty questions proposed to her by him, one book; the life of Saint Rupert, duke and confessor, one book; also the life of Saint Disibod, an Irish bishop, who, coming as a pilgrim for Christ into Germany, rests in the county of Sponheim, famous for many miracles, one book. On the Sunday Gospels she composed fifty-eight homilies, very obscure and intelligible only to the devout and learned. Likewise, on the Sacrament of the altar against certain heretics of this time, one book. Also a great volume which she entitled Scivias, that is, Know the Ways, namely of God and of the saints, concerning which she disputes very subtly and religiously. Another, which she inscribed Life of Merits, a work not to be despised, three books. Likewise another entitled Simple Medicine, one book, and another called Compound Medicine, one book. In these two she relates the marvelous and secret things of nature by subtle exposition to a mystical sense, so that, unless from the Holy Spirit, a woman could by no means know such things.

She wrote another large volume whose title is Divine Works, one book; to the clergy of the city of Trier, on the future calamities of the Church, one book; also to the people of Cologne on the same subject, one book. In these she foretells wonderful things, yet without determining the time. She also wrote, at the request of certain priests, an exhortatory book for secular persons, one book; to her sisters, a book of exhortation, one book; to the gray monks, one book. Various songs composed with sweet melody. To Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, one letter. Also a book of letters to various persons, of which I have read one hundred thirty-five; in all of them Catholic doctrine shines forth, by which she either confirms faith or instructs discipline. [unclear] in the same volume, stirred by the fame of her sanctity and divine revelations from regions of the world [unclear], commended themselves to her prayers through messengers and letters, and sought from her the solution of various questions.

She died under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1180, indiction 14, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the ninety-first year of her age, and was buried in the middle of the choir of the aforementioned monastery of Saint Rupert, before the high altar.

Werner, abbot of the monastery of Saint Blaise.

Theodoric, an abbot of the order of Saint Benedict, most chaste, a man practiced and learned both in sacred Scriptures and in secular letters, ready in talent, scholastic in speech, wrote for the edification of many the life of the same Hildegard, bride of Christ, one book; also various letters to diverse persons, and certain other things unknown to us. He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

most learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in secular letters: a philosopher, rhetorician, musician, and very celebrated poet. Under the name of Peregrinus he published many excellent volumes, in which the adorned arrangement of the thoughts and the pleasing elegance of the language show that their author was inferior to none of the ancients. Among these the following are reported: a notable work of dialogues under the names of Peregrinus the priest and Theodota, a virgin consecrated to God, which he entitled The Mirror of Virgins, 8 books; on the Gospels through the cycle of the year, a large volume, 1 book; On the Life of the Spirit, the Fruit of Death, 1 book; and another which is entitled The Matricularius, 1 book; another, Didascalon, 1 book; On Music, the Difference of Tones, 1 book; On the Praises of Saint Benedict, in verse, 1 book; various sermons, homilies, 1 book. He is also said to have written some other works, but they have not come into our hands. Whatever he wrote in prose, however, apart from sermons and letters, he arranged for the most part in the manner of a dialogue. There was another preacher who, according to the custom of the moderns, composed sermons to the people under the name of Peregrinus, not to be despised, but much inferior to our Peregrinus in learning and eloquence. For that man, in the manner of the declaimers of this time, content with simple speech, introduces frequent quotations from the Scriptures; but our author, echoing Ciceronian eloquence in the manner of the ancients, was not accustomed to make his discourse scarred with superfluous citations. He flourished under the emperor Conrad, the third of that name, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Dudechinus, priest of the church in Lobenstein, a studious and learned man, for the hope of eternal life went with many others to Jerusalem under the emperor Conrad III. Often fighting with the Saracens in naval battle, he shone forth with great devotion and steadfastness for the faith of Christ. Having returned to his homeland, at the request of Cuno, abbot of Mount Saint Disibod, then still [unclear] of our order, he [unclear] the history of his pilgrimage and how great things [unclear] with the unbelievers. And he published some things on various matters to different persons, and certain other things unknown to us. He flourished under the emperor Conrad, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Christian, archchancellor of the emperor Frederick I, afterward the thirtieth archbishop of Mainz, appointed by him, sat for eighteen years. He was a man most learned in secular literature, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, brilliant in talent, eloquent in speech; even Italy was amazed at him when he spoke. Among other monuments of his ability he wrote: The Deeds of the Emperor Frederick I, 1 book; also very elegant letters to various persons, and certain other things still unknown to us. Leo Tuscus, notary of Emmanuel, emperor of the Greeks, and a contemporary of this Christian, mentions him with praise in the book On the Prevarications and Errors of the Greeks. He flourished in the times of the same Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1180.

Eckebert, second abbot of the monastery of Saint Florin at Schoenau, of the order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, was the brother of the blessed Elisabeth, abbess and virgin of Christ. He wrote: on the Magnificat, 1 book; on the life and death of his holy sister, 1 book; Meditations on Jesus and Mary, 1 book; On the Praise of Our Savior, 1 book; also sermons, in the manner of the ancients, uncorrupted by citations of chapters, 2 books; letters to various persons, 1 book. He also published some other works which have not come into our hands. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1160.

Elisabeth, a nun, sister of the aforesaid abbot Eckebert, abbess of the convent of virgins of Christ which likewise is called Schoenau, is seen to be almost adjacent to the aforesaid monastery of men. A virgin of most holy manner of life, consecrated to the Lord from her infancy, she deserved to be divinely illuminated by many approved revelations, which, for the edification of the faithful, she duly committed to writing. Of these the following are read: she wrote a very beautiful work, namely, on martyrs, confessors, and virgins, 1 book; on the eleven thousand virgins crowned with holy martyrdom at Cologne Agrippina, 1 book; of her revelations, 2 books; to her brother Eckebert, still a canon at Bonn, 1 book; of letters to various persons, 1 book; to Saint Hildegard, virgin of Christ, one letter. Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

Caesarius, monk in Heisterbach. Caesarius, a monk in Heisterbach, of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Cologne, a devout man and an outstanding lover of regular discipline, and trained by long study in the divine scriptures. For the edification of novices, whose instructor he was by office, he wrote in simple and plain speech several little works, the reading of which is not to be despised by devout people. Among them I have found the following: a large volume of dialogues concerning miracles and various visions that occurred in his time in Germany, in [twelve?] books. Also homilies on the Sunday Gospels, two books; likewise on the Gospels concerning the saints, one book; many varied sermons pertaining to the instruction of novices, one book. The other works which he is said to have composed have by no means come to my knowledge through reading. He flourished under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1220.

Peter de Vineis, archchancellor of Emperor Frederick II. Peter de Vineis, archchancellor of Emperor Frederick II, a man very learned and eloquent in secular letters. He wrote, both in his own person and in that of the emperor, six books of letters to various persons; also one book on imperial power, and certain other things. He always defended Frederick’s party against the Roman Church and the supreme pontiff, the vicar of Christ; often in a public council, in the presence of the pope and the prelates, he tried by pleading with such eloquence to excuse his emperor’s rebellion that he turned everyone to admiration. But at last he was repaid by Frederick with a fitting reward, when he expelled him from his court and tore out the light of his eyes. This is the reward of those who defer to princes against obedience to the Roman see of the vicar of Christ; afterwards, unless they repent, they go down wretched to the lower regions. He flourished under the same Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

Jordan of the Order of Preachers. Jordan, of the Order of Friars Preachers, after Saint Dominic master general, a man sufficiently trained and learned in the divine scriptures, an outstanding preacher of the word of God, venerable no less for holiness than for knowledge, who by word and example converted many to the way of righteousness. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote many useful exhortatory letters to the brothers, in which the whole integrity of the spiritual life is seen. He is also said to have composed very useful sermons. He is reported also to have written a book on the institution of his order, and certain other things unknown to us. He flourished at the same time as Saint Dominic, under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1220.

Simon, monk of the monastery of Affligem. Simon, a monk of the monastery of Affligem, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in talent, distinguished in speech. He so turned into practice the counsel of our holy lawgiver Benedict, by which we are enjoined especially to love the divine scriptures in the monastery, that nothing in this life was sweeter to him than to devote himself to holy study, and he always turned over the little works of the holy fathers. Among other things he wrote: sermons on the Song of Songs, [unclear] books; also the admirable vision of a certain lay brother, one book; also several sermons and letters. He also abbreviated the Moralia of the blessed Pope Gregory in ten books, extracting all the better things that suited his purpose. The other works which he wrote have not come to my knowledge. From the time when the orders of the mendicant friars began, the study of letters perished in our order, and down to the present day it scarcely revives. For from the times of Emperor Frederick II down to the last year of Frederick III, in which we wrote these things, for nearly two hundred and seventy years, scarcely anyone appeared in our order who, after the example of the ancients, [unclear] knowledge and holiness of life [unclear], who because of knowledge and usefulness composed anything worthy for the edification of posterity, as is clear in what follows. But these things do not pertain to the matter.

John, bishop of Strasbourg and Bosnia. John, called from his fatherland the German, from the town of [Freiburg?], of the Order of Friars Preachers, of the convent of Strasbourg and afterwards bishop of Bosnia in Hungary, a man much trained and learned in the divine scriptures, and singularly learned in secular philosophy and canon law; later, abandoning that office, he returned to his own order. After Raymond he was appointed master general of the whole order. He wrote certain excellent volumes, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among them there is extant a notable summa on cases, which they call the Summa of Confessors, in five books. On the decrees of Gratian also, the first among the named doctors, he produced an apparatus. The other works which he composed have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250; he was buried in his own convent at Strasbourg, once famous for many miracles.

Otto, bishop of Freising. Otto, bishop of the church of Freising in the Noric province, which is now called Bavaria, as some write, nephew of Emperor Frederick I, a man in the divine scriptures

220
142 MVRIOHANNIS TRITHEMII HEINRICVS de Gandauo Archidiaconus Tornacensis omnium sui temporis facile doctissimus, & tam in philosophia seculari quā in diuinis scripturis valde eruditus, ingenio subtilis, & clarus eloquio, disputator quaestionum scriptrarum acutissimus, qui ob ingentem eruditionis suae gloriam doctor solennis appellari meruit. Scripsit inter multa ingenij sui opuscula. Summam insignem Theologia lib. 1. Super sentenias lib. 4. Quodlibetorum lib. 2. de sancta virginitate lib. 1. de poenitentia lib. 1. Sermones quoque varios, & diuersas in sacra pagina lecturas. In Metaphysicam Aristotelis lib. 14. in libros quoque physicorum lib. 8. & in alios libros Aristotelis multos. Alia praeterea multa scripsit, quae ad manus nostras non venertunt. Moritur sub Adolpho Imperatore. Anno Domini mill. cc. xciii. Indictione III. in die apostolorum Petri et Pauli. Sepultus Tornaci in ecclesia Dei geniticis. EMI CHO abbas Schonaugiensis coenobij ordinis diui patris Benedicti Treuerensis dioccesis Eckeberri supradicti abbatis quandam auditor atque discipulus, vir in diuinis scripturís studiosus et eruditus, secularis quoque literaturae non ignarus, ingenio promptus, & clarus eloquio, non minus vita quam scientia insignis. Scripsit tam metro quam prosa multa praeclara opuscula, de quibus tamen pauca in noticiam meam petuenerunt. Legio pusculum eius de laudibus diuae virginis Helisabeth Schonaugiensis. Item sermones mul tos et varios, & quaedā alia minora non inutilia. Caetera que composuit in manus nostras non venerunt. Claruit sub Eckeberto abbate. Anno Domini millesimo ducentesimo vel circa. CONRADVS de Media Ciuitate vulgariter Halberstat, ordinis fratrũ praedicato rum, vir tam in diuinis scriptris quam in seculari philosophia nō infime doctus, ingenio praestans et disputator egregius. Scripsit super sententias lib. 4. Summam quoque studentiū lib. 3. de triuo lib. 1. Lecturam notablem in librosancti abb. lib. 1. Sermones etiam multos et varios lib. 1. Alia quoque multa scriptisse dicitur, quae ad me non venerunt. In mul tos namque Bibliorum libros lecturas et explicationes fecisse dicitur. Denique ipse con cordantias noui et veteris testamenti per ordinem alphabeti primus ordinasse fertur. NIGOLAVS de Bybera gymnasij Erffordensis magister in scripturis secularibus nobiliter doctus et diuinarum scripturarum non ignarus, ingenio promptꝰ et clarus eloquio, metro exercitus et prosa. Scripsit gemino stylo non spernenda volumina, quibus memoriam sui posteris commendauit. Equibus ego tantum repperio: opus carmine et prosa mixtũ, de cauendo malo, quod praenotauit occultum lib. 1. Epistolarum quoque ad diuerfos lib. 1. & diuersa carmina. Caetera quae composuit, ad noticiam meam non venere runt. Claruit sub Rodulpho Imperatore. Anno Domini millefimo cc. nonagefi moque. HvGO de Argentina ordinis fratrũ prędicatorum doctor Parisiensis, in scriptris sanctis studiosus et eruditus, atque in seculari philofophia egregie doctus, ingenio subitilis et clarus eloquio. Scripsit inter alia ingenij sui exercitationis. Super sententias lib.4. Compendium quoque Theologicae veritatis, opus non abijciendum lib.6. Sermones etiam mul tos. Quodlibeta, quaestiones, disputationes, & varias in diuinis libris explanationes, atque alicuiam non pauca scriptisse dicitut, quae ad noticiam nostram minime venerunt. GERARDVS ciuifdem ordinis fratrũ prädicatotum lector conuentus Leodiensis, vir in diuinis scriptuiris studiosus eruditus, in sermonibus faciendis ad populum declamator egregius, ingenio promptꝰ, sermone scholasticus. Scripsit inter caetera valde vtilẽ tractatum de deoetis personis, quem praenotauit de doctrina cordis, docens septem dispositiones circa cor faciendas, multaque ad aedificationem pertinentia hinc inde de scri pturis diuinis sagaciter colligens. Item sermones (vt ferunt) de tempore de sanctis valde notabiles lib.2.Sed alia complura scripisse dicitur, quead noticiam nostrae lectionis adhuc mini me venerunt. ALANVS de Infulis magister Parisiensis vir in diuinis scptris eruditissimus, secularibus literis nulli suo tempore secundus, Theologus insignis, philofophus clarus, & poeta celeberrimus, qui Ecclesiasticae scholae Parisij multis tempore praefuit, vbi in omni scientia diuina pariter humana, clarus effulit, adeo vt nomen doctoris vniuerfalís nan cisci meruerit. Scripsit metro prosa pene infinita opuscula; de quibus ad mē noticiam non omnia fed pauca periuenerunt: super sententiaslib.4.Quodlibet lib.1.Ad abbatem sancti Aegidij, de vocabulis sacra scripturae opus non paruum, quod praenotauir; Oculum sacrae scripturae lib.1.de doctrina Moysi lib.totidem.In Cantica Canticorum lib.1.de poenitentia ad patriarcham Byturicensem lib.4.de aequiuocis mysticis

142 [unclear] of Johannes Trithemius

Heinrich of Ghent, archdeacon of Tournai, easily the most learned of all men of his time, and very well instructed both in secular philosophy and in divine scripture, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, a most acute disputant of written questions, who, because of the great glory of his learning, deserved to be called the Solemn Doctor. Among the many small works of his intellect he wrote: an outstanding Summa of Theology, 1 book; On the Sentences, 4 books; Quodlibets, 2 books; On holy virginity, 1 book; On penance, 1 book; also various sermons, and diverse lectures on sacred scripture; On Aristotle’s Metaphysics, 14 books; also on the books of the Physics, 8 books; and on many other books of Aristotle. He wrote many other things besides, which have not come into our hands. He died under the emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1293, in the third indiction, on the day of the apostles Peter and Paul. He was buried at Tournai in the church of the Mother of God.

Emicho, abbot of the monastery of Schönau, of the order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, once a hearer and disciple of the above-mentioned abbot Eckbert, a man studious and learned in divine scripture, and not ignorant of secular literature, ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, notable no less for life than for knowledge. He wrote many excellent small works, both in verse and in prose, though few of them have come to my knowledge. I have read his little work On the Praises of the blessed virgin Elisabeth of Schönau. Also many and various sermons, and certain other smaller works, not without usefulness. The rest that he composed have not come into our hands. He flourished under Abbot Eckbert, in the year of the Lord 1200, or thereabouts.

Conrad of Media Civitas, commonly Halberstadt, of the Order of Preachers, a man learned to no low degree both in divine writings and in secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect and an excellent disputant. He wrote On the Sentences, 4 books; also a Summa for students, 3 books; On the trivium, 1 book; a noteworthy lecture on the books of the holy abbot, 1 book; also many and various sermons, 1 book. He is said also to have written many other things, which have not come to me. For he is said to have made lectures and explanations on many books of the Bible. Finally, he is reported to have been the first to arrange the concordances of the New and Old Testament in alphabetical order.

Nicolaus of Bibra, master of the gymnasium of Erfurt, nobly learned in secular writings and not ignorant of divine scripture, ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote volumes in both styles that are not to be despised, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these I find only: a work mixed of verse and prose, On Avoiding Evil, which he entitled The Hidden, 1 book; also Letters to various persons, 1 book; and diverse poems. The rest that he composed have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Hugo of Strasbourg, of the Order of Preachers, a doctor of Paris, studious and learned in holy writings, and excellently learned in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. Among other exercises of his intellect he wrote: On the Sentences, 4 books; also a Compendium of Theological Truth, a work not to be rejected, 6 books; also many sermons; quodlibets, questions, disputations, and various explanations in the divine books; and he is said to have written not a few other things, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

Gerard, of the same Order of Preachers, lector of the convent of Liège, a man studious and learned in divine scripture, an excellent declaimer in making sermons to the people, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech. Among other things he wrote a very useful treatise On God and the Persons, which he entitled On the Doctrine of the Heart, teaching the seven dispositions to be made concerning the heart, and sagaciously gathering here and there from divine scripture many things pertaining to edification. Also sermons, as they say, on the season and on the saints, very noteworthy, 2 books. But he is said to have written several other things, which have not yet come to the knowledge of our reading.

Alan of Lille, master of Paris, a man most learned in divine writings, second to none in his time in secular letters, an outstanding theologian, a distinguished philosopher, and a most celebrated poet, who for a long time presided over the ecclesiastical school at Paris, where he shone brightly in every science, divine and likewise human, so that he deserved to obtain the name Universal Doctor. He wrote almost countless small works in verse and prose; not all, but only a few of these have come to my knowledge: On the Sentences, 4 books; Quodlibet, 1 book; To the abbot of Saint-Gilles, on the words of sacred scripture, a work of no small size, which he entitled The Eye of Sacred Scripture, 1 book; On the Doctrine of Moses, the same number of books; On the Song of Songs, 1 book; On Penance, to the patriarch of Bourges, 4 books; On Mystical Equivocations

140 IOANNIS TRITHEMII eruditus, & in secularibus literis non infime doctus, ingenio subtilis et clarus eloquio. Scripsit quandam de gestis transacti temporis historiam, quae à viris doctis et eruditis plu- rimum commendatur. Caetera si que scripsit, ad noticiam meam nondum venerunt. Huius Otthonis episcopi Aeneas Syluius qui et Pius papa secundus, in quadam oratione Franckfordiae habita non sine laude meminit. Sed in descriptione Europae Phrisiae situm declarans vocabulorum similitudine abductus, Frisiensem pro Frisingensi arbitratus est. Claruit sub Frederico secundo anno Domini M.CC.LX. DAVID ordinis fratrũ minorum, in diuinis scripturis studiosus et eruditus, & non minus vita et conuersatione quam scientia venerandus, in declamandis sermontibusad populum excellentis ingenij fuit. Scripsit ad edificationem simplicium fratrum non sper nenda opuscula, de quibus feruntur subiecta. Ad institutionẽ nouitiorum lib.2.Sermo- nes quoque varij ad populum, & quoedam his similia, quorum lectio deuotis fratribus ad modum vtilis iudicatur. Sepultus est in conuentu Augustensi. GALTERVS epifcopus Magolensis ex infulis oppido Flandriae oriundus, vir in diui- nis scripturis longo studio exercitatus, & secularium literarum non ignarus, ingenio prae- stãs et clatus eloquio, qui suo tẽpore propter doctrinã et eruditionẽ magno fuit in precio. Scripsit ad petitionem praepositi et clericorũ Insulensis ecclesiae, opus limato sermone decorum, super psalterio lib.1.Et qualdam ad diuetos (vt ferunt) non inelegantes epistolas. Alia quoque nonnulla edidit, que ad noticiam nostrae lectionis minime venerunt. ALBERTVS cognomento Magnus ordinis fratrũ praedicatorum, episcopus eccle- 20 siae Ratisponensis in Bauaria, oriundus ex Laugingen vico Sueuia, vir in diuinis serpturis eruditissimus, & in seculari philofophia nulli suo teipore secundus, ingenio subtilis, ter- mone scholasticus, vita et conuerfatione deotus atque sanctiffimus, qui diuises lite- ras et philosophiam Aristotelicam publice multis annis docuit, primo Parisij,deinde a- pud Coloniam Agrippinam,vbi inter altos sanctum Thomam Aquinatem habuit disci- pulum.Ad epifcopatum Ratifponensis ecclesie deinde assumptus, posteaquam illum ali- quamdiu rexisset, defertur, & amore studii falutaris ad cõuentum suum Coloniam reuer- sus est,vbi visque ad finem vitae sue doceando et scribendo permanit. Scripsit autem pene infinita opuscula,de quibꝰ ferũtur subiecta.Suma Theologie notabilis lib.4.Super sen- tentias quoque magistri Lumbardi lib.4.De quatuor Cooeuis lib.1.De homine lib.1.De co- 30 bono lib.1.De vita spiritali lib.1.Super officio Missae lib.1.De corpore Christi lib.1.Deco- dem sermones 32.De muliere forti lib.1.Super libris beati Dionyij Areopagitae lib.5.De multiplici timore lib.1.De laudi bus sanctae Mariae lib.1.Defensorum pro ordinibus fra- trum mendicantium lib.1.De formatione hominis lib.1.de partu hominis lib.1.de origi- ne animae lib.1.Super oratione Dominica lib.1.de modo praedicandi lib.1.de reparacione lapsi lib.1.de adhaerendo Deo lib.1.in Pentateucum lib.5.in lofuae lib.1.in iudicum lib.1. in Ruth lib.1.in regum lib.4.in paralipomenõ lib.2.in Estram et Neemiam lib.3.in Tho- biam lib.1.in Iudith lib.1.in Hester quoque lib.1.in prouerbia Salomonis lib.1.in Ecclesia- sten lib.1.in Cantica Canticorum lib.1.in librum Sapientie lib.1.in Ecclefiasticum lib.1. in libris Machabeorum lib.2.in Iob.lib.1.in Easiam prophetam lib.1.in Hieremia pro- 40 phetam lib.1.in Ezechielem prophetam lib.1.in Danielem lib.1.in duodecim prophetas minores lib.12.in Euangelium Matthei lib.1.in Euangelium Marcii lib.1.in Euangeliũ Lu- cae lib.1.in Euangelium Iohannis lib.1.in omnes epistolas Pauli lib.14.in Apocalypfin Io- hannis lib.1.Sermones de tempore et de sanctis per anni circulum lib.2.de animabus lib.1.Paradyfus animae praenotatus lib.1.Orationes super sententias. Of Johannes Trithemius

learned, and by no means poorly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence. He wrote a certain history of the deeds of the time past, which is very greatly commended by learned and erudite men. Other things, if he wrote any, have not yet come to my knowledge. Aeneas Sylvius, also Pope Pius II, mentioned this bishop Otto in a certain oration delivered at Frankfurt, not without praise. But in the Description of Europe, when setting forth the location of Frisia, led astray by the similarity of the words, he took “Frisian” for “Freisingian.” He flourished under Frederick II in the year of the Lord 1260.

David, of the Order of Friars Minor, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and venerable no less in life and conduct than in knowledge, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote, for the edification of simple brothers, little works not to be despised, of which the following are reported: On the Instruction of Novices, 2 books; also Various Sermons to the People, and certain similar things, the reading of which is judged very useful for devout brothers. He was buried in the convent at Augsburg.

Walter, bishop of [Maguelonne?], born from Lille, a town of Flanders, a man exercised by long study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, who in his time was held in great esteem because of his learning and erudition. At the request of the provost and clerics of the church of Lille, he wrote a work, elegant in polished speech, On the Psalter, 1 book; and, as they report, certain not inelegant letters to the rich. He also published some other works, which have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading.

Albert, surnamed the Great, of the Order of Friars Preachers, bishop of the church of Regensburg in Bavaria, born from Lauingen, a village of Swabia, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular philosophy, second to none in his time; subtle in intellect, scholastic in discourse, devout and most holy in life and conduct. He publicly taught the divine letters and Aristotelian philosophy for many years, first at Paris, then at Cologne Agrippina, where among others he had Saint Thomas Aquinas as a pupil. Afterwards assumed to the episcopate of the church of Regensburg, after he had governed it for some time he left it, and out of love for saving study returned to his convent at Cologne, where he remained teaching and writing until the end of his life.

He wrote almost countless little works, of which the following are reported: A Notable Summa of Theology, 4 books; also On the Sentences of Master Lombard, 4 books; On the Four Coeval Things, 1 book; On Man, 1 book; On the Good, 1 book; On the Spiritual Life, 1 book; On the Office of the Mass, 1 book; On the Body of Christ, 1 book; Ten Sermons, 32; On the Strong Woman, 1 book; On the Books of Blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, 5 books; On Manifold Fear, 1 book; On the Praises of Saint Mary, 1 book; A Defense on Behalf of the Orders of Mendicant Friars, 1 book; On the Formation of Man, 1 book; On the Birth of Man, 1 book; On the Origin of the Soul, 1 book; On the Lord’s Prayer, 1 book; On the Manner of Preaching, 1 book; On the Restoration of the Fallen, 1 book; On Cleaving to God, 1 book; On the Pentateuch, 5 books; On Joshua, 1 book; On Judges, 1 book; On Ruth, 1 book; On Kings, 4 books; On Chronicles, 2 books; On Ezra and Nehemiah, 3 books; On Tobit, 1 book; On Judith, 1 book; also On Esther, 1 book; On the Proverbs of Solomon, 1 book; On Ecclesiastes, 1 book; On the Song of Songs, 1 book; On the Book of Wisdom, 1 book; On Ecclesiasticus, 1 book; On the Books of Maccabees, 2 books; On Job, 1 book; On the Prophet Isaiah, 1 book; On the Prophet Jeremiah, 1 book; On the Prophet Ezekiel, 1 book; On Daniel, 1 book; On the Twelve Minor Prophets, 12 books; On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book; On the Gospel of Mark, 1 book; On the Gospel of Luke, 1 book; On the Gospel of John, 1 book; On All the Epistles of Paul, 14 books; On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book; Sermons for the Season and on the Saints through the Cycle of the Year, 2 books; On Souls, 1 book; Paradise of the Soul, so titled, 1 book; On Death and Life, 1 book; On Plants and Vegetables, 1 book; A Certain Summa of Philosophy, 1 book; On the Unity of the Intellect, 3 books; Questions against the Averroists, 1 book; On the Unity of Form, 1 book;
