166 IOANNIS TRITHEMII ris studiosus et eruditus, regularis disciplinae amator praecipuus, vita et conuersatione de uotus.Scripsit claro et aperto sermone pro fratrum suorum aedificatione quaedam non spernenda opuscula,quibus ingenium suum vtiliter occupauit. Equibus olim mihi exhibuit.de vinea spirituali opus non abijciendum lib. 1. item de pleniore institutione noui tiorum lib.i.Scripsit et alia quaedam parua sed vtilia pro religiosis exercitia, quae ad noticiam nostrae lectionis adhuc minime venerunt.Moritur senex et plenus dierum ac bono rum operum,sub Frederico Imperatore tertio,anno Domini mill.cccc.lxxxv. HEINRICVS Arnoldi natione Saxo, profelliione monachus ordinis Carthusiensis, domus Basiliensis,vir religione deuotos,ingenio clarus,affectu syncerus,mortibus grauis, eloquio dulcis,conuersatione affabilis,pius,humilis,mansuetus,exemplo fulgidus,in sacris literis plurimum exercitus,& pontificii iuris non ignarus.Qui cum officio notarius in sacro Basiliensi concilio multis annis fungeretur,fidelis,iustus ac prudentes cunctorũ testimonio probatus est.Tandemcernens omnia esse vanitatem,vniuersa pro Christi amorem electus,multis annis subditos sibi monachos,in magna pace et tranquillitate guber nauit.Scripsit autem multa opuscula valde deuota atque salubria,de quibus ferunt tur subiecta. Orationum multarum de diuersis sanctis lib.i.Sermones quoque multi lib.i.Historiae de multis sanctis lib.i.Passio Domini ex quatuor concordata lib.i.Meditationes de vita Christi lib.i.de immaculata conceptione beatae Mariae semper virginis li.i.de nouitiorum instructione lib.i.Dialogus inter lesum et Mariam lib.i.Dialogus inter sanctam Margaretham et eius seruulum de exercitijs spiritualibus lib.i.Alius dialogus inter eodẽ de cruce lib.i.de commendatione charitatis lib.i.de sancta humilitate sub forma oratio nis lib.i.iterum de humilitate lib.i.Chronicon domus Carthusiensis sue in Basilea lib.i.& quaedam alia.Moritur sub Frederico Imperatore tertio,& Innocentio papa octauo,anno Domini mill.cccc.Lxxxvii.indictionev. IODOCVS Eichman de Calvve,vico Sueuiae oriundus,in diuinis scripturis studiosus et amp; eruditus,aque in seculari philosophia nõ mediocriter doctus,ingenio promptus,sermo ne scholasticus,in gymnasio Heydelbergensi,legendo,docendo et amp; praedicando multis an nis in praecio fuit.vbi etiam iuxta morem in Ecclesia sancti spiritus praedicatoris aliquandiu gessit officium.Scripsit quosdam (vt ferunt) tractatus nõ abijciendos,sed ad noticiam nostrę lectionis minime venerunt.Extant eius et amp; multi et amp; instructi sermones lib.ii.Questiones quoque variae disputatae.Orationes etiam nonnullae ad patres. Scripsit etiam vocabularium praedicantium lib.i.Et quaedam alia.Claruit sub Frederico Imperatore tertrio,anno Domini mill.cccc.LXXXV.&amp; sub Innocentio papa moritur. HEINRICVS de Geilnhusen,monachus nostri coenobij in Spanhem,ordinis diui patris Benedicti,gymnasij Erffordensis Baccalaurius,&amp; quõdam in oppido natiuo Re ctor scholarium,vir seculati philosophia eruditus,metro exercitus et amp; prosa.Scripsit quaedam spernendae lectionis opuscula,qùibus ingenium suum vtiliter satis occupauit.Ad nouitos monasterij Portae Mariae ordinis sancti Wilhelmi scripsit longam et amp; instructum epistolam de profectu et amp; institutione spirituali lib.i.Vitam sancti Benedicti abbatiss carmine elegiacolib.i.Sermones de tempore et amp; de sanctis lib.1.Contra pluralitatem beneficiorum lib.i.Et quasdã ad diuersos epifolas.Moritur sub Frederico imperatore tertio,quinquagenerius,anno Domini mill.cccc,LXXXVIII.indictione sexta,vii.Calend.Aprilis,sepultus in parte ambitus mei dionali. PETRVS le Kyrslaken ordinis fratrum praedicatorum Hebraicae et amp; Latinae linguae peritus,declamator sermonum famosus.Scripsit ad Episcopum ecclesię Ratisponensis in Bauaria tractatum, contra perfidos ludaeos de conditionibus veri Messiae,id est Christi Claruit sub Frederico Imperatore tertiop̄,anno Domini mill.ccxc.LXXV. PHILIPPVS Kersbeele,ordinis fratrũ beatę Mariae semper virginĩs de monte Carmeli conuentus Gandensis,Philosophus et amp; Theologus Vincentij de Nouo castro,ordinis praedicatorum,contra puriffimam conceptionem diuę Mariae virginis latrantem,qñ Carolus Fernandus monachus diui ordinis Benedicti in Francia ad stylũ elegantiorem reformauit.Mortuus est Pa rifijs studens ante ferme triennium, NICO-

[Of] Johannes Trithemius

[unclear] studious and learned, an outstanding lover of regular discipline, devout in life and conduct. He wrote, in a clear and plain style, certain little works not to be despised for the edification of his brethren, with which he usefully occupied his talent. Of these he once showed me: On the Spiritual Vineyard, a work not to be rejected, one book; likewise On the Fuller Instruction of Novices, one book. He also wrote certain other small but useful exercises for religious, which have not yet come to the knowledge of my reading. He died old and full of days and good works, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1485.

Heinrich Arnoldi, a Saxon by nation, by profession a monk of the Carthusian order, of the house of Basel, a man devout in religion, distinguished in talent, sincere in affection, grave in character, sweet in speech, affable in conduct, pious, humble, gentle, bright in example, very much exercised in sacred letters, and not ignorant of pontifical law. When he held the office of notary for many years in the holy Council of Basel, he was approved by the testimony of all as faithful, just, and prudent. At length, seeing that all things are vanity, having chosen all things for the love of Christ, he governed the monks subject to him for many years in great peace and tranquillity. He wrote many very devout and wholesome little works, among which the following are reported: Many Prayers on Various Saints, one book. Also Many Sermons, one book. Histories of Many Saints, one book. The Passion of the Lord Harmonized from the Four, one book. Meditations on the Life of Christ, one book. On the Immaculate Conception of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin, one book. On the Instruction of Novices, one book. Dialogue between Jesus and Mary, one book. Dialogue between Saint Margaret and Her Little Servant on Spiritual Exercises, one book. Another Dialogue between the Same on the Cross, one book. On the Commendation of Charity, one book. On Holy Humility in the Form of a Prayer, one book. Again, On Humility, one book. Chronicle of His Carthusian House in Basel, one book; and certain other things. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1487, in the fifth indiction.

Jodocus Eichman of Calw, born in a village of Swabia, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and also not moderately instructed in secular philosophy, ready in talent, scholastic in speech, was held in esteem for many years in the Heidelberg gymnasium by reading, teaching, and preaching. There also, according to custom, he held for some time the office of preacher in the church of the Holy Spirit. He wrote certain treatises, as they say, not to be rejected, but they have not come to the knowledge of my reading. There are extant many learned sermons of his, two books. Also various disputed questions. Also some orations to the fathers. He also wrote A Vocabulary for Preachers, one book, and certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1485, and died under Pope Innocent.

Heinrich of Gelnhausen, a monk of our monastery in Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict, bachelor of the Erfurt gymnasium, and once rector of scholars in his native town, a man learned in secular philosophy, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, with which he occupied his talent usefully enough. To the novices of the monastery of Porta Mariae of the Order of Saint William he wrote a long and learned letter On Spiritual Progress and Instruction, one book. The Life of Saint Benedict the Abbot in elegiac verse, one book. Sermons on the Temporale and on the Saints, one book. Against the Plurality of Benefices, one book. And certain letters to various persons. He died under Emperor Frederick III, at the age of fifty, in the year of the Lord 1488, in the sixth indiction, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, buried in the southern part of the cloister.

Peter le Kyrslaken, of the order of the Friars Preachers, skilled in the Hebrew and Latin languages, a famous declaimer of sermons. He wrote to the bishop of the church of Regensburg in Bavaria a treatise against the faithless Jews On the Conditions of the True Messiah, that is, Christ. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Philipp Kersbeele, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Ghent, philosopher and theologian, [wrote?] against Vincent of Newcastle, of the order of Preachers, who was barking against the most pure conception of the divine Virgin Mary, which Carolus Fernandus, a monk of the divine order of Benedict in France, reshaped into a more elegant style. He died while studying at Paris almost three years ago,

Nico-

256
164 IOANNIS TRITHEMII bis incognita. Claruit sub Frederico Imperatore tertio, & Sixto papa quarto, anno Domini mill.cccc.lxx. IOHANNES de Lutra villula, dictus de Lutrea, vir in diuinis scripturis studiosus eruditus in philosophia scholastica egregie doctus, ingenio subtilis, sermone compositus, vita conuersatione honestus singulariter deuotus, amator virtutum, hostis vitiorum, fortissimus auaritiae contemptor, qui pluralitatem beneficiorum abhorruit, titulum Episcopatus sibi oblatum spreuit, qui primum in gymnasio Erffordensi Theologiam multis annis gloriose docuit, postea in Ecclesia Moguntina praedicatoris officium trennue gessit. Scripsit super sententias lib.IIII. Quaestiones quoque varias. Sermones de tempore de sanctis lib.II. Et quędam alia nobis incognita. Moritur sub Frederico Imperatore tertIO, Sixto papa quarto,anno Domini millesimo CCC.LXXIX.indictione XII. ALANVS de Rupe ordinis fratrũm praedicatorum,vir in diuinis scripturĩs eruditus,in declamandis sermonibus ad populum excellentissimae opinionis, vita conuerfatione Deo deuotus, beatae Marię semper virginis amator praecipuus, eiusque Rosarij mulatus promotor venerandus, perquam singulari dono supernae consolationis recreari meruit, crebris reuelationibꝰ miraculis que (vt ferunt) honōrari. Scripsit inter caetera ingenij sui opufcula: Compendium pfalterij beatae Marie semper virginis lib.I.de mi- ra culis quoque Rosarij eiusdem gloriosa virginis lib.I.Sermones multos varios lib.I.de fraternitate Rosarij lib.I.Et alia complura.Moritur in conuentu suo Svvoiensi, sub Frederico Imperatore tertiO, Sixto papa quarto anno Domini mill.cccc.LXXXIIII.indictione VII.in vigilia assumptionis Mariae. CONRADVS de Zabernia,in scriptutis sanctistudiosus eruditus, secularis literaturae non ignarus, musicus excellens, diuinī verbi praedicator egregius, ingenio clarus, sermone scholafticus, vita conuerfationẽ honestus. Scripsit aperto sermone quaedam nõ abijcienda opufcula.quibus ingenium suum vtiliter fructuose exercitans, etiam nominis sui memoriam posteris dereliquit. E quibus ego tantum repperi istade monochordo lib.I.de modo bene cantandi lib.I.de collectarũ conclusionibꝰ lib.I.Sermones multos varios.lib.I.Caetera qua composuit.ad noticiam nostrae lectionis minime venerunt. Claruit sub Frederico imperatore tertiO Sixto papa quarto,anno 30 Domini mill.cccc.LXXV.§.sub quibus mortuus est. IOHANNES de Dorfftein, ordinis fratrũ Eremitarum sancti Augustini, conuentus Erffordensis,vir in diuinisscripturis sudiosus eruditus,, secularis philofopiae nōignarus,ingenio subtilis ad difputandas enodandasque difficiles questionẽs scriptrarum satis idoneus,in declamandis quoque sermonibꝰ ad populum excellentis facundia.in gymnasio Erffordeni docendo prędicando excellit. Scripsit non contemnenda opufcula,de quibus feruntur subiecta: Quaestiones senteniarum lib.I.de vitij lingue lib.I.Sermones de tempore de sanctis lib.II.Et quaedam alia.Claruit Erffordiae sub Frederico Imperatore tetrio Sixto papa quartoanno Domini mill.cccc.LXXV. THEODERICVS de Herxen,congregationis fratrum clericorum in communivientium Visitator Rector, vir deuotus in diuinis scriptris studiofus eruditus, ingenio promptus, sermone scholafticus,Scripsit ad aedificationem fratrũm suorum multa praeclara opufcula.quibus ingeniũ vtiliter satis exercitans,memoriam sui posteris com-mendauit.E quibus extant subiecta.In pfalterio toto lib.III.Super oratione Dominica lib.I.Super salutationẽ Angelica lib.I.de passione Domini lib.I.de morienda quoque defiderio lib.I.Sermones complures ad fratres quaedam alia. Claruit sub Fredericko Impe-tore III.Sixto papa quarto anno mill.ccccc.LXXXI.indictione XIIII. ANGELVS de Brunsuco Saxoniaqui vulgo dicebatur Magister Engelinus,virin diuinis scripturã eruditissimus,in seculari philofophia egregie doctus,ingenio clarus, sermõne scholafticusz in declamandisz ad populum sermonibꝰ facundus, qui in gymna-sio Erffordensi docendo legendo clarius effulsit. Scripsit insigne opus super canone Missae,quod Moguntiiae coram clericis legisse perhibetur.Sermones multos varios lib.I.Quaestiones etiam diuerfas in scholis difputauit.Et quaedam alia.Moritur Argentinę in coenobio poenitentium sepultus, sub Frederico Imperatorem III.Anno Domini mill.CCCC.LXXXI.indictione XIII CRODENBERG,abbas monasterij mōtis sancti Iohannis Baptistae Rincaugiensis,Moguntine diocesis ordinis diui patris Benedicti,vir deuotus eruditus,, regularis seruantia nouiter introductae custos amator integerrimus, vnus ex his qui nostrae reformatiõe

Of Johannes Trithemius unknown to us. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1470.

JOHANNES of the little village of Lutra, called de Lutrea, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, learned and excellently taught in scholastic philosophy, subtle in intellect, composed in speech, honorable in life and conduct, singularly devout, a lover of virtues, an enemy of vices, a most steadfast despiser of greed, who abhorred plurality of benefices and scorned the title of a bishopric offered to him, first taught theology gloriously for many years in the school of Erfurt, and afterward vigorously performed the office of preacher in the church of Mainz. He wrote On the Sentences, four books; also various Questions; Sermons on the season and on the saints, two books; and certain other things unknown to us. He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1479, in the twelfth indiction.

ALANUS de Rupe, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, of most excellent reputation in declaiming sermons to the people, devoted to God in life and conduct, a special lover of blessed Mary ever virgin, and a venerable [unclear] promoter of her Rosary, deserved to be refreshed by a very singular gift of heavenly consolation, and, as they say, to be honored with frequent revelations and miracles. He wrote, among other little works of his talent: A Compendium of the Psalter of Blessed Mary Ever Virgin, one book; also On the Miracles of the Rosary of the same glorious Virgin, one book; many various Sermons, one book; On the Fraternity of the Rosary, one book; and many other things. He died in his convent of Zwolle, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1484, in the seventh indiction, on the vigil of the Assumption of Mary.

CONRADUS de Zabernia, zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, an excellent musician, an outstanding preacher of the divine word, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, honorable in life and conduct. He wrote in plain speech certain little works not to be rejected, by which, exercising his talent usefully and fruitfully, he also left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these I have found only the following: On the Monochord, one book; On the Manner of Singing Well, one book; On the Conclusions of the Collects, one book; many various Sermons, one book. The rest that he composed have not at all come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1475, under whom he died.

JOHANNES de Dorfftein, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, of the convent of Erfurt, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, sufficiently suited to disputing and resolving difficult questions of the Scriptures, and also of excellent eloquence in declaiming sermons to the people. In the school of Erfurt he excelled in teaching and preaching. He wrote little works not to be despised, of which the following are reported: Questions on the Sentences, one book; On the Vice of the Tongue, one book; Sermons on the season and on the saints, two books; and certain other things. He flourished at Erfurt under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1475.

THEODERICUS de Herxen, visitor and rector of the congregation of the Brethren Clerics Living in Common, a devout man, zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech. He wrote for the edification of his brethren many excellent little works, by which, exercising his talent usefully enough, he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Of these the following are extant: On the Whole Psalter, three books; On the Lord’s Prayer, one book; On the Angelic Salutation, one book; On the Passion of the Lord, one book; also On the Desire of Dying, one book; several Sermons to the brothers, and certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year 1481, in the fourteenth indiction.

ANGELUS de Brunsuco, a Saxon, who was commonly called Master Engelinus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently taught in secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, eloquent in declaiming sermons to the people, who shone out very brightly in teaching and lecturing in the school of Erfurt. He wrote a notable work On the Canon of the Mass, which he is said to have read at Mainz before the clergy; many various Sermons, one book. He also disputed diverse Questions in the schools, and certain other things. He died at Strasbourg and was buried in the monastery of the penitents, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1481, in the thirteenth indiction.

CRODENBERG, abbot of the monastery of Mount Saint John the Baptist of Rheingau, in the diocese of Mainz, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a devout and learned man, a most upright guardian and lover of the newly introduced regular observance, one of those who by our reformation

257
168 IOANNIS TRITHEMII secularis philosopiae non ignarus, ingenio promptus, sermone scholasticus, non minus honestate vitae quam scientia venerabilis. Scripsit nonnulla pręclara opuscula, quibus ingeniũ vtiliter occupans memoriam fui posteris commendauit. Equibus in praefato Erffordensi gymnasio fertur ordinarie legisse, in epistolas Pauli lib. xiiij. Orationes in laudẽ sancti Hieronymi varias habuit, sermones multos et diuersas quaestiones cum quibusdam alijs scripsisse dicitur, que in manus nostras adhuc minime venerunt. Moritur in monasterio sancti Petri Erffordidae sepultus, sub Maximiliano Rege Romanorum, anno Domini mill.cccc.xciii.indictione xii. IOHANNES Frytag de Dufeldorp, oppido Coloniensis diocesis, ordinis fratrumbeatae Mariae semper virginis de monte Carmeli, conuentus Mogintinensis et Prior Argentinensis, vir in diuinis scripturis studiosus et eruditus, doctor Coloniẽsis, ingenio acutus et vehemens, in declandis sermonibus ad populum nõ minus facundus quam doctus, vita et conuersatione deuotus, & regularis disciplinae amator pręcipuus. Scripsit de obseruantia dierum festorum lib.i.de locis terrae sanctae quam fuis pedibus terens oculis vidit lib.i.sermones varios de tempore et de sanctis lib.II.Et alia complura. Moritur sub Maximiliano Imperatore, anno Domini mill.ccxc.xciiij.indictione XII. Argentinę sepultus. SEBASTIANVS Murrho Colmariensis,presbyter et canonicus in Colmaria oppidonatiuitatis sua, vit in diuinis scripturus studiosus eruditus, in secularibus literis deductissimus philosophus, orator, poeta, astronomus Cosmographus celeberrimae opinionis, legum canonum notitia insignis, trium linguarum principalium, Hebraicae, Grecae Latinae peritissimus, architecture, musica, toto Quadruiuo nulli secundus, ingenio subtilis, eloquio differtus, vita conuersatione matutus. Scripsit ad Iacobum Wimpchengum Sletstatensem breue quidem, sed per pulchrum epito me de historia laudibus Germanorum principum populorum li.i.Carmina quoque multa elegantissima lib.i.Epistolas etiam multis ad diuerfos lib.i. Et varias orationes.Commentarios in Baptistam Mantuanum Carmelitamincepit, quos morte pręuentus non expeduit. Eosque Conradus Leontorius monachus Mulbronnensis terminandos suscepit propediem imprimendos concedet. Moritur non sine maxima studiosorum iactura peste sublatus, sub Maximiliano rege Romanorum, anno Domini millesimo cccc.xcv.indictione XIII. RODVLPHVS Langius,Monasteriensis Ecclesięin Wesphalia canonicus, vir indiuinis scripturis studosus, in secularibꝰ literis erudi tissimus, orator poeta clarus, ingenio subtilis,e loquio differtus. Scripsit tam metro quam prosa multa pręclara opufcula, quibus se praefentibus vtilem, posteris memorabilẽ fecit.E quibus subiecta feruntur.Ad Decanum Coloniensis Ecclesiae carminum diuerforum lib.i.de obsidione Nesiensis oppidi à Carolo duce Burgundie lib.i.de tribus Regibus sapphicum.De laudibus Alberti Magni carmen.Carmina multa, varias ad diuerfos Epistolas.Erquadam alia nobis incognita.Audio eum adhuc viuere senem,quanquam sint qui illum vita excessisse dicant hoc anno Domini mill.cccc.xcv. IACOBS de Stralen presbyter EcclesięColoniensis,vir in diuinis scripturar longostudio eruditus, secularis philofophiae non ignarus,ingenio subtilis,sermone scholafticus.qui olim in Ecclesia Basiliensi pradicatoris aliquandiu gessit officium. Scripsit multa commendanda quidem opufcula,quibus memoriam fui posteris commendauit. Equibusnonnulla in Erffordensi gymnasio publice legisse perhibetur.In Euangelium Iohannislib.I.Canonem Misse lib.i.de passione Domini lib.i.Itinerarium terrae sanctae lib.i.Quaestiones varias diputatas in scholis lib.i.Sermones multos, alia plura, viuit adhuc infere Wilhelmus de Aquisgrani.vir in diuinis scriptruris eruditus, secretaris philofophie nonignarus: ingenio subtilis,firmone scholasticus,vita conuerfatione pręclarus.qui olim inEcclesiaBasiliensipra dicatorisaliquandiugessitofficium.Scripsitmulta commendanda quidemopusculaquibusememoriamfuposteriscommendauit.Equi busnonnullainErffordenisigymnasiopublicelegisseperhibetur.InEuangeliumIohannislub.I.CanonemiMisselib.I.Depassionedomini.lib.I.Iterariumterraesanctaelib.I.Quaestionesvariasdiputatasinscholis.lib.I.Sermonesmultos,aliaplura,viiuitadhucinfere.

Johannes Trithemius not ignorant of secular philosophy, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, venerable no less for the integrity of his life than for his learning. He wrote several excellent little works, by which, usefully occupying his talent, he commended his memory to posterity. Of these, in the aforesaid gymnasium at Erfurt, he is said to have lectured in ordinary course: On the Epistles of Paul, 14 books. He delivered various orations in praise of Saint Jerome. He is said to have written many sermons and diverse questions, together with certain other things, which have as yet by no means come into our hands. He died in the monastery of Saint Peter at Erfurt, where he was buried, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1493, indiction 12.

Johannes Frytag of Dufeldorp, a town of the diocese of Cologne, of the order of the brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Mainz and prior of Strasbourg, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, a doctor of Cologne, sharp and forceful in intellect, no less eloquent than learned in delivering sermons to the people, devout in life and conduct, and an outstanding lover of regular discipline. He wrote: On the Observance of Feast Days, 1 book; On the Places of the Holy Land, which he traversed with his own feet and saw with his eyes, 1 book; various sermons on the season and on the saints, 2 books; and many other things. He died under Maximilian, Emperor, in the year of the Lord [1494?], indiction 12, and was buried at Strasbourg.

Sebastian Murrho of Colmar, priest and canon in Colmar, the town of his birth, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, a philosopher, orator, poet, and astronomer-cosmographer of very celebrated reputation, distinguished in knowledge of laws and canons, most skilled in the three principal languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, second to none in architecture, music, and the whole Quadrivium, subtle in intellect, rich in eloquence, mature in life and conduct. He wrote to Jakob Wimpfeling of Sélestat a brief indeed, but very fine, epitome on the history and praises of the German princes and peoples, 1 book; also many most elegant poems, 1 book; also many letters to various people, 1 book; and various orations. He began commentaries on Baptista Mantuanus the Carmelite, but, overtaken by death, did not bring them forth. Conrad Leontorius, monk of Maulbronn, undertook to finish them and will shortly permit them to be printed. He died, to the very great loss of scholars, carried off by plague, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1495, indiction 13.

Rudolf Langius, canon of the church of Münster in Westphalia, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, a distinguished orator and poet, subtle in intellect, rich in eloquence. He wrote many excellent little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he made himself useful to those present and memorable to posterity. Of these the following are reported: To the Dean of the Church of Cologne, a book of diverse poems, 1 book; On the Siege of the Town of Neuss by Charles, Duke of Burgundy, 1 book; On the Three Kings, a Sapphic poem; On the Praises of Albert the Great, a poem; many poems; various letters to various people; and certain other things unknown to us. I hear that he is still living, an old man, although there are some who say that he departed this life in this year of the Lord 1495.

Jacob de Stralen, priest of the church of Cologne, a man learned by long study in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, who once for some time held the office of preacher in the church of Basel. He wrote many little works indeed worthy of commendation, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these he is said to have read some publicly in the gymnasium at Erfurt: On the Gospel of John, 1 book; On the Canon of the Mass, 1 book; On the Passion of the Lord, 1 book; Itinerary of the Holy Land, 1 book; various questions disputed in the schools, 1 book; many sermons; and several other things. He is still living in [unclear].

Wilhelm of Aachen, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, excellent in life and conduct, who once for some time held the office of preacher in the church of Basel. He wrote many little works indeed worthy of commendation, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these he is said to have read some publicly in the gymnasium at Erfurt: On the Gospel of John, 1 book; On the Canon of the Mass, 1 book; On the Passion of the Lord, 1 book; Itinerary of the Holy Land, 1 book; various questions disputed in the schools, 1 book; many sermons; and several other things. He is still living in [unclear].

[unclear] laid the foundations for the Bursfeld reform. Since he was an outstanding lover of blessed Mary ever virgin, he wrote in her honor, in plain discourse, a very celebrated volume, taking the material of praise from each of her members under the figure of a cluster of grapes; he entitled it On the Vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth, one book. The Exercise of Novices, one book. On the Preparation of the Priest for Mass, one book. He delivered various addresses in our chapters, one of which begins: “The crown of our head has fallen”; another: “Catch us the little foxes”; a third: “Blessed is the servant,” etc. He also composed various sermons for the brothers, which are partly extant and partly have been lost through negligence. He died under Frederick III, emperor, and Innocent VIII, pope, in the year of the Lord 1486, in the fourth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. He was buried in the right apse of the choir toward the south side, before the altar of the holy father Benedict.

Georgius Molitoris of Neuenburg, a man trained by long study in the divine Scriptures, excellently learned, and not moderately instructed in scholastic philosophy, which they call Aristotelian; subtle and acute in intellect, honorable in life and conduct. In the school of Erfurt he taught theological science gloriously for not a few years. He wrote On the Sentences, three books; On the Passion of the Lord, one book; also many sermons and various questions. He died under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pope, in the year of the Lord 1490, in the second indiction.

Nicolaus of Wachenheim, doctor of Heidelberg, skilled in the holy Scriptures through long and sustained practice, an acute interpreter of Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, mature in life and conduct. In the school of Heidelberg, for almost fifty years, in teaching, lecturing, and writing, he was held in the highest esteem as a prince among theologians. He wrote works not to be despised in reading, by which he commended his memory to posterity; of these, however, very few have come to my knowledge. He flourished at Heidelberg under Frederick III, emperor. Questions on the Sentences, one book. Several sermons; speeches not useless to the clergy, [unclear]. He died at Heidelberg under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1480, a very old man, under Sixtus IV, pope; he died almost [seven years?] before this.

Heinrich, surnamed Prudent, a monk of the Carthusian order, prior of the house of the Valley near Bruges in Flanders, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in intellect, devout in life and conduct, singularly devoted to God. For the instruction of religious he wrote several devout little works, by which he commended his name to posterity. Among these there is extant a very celebrated work, especially suited to devotion, which he entitled Tetralogue of Devotion, three books. He also wrote many devout letters to various persons, and many other things not yet seen by me. He died in the new house of Saint Sophia of Constantinople near ’s-Hertogenbosch, in which he held the office of prior for some years, under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1483, in the second indiction.

Rudolphus Agricola of Groningen, a Frisian by birth, a man the most learned of all in secular letters in his time, not ignorant of divine letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, and most celebrated poet, skilled in the three principal languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin; subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech; formerly the teacher of Johann Dalberg, bishop of Worms, a man equally most learned. In the school of Heidelberg, by teaching and writing, he easily held first place in Latin. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these I have found the following: a heroic poem On Saint Anne, one book; Life of Francis the Patriarch, one book; also a very subtle Dialectic, three books; also many letters to various persons, several poems and epigrams, and various treatises. He composed an epitaph of this kind: “Envious fates have shut beneath this marble Rudolph Agricola, the hope and glory of Frisian soil; in this one man, namely, Germany earned whatever praise Latium has, whatever Greece has.” He was buried at Heidelberg in the convent of the Friars Minor.

Thilmann, prior or provost of the monastery of Saint Christopher at Ravengiersburg, at the edge of the diocese of Mainz toward Trier, in the place that from antiquity was called the retreat of the Huns, of the order of regular canons of Saint Augustine, a man in the divine Scriptures

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

Nicolaus of Crutzenach, from a town of the county of Spanheim, in the diocese of Mainz, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, distinguished in life, an acute disputant and an excellent preacher of sermons, taught theology publicly for many years in the university of Vienna. Both among the scholars there and before Emperor Frederick III he won great [unclear] and profit from his learning. He wrote certain distinguished volumes of his talent, of which the following are reported: On the Sentences, four books; On the Most Pure Conception of the Blessed Mary Ever Virgin, one book; Sermons on the Season and on the Saints, two books; many orations to [unclear]; various questions disputed in the schools; and certain other works unknown to us. He died at Vienna in Austria, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1491, in the ninth indiction.

Petrus Schot of Strasbourg, priest and canon of Saint Peter in Strasbourg, a man whose intellect was practiced in the divine Scriptures, most learned in both laws, and very learned in the other arts of humanity, a philosopher, rhetorician, and very celebrated poet, excellent in intellect, mature, honorable, and distinguished in life and conduct. He wrote certain beautiful little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his memory to posterity. On Saints John the Baptist, the Evangelist, and Chrysostom, he wrote a learned and delightful work in elegiac verse, one book; Diverse Poems, two books; Letters to Various Persons, one book; Brief praises of Andrew the Apostle in verse; Praises of John Gerson. Before the first [unclear] in the year of the Lord 1491, in the ninth indiction.

Petrus Schot of Strasbourg.

[unclear] a part of his works printed. He also published some other works which have not come to my knowledge. He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1492, in the ninth indiction, in the thirty-first year of his age. He was buried at Strasbourg in his church of Saint Peter; Jacob Wimpheling described his life, character, and intellect.

Nicasius of Voerda, by nation a Brabanter, having been deprived of his eyes from the third year of his life by the bitterness of measles, was made entirely blind, and for that reason utterly ignorant even of all letters. As if a second great miracle, in our time he showed himself a Didymus of Alexandria, since he appeared most learned in every doctrine and science, both divine and human. For in the university of Cologne, where he died, [unclear].

[unclear] delightful works in elegiac verse, two books; Diverse Poems, three books; Letters to Various Persons, five books; Brief praises of Andrew the Apostle in verse; Praises of John Gerson. Before the first [unclear] in the year of the Lord 1491, in the ninth indiction.

Nicasius of Voerda.

He recited [unclear] from memory. In the University of Louvain he first received the degree of master in arts; afterward he directed schools for some time in Mechelen; then, having returned to Louvain, he was appointed licentiate in sacred theology. He does not celebrate the divine rites by himself at the altar. Finally, using his memory as a book, he recites. [unclear] through the age, he was made doctor of canon law by the consent of all the doctors in the Cologne Academy, and at Cologne was a cautious interpreter of imperial laws. He published a very celebrated work which he read extraordinarily in that same University of Cologne, with more than one hundred students taking it down by the pen: On the Institutes, four books. Likewise at Louvain he published On the Sentences, four books. He disputed various questions in the schools, which are partly extant and partly have been taken away. He also gave many sermons to the people. He gave me several rather elegant letters, in one of which, quite full, he wove together the whole story of his fortune, when questioned by me; [unclear] that he had made little works, he was humble. He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1491, in the tenth indiction, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, at Cologne, in [unclear].

Third, in the year of the Lord 1590. For there was an error about him in [unclear]. He was buried in the church of Saint Columba, not in the major church. For there was an error about him in the Catalogue of Writers.

Johannes Pheffer of Widenberg, by nation an East Frank, a man learned in the divine Scriptures through long study, excellently taught in secular philosophy, excellent in intellect, devout, gentle, and distinguished in life and conduct. Sent from the University of Heidelberg, he illuminated the beginning of the university of Freiburg by his learning; there he taught sacred letters for many years with great glory, and thoroughly instructed many of his hearers. He wrote an outstanding volume on the Epistles of Paul, which, when read publicly, he entitled; Priestly Directory, thirteen books; also Questions on the Sentences, one book; sermons; and various treatises on the Scriptures, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III in the year of the Lord 1490. And he died almost two years before this.

CATALOGVS ILLVSTRIVM VIRORVM. in senate bona sub Maximiliano Rege, & Alexandro papa sexto; anno Domini millesi- mo cccc.xcv. GABRIEL Byel, ordinis clericorum in cõmuni viuentiũ, vir indiuinis scripturis lon- gostudio exercitatus, in seculari philosophia (quam Aristotelicam vocant) egregie do- ctus, ingenio clarus, sermone compositus, vita conuersatione deuotus, qui gymnasio Tubingensi ab exordio institutionis suae multis annis praefuit, vbi tam in philosophia quã in sacris literis claros discipulos erudiuit. Scripsit quaedam non spertenda opuscula, qui- bus nomen suũ notificauit. E quibus ordinarie legit in praefata Academia, in canonẽ Mis- sae volumen grande pulcherrimũ lib. i. Scripsit etiam de passione Domini lib. x. sermo- nes quoque multos li. r. Iam scribere dicitur super sententias opus singulare vtile; quod suis modo disciplinis legit. Alia quoque nonnulla scripsisse dicitur, que ad noticiã non ve- nerunt. Viuit adhuc prope septuagenarius, ecepto fortiter perstat in studio, sub Maximi- liano Rege Romanotum, anno Domini mil.cccc.xcv. indictio nexxit. IOHANNES de Lapide, monachus ordinis Carthusiensis, domus Basiliensis, vir indi- uinis scripturis eruditissimus, secularis litteraturę non ignarus, ingenio subtilis, sermo- ne disertus, vita conuersationẽ praeclarus, qui olim in gymnasio Parīsiensi magisterium in artium facultate assecutus, pluribus annis rexit in eadẽ studiumq́; sacrarum literarum docendo, legêdo ac disputando diligēter pꝛofequens, doctorali dignitate in schola Theo- logorum decorari meruit. Hic doctrinaem eorum Parisiensium qui Reales appellantur, primos adBasiliensium vnintersitatem transtalit, ibidemque plantauit, roborauit auxit. Interpraecipuos quoque Tubingẽsis gymnasij ineptores vnuꝫ fuit, qui denique post liberam plurium beneficiorum dimissionẽ ad canonicatũ praedicationis officium insignis Ec- clesię Basiliensis vocatus fuit, ac tandem paucis annis elapsis omnia pro Christi amore re- linquens, sacr̃ ordinis Carthusiensiß habitũ assumpsit. Scripsit autẽ multa praeclara volū- mina, quibus se prasen tibus vtile futurus memorabillem fecit, pauco rũ tamẽ ex his copia nobis obuenit. Introductorium Grammaticę lib. i. Dialogus de arte punctandi lib. de propositionibus exponibilibus lib. i. de arte soluendi sophificas argumentationes li. 1. Explanatio omnium librorum Logice Aristotelis lib. x. Explanatio librorum Physicę et lib. i. de his qua ad dignũ sacerdotē pertinent lib. i. Resolutorium dubiotũ peri- culorum circa Missam occurrentium lib. i. Summariũ passionis Domini li. r. de ascensio- ne Domini inter sermones Meffret, sermo vnus. Item inter sermões ipsius scripist tractatum lib. i. Et alia multa nobis incognita. Multos praeterea diuersorum austorum libros pertractatus capitula distinxit, singulis argumenta praemittens, quibus intentio semper virginis, obl̃tuens non minus sancte quam docte os loquentium iniqua. Qui tra- tatus cum praedictis sermonibus in plerisque exemplaribus habebitur impressus. Scripsit et- iam sermones tam ad clerũ quam ad populum complures lib. i. Orationes quoque Epi- stolas varias lib. i. Et alia multi nobis incognita. Moltos praetereà diuersorum austo- rum libros pertractatus capitula distinxit, singulis argumen ta praemittens, qui bus inten- tionibꝰ dilucide agnosci. Equibus sunt libri Cjeeronis de officijs, de amicitia, de sentētute, de somnio Scipionis. Item libri Logicę Aristotelis, Libri eiusdem de anima, libri Metaphysicę. Item libri beati Effrem diaconi, Iohan nis Chrysostomi, Augustini, li- ber Epistolarium eiusdem, omnes fere libri diui Ambrosij Episcopi, alia complura. Vi- uit adhuc senate bona in Carthusia Basiliensi, varia componit, multosque suis scriptis exemplo ad sancta studia prouocat. Sub Maximiliano Imperatore anno Domini quo hoc scripsimus mill.cccc.xcv. indictione xiii. Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

in good old age under King Maximilian and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1495.

Gabriel Biel, of the order of clerics living in common, a man exercised by long study in the divine Scriptures, excellently learned in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, distinguished in talent, composed in speech, devout in life and conduct, presided for many years over the school of Tübingen from the beginning of its foundation, where he trained notable pupils both in philosophy and in sacred letters. He wrote certain works not to be despised, by which he made his name known. Among these, in the aforesaid academy, he ordinarily lectured on the Canon of the Mass, a large and very beautiful volume, one book. He also wrote On the Passion of the Lord, ten books; also many sermons, [unclear] book[s]. He is now said to be writing on the Sentences, a singular and useful work, which he now lectures to his pupils. He is also said to have written several other things, which have not come to our knowledge. He is still living, nearly seventy years old, and persists vigorously in the study he has undertaken, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1495, indiction XIII.

Johannes de Lapide, a monk of the Carthusian order, of the Basel house, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, who formerly, in the school of Paris, obtained the mastership in the faculty of arts, governed there for several years, and, diligently pursuing the study of sacred letters by teaching, lecturing, and disputing, deserved to be adorned with the dignity of doctor in the school of theologians. He first transferred to the university of Basel the teaching of those Parisians who are called Realists, and there planted, strengthened, and enlarged it. He was also one of the principal founders of the Tübingen school. Finally, after the free resignation of several benefices, he was called to the canonry and office of preaching of the distinguished church of Basel; and at length, after a few years had passed, leaving all things for the love of Christ, he assumed the habit of the sacred Carthusian order. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he made himself memorable as one who would be useful to those now living and to those to come; yet only a few of these have come into our possession. An Introduction to Grammar, one book. A Dialogue on the Art of Punctuation, [unclear] book[s]. On Expoundable Propositions, one book. On the Art of Solving Sophistical Arguments, one book. An Explanation of All the Books of Aristotle’s Logic, ten books. An Explanation of the Books of the Physics, [unclear] and one book. On Those Things Which Pertain to a Worthy Priest, one book. A Resolutory Work on Doubtful Dangers Occurring around the Mass, one book. A Summary of the Passion of the Lord, [unclear] book[s]. On the Ascension of the Lord, among the sermons of Meffret, one sermon. Likewise among his sermons he wrote a treatise, one book. And many other things unknown to us. Moreover, he divided the books of various authors into treatises and chapters, prefixing arguments to each, by which the intention [unclear]. Always of the Virgin, not less holily than learnedly, stopping the mouth of those who speak wicked things. This treatise, with the aforesaid sermons, will be found printed in most copies. He also wrote several sermons both to the clergy and to the people, one book; also various prayers and letters, one book; and many other things unknown to us. Moreover, he divided many books of various authors into treatises and chapters, prefixing arguments to each, by which their intentions may be clearly recognized. Among these are Cicero’s books On Duties, On Friendship, On Old Age, and On the Dream of Scipio; likewise Aristotle’s books of Logic, the same author’s books On the Soul, and the books of the Metaphysics; likewise the books of blessed Ephrem the deacon, of John Chrysostom, and of Augustine, the same author’s book of letters, almost all the books of Saint Ambrose the bishop, and many others. He is still living in good old age in the Basel Charterhouse, composes various works, and by his writings and example summons many to holy studies. Under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we have written this, 1495, indiction XIII.

Conrad, called Hensel, by country a Hessian, pastor and rector of the church of Frankfurt, doctor of sacred theology and canon law, a very celebrated interpreter, most subtle in talent, composed in speech, who first, after absorbing letters in the school of Erfurt, publicly taught philosophy for some time, then in the school of Greifswald, and, having obtained the church of the imperial city of Frankfurt, vigorously governs to this day, and has for many years governed, by word and example the common people committed to him. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are extant. On the Sentences, [unclear] book[s]. Also On the Canonical Epistles, seven books. On the Song of Songs, one book. On Penance, Fasting, and Prayer, one book. On Faith, Hope, and Charity, one book. On the Four Virtues Which They Call Cardinal, one book. On the Sanctification of the Sabbath, one book. On the Gospels and Sunday Epistles through the cycle of the year, one book. Many various sermons, one book. Also On the Precepts of the Church and Evangelical Truth, one book. On the Interdict, one book. On Ecclesiastical Liberty, one book. Against Heretical Malefactors, one book. Against the Bohemian Hussites, one book. To the Archbishop of Cologne on the Office of the Mass, one book. To P

Johannes Trithemius

He composed very many scholastic [works], beyond number. In addition, for our common use he translated many little works from Greek into Latin: Xenophon’s Apology for Socrates; likewise Nestorius the heretic, whom Saint Cyril the bishop refuted at the Council of Ephesus; also the confession of a certain Cyprian the Greek; Proclus on the praises of blessed Mary ever virgin; some of Lucian’s Dialogues of the Dead; a dialogue by the same author on the council of the gods. He also translated metrically into the German language the single combat from Homer’s Iliad, on the duel of Paris and Menelaus. Likewise he rendered into Latin Ephanius on the life and death of the prophets, and also Maximus Tyrius, the Platonic philosopher, in the oration: If God made good things, whence do evils come? Besides these he translated some other things, which forgetfulness has now taken from our memory. He lives near Stuttgart, bound by the bond of marriage, yet no less applying himself to letters and writing various things, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Wilhelmus de Velde

Wilhelmus de Velde, by homeland a Gueldrian, canon of the order of the regulars of Saint Augustine in Frankenthal in the diocese of Worms, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, a philosopher and astronomer, and a cosmographer of celebrated reputation, deep in intellect, acute, and very subtle; composed in speech, devout in life and conduct. He wrote and is writing certain very beautiful and wondrous volumes, in which he clearly shows to readers the sharpness of his intellect. Of these he recently showed me the following: Statutes of the sisters of his order, one book; a most subtle work on the whole universe, that is, on the beginning, middle, and end of the world, which he entitled The Greater Empyrean, 24 books; likewise a compendium of this work, which he entitled [unclear]; also many tables on various subjects, no less useful than subtle; many sermons to the people; epigrams and various poems; also some things not to be rejected in mathematics; also many letters to me and to others. Finally he composed some other things, which will come to light in their own time. He is still living, fifty years old, in Darmstein, a village of the territory of Worms, serving as parish priest, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 8.

Petrus Bo-Landan Lautenburger; Petrus Bolandanus of Ladenburg; Petrus

Petrus Bolandus of Ladenburg, parish priest in the town of Schriesheim in the diocese of Worms, a man most learned in every respect, a distinguished philosopher, mathematician, theologian, and very celebrated poet, ready in intellect, eloquent in expression, excellent in verse, and also an outstanding declaimer of sermons in prose. He wrote some splendid volumes, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Yet few of these have come to my knowledge: a Sapphic poem for Emperor Frederick III; a Sapphic poem on the death of Rudolf Agricola; innumerable epigrams from the sayings of Seneca and Plato; a long Sapphic poem on the divine Mary; a heroic poem on the work On the Threefold Whiteness; a heroic poem on our work On the Misery of Prelates; elegiac poems, Sapphic poems, and letters to Johann Camerarius Dalburg, his bishop of Worms. He wrote a poem to the students of Heidelberg on account of the plague; of epigrams and elegies almost innumerable, one book; besides these many sermons and elegant orations, and very ornate letters to various persons. He is also said to be writing many other things, but in secret. He is still living in Schriesheim, not far from Heidelberg, being 50 years of age, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Johannes Bertram of Neuenburg; Johannes

Johannes Bertram Nuenburghen wrote to Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, a long letter in the form of a little book, On the Value of Masses, one book. He also explained various questions disputed in the schools. He is now writing and lecturing ordinarily on the epistles of Paul. Almost ten years before he had lectured on Genesis, a great and pleasing work. He is still living in the academy of Mainz, having passed his forty-fifth year of age, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction 14.

Rudolphus de Euschringen

Rudolphus de Eufstringen, of Baden, [unclear] of the archbishop of Trier, a man most learned in every respect and a most [unclear] cultivator and investigator of all antiquity, a supreme philosopher, a most sagacious interpreter of law, and a most eloquent lover and [unclear] of the divine Scriptures, subtle and ready in intellect, in speech

170 [Works] of Johannes Trithemius

…the same on the Psalter according to the exposition, one book. From parts of Saint Thomas he [unclear], one book. He began a lecture on the Apocalypse of John, which he will continue in the school at Mainz. He also wrote notably on Aristotle’s books of Economics. He likewise disputed and wrote notable questions on the Ethics. He also composed many other things which have not come to my knowledge. He is still living, almost sixty years old, in the city of Frankfurt, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495.

Johannes Gotfridi of Odernheim, pastor of the church of Saint Catherine in Oppenheim, not far from Mainz, bachelor of sacred theology, a man excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote many and various treatises, which he has not yet allowed to come to light. He also composed many elegant sermons for the cycle of the year and on various subjects. He wrote letters both to me and to others, composed with grace of eloquence. Finally, he translated many treatises of the ancient authors from Latin speech into the vernacular tongue, with no less eloquence than [unclear], if indeed charm and ornament are allowed to exist in the German language. Among these I have seen Cicero’s On the Nature of the Gods, which he translated at the urging of the valiant knight Frederick, chamberlain of Dalberg, no less elegantly than learnedly. He also began to translate Augustine’s City of God for the same Frederick, and has now completed almost twelve books. He also wrote and translated many other things, which will come to light in their own time. He is still living in good old age at Oppenheim, writing various things, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495.

Werner Rolevinck of Laer, a Westphalian by country, sprung from the diocese of Münster, a monk of the Carthusian order, of the house of Saint Barbara in Cologne, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, subtle in intellect, devout in life and conduct. He wrote many distinguished volumes, among which the following are extant: On all the Epistles of Paul, three great volumes, which work he entitled The Teaching of Paul, fourteen books. Life of Paul, seven books. Paradise of Conscience, one book. On the sacrament of the altar and the value of Masses, one book. To John, bishop of Münster, Form for God-fearing Bishops, one book. Form of Living for Canons and Secular Priests, one book. On the dignity and power of priests, one book. On true nobility and its origin, one book. To Everwin, count of Bentheim, on the best manner of governing the commonwealth, one book. On the government of rustics, one book. On hospitallers and those occupied with works of mercy, one book. On fraternal correction and monastic visitation, and on those who hinder its good progress, one book. Twelve questions on those to whom it belongs to treat sacred Scripture, and on the degrees conferred in the schools, one book. Ten questions on the advancement of religious, one book. Eight questions, one book. Fasciculus temporum, with circles from the beginning of the world down to the times of Pope Sixtus IV, one book. On the praise of Westphalia and its conversion to the faith, one book. On the origin of the Frisians, one book. On contracts, whether they are lawful, one book. On the calendar and martyrology, one book. Twenty rules useful for prelates, one book. A long sermon on Saint Benedict, printed some time ago, which begins thus: “I in my innocence have entered.” A question whether Christ on the cross prayed for all, one book. On the excellence of Albert the Great, one book. To a certain abbot of our order who was compelled to accept the episcopate, one book. On the common brotherhood of those feasting together, one book. On the instruction of novices, one book. On the difference of passions and what a passion is, one book. On the security of the license of prelates, one book. On holy desires and the manner of conducting oneself in them, one book. On the contemplation of simple persons, one book. On devoutly paying the canonical hours, one book. Many synodal, chapter, and popular sermons, the number of which is uncertain. He also wrote almost countless letters both to me and to others. These are the things which he recently confessed to me that he had written, in the seventieth year of his age and the forty-eighth of his conversion, when I was in his cell, under Emperor Maximilian and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1495, indiction 13, on the sixth day before the Ides of May. Many other unfinished works are moreover still in his hands, to be completed in their own time.

Johannes of Keysersberg, priest and distinguished preacher of the church of Strasbourg, a man devoted to and learned in the divine writings, and excellently learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, an unafraid herald of truth, a lover of virtue, an enemy of vices, who has often pursued the crimes of the wicked with free voice even to the point of envy. He wrote several distinguished little works, of which, however, he has as yet allowed few to come to light. There are extant his most beautiful sermons to the people, two books. 174 IOHANNIS TRITHEMII se praesentibus vtilem posterisque memorabilem reddidit. E quibus extat summa nota- bilis de contractibus, quantum ad conscientiae forum pertinet, & Theologicam decisio- nem, plusquam per centum quaestiones distincta li.vii. Oratio quoque non inelegans de reformatione monachorum. Caetera quae scripsit vsque adeo eclare semper studuit, vt ne mihi quidem amicitiae foedus ea revulare vnquam potuerit. Epistolas ad me et alios plu- res dedit. Viuit adhuc regens Theologicam scholam in gymnasio Tubingensi, oppido Sueuiae Ducis Eberhardi Wirtenbergensis, & varia conscribit, sub Maximiliano Rege an- no Domini mill.cccc.xcv. CONRADVS Celtis Proticius, Francus orientalis, ex Syveinfordia natus, vir vn- decunque doctissimus philofophus clarus, orator facundus, Astronomus et Cosmogra- phus insignis, & Poeta laureatus, diuinarum quoque scripturarum non ignarus, Graece et Latinae linguae peritus, ingenio excellens et disertus eloquio. Scripsit metro et prosa multa praeclara volumina: quibus memoriam sui posteris commendauit. Equibus mihi aliquando legit subiecta. Ad Maximiianum regem in vtramque Ciceronis Rhetoricam, Epitoma id est compendium seu Breuarium lib.i. Carmen de laudibus eloquentiae lib.i. de arte verificandi lib.i.de condendi Epistolis lib.i.de situ vtibis Norici montis, quod opus Nurenbergam praenotauit lib.i.Peregrinationem suam Sarmaticam lib.i. Carminũ seu Epigrammaton lib.iiii.Amnorum qui secundum quatuor Germaniae latera, lstulae inscribuntur lib.iiiii.Panegyrin Duci Bauariae lib.i.Carmen sapphicum in vitam sancti Sebaldi patroni Nurenbergensium.librum vnū; Germaniam lib.i.Orationes multis et varias lib.i.Epistolas tam ad me quam ad alios multas elegantissimas metro et prosae- didit,& in Cosmographia,cuius scientiffimus est varia scripsit, quae posthac in lucem suo tempore ventura sunt. Viuit adhuc in gymnasio Engolstatensi in Bauaria, ordinarie le- gens in poesi et oratoria, annos habens aetatis x x v. sub Maximiliano Imperatore, anno Domini quo haec scribusmus,millefimo CCC C XCV.indictione XIIII. IOHANNES de Veteri aqua, alias de Gauda, patria Hollandinus, educatio- ne Brabantinus, ordinis fratrum beatae Mariae semper virginis de monte Carmeli, conuentus Mechliniensis,hoc tempore Subprior Cassellensis in Hassia, vir in diuinis scripturis studiosus, & longa exercitatione peritus, in declamandis ad populum fer- monibus excellentis ingenij, ordinisque sui feruens amator cultorque deuotus.Scri- pfit ad multorum fratrum infan̄tiām et Aedificationēin, de initio et profectū ordinis sui commendabile opus, quod praenotauit: Fasticulum temporum tripartitum or- dinis Carmelitarum lib.iiii.In quorum primo Heliam et Prophetas ordinis Carme- litici fundatores extitisse probat.in secundo sanctos et Canonifatos ex eodem enume- rat, in tertio successiones Priorum generalium totius ordinis sui secundum tempo- ra locat. Scripsit etiam de puriffima semper conceptione beatae Mariae virginis lib.i.Sermones quoque innumeros ad populũ lib.ii.Epistolas tam ad mequamad alios pene infinitas. Scripsit praeterea multas Epistolas contra quendam Wigandum ordinis prae- dicatorum conuentus Franckfordensis lectorem, conceptionem purissimam Dei ge- nitricis, temere impugnantem. Is enim sęptimum capitulo tractatus nostri de sancta Anna vesana loquacitate impugnans, contra me scripsit longam et procacem Epi- stolam.in qua se pensantem manus subscripsit, & nomen suum proprium fraudulen- ter subticuit, cuius temeritati tum per istum Iohannem Carmelitam, tum per alios viros eruditos satis admodum est responsum. Ego enim vnas tantum literas rescri- bens, nolui diutius cum Barthologo contendere verbis.Caetera vero quae Iohan-nes iste composuit, in manus nostras non venerunt.Viuit adhuc in conuento Cas- sellensi Subprioris gerens officium et varia conscribit.Annos aetatis habens plusquam sexaginta, sub Maximiliano Imperatore anno Domini quo haec scripsimus mill.cccc. xcv.indictione XIIII RVTGERVS Sicamber de Venray patria Gelrensis,ordinis canonicorum regula- tium sancti Augustini,coenobij diui Apostoli Petri Dumetensis, vulgariter Heynensis, 59 non longea Wormacia,vir in diuinis scripturís studiosus et eruditus, & in secularibus literis egregie doctus, ingenio acutus, sermone disertus, vita et conuerfatione de- uotus, metro excellens et prosa.Scripsit tam carmine quam oratione soluta,multa commendanda opufcula, quorum lectio non minus vtilis est quam iucunda.Ex his legi subiecta.Dialogum de institutione puerili lib.i.Dialogum de inquisitione beatae vitae li.ii.Hymnorũ de sancta Maria vario genere metri li.ii.qui continent ferme duode- cim millia verfuū.Dialogũ de vario vfù literarũ li.iii.Dialogũ dere-

Johannes Trithemius

... made himself useful to those present and memorable to posterity. Of these there is extant a notable Summa on contracts, insofar as it pertains to the forum of conscience and to theological decision, divided into more than one hundred questions, seven books. There is also a not inelegant oration on the reform of monks. The other things that he wrote he always strove so much to keep hidden that not even the bond of friendship could ever induce him to reveal them to me. He sent letters to me and to several others. He is still living, directing the theological school in the college of Tuebingen, a town of Swabia belonging to Duke Eberhard of Wuerttemberg, and he is writing various works, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1495.

Conrad Celtis Proticius, an East Frank, born at Schweinfurt, a man most learned in every respect, a famous philosopher, an eloquent orator, a distinguished astronomer and cosmographer, and a poet laureate, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, skilled in Greek and Latin, excellent in intellect and fluent in speech. He wrote many splendid volumes in meter and prose, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these he once read the following to me: To King Maximilian, on both Rhetorics of Cicero, an epitome, that is, a compendium or breviary, one book; a poem on the praises of eloquence, one book; On the Art of Versifying, one book; On Composing Letters, one book; On the Site of the City of Noricus Mons, which work he entitled Nuremberg, one book; his Sarmatian Journey, one book; Poems or Epigrams, four books; Loves, which according to the four sides of Germany are inscribed [Istulae], [four?] books; a Panegyric to the Duke of Bavaria, one book; a Sapphic poem on the life of Saint Sebald, patron of the people of Nuremberg, one book; Germania, one book; many and various orations, one book. He has issued very many most elegant letters, both to me and to others, in meter and prose, and in cosmography, of which he is most learned, he has written various things which hereafter, in their own time, will come to light. He is still living in the college of Ingolstadt in Bavaria, lecturing ordinarily on poetry and oratory, being twenty-five years of age, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, in the fourteenth indiction.

Johannes of Veteri Aqua, otherwise of Gouda, a Hollander by homeland, a Brabanter by upbringing, of the order of the Brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Mechelen, at this time subprior of Kassel in Hesse, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and skilled by long practice, of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, and a fervent lover of his order and a devout cultivator of it. For the instruction and edification of many brothers he wrote a commendable work on the beginning and progress of his order, which he entitled The Three-Part Fascicle of Times of the Order of Carmelites, four books. In the first of these he proves that Elijah and the prophets were founders of the Carmelite order; in the second he enumerates the saints and canonized persons from the same order; in the third he places in chronological order the successions of the priors general of his whole order. He also wrote On the Most Pure Conception Ever of the Blessed Virgin Mary, one book; also countless sermons to the people, two books; letters both to me and to others, almost infinite in number. He wrote besides many letters against a certain Wigand, of the Order of Preachers, lecturer of the Frankfurt convent, who rashly attacked the most pure conception of the Mother of God. For he, attacking with mad loquacity the seventh chapter of our treatise on Saint Anne, wrote against me a long and impudent letter, in which he signed himself “the one weighing,” and fraudulently suppressed his own proper name. To his rashness answer has been made quite sufficiently, both by this Johannes the Carmelite and by other learned men. For I, writing back only one letter, did not wish to contend any longer in words with a Barthologus. The other things which this Johannes composed have not come into our hands. He is still living in the convent at Kassel, holding the office of subprior, and is writing various works. He is more than sixty years of age, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, in the fourteenth indiction.

Rutger Sicamber of Venray, by homeland a Gelderlander, of the order of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine, of the monastery of the holy Apostle Peter of Dumetum, commonly called Heyen, not far from Worms, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and outstandingly learned in secular letters, sharp in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout in life and conduct, excellent in meter and prose. He wrote, both in verse and in prose, many commendable little works, the reading of which is no less useful than pleasant. Of these I have read the following: A Dialogue on the Education of Boys, one book; A Dialogue on the Inquiry into the Blessed Life, two books; Hymns on Saint Mary in various kinds of meter, two books, which contain almost twelve thousand verses; A Dialogue on the Various Use of Letters, three books; A Dialogue on [unclear]...

Catalogue of Illustrious Men.

[unclear] various addresses to the clergy, one book. He also wrote many very elegant letters both to me and to others. His other works have not come to my knowledge. With great expense and long labor he collected the works of Johannes de Gerson, formerly Chancellor of Paris, of which at last he brought many to us from France, dividing them into three parts in a very fine order and making a quite useful table of all the books; he gave that whole work to the press. Therefore he deservedly ought to be loved in a special way by all learned and devout men, since by his labors and expenses he brought to light so many volumes of that most learned and most devout doctor. He is still living, fifty years old, in the city of Strasbourg, under the Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Johannes Wyric of the town of Neuss, a native of the diocese of Cologne, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Cologne, provincial prior of Lower Germany, doctor of divine Scripture, a learned interpreter, a very acute expounder of Aristotelian philosophy, ready in intellect, orderly in speech, devout in life and conduct, a sharp disputant, an excellent preacher of the divine word. He wrote certain commendable little works, by which he made himself useful to those now living and memorable to those to come. Among them there is an outstanding volume on the Sentences, four books; also many sermons to the people, and various questions disputed in the schools; but certain other things are to be brought to light in their own time. He is still living in mature age, residing at Cologne, under the Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Johannes Camerarius Dalburgius, Bishop of Worms, a most celebrated jurisconsult, most learned both in divine Scripture and in secular letters, skilled in the three principal languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, a very distinguished rhetor and poet, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, notable for experience of many matters, who magnificently adorns the nobility of his family by his character and learning. He wrote and writes, both in verse and in prose, certain works of excellent talent, and he has not yet allowed them to come to light, because, being too much occupied with the affairs of the commonwealth, he cannot complete them to the degree that is his purpose. Yet some of them have become known to us: a Sapphic poem on the death of Rudolf Agricola, his teacher in Greek; [unclear]; On the Origin and Theory of Coinage, one book; very many elegant orations; also many poems and epigrams; and several very elegant letters to various persons; and certain other things. He is still living, [unclear] forty, [unclear] he will write various things in Latin, under the Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, in the thirteenth indiction.

Johannes de Arundine, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin [unclear], [unclear] of Camerarius, Bishop of Mechlin, Bishop of [unclear], a man studious and learned in divine Scripture, and also excellently instructed in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian; subtle in intellect, clear in eloquence, notable as a declaimer of popular sermons. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are reported: a notable lecture on the Book of Wisdom, one book; on the Epistle of Paul to the Romans, one book; sermons on the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” one book; also sermons for the season and on the saints, two books. He is said to have written many other things too, which have not come to my knowledge. He is still living in the city of Lower Utrecht, being vicar of the bishop of that place in pontifical matters, under the Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, in the fourteenth indiction.

Johannes Capnion, otherwise Reuchlin, a native of the town of Pforzheim in Swabia, my teacher in Greek, an outstanding doctor of imperial law, and counsellor of the illustrious duke Eberhard of Württemberg, at once most eloquent and most upright in law and faith, a most diligent investigator of all the most ancient philosophy and literature, a most skilled interpreter of the three principal languages, Hebrew together with Chaldaic, likewise Greek and Latin. He is also especially distinguished in French and in the more polished form of our vernacular, most learned in every respect both in divine writings and in secular letters, since he has for many years penetrated with the greatest effort the secret mysteries of the Greeks and Hebrews. Truly he is worthy to devote himself to letters alone, not also to be burdened in the noisy popular court. For not only Italy, but not even our age, could set against us anyone equal to so great a man. He wrote many excellent volumes, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Among these there is a volume furnished no less with eloquence than with learning, which he wrote to lord Johannes Camerarius Dalburgius, bishop of the Vangiones, on all the secret and hidden mysteries of the philosophy of the Greeks, Hebrews, and Christians, which he entitled, from the name of his family, with the Greek title Capnion, or On the Wonder-working Word, one book; On the Preliminary Exercises of Rhetoric, ten books; On the Diversity of the Four Idioms of the Greek Language, one book; epigrams and elegies, one book; a funeral oration on the death of Rudolf Agricola; letters both to me and to others; orations

[In speech?] elegantly composed, worthy of the presbyterate in life and conduct. He wrote most ornate orations delivered by him before various princes, and also many very elegant letters both to me and to various others, and certain other things still wholly unknown to me. If only he could have leisure for letters as much as he is compelled to give himself to affairs of the commonwealth, our Mosellan land would have no one equal to him in learning and in the publication of books. He is still living with his archbishop of Trier, whose illustrious name he makes more illustrious by his talent and prudence, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Heinrich [Euticus?], an easterner from Mount Noricus, otherwise Nuremberg, a most skilled doctor of the arts, philosophy, and medicine, who for a long time practised his art in Augsburg and now practises it in Frankfurt, a man certainly most learned in every respect, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote, in a varied kind of meter, a polished and very bright work which he entitled Scommata, or the Urbane and Witty Jests of Young Men, one book; also a satire against the Sophist Dialecticians, enemies of the study of humanity, one book; In Praise of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin, one book; also various epigrams, and many most ornate letters to various people, and several other things unknown to us. He is still living in the imperial [unclear], also a philosopher and a very celebrated rhetorician, ready in talent, eloquent in speech, mature in life and conduct. He wrote certain distinguished treatises, with which he profitably occupies his talent and commends his memory to posterity. Yet he conceals the things he writes, either to avoid the [unclear] of vain glory, or so that he may correct what he has written with the file of mature examination. For few of his works have become known to us: On the Method of Single Combat, one book; also On War Machines, [unclear]; learned and studious in [unclear], and outstandingly learned in secular letters, professor of both laws; On the Care of Soldiers' Horses, one book; elegant orations delivered on other occasions in synods. [unclear] he adorns in [unclear] fashion. He wrote many distinguished little works both in verse and in prose, and in addition published many letters, both to me and to others, full of every charm; from these it is easily apparent to readers how much he is worth in learning, in eloquence, and in experience of many things. He is still living in the church of Speyer, thirty-five years of age, under Emperor Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we have written these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Sebastian Titio, otherwise Brant, citizen of Strasbourg, distinguished doctor of both laws, and very learned both in the divine scriptures and in other humane letters, no mean master of poetry, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, outstanding in counsel and action, who has spread his name far and wide. Among his works the following are extant: On the Titles of Both [Laws?] and [unclear] to be recovered, one book; to the same, an epilogue, [The Kingdom?] of Jerusalem, in elegiac verse, one book; In Praise of the Glorious Virgin Mary and of many saints, many poems of various kinds, one book; Of Various Epigrams, one book; a Sapphic poem in our book On the Misery of Prelates; Against Slanderous Advocates; On the Captivity of King Maximilian; commendatory poems for various printings. Furthermore, with wondrous skill and industry, though in the common vernacular tongue, he compiled a certain little book which he called the Ship of Narragonia, in which he so elegantly expressed the cause and root of all follies, censures the morals of fools, and gives certain remedies for each, that it is [unclear] called not a book of fools, but [unclear]. For he weaves together various things under Emperor Maximilian, whom he singularly loves, and composed about him and to him several very charming poems, even secret ones, as they say, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1495, indiction 13.

Conrad Summenhart, eminent professor of sacred theology, studious and learned in the holy scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, and outstandingly learned in canon law, subtle in talent, composed in speech, who ordinarily reads and teaches divine letters in the school of Tübingen. Multos denique veterum auctorum tractatus in vernaculam linguam de latino sermone convertit, non minori eloquentia quam repperit, si ramen Theutonicae linguae lepos et ornatus concedatur inesse.
