Alia quoqque pro- to vtilitate ecclefatica multa cóposuit quae nos latent. Claruit sub Galba et amp; Volufiano prin- cipibus. Anno domini. 255. NOVATIANVS Romanae ecclefae presbyter, aduerfus Cornelium cathedram e- piscopalem conatus inuadere, cum non posset, primum in ecclefia schisma con- citauit, &amp; haeresim Nouatianorum confttituit, nolens apostatas poenitentes recipere, atque rebaptizans rite baptizatos. Huius erroris autor Nouatus Cypriani presbyter fuit. Scripfit autem: De Pascha lib.i. De cibis Iudaicís lib.I. De Sabbato lib.I. De instantia lib.I. 40 De Circumcisione lib.I. De Attalo lib.I. De Sacerdote lib.I. De sancta Trinitate lib.I. De Oratione lib.I. Epistolas plures ad diuerfos. Alia infuper nonnulla scripfle dicitur, que ad notitiam meam nó venerunt. Claruit tẽ- poribus Philippi Imperatoris. Anno domini. 260. MALCHION Antiochenae ecclefae presbytey, vir eruditus atque difertissimus, quip- pe qui rhetoricam in eadem ciuitate multis annis florentiffime docuit. Edidit nonnulla pręclara opufcula, quae suo tempore ad fidei Christianae defenfionem contra haereticos multum conducere videbantur. De quibus extat opus insigne dialogorum. Contra Paulum Samofatenum lib.i. 50 Ad Dionysium papam ex Synodo epi.I. Claruit sub Claudio et amp; Aureliano principibus. Anno domini. Z7O. VICTORINVS episcopus Pictauienfis, vir in diuinis scripturis valde eruditus, Grę- co et amp; Latino inftructus eloquio, scripfit multa pręclara opufcula, in quibus magnifice fuū exercitauit ingenium. Fuit autem diuini verbi prędicator insignis, &amp; tandẽ pro fide Chri- fti martyrio coronatus legitur. De cuius scriptis subiecta feruntur. In Genesim lib.I. In Abacuc lib.I. In Exodum lib.I. In Ecclefiaften lib.I. In Leuiticum lib.I. In Cantica canticorum lib.I. In Efaiam prophetam lib.I. In Apocalypfim lib.I. R 4 In Ezech-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

and a distinguished declaimer; coming into Gaul after the glorious triumph of his master, he obtained the palm of martyrdom for the faith of Christ at the city of Cimella. This Pontius, by his honey-sweet preaching and zeal, converted the two Philips, emperors, to Christ, and persuaded them to be the first among the Roman rulers to renounce idols. He also wrote, in an elegant style, a notable volume, which contains:

The Life of Saint Cyprian, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Philip, in the year of the Lord 240.

Dionysius, the thirteenth bishop of the city of Alexandria, formerly a hearer and disciple of Origen, while he was still a presbyter held the public school under Heraclas and acquired great glory for his learning. For he was a man most learned in every science, a philosopher, rhetorician, and distinguished theologian, who, agreeing with the doctrine of Cyprian and the African synod on rebaptizing heretics, wrote very many letters on that matter to various persons. Among them these are counted:

On repentance, to Fabius, one letter. On the Sabbath, one book. To the Romans, one letter. To Hermonion [Hermammon?], one book. To Saint Sixtus, pope, two letters. On the persecution of Decius, one book. To Philemon and Dionysius, presbyters, two letters. Against Nepos, the Chiliast, one book. To Dionysius after he became pope, two letters. Against Sabellius, one book. To Novatian the heretic, one letter. To Ammon, bishop of [Berenice?], one letter. [unclear: Dionysius Novatianus]. To Pope Dionysius, one book. To Dionysius and Didymus, one letter. To Thelephorus, one letter. To the Laodiceans, on repentance, one letter. To Euphranon, one letter. To Origen, on martyrdom, one letter. A canon on repentance, one book. On the order of offences, one letter. On nature, to Timothy, one book. To the Alexandrians, on exile, one letter. On temptations, one book. On Easter, one book. Commentaries on Ecclesiastes, one book. To Bishop Heraclas in Egypt, one book. On Jewish foods, one book.

Several letters of his to Basilides are also reported. A distinguished letter of his Against Paul of Samosata is extant, which he had written a few days before his death. He also composed many other things for ecclesiastical use, which are unknown to us. He flourished under the rulers Gallus and Volusianus, in the year of the Lord 255.

Novatian, presbyter of the Roman church, having attempted to usurp the episcopal chair against Cornelius, and being unable to do so, stirred up the first schism in the church and established the heresy of the Novatians, refusing to receive apostates who repented, and rebaptizing those duly baptized. The author of this error was Novatus, Cyprian’s presbyter. He wrote:

On Easter, one book. On Jewish foods, one book. On the Sabbath, one book. On earnestness, one book. On Circumcision, one book. On Attalus, one book. On the Priest, one book. On the Holy Trinity, one book. On Prayer, one book. Several letters to various persons.

He is also said to have written some other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Emperor Philip, in the year of the Lord 260.

Malchion, presbyter of the church of Antioch, a learned and most eloquent man, since indeed he taught rhetoric in that same city for many years with the greatest distinction, published some excellent little works which in his own time seemed to contribute greatly to the defense of the Christian faith against heretics. Of these there is extant a notable work of dialogues:

Against Paul of Samosata, one book. To Pope Dionysius from the synod, one letter.

He flourished under the rulers Claudius and Aurelian, in the year of the Lord 270.

Victorinus, bishop of Pictavium, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and trained in Greek and Latin eloquence, wrote many excellent little works, in which he splendidly exercised his talent. He was also a distinguished preacher of the divine word, and it is recorded that at last he was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ. Of his writings the following are reported:

On Genesis, one book. On Habakkuk, one book. On Exodus, one book. On Ecclesiastes, one book. On Leviticus, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. On the prophet Isaiah, one book. On the Apocalypse, one book. On Ezek-

300
202 ABBAS SPANHEMENSIS In Ezechielem lib.r. Et alia multa. Claruit temporibus Valeriani et Galieni principum. Anno domini 270. PAMPHILVS presbyter Eusebii Caesariensis, tantos apud Caesariam libros amore scripturam congregauit, vt in omni terra eo tempore nulla bibliotheca celebrior extite-rit. Magnam denique partem librorum Origenis propria manu descripsit, & in eandem librariam Caesariensem reposuit. Ab eo cognomen Eusebius Pamphili fortitus est. Scri-psit autem antequam Eusebius scribere inciperet non spernendae authoritatis opuscula. De quibus tantum reperi. Contra Mathematicos lib.i. Apologeticum pro Origene lib.i. Fertur etiam quasdam plenas fide et eruditione scripsisse epiftolas. Tandem poft bea-ta ftudia, & multos pro ecclesia Dei labores, pro fide Christi apud Caefaereā Palęftinae mat-tyrio coronatus est, sub perfeccutione Maximiani qui imperauit circa annos domini 240. ANATHOLIVS Alexandrinus, Laodiceae, Syriae episcopus, vir in diuinis scripturis peritus, & in secularibus literis nulli suo tēpore fecũdus, Rhetor, Astronomus, & Geome-ter infignis, reliquit ingenii sui multa praeclara opufcula, de quibus tamen pauciffima ad nostram notitiam peruenerunt. Extat eius infigne volumen praenotatum. De Pascha lib.r. De arithmetica institutione lib.io. Claruit sub Probo et Charo principibus. Anno 285. ARCHELAVS episcopus Mesopotamiae, Syrie, vir doctus et disputator acutus. Scri-pfit Syro fermonẽ nonnulla opuscula, quae apud Latinos raro inueniuntur. Hic contra Manichaeum herefiarcham excuntem de Perfide valenter difft utauit, & omnia eius argu-men ta confudit, quamuis ab errore illum reuocare nequiuerit. Scripfit auteē eandem difputationem. Contra Manichaeum lib.i. Aliar vero nobis incognita funt. Claruit sub Aureliano et Probo principibus. Anno domini. 280. LVCIANVS Antiochenae ecclesiae presbyter, vir tantae doctrinae et eloquentiae, vt doctus atque differtus, in declamandi Homiliis ad populum excellentis ingenii fuit, & non minus vita quam eruditione scripturarum venerabilis sub perfecutione Maximiani pro fide CHRISTI martyrio laureatus est. Helinapoli Bithyniae sepultus. Scripfit inter caetera. De fide nostra lib.r. Et alios diuerfos tractatus, fermones et homilias atque epiftolas. Claruit sub Maximi-ano Imperatore. Anno domini. 240. PIERIVS ecclesiae Alexandrinae presbyter, vir nobilis atque doctiffimus, Origenes iunior vocaretur, in homiliis ad populum declamandis excellentissimus fuit. Hic sub Theona episcopo Alexandrinorum, vita et doctrina clarissimus effulgens, volun-tarie paupertatis pro Christi amore cultor fuit infignis, & doctor populi admirabilis. Scri-pfit infinitos tractatus, qui tamen ad notitiam nostram non venerunt. Extat eius longif-40 simus in vigilia Paschae ad populum habitus. Iu Ozee prophetam lib.i. Claruit sub Diocletiano Imperatore. Anno domini .290. PHILEAS episcopus Thebaidae ciuitatis in Aegypto, vir nobilis atque dottissimus, non minus moribus quam eruditione scripturatrum infignis, poft multos labores, & editos pro vtilitate fideliũ varios tractatus, tandem sub Maximiano Imperatore pro fide Christĩ martyreffetus euolauit ad superos. De cuius scriptis extat difputatio habita. Contra iudicem iniquum lib.r. Delaude martyrum Alia quae feripsit nobis incognita funt, quamuis multa ferantur à patribus. Claruit sab Maximianno principe. Anno domini 240. ARNOBIVS presbyter, philofophus et rhetor infignis, cum adhuc gentilis rheto-ricam doceret, diuina miseratione vocatus, Christianum se coepit profiteri. Cumque ad epi-fcopos accedens se baptizari expeteret, non credebant, veriti ne vir seculari tum ens elo-quentia facramentis fidei conaretur illudere, & ideo sententiam differebant. Arnobius vero cernens fibi fidem minime adhiberi, in argumentum syncritatis fuae scripfit et ob-tulit episcopis infigne volumen. Aduerfum Gentes lib.7. In Pfalterium quoque lib.i. Derhe-

202 The Abbot of Sponheim

On Ezekiel, one book. And many other things. He flourished in the times of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, in the year of the Lord 270.

Pamphilus, priest of Eusebius of Caesarea, out of love for the Scriptures gathered so many books at Caesarea that at that time no library in all the earth was more celebrated. Indeed, he copied out with his own hand a great part of the books of Origen and placed them in that same Caesarean library. From him Eusebius obtained the surname Pamphili. But before Eusebius began to write, he wrote some little works of no contemptible authority. Of these I have found only:

Against the Mathematicians, one book. An Apology for Origen, one book.

He is also said to have written certain letters full of faith and learning. At last, after blessed studies and many labors for the Church of God, he was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ at Caesarea in Palestine, under the persecution of Maximian, who ruled around the year of the Lord 240.

Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures and second to none in secular letters in his time, a distinguished rhetorician, astronomer, and geometer, left many splendid little works of his genius; yet very few of them have come to our knowledge. There survives his notable volume entitled:

On Easter, one book. On Arithmetical Instruction, ten books.

He flourished under the emperors Probus and Carus, in the year 285.

Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia in Syria, a learned man and acute disputant, wrote some little works in the Syriac language, which are rarely found among the Latins. He vigorously disputed against Mani, the heresiarch coming out of Persia, and confounded all his arguments, although he was unable to recall him from error. He wrote that same disputation:

Against Mani, one book.

Other works are unknown to us. He flourished under the emperors Aurelian and Probus, in the year of the Lord 280.

Lucian, priest of the church of Antioch, a man of such learning and eloquence that, learned and eloquent, he was of excellent ability in delivering homilies to the people, and venerable no less for his life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ under the persecution of Maximian. He was buried at Helenopolis in Bithynia. Among other things he wrote:

On Our Faith, one book.

And various other treatises, sermons, homilies, and letters. He flourished under the emperor Maximian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Pierius, priest of the church of Alexandria, a noble and most learned man, was called the younger Origen; he was most excellent in delivering homilies to the people. Under Theonas, bishop of the Alexandrians, shining forth as most renowned in life and doctrine, he was a distinguished cultivator of voluntary poverty for love of Christ and an admirable teacher of the people. He wrote countless treatises, which nevertheless have not come to our knowledge. There survives his very long discourse delivered to the people on the vigil of Easter:

On the Prophet Hosea, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Diocletian, in the year of the Lord 290.

Phileas, bishop of the city of Thebaid in Egypt, a noble and most learned man, distinguished no less in character than in knowledge of the Scriptures, after many labors and various treatises published for the benefit of the faithful, at last under the emperor Maximian flew away to heaven as a martyr for the faith of Christ. Of his writings there survives a disputation held:

Against an Unjust Judge, one book. On the Praise of Martyrs.

The other things he wrote are unknown to us, although many are reported by the fathers. He flourished under the emperor Maximian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Arnobius, priest, philosopher, and distinguished rhetorician, while he was still a pagan teaching rhetoric, was called by divine mercy and began to profess himself a Christian. And when, going to the bishops, he sought to be baptized, they did not believe him, fearing that a man then swollen with secular eloquence was attempting to mock the sacraments of the faith; and therefore they deferred their judgment. But Arnobius, seeing that no trust was being placed in him, as proof of his sincerity wrote and offered to the bishops a notable volume:

Against the Nations, seven books. Also On the Psalter, one book.

DE SCRIPT. ECCLESIAT. De Rhetorica institutitone lib.i. Alia quoque multa edidit quae ad notitiam meam non venerunt. Dociuit in Aphrica retoricam sub Diocletiano principe, habuit multos egregios &; nobiles discipulos qui viri doctissimi euaferunt. Claruit ergo annos domini nostri lesu Christi. 300. Iohannes Clymachus quod latine sonat scholasticus, abbas montis Synai, vir in diuinis scripturis studiosus &; eruditus, ingenio excellens, mitis, &; humilis, vita &; conuersatione deuotus atque sanctiffimus, cum adhuc sedecim esset annorum, mundum cū suis oblectamentis deferuit, &; in dicto coenobio monachum se fieri instantissime petiit &; obtinuit. Deinde post annos decem &; nouem cum iam solitarius pugnare &; vincere secundum regulā monachorum didicisset, cum licentia abbatis sui heremum petitit, in qua multis annis in omni sanctitate solus cum Deo habitauit. Postremo cum vita eius sanctiffima omnibus innoutuisset, vnanimi omnium consensu in abbatem eligitur, &; renitens, ad coenobium reuocatur. Scripsit ad Ioannem abbatem de Raythu opus celeberrimum, &; proinstitutione monachorũ valde accommodū, habens fermones triginta quod prenotatur. De triginta gradibus lib.i. Abono &; super bono. Ad paftorem sermonem lib.i. In inferiori quidem libro. Epiftolas plures ad monachos lib.i. Et quaedam alia In quibusdam locis, maxime vbi de hominis spiritalis mortificati impaffibilitate tractat, à modernis theologis reprehenditur, ficut apud Iohannem de Gerfon in certis tractatibus intuenitur. Claruit circa tempora Constantini, Constantii &; Constantis, frattum imperatorũ, qui regnauerunt. Anno domini. 346. Hildefonsvs Toletanae sedis post S. Eugenium episcopus, vir in diuinis scripturis etuditissimus, &; secularis quoque literaturae non ignarus, metro excellens &; profa ingenio subtilis, sermone disertus, &; super omnes sui temporis episcopos facūdus &; eloquens, vita &; conuerfatione Deo dignus atque sanctiffimus. Fuit enim timoris Dei instantia pręditus, religione deuotus, compunctione profufusus, incessu grauis, honeftate laudabilis, pasto tientia singularis, differendi ingenio clarus, sapientia summus. Qui cum adhuc puer esset diuino spiritu attactus, res mundi, parentūque affectiones contemptens, Agalienfe monafte-riũ petitit, monachūque se in eo multis decenter exhibuit. Coenobiũ quoque virginum in Debienfi villula construxit, quod de parentum fuorum opibus dotauit. Abbas deinde effectus Agalienfs coenobii, monachorum mores exercuit, rem discreuit, vitamque fer-uauit. Principali post haec violentia Toletum reducitur, atque inibi post decefforis fui ob-itum pontifex furrogatur. Scripfit multa praeclara opufcula. De quibus feruntur subiecta. De sancta Trinitate lib.i. De cognitione Baptismi lib.i. De imbecillitate propria lib.i. De progreflu spiritualis deferti lib.i. De virginitate S. Mariae lib.i. Hymnorum diuersi generis lib.i. Annotationes actionis diurnae lib.i. Sermones varii lib.i. Annotationum in facris lib.i. Epigrammata multa lib.i. Annorationum in sacramentis lib.i. Demiffa quoque lib.i. E t alia cōplura. Cum beatissimus iste presul Hildefonfus librũ de virginitate puriffimae Dei genitricis Mariae ad finem vsque complesset, cui omni studio quo poterat femper devoteffime seruire follebat, apparuit ei domina mundi sacrattiffima esse affirmabat, Ille ve-ro cupiens eam altius honorare, conftituit vt celebraretur folennitas eius fingulis annis o-cetaua die ante natalem domini, quae folennitas iam obtinuit, vt per vniuerfam fidelium ec-jo cleffā in honore purifimae conceptionis illius celebretur. 6. Iduū Decemb. Vnde rurfum ei beata Dei genitrix apparens vestimentum facerdotale, quod nos Albam vocamus, &; cathedrali illi attulit, de quibus multa miranda &; gloriofa narrantur. Claruit. Firmianvs Lactantius, Atnobii retoris quondam auditor atque discipulus, vir in secularibus literis abundanter doctus, &; in ditinis scripturis nobiliter nfitutus, ita vt in arte dicendi post Ciceronem facile obtinuerit principatum: retoricam primum Nico-medix, deinde Romae sub Dyocletiano ab eo vocatus gloriofe docuit. Vbi cum penuria discipulorum ad paupertatem deueniffet, ad extremum Caefaris Cryffi filii Constantini praeceptor, iam fenex in Gallia factus eft. Scripfit 10

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On Rhetorical Instruction, one book.

He also published many other works which have not come to my knowledge.

He taught rhetoric in Africa under the emperor Diocletian, and had many excellent and noble pupils, who became very learned men. He therefore flourished in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 300.

John Climacus, which in Latin means Scholasticus, abbot of Mount Sinai, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent, gentle and humble, devout and most holy in life and conduct, when he was still sixteen years old, abandoned the world with its delights, and most earnestly sought and obtained permission to become a monk in the said monastery. Then after nineteen years, when he had already learned, according to the rule of monks, to fight and conquer as a solitary, with the permission of his abbot he sought the wilderness, in which for many years he lived alone with God in all holiness. Finally, when his most holy life had become known to all, by the unanimous consent of all he was elected abbot and, though resisting, was called back to the monastery. He wrote to John, abbot of Raithu, a very celebrated work, very suitable for the instruction of monks, containing thirty sermons, which is entitled:

On the Thirty Steps, one book. “From the good and above the good.”

To the Shepherd, one sermon, one book. “In the lower book indeed.”

Several letters to monks, one book.

And certain other things.

In certain places, especially where he treats of the impassibility of the mortified spiritual man, he is criticized by modern theologians, as may be seen in certain treatises in John Gerson. He flourished around the times of Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, brother emperors, who reigned in the year of the Lord 346.

Ildephonsus, bishop of the see of Toledo after Saint Eugenius, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature either, excellent in meter and subtle in talent in prose, eloquent in speech, and above all the bishops of his time fluent and eloquent, worthy of God and most holy in life and conduct. For he was endowed with constant fear of God, devout in religion, overflowing with compunction, grave in his gait, praiseworthy in integrity, singular in pastoral patience, distinguished in talent for disputation, supreme in wisdom. When he was still a boy, touched by the divine spirit, despising the things of the world and the affections of his parents, he sought the Agaliense monastery, and for many years conducted himself fittingly in it as a monk. He also built a convent of virgins in the little estate of Dehbia, which he endowed from his parents’ resources. Then, having been made abbot of the Agaliense monastery, he trained the morals of the monks, managed the property, and preserved the life. After this, by royal violence, he was brought back to Toledo, and there, after the death of his predecessor, was appointed bishop. He wrote many distinguished little works. Of these the following are reported:

On the Holy Trinity, one book. On the Knowledge of Baptism, one book.

On His Own Weakness, one book. On the Progress of the Spiritual Desert, one book.

On the Virginity of Saint Mary, one book. Hymns of various kinds, one book.

Annotations on the daily office, one book. Various sermons, one book.

Annotations on sacred matters, one book. Many epigrams, one book.

Annotations on the sacraments, one book. Also On the Mass, one book.

And many other things. When this most blessed bishop Ildephonsus had completed to the end the book on the virginity of Mary, the most pure Mother of God, whom he was always accustomed to serve most devoutly with all the zeal he could, the most sacred Lady of the world appeared to him and affirmed [unclear]. But he, wishing to honor her more highly, established that her solemnity should be celebrated each year on the eighth day before the Nativity of the Lord; this solemnity has now prevailed, so that throughout the whole Church of the faithful it is celebrated in honor of her most pure conception, on the sixth day before the Ides of December. Hence again the blessed Mother of God appeared to him and brought him a priestly vestment, which we call an alb, and that cathedral [unclear], concerning which many wondrous and glorious things are told. He flourished.

Firmianus Lactantius, once a hearer and disciple of Arnobius the rhetor, a man abundantly learned in secular letters and nobly instructed in the divine Scriptures, so that in the art of speaking he easily obtained first place after Cicero: he first taught rhetoric gloriously at Nicomedia, then at Rome under Diocletian, after being summoned by him. There, when through lack of pupils he had fallen into poverty, at last, already an old man, he was made in Gaul the tutor of Caesar Crispus, son of Constantine.

He wrote

EVSEBIVS ecclesiae Caesariensis Palaestinae episcopus, cognomento Pamphili, Do- rothaei Eunuchi viri doctissimi quondam discipulus, in diuinis scripturis studiosissimus, &; bibliothecae ecclesiasticae vna cum Pamphilo martyre diligentiissimus instaurator, qui 20 cum Arrianus esset, ad primum concilium patrum apud Niceam habitũ accedens, errorẽ deposuit, patrumque sententiam sequutus, eorum iussu symbolum (quod Nicenum dicitur) composuit, &; in fidei sue purissime testimonium illis obtulit legendum &; confirmandum. In quo errores Arrianorum fortiter contriuit, nihilque eius editioni vel additum est vel sub- tractum, sed vsque in hodiernum diem in ecclesia Dei publice cantatur. Post hac in ortho- doxa fide perfeuerans sanctissime consummatus est. Scripsit graeco sermone multa prae- clara volumina. De equibus apud Latinos feruntur subiecta, Videlicet. Contra Porphyrium lib.30 Explicationes Euangelica lib.20 30 In Esaiam prophetam lib.i.4. Cum quidsit Christiianis; De praeparatione Euangelica lib.10. Successiones sanctorum. Ecclesiastica historia lib.i. Mosen gentis Hebraï. Epitoma chronicae lib.i. De dissonantia Euangelistarum lib.i. Tophanias lib.i. Apologia pro Origine lib.6. Topicorum lib.3. In Psalterium totum lib.i. De vita Pamphili lib.i. Alia quoque multa composuit, quae ad notitiam meam non venerunt. Claruit sub Con- Martyrologium lib.i. stantino imperatore magno, cui amicissimus fui propter eximiam doctrinam, &; vitae san- ctitatem. Anno domini. 320. RETHICVS Eduorum Augustudunensis episcopus, vir in diuinis scripturís stu- 49 diosus, &; suo tempore doctor famatae opinionis. Fertur non pauca scripfisse opuscula, & praecipue in diuinos libros commentarios, sed paucos ad notitiam nostram meminimus peruenisse. Videlicet. In Cantica canticorum lib.i. Contra Nouatianum lib.i. Expositionem eius in Cantica, S.Hieronymus vt ineptam reprehendit. Claruit in Gal- lia sub Constantino magno. Anno domini. 3:20. IACOBSVLS, cognomento sapiens, Nisebenę vrbis Perfarum episcopus, vir magnae doctrinae, &; incomparabilis sanctitatis, vnus ex numero confessorũ sub Maximiano per- sequutore vincentium, Nicaeno concilio interfuit, & Arrium impiissimum homousion appositione damnauit. Hic vir sanctissimae conuersationis, vrbesibi commissam oratio- 50 nibus suis à multis periculis sape liberauit. Scripsit addicationem fidelium, sermone Syro non pauca opuscula, de quibus feruntur. De fide lib.i. De dilectione proximi lib.i. De charitate generali lib.i. De oratione lib.i. De ieiunio lib.i. De vita post mortem lib.i. De resurrectione lib.i. De patientia lib.i. De humilitate lib.i. De satisfactione lib.i. Depoenitentia lib.i. De vir-

The Abbot of Spanheim

He wrote many excellent volumes. Of these the following are reported:

On the Divine Institutes, one book. It begins: “Great and excellent.” On the Origin of Error, one book. It begins: “Although in the first book.” On False Wisdom, one book. It begins: “I should wish it to be declared to me.” On True Wisdom, one book. It begins: “As I was thinking, and with my mind.” On Justice, to Constantine, one book. It begins: “There is no doubt with me.” On True Worship, one book. It begins: “That was its duty.” On the Blessed Life, one book. It begins: “It is well.” On the Anger of God, to Donatus, one book. It begins: “I have often observed, Do[natus].” On the Workmanship of God, one book. It begins: “How very little at rest I am.” To Asclepiades, one book. Letters to Probus, four books. On Persecution, one book. Symposium, in hexameter verse, one book. Letters to Severus, two books. Entitled The Grammarian, one book. An Epitome against the Gentiles, one book. It begins: “There is a happy place in the first.” On Paradise, in hexameter, one book.

He is said to have written not a few other works besides, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished under the emperor Constantine, to whom he was very dear, in the year 320.

Eusebius, bishop of the church of Caesarea in Palestine, surnamed Pamphilus, formerly a disciple of the eunuch Dorotheus, a most learned man, very devoted to the divine Scriptures, and, together with the martyr Pamphilus, a most diligent restorer of the ecclesiastical library: although he was an Arian, when he came to the first council of the fathers held at Nicaea, he put aside his error and, following the opinion of the fathers, at their command composed the creed which is called Nicene, and offered it to them to be read and confirmed as testimony of his own most pure faith. In it he powerfully crushed the errors of the Arians, and nothing has been either added to or taken from his edition, but it is sung publicly in the Church of God down to the present day. After this, persevering in the orthodox faith, he was most holily brought to his end. He wrote many excellent volumes in Greek. Of these the following are reported among the Latins, namely:

Against Porphyry, thirty books. Explanations of the Gospel, twenty books. On Isaiah the Prophet, [fourteen?] books. It begins: “Since what is for Christians.” On the Preparation of the Gospel, ten books. Successions of the Saints. Ecclesiastical History, one book. It begins: “Moses of the Hebrew people.” Epitome of the Chronicle, one book. On the Disagreement of the Evangelists, one book. Theophany, one book. Apology for Origen, six books. Topics, three books. On the Whole Psalter, one book. On the Life of Pamphilus, one book. Martyrology, one book.

He also composed many other works which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the great emperor Constantine, to whom he was very dear because of his distinguished learning and the holiness of his life, in the year of the Lord 320.

Rheticus, bishop of the Aedui at Autun, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and, in his time, a teacher of renowned reputation. He is said to have written not a few little works, and especially commentaries on the divine books, but I recall that few have come to our knowledge, namely:

On the Song of Songs, one book. Against Novatian, one book.

Saint Jerome censures his exposition on the Song of Songs as foolish. He flourished in Gaul under Constantine the Great, in the year of the Lord 320.

Jacob, surnamed the Wise, bishop of the city of Nisibis of the Persians, a man of great learning and incomparable holiness, one of the number of the confessors who were victorious under the persecutor Maximian, was present at the Council of Nicaea and condemned the most impious Arius by the addition of homoousion. This man of most holy conduct often freed the city entrusted to him from many dangers by his prayers. For the edification of the faithful he wrote not a few little works in the Syrian tongue, of which the following are reported:

On Faith, one book. On Love of Neighbor, one book. On General Charity, one book. On Prayer, one book. On Fasting, one book. On Life after Death, one book. On the Resurrection, one book. On Patience, one book. On Humility, one book. On Satisfaction, one book. On Penance, one book. On

Aduersum gentes lib.i. De constructione tabernaculi lib.i. De conversione gentium lib.i. De regno Persatum lib.i. De perfequutione Christianorum lib.i. Chronica temporum lib.i. ANTONIVS monachus et amp;amp; abbas, natione Aegyptius, vir sanctissimus, heremiꝗque cul- tor insignis, cuius praeconia laudum vniuersus personat orbis, multis religiosae ac beatae vitae normam praebuit, qui etsi literas non didicerit, in diuinis tamen scripturis adeo eru- ditus fuit, vt nullus doctorum seci praeferre praesumeret. Habebat memoriã pro libros, intellectũ et amp;amp; sensum pro literis, gratiã pro studio lectionis. Dictauit Aegyptiaco sermone ad diuerfa coenobia apostolici sensus atque sermonis, varias epistolas. E quib. extat insignis illa. 10 Ad Arsenoitas epist.1. Ad alia coenobia epist.6. Eius vitam beatus Athanasius episcopus Alexandrinus insigni volumine Greco sermo- ne descripsit. Legi opus insigne quod hexametris pentametrisque versibus composuit. 40 De quatuor Euangeliis lib.4. Immortale nihil mun. ATHANASIVS Alexandrinę vrbis nonusdecimus episcopus, vir sanctus atque in diuinis scripturis doctissimus, multas pro fide catholica perfeiones ab Arrianis sus- tinuit. In hoc loco multis annis, vt diximus, latitans, solem non vidit, ibique symbolũ: Quicunque vult saluus effe com-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On Virginity, one book. On the Sense of the Soul, one book. On Circumcision, one book. On the Blessing of Unleavened Bread, one book. On Christ, That He Is the Son of God, one book. On Chastity, one book. Against the Nations, one book. On the Construction of the Tabernacle, one book. On the Conversion of the Nations, one book. On the Kingdom of the Persians, one book. On the Persecution of Christians, one book. A Chronicle of the Times, one book. On the Words of Isaiah, one book. Thus the whole work just designated comprises 25 books. He flourished under the great emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 330.

Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia, and afterward of Tyre, learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, a confessor and distinguished defender of the Christian faith, and a diligent emulator of evangelical perfection, after the publication of many volumes, was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ under the last persecution, or, as others affirm, under Decius and Valerian, at Chalcis in Greece. He wrote, in a polished and well-ordered style, not a few volumes, of which the following are reported:

Against Porphyry, two books. The Symposium on the Ten Virgins, one book. On the Resurrection, one book. On the Pythoness, one book. On the Departure of the Soul, one book. On Genesis, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. “For it must be known, brothers,” one book. On the Last Times, one book. Also a Chronicle, one book.

He flourished under the great emperor Constantine, or, as others prefer, under Decius and Valerian, in the year of the Lord 355.

Antonius, monk and abbot, Egyptian by nation, a most holy man and distinguished cultivator of the desert, whose praises the whole world proclaims, furnished to many a rule of religious and blessed life. Although he had not learned letters, he was nevertheless so learned in the divine Scriptures that none of the doctors of his age would presume to put himself before him. He had memory in place of books, understanding and sense in place of letters, grace in place of the study of reading. In the Egyptian language he dictated various letters, of apostolic sense and speech, to different monasteries. Of these, that distinguished one is extant:

To the Arsenoites, one letter. To other monasteries, six letters.

Blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, described his life in an outstanding volume in the Greek language. He flourished under Constantine the Great and during the reigns of his sons, in the year of the Lord 330, shining with many miracles.

Juvencus, priest, Spanish by nation, a noble man and a most learned philosopher, distinguished poet, rhetorician, and theologian, and venerable to the Church no less for his conduct than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, published for the edification of readers many excellent volumes, both in meter and in prose; but few of them have come to my knowledge. I have read the distinguished work which he composed in hexameter and pentameter verses:

On the Four Gospels, four books. “Nothing immortal [unclear].” On the Sacraments, one book.

The rest which he is said to have composed have not come into our hands. He flourished under Constantine the Great and his sons, in the year of the Lord 350.

Against the Arians, three books. On the Soul, one book. Almost innumerable Letters, one book. Against Origen, one book.

He flourished in the times of Constantine and his sons, in the year of the Lord 350.

Athanasius, nineteenth bishop of the city of Alexandria, a holy man and most learned in the divine Scriptures, endured many persecutions from the Arians on behalf of the catholic faith. Indeed the whole world was narrow for him, with the Arians persecuting him everywhere; they nowhere seemed to be wholly secure. For a man’s enemies were those of his own household. Therefore, fleeing from the face of the emperor and of the Arians, he came to the city of Trier in Gaul, and, honorably received by Saint Maximianus the archbishop, for [unclear] years hid with him in a cistern without water, which to this day is shown in the crypt at the monastery of Saint Maximinus in Trier. While lying hidden in this place for many years, as we have said, he did not see the sun, and there the creed “Whoever wishes to be saved”

Moritur tempore Va-lentiniani et amp; Valentis imperatorum. Anno Domini. 379. facerdotii sui. 46. 6. nonas Maii. Indictione. 7. THEODORVS Heracliae Thraciarum episcopus, in diuinis scripturis studiosus et amp;cruditus, &amp; declamator egregius compositique sermonis, edidit in sacris voluminibus non contemnendae lectionis commentarios. De quibus subiecti feruntur. In Psalterium lib.i. In epifolias Pauli li.14 40 Alia quoque nonnulla scripsisse dicitur, sed ad notitiam meam non venerunt. Claruit temporibus Constantini secundi. Anno domini. 340. EVSEBIVS episcopus Emisenus, vir in diuinis scriptoris eruditissimus, &amp; in declandis homiliis ad populum nulli suo tempore secundus, rhetor, &amp; theologus omnium opinione celeberrimus. Fertur multa et amp; pene infinita scripsiße opuscula, sed nos paucoru folos titulos et amp; numeros potuimus inuenire. Scilicet Aduerfum Gentes lib.i. Sermones ad populum li.to Aduersum Iudaeos lib.i. Homiliarum multarun lib.i. Clauit Constamtino &; fratribus eiusregnantibus. Anno domini350. Fertur eius expositio In Cantica canticorum lib.i. Clauit temporebus Constantii Imperatoris. Anno domini 340. SERAPION ex monacho Thomufeos episcopus, &amp; beato Antonio abbati amicifsimus,vir tantę eruditionis et amp; eloquentiae, vt propter excellentiam ingenii cognomentum schola-

Abbot of Sponheim he composed, until at last, betrayed by a certain girl, by the will of God he escaped by flight. If anyone wishes to know his deeds more fully, let him read the Tripartite History. He wrote in the Greek language almost innumerable little works, of which I have found the following among the Latins.

On the Unity of the Trinity, one book. “You, one God, God the Father.” On the proper persons of the Trinity, one book. “Now through each [unclear].” On the Assumption of Man, one book. “Just as in one.” On the Names of the Trinity, one book. “Here now concerning the names of each.” On the One Substance of the Trinity, one book. “Here, contradicting, the person.” On the Blessedness of Faith, one book. “I ask of you concerning the one.” One book. “For which reason most earnestly.” On the Profession of the Catholic Rule, one book. “Before the beginning of times, above.” On the Unity of Faith, one book. “When you have read this faith.” On the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, one book. “To those who say that the Son of God was created.” On the Trinity and the Holy Spirit, one book. “To the most blessed lord and.” To Lucifer the Bishop, one book. “The first objection of these men is.” Against the Objections of the Arians, one book. “When at Nicaea [unclear].” A Disputation against Arius, etc., one book. “The Arians, behaving childishly.” Against Valens and Ursatius, one book. On the Titles of the Psalms, one book. “All things whatsoever our Lord.” One book. “The letters of holy charity.” One book. “Of divine worship and of [unclear].” Book 2. “Even if I have boasted of anything.” Against the Arians, one book. “Heresies, as many as he himself.” One book. “Whoever wishes for salvation.” Against the same, fourteen books. “Paul, and [unclear]. Nor Moy[ses?].” One book. “The Arians, behaving childishly.” On the Homoousion of the Father and the Son, one book. “Those who maliciously [treat] divine things.” Dialogue with an Arian, one book. “It was brought about by the providence of God.” An Exhortation to Monks, one book. “Even if someone boasts in.” Life of Saint Antony, one book. “Excellent, in these matters, brothers.” Symbol of His Faith, one book. “Whoever wishes to be saved.” On All the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books. Sermons to the People. On the Persecution of the Arians, two books. He flourished when Constantine and his brothers were reigning, in the year of the Lord 350. On His Flight and Exile, one book. On the Gospel of John, one book. Many Homilies. He published several letters to various persons, and also sermons and various treatises, which either have not yet been translated into Latin or have not come to my knowledge. He died in the time of the emperors Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 379, the forty-sixth year of his priesthood, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the seventh indiction.

Theodorus, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, an outstanding declaimer and a man of polished speech, published commentaries on the sacred volumes that are not to be despised in reading. Of these the following are reported.

On the Psalter, one book. On the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books. He is also said to have written some other works, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Constantine II, in the year of the Lord 340.

Eusebius, bishop of Emesa, a man most learned in the divine writings, and, in delivering homilies to the people, second to none in his own time, a rhetorician and theologian most celebrated in the opinion of all. He is said to have written many, indeed almost countless, little works, but we have been able to find the titles and numbers of only a few, namely:

Against the Gentiles, one book. Sermons to the People, ten books. Against the Jews, one book. Many Homilies, one book. He flourished when Constantine and his brothers were reigning, in the year of the Lord 350.

Triphilius, bishop of Cyprus or of Leucontheon, a man most learned in both divine and secular writings, and easily the most eloquent prelate of his age, is said to have written not a few volumes and to have expounded the divine Scriptures in many ways, but I do not recall that any of his works have come into our hands. His exposition is reported:

On the Song of Songs, one book. He flourished in the times of the emperor Constantius, in the year of the Lord 340.

Serapion, formerly a monk, bishop of Thmuis, and a very close friend of the blessed abbot Antony, a man of such learning and eloquence that, because of the excellence of his talent, the surname schola-

DE SCRIPTORIB. ECCLES. scholastici sortitus fuit. Multa fertur scripsisse opuscula. De quibus extant subiecta. lib. 1. De Psalmorum titulis lib. 1. Contra Manichaeum. Epistolae plures ad diuerfos. Floruit sub Constantio principe. Anno domini. 340. Achacius Caesariensis Palaestinae episcopus, vir quidem in diuinis scripturis exercitatus, sed Arriana impietate peruersus, in tanta reuerentia à Constantio Imperatore habitus, vt in locum Liberii papae Romae Foelicem presbyterum epifcopum constitui obtinuerit. Hic Achacius quia luscus erat monoculus vocabatur. Scripsit autem multos &; varios tractatus, qui reuera fuissent vtiles, si catholicum habuissent authorem. Equibus potiores feruntur quos subiecimus. lib. 17. Sethematon lib. 1. Simmicton. Claruit sub Constantiõ Imperatore. Anno domini. 550. Hilarius Pictauiensis Aquitanie episcopus, vir moribus, vita, &amp; doctrina valde venerabilis, multas ab Arrianis pro fide Christi fustinuit iniurias. Nam factione Saturnini Arelatensis episcopi, de synodo Biterensi Phrygiam relegatis, annis quatuor constanimo durum portabat exilium, vbi orationibus iuis mortuum legitur reuocasse ad vitam. Qui cum esset vir vndecumque doctiffimus, multa composuit opuscula. De q̃orum numero feruntur subiecta. Contra Dioscorum. lib. 1. Contra Valentem et amp; Vsatium, lib. 1. VICTORINVS Afer, vir confularis, rhetor omnium suo tempore celeberrimus qui in vrbe Roma sub Constantino imperatore diu rhetoricam docuit, vbi propter excellentiam doctrinae in foro Traiani etream statuan promeruit. Conuersus ad fidem Christi in fenectute sua multos in scripturis sanctis tractatus edidit more dialectico satis obsecuros, &amp; viris doctiffimis vix peruios. De q̃ibus extant subiecti. TITVS episcopus Botrenus, vir in diuinis scriptris eruditissimus, &amp; in secularibus litteris egregie doctus, ingenio acer et amp; vehemens, multa fertur cudisse opuscula, qui bus memoriam fui nominis cum gloria tranfumisit ad posteros. DAMASVS papa natione Hispanus, sedit post Liberium in cathedra Petri an- nis decem et amp; octo, vir in diuinis eruditissinus, &amp; in seclaribus litteris egregie doctus, rhetor, &amp; poetę celeberrimus, &amp; in componendis versibus peritissimus, ingenio subtilis, vita S

On Ecclesiastical Writers

he obtained the rank of scholasticus. He is said to have written many short works. Of these the following are extant.

One book. On the Titles of the Psalms, one book.

Against the Manichaean.

Several letters to various persons. He flourished under the prince Constantius, in the year of the Lord 340.

Achacius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, a man indeed well exercised in the divine Scriptures, but corrupted by Arian impiety, was held in such reverence by the emperor Constantius that he obtained the appointment of Felix the presbyter as bishop at Rome in the place of Pope Liberius. This Achacius, because he was one-eyed, was called Monoculus. He wrote many and various treatises, which would truly have been useful if they had had a catholic author. Of these the better are said to be those which we have set below.

Seventeen books of [Zethematon?]. One book of [Simmicton?].

He was distinguished under the emperor Constantius, in the year of the Lord 350.

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers in Aquitaine, a man very venerable in morals, life, and doctrine, suffered many injuries from the Arians for the faith of Christ. For, through the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles, after being banished from the synod of Beziers to Phrygia, for four years he bore hard exile with a constant spirit, where by his prayers he is read to have called a dead man back to life. Since he was a man most learned in every respect, he composed many short works. Of their number the following are reported.

Against Dioscorus, one book. Against Valens and Ursacius, one book.

On the Holy Trinity against the Arians, two books, “As I look around...”

One book, “God who everywhere...”

Defense of the Catholic Faith, one book, “To the most beloved brothers...”

One book, “The degree which Matthew...”

On the Gospel of Matthew, one book.

To the Emperor Constantius, three books, “Now is the time to speak...”

One book, On the Book of Job.

One book, “To the most blessed and glorious...”

One book, On the Song of Songs, one book.

Mysteries, four books. Letters to various persons, one book.

One book, On the Canonical [unclear] concerning fasts and abstinence.

Against Auxentius, one book, [unclear]. “In the first sermon...”

On Heresies, one book, [unclear]. “Logos, or...” etc.

Chronicle, one book, [unclear]. “He lives and [unclear]...”

Two books, [unclear]. “Be present, true light...”

He also published some other works, which have not come into our hands. At length, having returned to his city from his exile, he died under the emperor Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 371, in the fourteenth indiction; his feast is celebrated on the Ides of January.

Victorinus the African, a man of consular rank, the most celebrated rhetorician of all in his time, taught rhetoric for a long time in the city of Rome under the emperor Constantine; there, because of the excellence of his learning, he earned a bronze statue in the Forum of Trajan. Converted to the faith of Christ in his old age, he published many treatises on the holy Scriptures in a dialectical manner, obscure enough and scarcely accessible even to the most learned men. Of these the following are extant.

Against the Arians, two books, [unclear]. “In the first sermon...”

On the Holy Trinity, one book, [unclear]. “Homoiotypos...”

Against the heretics, one book, [unclear]. “He lives and [unclear]...”

On the homoousion also, one book, [unclear]. “Be present, true light...”

On the letters of the apostle Paul, four books, [unclear].

And certain other things.

He was distinguished at Rome under the emperor Constantine, in the second year, 360.

Titus, bishop of Bostra, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular letters, sharp and vehement in talent, is said to have fashioned many short works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. Of their number the following are reported.

Two books. Commentaries on the Gospel, one book.

Against the Manichaeans. And many other works besides.

He was distinguished in the year of the Lord 349, and died under the emperor Valens.

Damasus, pope, a Spaniard by nation, sat after Liberius in the chair of Peter for eighteen years; a man most learned in divine matters and excellently instructed in secular letters, a rhetorician and most celebrated poet, and most skilled in composing verses, subtle in talent,

life

Claruit sub Valentiniano et Valente. Anno domini. 370. APOLLINARIS Laodicenus Syriae episcopus, vir in diuinis scripturis studiosus et eruditus, & grammaticae institutionis longe doctissimus ingenio acer et vehemens, sermone clarus, scripsit pro defensione catholica fidei quaedam praeclara volumina, quibùs equilibus exat opus celeberrimum Contra infanum Porphyrium, lib.30. Abbot of Spanheim.

...devout and most holy in life, a very great lover of the blessed priest Jerome. He wrote various little works in both kinds. Of these the following are extant.

The deeds of the supreme pontiffs, 1 book. “The blessed apostle Peter...” On the faith, against heretics, 1 book. “Since after the Nicene council...” Letters to various persons, 1 book. “Bishop Damasus...” Various poems. And other works.

He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370.

Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and by far most learned in grammatical training, sharp and forceful in talent, distinguished in speech, wrote certain notable volumes in defense of the Catholic faith; among them there is extant the very celebrated work:

Against the mad Porphyry, 30 books. And certain other works.

He flourished under the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

Didymus of Alexandria, deprived of his eyes from early childhood, and for this reason wholly ignorant even of the elements, displayed so great a miracle of himself that he perfectly learned dialectic and geometry, which especially require sight. In the divine Scriptures he was very learned, the teacher of the blessed Jerome and a very close friend of Saint Antony, sharp in talent, distinguished in life. He wrote the following works in Greek:

Against the Arians, 2 books. Also On Doctrines, 1 book. On the canonical epistles, 7 books. “James, etc. [unclear]...” On the Holy Spirit, 1 book. “All indeed which are divine...” On the books of Saint Job, 1 book. On Isaiah the prophet, 10 books. [unclear], 3 books. On Zechariah, to the same, 5 books. On Hosea, to Jerome, 1 book. On the Gospel of John, 1 book. Also On the Psalter, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished as an octogenarian under the emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 395.

Optatus, bishop of Milevis, an African by nation, a man learned in the study of the divine writings, outstanding in talent, devout in life, a Catholic, is said to have written certain notable little works in defense of our faith, in which he magnificently exercised his abundant talent. Among these there is said to be extant a great and distinguished volume which he wrote:

Against the Donatists, 6 books. And several letters. And many other works.

He flourished under the rulers Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370.

Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a learned and most holy man, had such authority among the Greeks that no one, however slightly learned, ever dared to contradict his teaching or writings in any matter. He wrote many notable little works in Greek, but few of them have come into our hands.

On the Holy Spirit, 1 book. Against Eunomius, 9 books. “In the beginning, etc. [unclear]...” A rule for monks, 1 book. “The human race...” An exhortation for monks, 1 book. “Hear, my son, the admonition...” On the education of boys, 2 books. “Indeed of God, without [unclear]...” On faith, 1 book. “Every scripture [unclear] by divine...” Several homilies, 4 books. “It is time to cry out...”

In addition he composed other treatises, sermons, and letters to various persons.

He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, in the year 380.

Ephrem the monk, a distinguished inhabitant of the desert, deacon of the church of Edessa, ordained priest by the blessed Basil, because of humility never approached to perform the divine mysteries, although before God and men he was considered worthy. Nevertheless, so far as belonged to his office, in admonishing the people he delivered innumerable homilies. This man, as is read in the Lives of the Holy Fathers, was seen by an angel to have received a book written in golden letters; from this, soon on the next day and thereafter, with the Holy Spirit speaking in him, he had so great a grace of declaiming that he found no one like himself in his time. He wrote in the Syrian language

Gregorius sex monacho episcopus Nazianzenus, vir tantae doctrinae integritatis eloquentiae, vt nec aduersarũ quidem eius his quae ab illo dicebantur vllatenus contra- dicere auderent, ita vt ad confirmationem authoritatis Gregorum tantùm aliquid dixif- se sufficeret. Hic monasticae conuersationis cultor amator, cum propter excellentiam doctrinae vitae sanctitatem ad Episcopatum vocaretur, fugiens se abscondit, malens ab- iectus esse in domo domini, quam in turba honoribus caducis extolli. Sed omnipotens Deus noluit tam clarum iubar sub modio praefatae conuerfationis abscondi, quod ad mul- torum salutem potuit extendi. Inuentus ergo diuino indicio, ad sedem episcopeam à po- pulo ducitur, moxque in fugae suae excusationem solennis homilia dictatur; in qua ars ar- tium animarum regimen esse ostenditur. Hic ob insignem doctrinam vitae sanctitatem Gregorius magnus, ante beatum Papam eiusdem vocabuli dicebatur. Scripsit autem grae- co sermones plura opuscula. De quibus extant subiecta. lib.i. [unclear] certain little works for the instruction of readers. Of these the following are found among the Latins, namely:

On the Holy Spirit, book 1. “Grief compels me.” On Compunction of Heart, book 1. “Come, dearest beloved.” On Contrition of Heart, book 1. “Our Lord Jesus Christ.” On Penitence, book 1. “In the struggles of this...” On the Struggles of the Age, book 1. “Come, most beloved.” On the Day of Judgment, book 1. “Glory to almighty God.” On the Resurrection, book 1. “Blessed is he who has hated...” On the Blessedness of the Soul, homily 1. “In the holy Scriptures.” On Thoughts, homily 1. “As often as, brothers...” On Severe Preaching, homily 1. “I ask you, brothers.” On the Celebration of the Mysteries, book 1. A Lament over the City of Edessa.

He also published not a few other works, especially sermons and homilies to the people, which have not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, a very close friend of blessed Basil, as you will be able to find in his legend. In the year 380.

Book 1. “I understand man from the soul...”

Gregory, bishop of Emesa, brother of blessed Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a man very devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, stirred also by his brother’s zeal, himself wrote several little works in Greek. Of these, among our writers, I have found only:

On the Image and Condition of Man, book 1. Against Eunomius, 2 books.

He flourished, younger than his brother, under the princes Valentinian and Valens; he composed various works. In the year of the Lord 380.

Gregory, formerly a monk, bishop of Nazianzus, a man of such learning, integrity, and eloquence that not even his adversaries dared in any way to contradict what was said by him, so that, for the confirmation of authority, it sufficed merely to say that Gregory had said something. He was a cultivator and lover of the monastic life; when, because of the excellence of his teaching and the holiness of his life, he was called to the episcopate, he fled and hid himself, preferring to be abject in the house of the Lord than to be exalted in a crowd by fleeting honors. But almighty God did not wish so bright a radiance to be hidden under the bushel of the aforesaid way of life, since it could be extended to the salvation of many. Found therefore by divine indication, he was led by the people to the episcopal see, and immediately, in excuse for his flight, a solemn homily was delivered, in which the government of souls is shown to be the art of arts. On account of his distinguished learning and holiness of life he was called Gregory the Great before the blessed pope of the same name. He wrote many little works in Greek. Of these the following are extant:

Book 1. On the Praise of Maximus the Philosopher, book 1. Against the Same, in Reproach, book 1. On the Death of His Brother Caesarius, book 1. On Virginity, in hexameter. On the Praise of Cyprian the Martyr, book 1. “I have been overcome, I confess.” On the Holy Spirit, 2 books. “Christ, being born, [unclear] glory...” Apologetics, When He Had Fled, book 1. “Again Jesus [unclear].” On the Nativity of the Lord, book 1. “I was longing for you.” On the Second Epiphanies, book 1. “My belly grieves me.” On the Holy Spirit on the Day of Pentecost, book 1. “Our tongue alone...” On Himself, Returned from the Country, book 1. “What praiseworthy thing alone...” On Jeremiah, with the Emperor Present, book 1. Against Julian the Apostate, book 1. On the Reconciliation of a Monk, book 1. On the Devastation by Hail. Against Eunomius.

He published several sermons and homilies, and various treatises on diverse subjects, which have not come to my knowledge. At length, worn out by old age, when he saw that he could no longer be equal to the government of the people, after another bishop had been ordained in his place, he returned to the pursuit of the solitude he had left behind.

He flourished under Valentinian and Theodosius. In the year of the Lord 390.

Eutropius, monk and priest, a man of a very religious manner of life, in the divine

very devoted to and learned in [unclear] scriptures, and fully instructed in secular letters, he is said to have composed several little works. Of these the following alone are extant for us, known by title:

To two virgins, sisters, 2 books. Of Chronicles down to his own times, 1 book.

He flourished under the emperors Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370. There are also those who write that he was a disciple of Augustine and flourished in the year of the Lord 430.

[Hesychius?], priest and monk, formerly hearer and disciple of blessed Gregory Nazianzen, bishop, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, admonished by the example of his teacher, is said to have written many little works of explanations on the divine books, and to have labored over various volumes on both the New and the Old Testament, which have not yet come into our hands. I have read only that notable and very large work which he wrote to Eutychianus, the venerable deacon.

On Leviticus, 1 book. To the venerable deacon.

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 400.

Ambrose, bishop of Milan, a Roman by country, a man most celebrated for faith and holiness, easily the most learned of all in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, perfectly instructed in the Greek and Latin tongue, whose merit the whole world proclaims, whose works Holy Mother Church confirms as books with a great commendation of authority. In expounding and explaining the divine scriptures he surpassed all doctors, so that, although many bishops were banished into exile for the faith, no one ever dared to touch Ambrose. For he was a most steadfast hammer of heretics, whose tongue, speaking in the faith of Christ, no human authority could ever impose silence upon. Always ready to undergo any dangers for the faith, with the Lord protecting him he escaped everywhere free and unharmed. He wrote many distinguished little works, of which I have found only those set down below.

On Duties, 3 books. “Not to seem arrogant.”

On the Calling of the Gentiles, 2 books. “Among the defenders [unclear].”

Hexaemeron, 6 books. “Only lest of opinion.”

On Human Dignity, 1 book. “Let us make man.”

On Paradise, 1 book. “Concerning Paradise [unclear].”

On Cain and Abel, 1 book. “Concerning Paradise in the preceding.”

On Noah’s Ark, 1 book. “Of holy Noah we undertake.”

On Abraham the Patriarch, 2 books. “Abraham, of this book.”

On Isaac, or the Soul, 1 book. “In the father of holy [unclear] for us.”

On the Good of Death, 1 book. “Since concerning the soul above.”

On Flight from the World, 2 books. “Frequent for us concerning [unclear].”

On Jacob and the Blessed Life, 1 book. “Necessary for learning.”

On Joseph the Patriarch, 1 book. “The life of the saints to others.”

On the Blessings of the Patriarchs, 1 book. “First of all, how great.”

On Naboth the Jezreelite, 1 book. “The story of Naboth [unclear].”

On Elijah and Fasting, 4 books. “Many disturbances for us.”

Apology of David, 1 book. “The apology of the prophet.”

On Interpellations, 5 books. “The queen of the South came.”

On Solomon, 3 books. “[Jeroboal?] under the tree.”

On the Mysteries of Those Being Initiated, 6 books. “Concerning morals daily.”

On the Sacraments, 1 book. “I wish, brothers, [unclear].”

On Pastoral Care, 1 book. “The mystery of Passover concerning.”

On Faith, to Gratian, 2 books. “We have brought down, brother.”

On the Holy Spirit, 1 book. “In the preceding book something.”

On Faith, the Creed, 2 books. “If that is the end of virtues.”

On the Incarnation of the Lord, 1 book. “I admonish you, brothers.”

On the Mystery of Passover, 2 books.

On the Death of His Brother, 1 book.

On Penitence, 1 book.

An Exhortation to Penitence, 1 book.

Anno domini 380. PHILASTRIVS episcopus Brixiensis, vir in diuinis scripturis doctissimus, &; se- cularium literarum non ignarus, beato Ambrosio Mediolanensi, &; notus familiaris, cu- ius meminit sanctus Augustinus in quadam epistola, ad Quod vult deum, scripsit pro vti- litate communi quaedam praeclara opuscula, è quibus nullum ad manus nostras memini peruenisse. Fertur eius beato Augustino vbi supra testante insigne opus quod scripsit. De156.haeresibus. lib.I. Symoniani a Symone Caetera non vidi. Claruit sub Theodoso Imperatore Christianissimo. Anno domini380. EVAGRIVS monachus &; discipulus sancti Macharii, Aegyptii, &; postea episcopus Antiochenus, vir vnde cumque doctissimus, tam secularibus quam diuinis scripturis eru- ditus, Graeco &; Latino peritus eloquio, etiam in episcopatu prioris vitae austeritatem cu- stodiens, tantae abstinentie fuit, vt miraculo haberetur. Hic primus vitam sanctorum pa- trum scriptis commendauit, de sua vena multa opuscula edidit. De quibus tamen pau- cissima ad notitiam meam peruenerunt. Feruntur autem eius subiecta. Ad Anachoretas valde vtilis. lib.I. De octo vitiis principalibus lib.I. Ad Coenobitas quoque. lib.I. Exhortatorii ad virginem lib.I. Vitam Antonii Latinam fecit. lib.I. Presbyter Euagrius De vita sanctorum patrum lib.I. Alia quoque multa scripsit, de Graeco in Latinum transtulit incognita nobis. Claruit sub Gratiano principe. Anno domini380. MAXIMVS episcopus Constantinopolitanus, natione Alexandrinus, philosophus theologus insignis, in cuius laudem Gregorius Nazianzenus librum edidit, multas in- joc iurias ab Arrianis sustinens, episcopatu tandem pulsus, multa in eos scripsit. E qui- planationes composuit, quae apud Graecos eo tempore magno pretio habebantur. E qui- bus haec apud nos feruntur. Contra Arrianos. lib.I. Caetera mihi incognita sunt. Claruit in Graecia sub Gratiano principe. Anno dominij 380. AMBROSIVS presbyter natione Alexandrinus, Didymi coeci quondam auditor atque discipulus, quo explanante scripturas diuinas magnifice didicit, varias in illas ex- Commentariorum in Iob. lib.I. Contra Apollinem Laodicaenum. lib.I. S 3

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On virgins, three books: “If, in accordance with the heavenly [unclear].”

On widows, one book: “It has happened well, brothers.”

An exhortation to virgins, one book: “You who to the great banquet.”

To a devout virgin, one book: “Hear, daughter, and see,” and one book: “Hear me now, you who.”

To a fallen virgin, one book: “Ambrose, bishop, [unclear].”

Against Symmachus, one book: “And if the increase.”

A consolatory work for Valentinian, one book: “Dalmatius [unclear] me.”

Against Auxentius, one book: “I see that you, beyond what is usual.”

On the handing over of the basilicas, two books: “You entrust me with a pledge.”

On the instruction of a virgin, one book: “This movement [unclear] for us.”

On the death of Theodosius, one book: “You have undertaken the office, sacred [unclear].”

On the instruction of priests, one book: “No ordinary [unclear].”

On circumcision, one book: “An army always with continual [unclear].”

On the synagogue, to Theodosius, one book: “To the lady sister of life and [unclear].”

The revelation of Gervasius and Protasius, two books: “Ambrose to the virgins.”

On the passion of Saint Agnes, one book: “Concerning judgments.”

On choosing a pontiff, one book: “Into the Epistles of Paul.”

On Saint Job, one book: “Although also mystical [things].”

Of hymns and prefaces, one book: “You warn well, brother.”

On the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” ten books: “As we are about to write into the book of the Gospel [unclear].”

Letters to various persons, ten books: “We gladly preach.”

On the Gospel of Luke, one book: “The Simonians from Simon.”

Of many sermons, one book: “On the forty-two stopping-places.”

On certain psalms, two books.

He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. Finally, he is said to have made Hegesippus and certain others Latin from the Greek.

He flourished under the most merciful emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 380.

PHILASTRIUS, bishop of Brescia, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, known and familiar to blessed Ambrose of Milan, whom Saint Augustine mentions in a certain letter to Quodvultdeus, wrote for the common benefit certain distinguished little works, none of which I remember to have come into our hands. His notable work, which he wrote, is reported, with blessed Augustine bearing witness in the place cited above:

On 156 heresies, one book: “The Simonians from Simon.”

The rest I have not seen.

He flourished under the most Christian emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 380.

EVAGRIUS, monk and disciple of Saint Macarius the Egyptian, and afterwards bishop of Antioch, a man most learned from every point of view, instructed in both secular and divine writings, skilled in Greek and Latin eloquence, preserving even in the episcopate the austerity of his former life, was of such abstinence that he was held to be a miracle. He was the first to commend to writing the life of the holy fathers; from his own vein he published many little works. Of these, however, very few have come to my knowledge. The following are reported as his:

To anchorites, very useful, one book.

On the eight principal vices, one book.

Also to cenobites, one book.

An exhortatory work to a virgin, one book.

He made the Life of Antony Latin, one book: “The presbyter Evagrius.”

On the life of the holy fathers, one book.

He also wrote many other works, and translated from Greek into Latin works unknown to us. He flourished under the prince Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

MAXIMUS, bishop of Constantinople, an Alexandrian by nation, a distinguished philosopher and theologian, in whose praise Gregory Nazianzen published a book, enduring many injuries from the Arians and at last driven from the episcopate, wrote many things against them. He composed explanations, which among the Greeks at that time were held in great esteem. Of these the following are reported among us:

Against the Arians, one book. The rest are unknown to me.

He flourished in Greece under the prince Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

AMBROSIUS, a presbyter, an Alexandrian by nation, once a hearer and disciple of Didymus the Blind, from whose exposition of the divine Scriptures he learned magnificently, composed various explanations on them.

Commentaries on Job, one book.

Against Apollinaris of Laodicea, one book.

The Abbot of Spanheim

He flourished under the princes Theodosius and Arcadius in the year 400.

Petronius, bishop of Bologna, a monk in his manner of life, very learned and eloquent in the divine Scriptures, and no less worthy of reverence for holiness than for knowledge, shone with many miracles in life and after death, as is read in his history. Among other things he wrote:

On the Life of the Holy Fathers, book I. On the Ordination of a Bishop, book I.

And other things unknown to us.

He died under Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 385, in the thirteenth indiction.

Pachomius, abbot, a most magnificent founder of the monks of his time, founder of many monasteries, and a man of most holy life, shining with many miracles in life and after death, was a learned man, instructed in the divine Scriptures. For the edification of the brothers he wrote many letters, of which the following are reported:

To Abbot Cornelius, letter I. To the provosts of the monasteries, letter I.

To Abbot Syrus, letter I. To the working brothers, letter I.

Also a Rule of Monks, book I.

He flourished under the princes Valentinian and Theodosius in the year 390.

Aurelius Clemens Prudentius, a Christian poet, a man most learned in secular letters, sufficiently skilled in the divine Scriptures, excellent in meter and prose, was held fast for fifty-seven years by the loves of the world; he read and expounded many little works of the poets, and from his own vein wrote many profound poems. At last, however, in old age, having rejected the vanity of the world, he betook himself to the sacred Scriptures, and in verse and prose expounded many hidden things of both Testaments. He wrote many excellent little works, of which I found the following made in metrical measure:

Against Symmachus the Idolater, book I. “Paul, herald of God.”

On the Conflict, book I. “The faithful old man first.”

On Divinity, book I. “God is three, the highest.”

Against the Patripassians, book I. “There are very many, but.”

Against the Sabellians, book I. “Yield, profaner.”

Against the Jews, book I. “These things, if [unclear] Jewish [unclear] in 30.”

Against the Homuncionites, book I. “There are those who [unclear].”

Against the Phantastics, book I. “It is worth the trouble [unclear].”

On the Origin of Sins, book I. On the Hexaemeron, book I.

On the Holy Trinity, book I. “The winged herald of the day [announces] the light.”

Of Various Hymns, book I. “Blessed martyr, near.”

Praises of Saint Vincent, book I. “Ancient [unclear].”

Praises of Saint Lawrence, book I. “Roman, of Christ [unclear].”

Of Histories, book I. “Behold, there was a dove.”

On the Nature of the Soul, book I. “A doubtful person meets here.”

On the Resurrection of the Flesh, book I. “I ask with me in Christ.”

On the Martyrs, book I. “They have been written in heaven.”

On the State of the Soul, book I. “Whoever [says] souls [unclear] errs.”

Hamartigenia, book I. “Brothers, [unclear] the digger.”

On the Hope of Pardon, or a Prayer, book I. “O God, parent of [unclear].”

Against the Marcionites, book I. “As often as [unclear] rage hurls down.”

Peristephanon, book I. “Pious, faithful, innocent.”

He also wrote not a few letters.

He also published some other works which have not come into our hands.

He flourished under the emperor Gratian in the year of the Lord 380.

John, monk and priest of Damascus, a learned and holy man, of whom wondrous things are told on account of the excellence of his teaching and the sincerity of his life, held in high esteem at Constantinople and appointed prelate of the monks, turned many away from iniquity. In the Greek language he wrote little works of profound meaning, but few of them have come into our hands. I have read only that famous work:

On the Tradition of the Orthodox Faith, book I. “No one has ever seen God.”

The History of Barlaam and Josaphat, book I. I have seen nothing of the rest.

He flourished under the most devout prince Theodosius in the year of the Lord 390.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Ticonius the African, whom blessed Augustine, in the third book of On Christian Doctrine, records as having belonged to the Donatist party, although in some matters he disagreed with them, was certainly a keen man and much practiced in the divine Scriptures. He wrote not a few short works. Of these the following are reported, namely:

On Internal War, three books. An Expository Work on Various Questions, one book. On the Apocalypse of John, one book. The Rules of Sacred Scripture, one book. Several letters to various persons. And many other things. He flourished when Theodosius and his sons were ruling, in the year of the Lord 390.

Heraclides the monk, a man holy in conduct, distinguished for learning in the divine Scriptures, a most diligent investigator and imitator of the holy fathers, anchorites and monks, who, like a resourceful bee, gathered the flowers of virtues from the way of life of each into the little cell of his breast and produced the honey of spiritual sweetness. Among other things, for the edification of readers, he wrote a notable work on the life and conduct of the holy fathers living in the desert or in monasteries under a rule, whose title is:

Paradise, one book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, a man very devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures [unclear], wrote, among other things, a useful work:

On the Holy Spirit, one book.

Of the other works which he is said to have composed, nothing has come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of the devout emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.

| 212 | ABBAS SPANHEMENSIS | non ignarus, partis Luciferiani, & ob id merito reprehensibilis. Scripsit multa egregia vo- | Clauit sub Valentiniano et Theodosio. Anno domini. 390. | lib.1. | | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Hieronymus presbyter et monachus, patre natus Eusebio ex oppido Stridonis, vir in secularibus literis valde eruditus, & in diuinis scripturis inter omnes doctores eruditissimus, multarum linguarum peritia insignis, sacrae legis interpres, haereticorum malleus et expugnator fortissimus. Hie est verus dispensator euangelicus, fidelis et pru- dens; qui proferens de thesauro suo noua et vetera, dansque in tempore spiritualis tritici mensuram conferuis suis, Hebraeos superbos spoliavit humilesque ditauit latinós. Hic est Ecclesiae Christi doctor egregius qui vestes Esau per deuia errorum vagantis domino otiose reconditas cum pia matre Rebecca, id est gratia Dei protulit, ac mansuetum Iacob fidelemque Christo seruientem vestiuit. Hie est Hieronymus Iesu Christi syncerus amator, qui nullum tempus otiose transiens, die ac nocte in lege domini meditabatur, & vix cor- pori necessario somno indulto, semper diebus ac noctibus scripsit, legit, docuit vel oratuit, quod testantur pene infiniti libri quos edidit. Hie veritatis defensor, cultor virtutis, vitiorum ac errimus hostis; cum esset Ecclesiae Ramanae presbyter, & scelera clericorum constanter argueret, eorum inuidia fecerit ex vrbe, veniensque in Iudaeam gloriosum domini visitauit sepulchrum, atque iuxta praesepe Bethleemiticum locum sibi habitationis constituens, toti mundo clarus innōtuit, disponente id nimirum diuina prouidentia, vt ibi lux mundi quiesceret, vbi verus sol iustitiae hominibus nascendo innotuisset. Sanctissimi loci habitator sanctus atque conueniens, fide firmus, charitate ignitus conuersatione maturus qui seduci rebus secundis non potuit, quem à sancto proposito nulla vnquam aduersitas deiecit. Sed quid foedus laudator viri sanctum verticem labris contingo impuris? Silēduni magis humiliter mihi fuerat, quam de sanctissimo viro insufficienter loquendum. Nunc ergo quā de scriptis et opusculis eius inuenimus per ordinē cōsignemus. The Abbot of Spanheim ... not unaware of the Luciferian party, and for that reason deservedly blameworthy. He wrote many excellent [unclear]. He flourished under Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390. One book.

Jerome, priest and monk, born of his father Eusebius from the town of Stridon, a man very learned in secular letters and, among all the doctors, most learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished by skill in many languages, interpreter of the sacred law, hammer of heretics and most powerful assailant. This is the true evangelical steward, faithful and prudent, who, bringing forth from his treasury new things and old, and giving to his fellow-servants in due season the measure of spiritual wheat, despoiled the proud Hebrews and enriched the humble Latins. This is the eminent doctor of the Church of Christ, who, with his pious mother Rebecca, that is, the grace of God, brought forth the garments of Esau, wandering astray through the byways of errors, laid up unused for the Lord, and clothed the meek Jacob, faithful and serving Christ. This is Jerome, sincere lover of Jesus Christ, who, passing no time in idleness, meditated day and night on the law of the Lord, and, scarcely granting his body the sleep it required, always by days and nights wrote, read, taught, or prayed, as the almost countless books which he published bear witness. This defender of truth, cultivator of virtue, and most bitter enemy of vices, when he was priest of the Roman Church and constantly reproved the crimes of the clerics, [unclear] from the city through their envy; and, coming into Judaea, he visited the glorious sepulchre of the Lord, and, establishing for himself a dwelling-place beside the manger at Bethlehem, became renowned throughout the whole world, this no doubt being arranged by divine providence, so that the light of the world should rest there where the true sun of justice had become known to men by being born. A holy and fitting inhabitant of a most holy place, firm in faith, kindled with charity, mature in conduct, who could not be led astray by prosperity, whom no adversity ever cast down from his holy purpose. But why do I, a foul praiser, touch the holy head of the man with impure lips? It would have been more fitting for me to keep humble silence than to speak inadequately about so most holy a man. Now therefore let us set down in order what we have found concerning his writings and little works. Among these are:
