260 ABBAS SPANHEMENSI S WINDICHINVS monachus Corbeiensis coenobii in Saxonia, ordinis sancti Be- nedicti, natione Theutonicus, vir in diuinis scripturis doctus, & in secularibus literis e- ruditissimus, ingenio promptus clarus eloquio, metro excellens prosa. Scripsit alter- no stylo multa praeclara opuscula. De quibus ego tantum adhuc reperi subiecta. Ab exor- dio Saxonum vsque ad mortem Ottonis Imperatoris primi, scripsit ad Mechtildam eius filia. Historiam Saxonum lib.3. Flore virginali cum ma. Gesta Ottonis primi lib.1. Passionem Teclę virginis metrice lib.2. Vitam Pauli primi heremitę lib.1. Claruit sub Ottone Imperatore primo. Anno domini. 150. EVTRANDVS Ticinensis ecclesię diaconus natione Italus, ex Papia ciuitate ori- undus, Berengarii regis Italiae quondam scriba Secretarius, vir in secularibus litteris val- de eruditus, diuinarum scripturarum non ignarus, ingenio acer vehemens, Graeco Latino fermone peritus non minus carmine excellens quam prosa. Fertur nonnulla praeclara scripsisse opuscula, quibus nomen suũ notificauit. A Berengario rege Italia pul- fus, venit in Germaniam, apud Franckfordiam positus. Scripsir insigne opus historiam sui temporis tyrannidem ipsius Berengarii continentem, quod quasi pro vicissitudine iniuriarum ab eo perceptarum praenotauit. Autapodosim, id est retributionem lib.7. Regnantibus, imo senien. De aliis nihil vidi. Scripsit autem praefatum volumen ad Regimundum episcopū Li- beritanae Hispaniarum ecclesię, in quo aliquando catmine vtitur, aliquando Graeco fer- mone, multa de Germanorum gestis interieretens. Claruit sub Ottone primo Imperatore. Anno domini.950. ALBO Floriacensis monasterii abbas, ordinis S. Benedicti, vir in diuinis scripturis iugilectione studio exercitus, in secularibus disciplinis egregie doctus, vita quoque conuerfatione insignis, vsque ad martyrii coronam dignus comprobatus, dum in Va- stonia verbũ Dei praedicaret, fidei Christianae testis sanguinis effusione factus est. Scripsit, Super calculo Victorii lib.1. Additiones in eundem lib.i. Et quaedam alia. Claruit temporibus Ottonis primi. Anno domini. 970. RVPERTVS rex Francię, nobilis, fortis, iustus, doctus religiosus, inter ecclesiasti- cos scriptores locum metito recipit, quippe qui cantus responsoria dulei regulari modulamine ad honorem ecclesię catholicę composuit. In literis humanitatis, prefertim in musica doctissimus fuit, tantę autem religionis vt horas canonicas in ecclesia decanta- ret cum clericis, foris apud se legeret cum suis. Tantae pietatis miserationis extitit in pauperes, vt suis se aliquando vestimentis spolians eorum nuditates multis vicibus operi- ret. De eius manibus liber nunquam recedebat, adeo vt pro tribunali fedens, inter iudici- orum causatum strepitus in sinu apertum haberet Psalterium. Vnde post mortem mi- raculis coruscasse legitur. Eius est illa vulgata sequentia, quae cantatur diebus pentecostes. De Sancto Spiritu .s. Veni Sanctè Spiritus. Responsorium de S. Petro .s. Cornelius Centurio. De natiuitate Domini .s. Iudaea Hierusalem no. Et illud Alleluia .s. Eripe me de inimicis. Et alia multa quae nescio. Responsorium, Cornelius Centurio, Romae summo ponti- fice missam celebrante, S. Petro in altari offertori temꝑore cum magna deuotione obtu- lit. Accurrentes autem ministri altaris, arbitrati sunt magni ponderis aurum obtulisse di- uitem regem, sed schedulã reperiētes scriptam notatam admirabātur, ingeniũ deuo- tionem principis collaudantes. Hinc papa decrevit ob memoriam sanctissimi regis, rogâ- tibus clericis, vt hoc responsorium in honorem S. Petri deinceps cantaretur. Claruit sub Ottone secundo Imperatore. Anno domini. 980. AMMONIVS monachus Floriacensis coenobii, ordinis S. Benedicti nationis Gal- licus, vir in diuinis scriptris studiosus eruditus, atque in secularium literarum discipli- nis sufficienter instructus. Fertur tam metro quam prosa nonnulla composuisse opuscula, sed ad manus nostras minime venerunt. Scripsit post ad Renaldum monachum volu- men vnum. Demiraculis S. Benedicti lib.i. Claruit sub Ottone imperatore tertio. Anno domini. 990. HERIGERVs abbas Lobiensis coenobii ordinis S.Benedicti,in diuinis scripturis eru- ditissimus, in secularib. literis nobiliter doctus,carmine excellens prosa.Cuius Berno abbas

Abbot of Sponheim

Widukind, a monk of the monastery of Corvey in Saxony, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and very well instructed in secular letters, quick in talent, clear in eloquence, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote many distinguished little works in an alternating style. Of these I have so far found only the following. From the beginning of the Saxons down to the death of Otto, the first emperor, he wrote to Mechthild, his daughter:

A History of the Saxons, 3 books. Flore virginali cum ma [unclear]. The Deeds of Otto I, 1 book. The Passion of Thecla the Virgin, in verse, 2 books. The Life of Paul the First Hermit, 1 book.

He flourished under Otto, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 950.

Liutprand, deacon of the church of Ticinum, Italian by nation, born from the city of Pavia, formerly scribe and secretary of Berengar, king of Italy, a man very learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, sharp and forceful in talent, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, no less excellent in verse than in prose. He is said to have written several distinguished little works, by which he made his name known. Driven out of Italy by King Berengar, he came into Germany and stayed at Frankfurt. He wrote a notable historical work on his own time, containing the tyranny of that Berengar; this, as if in recompense for the injuries received from him, he entitled:

The Antapodosis, that is, Retribution, 7 books. Regnantibus, imo senien [unclear].

Of the others I have seen nothing. He wrote the aforesaid volume to [Recemund?], bishop of the church of Elvira in Spain; in it he sometimes uses verse, sometimes Greek speech, interspersing many things about the deeds of the Germans.

He flourished under Otto I, emperor, in the year of the Lord 950.

Abbo, abbot of the monastery of Fleury, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures by constant reading and study, exceptionally learned in secular disciplines, and also distinguished in life and conduct, was proved worthy even to the crown of martyrdom: while he was preaching the word of God in Vasconia, he was made a witness of the Christian faith by the shedding of his blood. He wrote:

On the Reckoning of Victorius, 1 book. Additions to the same, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Otto I, in the year of the Lord 970.

Robert, king of France, noble, brave, just, learned, and religious, rightly receives a place among ecclesiastical writers, since he composed chants and sweet responsories in regular melody for the honor of the catholic Church. In humane letters, especially in music, he was most learned; and he was of such religion that he sang the canonical hours in church with the clerics, and outside, at home, read them with his own people. He was of such compassion and mercy toward the poor that, sometimes stripping himself of his own garments, he many times covered their nakedness. A book never left his hands, so much so that, sitting on the tribunal amid the noise of judicial cases, he would have the Psalter open in his lap. Hence he is read to have shone with miracles after death. His is that well-known sequence which is sung on the days of Pentecost:

On the Holy Spirit, namely, “Come, Holy Spirit.” A responsory on Saint Peter, namely, “Cornelius the Centurion.” On the Nativity of the Lord, namely, “Judaea Jerusalem no” [unclear]. And that Alleluia, namely, “Deliver me from my enemies.” And many other things which I do not know.

The responsory “Cornelius the Centurion,” when the supreme pontiff was celebrating Mass at Rome, he offered with great devotion to Saint Peter on the altar at the time of the offertory. The ministers of the altar, hurrying up, thought that the rich king had offered gold of great weight; but, finding a written and notated sheet, they marveled, praising the talent and devotion of the prince. Therefore the pope decreed, at the request of the clerics and in memory of the most holy king, that this responsory should thereafter be sung in honor of Saint Peter.

He flourished under Otto II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 980.

Ammonius, a monk of the monastery of Fleury, of the Order of Saint Benedict, French by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters. He is said to have composed several little works both in verse and in prose, but they have by no means come into our hands. He afterwards wrote one volume to the monk Renald:

On the Miracles of Saint Benedict, 1 book.

He flourished under Emperor Otto III, in the year of the Lord 990.

Heriger, abbot of the monastery of Lobbes, of the Order of Saint Benedict, most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose. Berno the abbot

361
DE SCRIPT. ECCLESIAT. abbas Augiensis meminit in libro quodam ad Aribonem archiepisco- pũ. Scripsit dialogũ insignẽ sub persona sui Adelboldi clerici monachi tũc Romę exi- stentis postea episcopi Traiectẽtis, de quo statim nobis sermo habēdus est, pręnotatum. De dislonantia ecclesiae lib.i. Vitam S. Vrsinari metrice lib.i. Ad Hugonem de quaestionibus lib.i. De diuinis officiis lib.i. Gesta episcoporum Lobiensium lib.i. De corpore sangine Domini lib.i. Et alia plura. Claruit sub Ottone Imperatore tertio. Anno Domini. 990. FLAVALDVS monachus Remensis, ordinis S. Benedicti, in scripturis diuinis eru- ditus, in secularibus literis egregie doctus, ingenio subtilis, disertus eloquio. Scripsit non contemnendae lectionis opulcula, quorum studio nomen suum cum gloria transmi- to E quibus fertur opus infigne à conditione Remensis ciuitatis, quam mili- fit ad posteros. Remi à fratre Romulo nec ati fugatos ob memoriam Domini sui construxisse, sic ap- tes valde eruditus, cum adhuc monachus esset, apud Lobias publicam scholam mona- pellasse commemorant, vsque ad sua tempora, in quo multa de sanctis martyribus aliis rebus ac gestis inter seretens, volumini hunc titulum dare voluit. Gesta Remensium pontificum lib.i. Vitas quoque multorum sanctorum l.b.i. Alias plurium sanctorum lib.i. Cantus in honore sanctorum. Et quađam alia. Claruit in multa religione disciplina temporibus Ottonis Imperato- ris secundi. Anno domini. 880. ARIBO Moguntinus archiepiscopus, decimusonus post S. Bonifacium martyrem, ad quẽ Berno abbas Augiensis coenobii de aduentu Domini conscripsit tractatum, vir in diuinis scripturis studiosus eruditus, celebrata Synodo apud Selgenstat cum Burckar- do episcopo Wormaciensis episcopi, vir in diuinis scripturis doctus, sic aperi- tes valde eruditus, Cum adhuc monachus efferet, apud Lobias publica scholam mo- narchum tenuit, in qua Burckardum vna cum aliis in vtraque literatura erudiuit. Scripsit inter alia sui ingenii opera. In Psalmos 15. graduum lib.i. Ad Bernonem abbatem epi.i. Et quađam ad alios epistolas Moritur sub Contrado iuniore Imperato- re. Anno domini. 1023. multa utilia constituit, quae in scripturis authenticis habentur. Scripsit etiam, BVRCKARDVS ex monacho Lobiensis coenobii ordinis S. Benedicti Constipsat scripsit tractatum, vir in diuinis scripturis studiosus eruditus celebrata Synodo apud Selgentat cum Burckar- do episcopo Wormacensis episcopi, vir in diuinis scripturis doctus, , sic aperi- tes valde eruditus. Scripsit ex sententiis sanctorum patrum generalium con- diosiffimus valde eruditus. Ego sunt seruorum pontificum, magnũ infigne opus post Isidorum, videlicet. Decretorum quod diuisit in li.20. In nouo testamento prius. Epistolarum ad diuerfos lib.i. Claruit sub sancto Henrico Imperatore. 40 Annodomini. 1020. BERNO abbas Augiesis coenobii ordinis s. Benedicti Constatiensis diccesis, natione Teutonicus, vir in diuinis scriptoris doctus, in secularib. literis valde nobiliter eruditus Musicus, Poeta, nulli suo tẽpore secundus, vita conuersatione pręcipuus. Scripsit tam metro quam prosa quaedam praeclara volumina, de quibus ego tantum reperi subiecta. Ad Piligrimum archiepiscopum Coloniensem egregium, vtile volumen componuit. De Musica seutonis lib.i. Omnis igitur regularis Mo. 50 Deinstrumentis Musicae lib.i. Musicum non esse content. De aduentu Domini ad Aribonem lib.i. Summae dignitatii. De officio quoque missae lib.i. De leiuonio quatuor temporum lib.i. De leiunio sabbati lib.i. De mensura monochordi lib.i. Epistolarum ad diuerfos lib.i. Alia infuper multa edidit, quae ad notitiam meam nondum venerunt. Claruit tempo- ribus S. Henrici Imperatoris primi, sed regis secundi quia primus coronam imperii non accepit. Anno domini.1020. ADELBOLDVS epifcopus Traiectensis, ex monacho, vt ferunt Lobiensi ordinis S.Benedicti, sub cuius persona Herigerus abbas dialogum de aduentu domini compo- fuit, vir in diuinis scripturis eruditus in secularib.literis nobiliter doctus, in etria S.Hen- riei imperatoris in magno pretio habitus, nõ minus armis eruditione pręstrauit ini- fideles.Scripsit, Vitam

On Ecclesiastical Writers

the abbot of Reichenau mentions [him] in a certain book to Archbishop Aribo. He wrote a notable dialogue under the person of his Adelbold, a cleric and monk then living at Rome and later bishop of Utrecht, of whom we must speak presently, entitled [unclear].

On the [unclear] of the Church, one book. The Life of St. [Ursmar?], in verse, one book. To Hugh, on Questions, one book. On the Divine Offices, one book. The Deeds of the Bishops of [Liège?], one book. On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book. And many other things. He flourished under the emperor Otto III, in the year of the Lord 990.

Flodoardus, a monk of Reims of the Order of St. Benedict, learned in the divine Scriptures, excellently instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by study of which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Among these there is said to be a distinguished work from the founding of the city of Reims, which, they record, the soldiers of Remus, [after Remus had been killed by?] his brother Romulus and [they had been] driven out, built in memory of their lord and so named, down to his own times; in it, interweaving many things about the holy martyrs and other matters and deeds, he chose to give the volume this title:

The Deeds of the Bishops of Reims, one book. Also Lives of Many Saints, one book. Other [lives] of several saints, one book. Songs in honor of the saints. And certain other things. He flourished in much religious discipline in the times of the emperor Otto [unclear], in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, the nineteenth after St. Boniface the martyr, for whom Berno, abbot of the monastery of Reichenau, wrote a treatise On the Advent of the Lord, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures: after holding a synod at Seligenstadt with Burchard, bishop of Worms, he established many useful things, which are contained in authentic writings. He also wrote, among other works of his talent:

On the Fifteen Gradual Psalms, one book. To Abbot Berno, one letter. And certain letters to others. He died under the emperor Conrad the Younger, in the year of the Lord 1023.

Burchardus, from a monk of the monastery of Lobbes of the Order of St. Benedict [became] bishop of Worms, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and very learned in secular letters. While he was still a monk, he kept a public school of monks at Lobbes, in which he instructed [unclear], together with others, in both literatures. He wrote, from the opinions of the holy Fathers, of general councils, and of various pontiffs, a great and notable work after Isidore, namely:

Decrees, which he divided into twenty books. “In the New Testament first...” Letters to Various Persons, one book. He flourished under the holy emperor Henry, in the year of the Lord 1020.

Berno, abbot of the monastery of Reichenau of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Constance, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, very nobly instructed in secular letters, a musician and poet second to none in his time, distinguished in life and conduct. He wrote certain excellent volumes both in verse and prose; of these I have found only the following. For Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne, he composed an excellent and useful volume:

On Music, or on Tones, one book. “Every regular [unclear]...” On the Instruments of Music, one book. “The musician is not to be content...” On the Advent of the Lord, to Aribo, one book. “Of the highest dignity...” Also On the Office of the Mass, one book. On the Fast of the Four Seasons, one book. On the Saturday Fast, one book. On the Measurement of the Monochord, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He published many other things besides, which have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of St. Henry, the first emperor but the second king, because the first did not receive the crown of empire, in the year of the Lord 1020.

Adelboldus, bishop of Utrecht, formerly, as they say, a monk of Lobbes of the Order of St. Benedict, under whose person Abbot Heriger composed the dialogue On the Advent of the Lord, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, held in great esteem at the court of St. Henry the emperor; no less by arms than by learning he [unclear] the unbelievers. He wrote,

The Life

OSBERTVS monachus Cantuariensis, ordinis sancti Benedicti,vir in diuinis scri- pturis eruditus,&amp;in Musica arte peritissimus, ingenio subtilis et amp; clarus eloquio, varios in vtraque literatura tractatus edidit, quibus famã sui nominis ad posteros transmisit. RVPERTVS abbas monasterii Cassinensis,ordinis S.Benedicti, vir in diuinis sCri- pturis studiofus et amp; eruditus atqꝫ in secularibus literis egregie doctus, regularis disciplinae 40 zelosus et amp; streuus gubernator vt ouiũ sibi cõmissarum verbo et amp; exẽplo pastor vtilis pos- set haberi.Scrip̄sit ad aedificationem fratrum fuorum pulchrorũ et amp; elegantes, Sermones lib.I. GVIDO monachus et amp; abbas coenobii de cruce sancti Leufredi, ordinis diui patris Benedicti,patria Aretinus,vir in diuinis scripturus exercitus,atque in secularibus disci- plinis etuditi issimus,Dialecticus et amp; Musicix insignis.In hoc etiam praeferendus ecatetis, quod ignotos cantus etiam pueri et amp; puellae per eius regulam in manu sua facilius disciant per se,quam per vocem magistri,aucter per aliciuis instrumenti. Et alia quae non vidi. Claruit sub Conrado iuniore Imperatore.Anno domini.1030. The Abbot of Sponheim

The Life of St. Henry the Emperor, one book. On the praise of the holy cross. On the praise of blessed Mary. But he also published some other works, both in verse and in prose, which have not come to my knowledge. He died under Conrad the younger, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1027, in the tenth indiction, in the eighteenth year of his episcopate, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December.

Osbert, a monk of Canterbury, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in the art of music, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, published various treatises in both kinds of literature, by which he transmitted the fame of his name to posterity. He wrote, among other things: The Life of St. Dunstan, archbishop, one book. Also On Music, one book. He flourished in the times of St. Henry the emperor, in the year of the Lord 1026.

Odilo, fourth abbot of Cluny, of the Order of St. Benedict, a holy and learned man, presiding over the monastery for fifty-six years, led the souls of many to Christ by word and example; Peter Damian, bishop and cardinal of Ostia, described his life, full of virtues and miracles, in a lucid discourse. He composed for the edification of his brothers: Elegant Sermons, one book. He died under Henry II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1048, in the first indiction, in the eighty-seventh year of his age, on the first day of the month of January.

Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in the disciplines of secular letters, the most learned of teachers in all his time, a distinguished poet and dialectician, presiding for many years over the public school, produced very many highly learned hearers. In life also most holy, he is read to have shone with many miracles. Among other things, he is said to have written: Letters to various persons, one book. In Praises of St. Mary, one book. Various hymns and prayers. And certain other devotional works. He flourished in the times of Henry, the first king, in the year of the Lord 1016.

Bruno, bishop of Wurzburg, paternal cousin of Conrad II, emperor, German by nation, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures, most holy in life and conduct, who, because of the excellence of his merits, was inscribed in the catalogue of the saints and is held to be the special patron of East Francia. He gathered from the writings of the ancient fathers a fine exposition: On the Whole Psalter, one book, "Blessed is the man who has not gone away." Whether he wrote anything else I do not know. He died under Henry II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1045, in the thirteenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Cassino, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally instructed in secular letters, zealous for regular discipline and an active governor, so that he could be considered a useful shepherd of the sheep committed to him by word and example. He wrote for the edification of his brothers fine and elegant Sermons, one book. He also published some other works, which have not yet come to our knowledge.

Guido, monk and abbot of the monastery of the Cross of St. Leufredus, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, by homeland an Aretine, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular disciplines, an outstanding dialectician and musician. In this too he is to be preferred to the rest: that even boys and girls may learn unknown songs more easily by themselves through his rule on their hand than through the voice of a master or by any instrument. He wrote, among the other little works of his intellect, against Berengar, cleric of the church of Tours: On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book. Also On Music, two books, "Therefore those who [unclear] our discipline." And other works which I have not seen. He flourished under Conrad the younger, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1030.

Egelnoth, archbishop of the church of Canterbury in England, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, most holy in life and conduct, a most merciful advocate of the poor. At his exhortation Cnut, king of England, made many alms, especially to the church of Chartres, over which the most learned man Fulbert, bishop, then presided, of whom we have made mention above. He is said to have written, to the honor of almighty God, a fine work: In Praise of St. Mary, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Conrad the younger, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1039.

Adelmann the grammarian, from a cleric of Liege bishop of Brescia, formerly a hearer of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, a man zealous and learned in the divine writings, a philosopher and dialectician famous in his time, excelling in verse and prose. He wrote in both

DE SCRIPT. ECCLESIAT. que stylo quedam commendanda opuscula, de quibus ad lectionis nostrę notitiam pauca peruenierunt. Scripsit ad Berengarium Thuronensem olim apud Fulpertum condiscipulum suum, tunc errare et dogmatizare incipientẽ valde prolixe et amice eum corripiens. De corpore sanguine Domini lib.i. Collectaneum te voco. Epistolarum ad diuerfos. lib.i. Alia insuper multa tam metro quam prosa scripsisse dicitur, quae non vidi. Claruit sub Henrico rege tertio. Anno domini. 1040. HERMANNVS qui dicebatur contractus, monachus coenobii S. Galli, ordinis diui patris Benedicti, natione Teutonicus, filius comitis de Veringen in Sueuia, vir in diuinis scripturis eruditissimus, in secularibus literis vniuerfaliter doctissimus, Philosophus, Poeta, Astronomus, Rhetor, Musicus, nulli suo tempore secundus, trium linguarũ Gręcę, Latinae, Arabicae peritissimus. Scripsit carmine prosa multa praeclara volumina, de quibus ego tantum reperi subiecta, videlicet, De Musica lib.i. De monochordo lib.i. In consideranda mono. De sex aetatibus mundi lib.i. Prima est mundi huius. De compositione astrolabii lib.i. In metienda igitur sub. De vtilitate astrolabii lib.1. Quicunque Astronomicae. De eclipsibus lib.i. De computo lib.i. 20 De quadratura circuli lib.i. De conflictu rhythmimachiae lib.i. Qui peritus Arithmet. De Physiognomia lib.i. Clari viri prudentis. Vitas plurium sanctorum lib.i. Hymnos prosas varias. Composuit etiam dulci regulari melodia, cantus prosas pulcherrimas. E quibus est illa de beata virgine Maria dulcissima, Salue regina. Et alma redemptor mater, ceterae quatum copiosus est numerus. Transtulit etiam nonnulla Gręcorum philosophorum Arabum Astrologorum volumina in Latinum. Membris fuit iuxta nomen suum contractus, sed semper in gratiarum actione perfecerans, vnde perbeatam virginem Dei genitricem interius mirabiliter consolari illustrari meruit. Claruit temporibus Henrici Imperatoris secundi. Anno domini. 1640. GVIMVDVS archiepiscopus Auertsanus, ex monacho Coenobii de cruce S. Leu-fredi, ordinis sacratissimi patris Benedicti, vir in diuinis scripturis nobiliter doctus, in secularibus litteris ad perfetus, secularium quoque literatum non ignarus. Scripsit quedam tempore astronomorum volumina in Latinum, Membris fuit iuxta nomina suum prosa multa tantum reperi subiectas, videlicet, De corpore sanguine Domni lib.i. Ad rem his temporibus. Et quaedam alia nobis inuisa. ALPHANVS archiepiscopus Salernitanus, ex monacho Cassinensis coenobii, ordinis S. Benedicti, vir in diuinis scripturus nobiliter doctus, & in secularibus letteris ad perfetus, seclarium quoque celeberrimę opinionis. Scripsit quaedam tempore astronominus ingenium sua excita, nomen etiam posteris profundi sensus opuscula, quibus ingenium sua spernenda, De quibus ego tantum notificauit. E quibus extant. De vnione verbi Dei hominis lib.i. De quatuor humoribus corporis lib.i. Alia quoque in omni literatura volumina composuit, quae ad nos minime venerunt. CAMPANVS natione Lombardus, Philosophus Astronomus omnium opinio-ne suo tẽpore celeberrimus, ingenio acutus, sermone scholasticus, diuinarum quoque scri-pturarum nõ ignarus, calculator computista insignis. Edidit ingenii sui non pauca opu- fo legi subiecta, opus magnum insigne. De computo ecclesiastico lib.i. Rogauit me vnu ex. De compositione quadrantis lib.i. Scire debes quod circulus. Alià quoque multa in Astronomi composuit, quae ad manus nostras non venerunt. Claruit sub Henrico re ge tertio. Anno domini .1030. HELPERICVS monachus coenobii S Galli, ordinis di ui patris Benedicti, natione Teutonicꝰ, vir in diuinis scripturis multũ eruditꝰ, in secularib. literis doctissimus, Philo- Poeta, Astronomus insignis, ingenio subtilis sermone cõpositus Scripsit tam metro

On Ecclesiastical Writers

and certain little works worthy to be commended for their style, of which few have come to our knowledge for reading. He wrote to Berengar of Tours, formerly his fellow pupil under Fulbert, then beginning to err and to teach dogmatically, correcting him at great length and in friendly fashion.

On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book. “I call you a collector.” One book of letters to various persons. He is said besides to have written many other things, both in verse and in prose, which I have not seen. He flourished under King Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1040.

Hermann, who was called Contractus, a monk of the monastery of St. Gall, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, son of the count of Veringen in Swabia, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, most thoroughly instructed in secular letters, a philosopher, poet, astronomer, rhetorician, musician, second to none in his time, and highly skilled in the three languages Greek, Latin, and Arabic. He wrote many distinguished volumes in verse and prose, of which I have found only the following, namely:

On Music, one book. On the Monochord, one book. “In considering the mono-.” On the Six Ages of the World, one book. “The first is of this world.” On the Construction of the Astrolabe, one book. “Therefore in measuring under-.” On the Usefulness of the Astrolabe, one book. “Whoever of astronomical-.” On Eclipses, one book. On Computation, one book. On the Squaring of the Circle, one book. On the Conflict of Rhythmomachy, one book. “He who is skilled in arithmetic-.” On Physiognomy, one book. “Of a distinguished prudent man.” Lives of Several Saints, one book. Various hymns and sequences. He also composed, in sweet and regular melody, most beautiful chants and sequences. Among these is that very sweet one concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary, “Salve regina,” and “Alma redemptoris mater,” and others, of which the number is abundant. He also translated into Latin some volumes of Greek philosophers and Arab astrologers. In his limbs he was, in accordance with his name, contracted, but always persevering in thanksgiving; hence he deserved to be inwardly wonderfully consoled and enlightened by the most blessed Virgin, Mother of God. He flourished in the times of Emperor Henry II, in the year of the Lord [1040?].

Guimundus, archbishop of Aversa, formerly a monk of the monastery of the Cross of St. Leufredus, of the order of the most holy father Benedict, a man nobly learned in the divine Scriptures, perfected in secular letters, and also not ignorant of secular literature. He wrote certain volumes in Latin [unclear] in the time of the astronomers. In his limbs he was, in accordance with his name, [unclear]. I have found only the following prose works, namely:

On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book. “To the matter in these times.” And certain other works unseen by us.

Alphanus, archbishop of Salerno, formerly a monk of the monastery of Monte Cassino, of the order of St. Benedict, a man nobly learned in the divine Scriptures and perfected in secular letters, and also of very celebrated reputation among secular writers. He wrote certain little works [unclear], by which he made known to posterity the name also of profound understanding and his talent [unclear]. Of these there survive:

On the Union of the Word of God and Man, one book. On the Four Humors of the Body, one book. He also composed other volumes in every branch of literature, which have by no means come down to us.

Campanus, a Lombard by nation, philosopher and astronomer, in the opinion of all most celebrated in his time, keen in talent, scholastic in speech, and also not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, an outstanding calculator and computist. He published not a few works of his talent, of which I have read the following, a great and distinguished work:

On Ecclesiastical Computation, one book. “One of [them] asked me from-.” On the Construction of the Quadrant, one book. “You must know that the circle.” He also composed many other things in astronomy, which have not come into our hands. He flourished under King Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1030.

Helpericus, a monk of the monastery of St. Gall, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, most instructed in secular letters, a philosopher, poet, distinguished astronomer, subtle in talent, composed in speech. He wrote both in verse

De Musica quoque lib.i. De ceteris nihil vidi. Claruit sub Henrico Imperatore tertio. Anno domini. 1069. BERTHORIVS abbas monasterii Cassinēsis, ordinis S.Benedicti,vir in sanctis scriptu- ris studiosus &; doctus,&amp; in disciplina seculariū literarum nobiliter eruditus, Philosophus et amp; medicus insignis. Benedicti,vir in diuinis scripturis eruditissimus,&amp; in secularib.literis nobiliter doctus,ingenio et amp; eloquio elatus, quem Leo 5º papa nonus propter scientiã literarũ duxit et amp; episcopū cardinalẽ ordinauit, missus ab eo Constantinopolum ad confutandas haereses Graecorũ,a deo Nicętam pecto- ratum monachum in praesentia Imperatoris Constantini et amp; Michaelis patriarchae confe- tauit et amp; deuicit vt libroꝫ suum quē contra Latinorũ ecclesiam conscripserat, anathema- tizaret,&amp; cum manu propria igni comburendũ iniiceret.Et quicquid ibidem disputando dixit aut fecit,lueulẽter conscripsit, sub nomine Romani et amp; Constantinopolitanī. Dialogorum more lib.I.Scripsit etiam quaedam alia. Claruit sub Henrico imperatore secundo. Anno domini.1050. ANSEL-

The Abbot of Spanheim some little works in verse as well as in prose. Of these I have been able to find only a distinguished work:

On ecclesiastical computation, one book. “When with our brothers [unclear]...” Also On Music, one book. Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1069.

Berthorius, abbot of the monastery of Cassino, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the Holy Scriptures, and nobly educated in the discipline of secular letters, an eminent philosopher and physician. Before his conversion he is said to have written many little works in his own faculty. But afterward changing his study, and having been made a physician of souls, he wrote for the edification of his brothers:

Elegant Sermons, one book.

He also published other various treatises, knowledge of which has not reached me.

Rogerius, a monk of the Order of St. Benedict, to whom Guimundus of Aversa, bishop, while still established in the monastery, is said to have written three books Against Berengar; a learned man, educated both in divine and in secular letters, described, for the edification of many, in a sufficiently lucid style:

The Life of Bruno, Bishop of Cologne, one book.

And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Henry II, in the year 1040.

Algerus, from a scholastic a monk of Corbie in Saxony, German by nation, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man trained by constant study in the sacred writers, rich in reading of the ancients, and magnificently learned in secular books, cautious in intellect and sufficiently eloquent in speech, strong in verse and prose. He wrote in a very polished style a notable volume:

On the Sacrament of the Altar, two books. “Because the saints concerning the body...” On Grace and Free Will, one book. “It must be known that free...” And certain letters.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come into our hands.

Albertus, a monk of Metz, of the Order of St. Benedict, French by nation, a man skilled in the Holy Scriptures through continual exercise, and not ignorant of the arts of humanity, which we call liberal, in order to transmit his name to posterity, wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised. Of these there is said to be a short but useful work, containing the history of the events of his own time, which he dedicated:

To the Bishop of Metz, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Conrad the Younger, in the year of the Lord 1030.

Eckebertus, cleric of the church of Liege, German by nation, elegantly learned in the divine Scriptures and perfectly instructed in the disciplines of secular letters. He wrote some little works both in verse and in prose, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there survives a volume composed in elegant verse, which he entitled:

On Rustic Riddles, one book. “On the same matter, greater than others...”

And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Leo, Pope IX, formerly bishop of the city of the Leuci, which is called Toul, under the archbishop of Trier, sat in the chair of Peter after Damasus for seven years. Previously called Bruno, a learned and holy man. He wrote some distinguished little works, in which the grace of expression and sublimity of thought are deservedly commended. Of these, to Constantine the monk [unclear]:

Against the Errors of the Greeks, one book. To the Patriarch of Constantinople, two books. Letters to Various Persons, three books. To the bishops of Africa and Egypt.

He died under Henry the third king, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 1054, in the seventh indiction, shining with many miracles.

Humbertus, a monk of Toul, of the Order of St. Benedict, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly learned in secular letters, lofty in intellect and eloquence, whom Pope Leo IX, because of his knowledge of letters, brought forward and ordained cardinal bishop. Sent by him to Constantinople to refute the heresies of the Greeks, by God’s aid he refuted and defeated Nicetas Pectoratus, a monk, in the presence of Emperor Constantine and Patriarch Michael, so that he anathematized his book which he had written against the Church of the Latins and with his own hand threw it into the fire to be burned. And whatever he said or did there in disputation, he wrote out lucidly under the name of the Roman and the Constantinopolitan:

In the Manner of Dialogues, one book. He also wrote certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Henry II, in the year of the Lord 1050.

Ruthenorum ex monacho, ordinis S.Benedicti,natione Italus, vir in diuinis scripturisdoctus, declamator homiliarum ad populum egregius, sanctus Z denique

On Ecclesiastical Writers

ANSELM, a monk of Reims, of the Order of St. Benedict, a Frenchman by nationality, a man having a mind trained in the divine scriptures, wrote certain small works of his own study, which have not yet come into my hands. And among other things he gathered into one volume the deeds of Pope Leo IX performed throughout Gaul in councils and assemblies, in order to make known with how great authority he held a synod at Reims, or in other cities; with how great industry and subtlety he examined ecclesiastical cases; with what apportionment he corrected sinners; and how divine power worked together with him, as was sufficiently clear in one case of the Synod of Reims, where, when the bishop of Freising acted contumaciously against apostolic authority, by God’s vengeance he suddenly became mute before the eyes of all. He wished this work to be entitled:

The Itinerary of Pope Leo, one book.

He flourished under Henry III, king, in the year of the Lord 1050.

LANFRANC, archbishop of the church of Canterbury in England, formerly abbot of the monastery of Caen, of the Order of St. Benedict, an Italian by nationality from the city of Pavia, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, and in secular letters, especially in dialectic, by the opinion of all the most learned of his time, famous no less for holiness than for knowledge, left outstanding monuments of his intellect. Of these I have found only the following, a distinguished work:

On All the Epistles of Paul the Apostle, four books. Commentaries on the Psalter, one book. Against Berengar, one book, “Lanfrancus misericor.” The Deeds of Count William, one book. Of the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1060.

PETER DAMIAN, formerly a monk of the holy father Benedict, bishop of Ostia, cardinal of the most holy Roman church, a man devoted to the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, gentle and keen in intellect, pleasing and polished in speech, sufficiently capable in persuasion, shone forth as distinguished and famous no less for holiness than for learning. Following the example of the great bishop Gregory, through love of solitude and quiet he abandoned his episcopate, and after he had governed it strenuously for some years he returned to his monastery, thereafter spending his life with his brothers in tranquility of mind. But when he was reproved by the supreme pontiff with a charitable rebuke as to why, being a useful and suitable man, he had relinquished the episcopate through love of private salvation, he issued apologetic writings to the Roman pontiffs who succeeded one another, Nicholas II, Alexander II, and Gregory VII; in these, humbly excusing his action by authority, reason, and example, he appeased their minds. Of his small works the following are reported: To Leo the Hermit, whether a solitary person praying the canonical hours ought also to say “The Lord be with you,” when there is no one to answer; an instructive little work, entitled:

The Lord Be with You, one book, “To Lord Leo, with love.” Apologetics, one book, “To his lord Nicholas alone.” On the Incontinence of Priests, one book, “Recently, having with some.” On the Wives of Clerics, one book, “I address you, O [unclear].” Rule of Solitaries, one book, “While the fervor of holy [unclear].” Exhortation to Monks, one book, “To the brothers in Gangra.” Miracles of His Own Time, one book, “To the most beloved Gerard.” On the Progress of Monks, one book. Antilogion against the Jews, one book. one book, “Hugh, abbot of Cluny.” Life of Abbot Odilo, one book, “To Blanche, formerly countess.” On the Terror of Death, one book, “Indeed it must be considered.” On Meditation on Death, one book. Against a Certain Bishop, one book. Against Simoniacal Bishops, one book. On the Insolence of Wicked Men, one book, “To Lord H. of Ravenna.” Most Pleasing or Most Approved, one book. On the Natures of Certain Animals, one book. Of Rhetorical Declamation, one book, “Still, most beloved men.” On Flora Lucilla, one book, “Admirable, glorious.” On Cassian the Martyr, one book, “The glorious [unclear] of blessed Boniface.” On St. Boniface, one book, “To the fair, brothers, [unclear].” On St. Anastasius, one book. And many other things which I have not seen. Sermons and homilies [unclear].

He flourished under King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1050.

The Abbot of Sponheim

...and finally worthy of God, since, preaching the Catholic faith in Prussia, he is read to have been crowned with martyrdom by the enemies of Christ. He wrote some distinguished little works of his talent. Of these there survive, of commentaries:

On Genesis, 2 books.

And certain others. He suffered at the hands of the Prussians under St. Henry of Bamberg, who was the second king of this name and the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1008, indiction 6. After afflicting him with many tortures and cutting off his feet and hands, they at last made him a martyr of Christ by beheading.

Erhard, a monk of the order of St. Benedict, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and learned by continual exercise, subtle in intellect and ready in speech, was of excellent industry in delivering homilies to the people. By expounding the divine Scriptures he made his name known, and by frequent study of them became an outstanding teacher. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, of which there are reported:

Commentaries on Genesis, 1 book. On Exodus, 1 book.

On Leviticus, 1 book. On Numbers, 1 book.

On Deuteronomy, 1 book. Also of homilies, 1 book.

He also published some other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Bernold, priest of the church of Constance in Swabia, a German by nation, a devout man, zealous and learned in the holy Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in the discipline of secular letters, distinguished in intellect and [unclear] in eloquence, left some little works of his study, which nevertheless have not at all come to the knowledge of our reading. He is said to have composed, for the usefulness of the ecclesiastical commonwealth, a volume which he entitled:

The Roman Order, 2 books.

He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1060.

Marbod, bishop of Rennes, very zealous in the divine Scriptures, learned by reading the ancients, and nobly instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, excellent in verse and prose. He wrote not a few volumes in both styles, which could no less please readers than profit them. Among these there excels a notable work which he composed in elegant meter with a threefold sense:

On the Song of Songs, 1 book. The Passion of the Theban Martyrs, in verse, 1 book.

And certain others. He flourished in the times of Henry III, in the year of the Lord [1050?].

Marianus, a monk of Fulda, of the order of St. Benedict, a Scot by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, a historian and distinguished computist, left his homeland and came into Germany as a pilgrim for the love of Christ. First, at Cologne, he was made a monk at St. Martin's, and, from desire for solitude, was enclosed; he remained there for two years. Afterwards, however, transferred to Fulda, he remained enclosed there for 12 years, until at length, on account of his learning and sanctity, by order of the bishop of Mainz and the abbot of Fulda, he moved to Mainz and, staying again enclosed at St. Martin's for 17 years, was held by all in great honor. He wrote from the beginning of the world down to his own times:

A notable Chronicle, 2 books. We are instructed by the divine.

On the Harmony of the Evangelists, 1 book. It was in the days of Herod.

Also On Computus, 1 book.

And certain others. He died under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1086, indiction 9, in the 58th year of his age, and was buried at Mainz at St. Martin's, in the greater church, not without a reputation for sanctity.

Weneric, bishop of Vercelli, formerly a cleric of the church of Trier, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in the discipline of secular letters, made his name known to posterity by writing, although his little works have not come to the knowledge of our reading. In that discord which existed between Hildebrand, Pope Gregory VII, and Henry, third emperor or fourth king, he wrote, in the person of Theoderic, bishop of Verdun, while he was still a cleric at Trier, to that same pope, beseeching him as a father and, with friendly affection, as though grieving, suggesting to him all the things which talkative rumor had spread abroad that he had done or said against the right of laws and the justice of equity. He entitled it:

On the Discord of the Kingdom and the Priesthood, 1 book. I have found nothing concerning the rest.

He flourished under King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080.

Theoderic, a monk of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in speech. He is said to have written certain little works of reading not to be spurned, of which few have come to my knowledge. I have read only, addressed to Richard, abbot of Fulda:

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Life of St. Benedict, one book. It begins: “When the heavenly sacrament...” On the Translation of the Body of the Same, one book. It begins: “When for a long time the Lombard people...” Letters to Various Persons, one book. He also composed many other works, both in verse and in prose, which have not come down to us. He flourished under King Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1049.

Adam, abbot of Persema, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures through constant exercise, rich in reading the ancients, and sufficiently trained in knowledge of secular letters, of very celebrated reputation in delivering homilies, transmitted his name with praise to posterity by composing various treatises. There are extant his devout and useful works:

Sermons to the Brethren, one book. On the Saints and Various Subjects, one book.

He is also said to have explained certain treatises of sacred Scripture, in which he showed the abundant vein of his talent; but they have not come to my knowledge.

Anselm, bishop of Lucca, a man most learned in the divine writings and not meanly instructed in secular letters, the tireless co-worker of Pope Gregory VII and an outstanding defender of him against Guibert, who had been set under him by Henry, so that he defended all his deeds, sayings, or writings against Emperor Henry by the authority of law and of the Scriptures. He left very famous monuments of a great talent, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant:

Against Guibert the Antipope, one book. On the Psalter, also one book. And Several Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1080.

Willeram, abbot of Mersburg, of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, practiced in verse and prose, after he had for some time devoted himself to the study of letters at the University of Paris, returned to his homeland and was made scholasticus of the church of Bamberg. At length, considering that the glory of the world passes away with time, and despising the world, he put on the monk in the monastery of Fulda for love of Christ; and finally, as his merits increased, he was consecrated abbot in the monastery of St. Peter near Mersburg, and by writing made his name known to posterity. Of his little works I have read only a volume, composed with fine variety in mixed prose and verse, on the marriage of Christ and the Church:

On the Song of Songs. It begins: “When I look upon the studies of the elders...” On Jeremiah the Prophet, one book. And Several Letters to Various Persons, one book.

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1070.

Franco, scholasticus of the church of Liège, a German by nation, a man magnificently learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, also outstanding as an astronomer and computist, and venerable no less for religion than for knowledge. He is said to have composed some treatises on the sacred Scriptures, which have not yet come to my knowledge. He wrote to Hermann II, archbishop of Cologne, a subtle and excellent work, a volume in mixed prose and verse, composed with fine variety, on the marriage of Christ and the Church:

[unclear], one book. On the Squaring of the Circle, one book. And many other works.

He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Bernard, a monk of Cluny, of the order of St. Benedict, a man practiced in the holy Scriptures by constant meditation, and not ignorant of secular literature, also in religion and [unclear].

The Customs of Cluny, one book.

Bernard, a monk of Corbie in Saxony, of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man nobly learned in the divine writings and very skilled in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech. He wrote to Hartwin, archbishop of Magdeburg, in a clear indeed but bitter discourse, a volume:

Against Henry IV, one book. And other works which I have not seen.

He also wrote other things. He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1050.

Ivo, bishop of Chartres, formerly provost of St. Quentin of Beauvais, of the order of regular canons of the divine father Augustine, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures and a most careful interpreter of the canons of the holy fathers and general councils, and revered no less for holiness than for knowledge, magnificently reformed his order, which had long since collapsed. After Burchard, bishop of Worms, he wrote from the canons of the saints a concise decretal collection, which jurists used before the time of Gratian, and which he entitled:

Panormia, ten books. Excerptiones ecclesi[asticae?] [unclear]. Letters to Various Persons, one book. [unclear] the Church of Chartres. And

268 The Abbot of Sponheim And certain other things. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1090.

Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans and afterwards archbishop of Tours, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular learning second to none in his time; sharp in intellect and very eloquent in speech; formerly a disciple of Berengar of Tours, but a persecutor of his error; who endured many persecutions and tribulations, even to imprisonment, for ecclesiastical liberty. He wrote in both styles, namely verse and prose, certain excellent little works, of which as yet only a few have come to our knowledge for reading. He wrote, in elegant meter, a very beautiful and useful exposition:

On the Whole Office of the Mass, one book: “I have proposed to write what...” On His Exile, one book: “Recently I was wealthy in...” On the Misery of This Life, one book: “We are taken from the midst [unclear]...” On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. Of Hymns and Prayers in Diverse Meter, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book: “If anyone [says] one nature...”

He comprised the epitaph of Berengar, once his teacher, in fifty-two verses. He wrote also many other things still unknown to us. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1090.

Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury in England, formerly abbot of the monastery of Bec in Normandy, of the Order of St Benedict, once a hearer and disciple of Lanfranc; a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in knowledge of secular letters; upright and most holy in life and conduct; devout in mind, eloquent in speech, continual in action, angelic in countenance, mature in bearing, exemplary in progress, in the study of the Scriptures:

Against the Gentiles, Why God Became Man, one book: “Often, earnestly, by many...” On the Incarnation of the Word, against the Jews, one book: “To the lord father of the whole...” On the Virginal Conception, one book: “Since in all things, religious...” Proslogion, one book: “Come now, little man...” Monologion, one book: “Anselm, servant, etc.” On the Holy Spirit, against the Greeks, one book: “It is denied by the Greeks that the Spirit...” On the Fall of the Devil, one book: “That saying of the Apostle, ‘What have you...’” On the Diversity of the Sacraments, one book: “To the lord and friend Waltram...” On Leavened and Unleavened Bread, one book. On the Song of Songs. On the Will of God, one book: “Human reason, when concerning...” On the Holy Trinity, one book. Dialogue of a Christian and a Gentile. On Peace and Concord, one book: “Wherever sacred Scripture...” On Grace and Free Will, one book. On Blessed Sufficiency. Dialogue on Truth, one book: “Since God is truth...” On Similitudes, one book: “The will in three ways...” Measurement of the Cross, one book: “Jesus of Nazareth, by [unclear]...” Meditations, one book: “[unclear] whether it is...” Against the Fool, one book: “Since he does not rebuke me...” On the Misery of Man, one book: “My life terrifies me...” On Antichrist, one book. To Lanfranc the Archbishop. On the Eight Beatitudes, one book. On St John the Baptist. On the Members Attributed to God, one book: “Since your probity...” On the Sacraments and Divine Offices, one book: “Servant of the servants of God, in...” Proverbs, that is, On the House of Conscience, one book: “[Jesus] entered; what...” On the Hexaemeron, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. On the Grammarian, one book: “A desertory, on account of the second place, whatever is...” On the Assumption of St Mary, one book. On Servitude, on account of the second place, whatever is... To William of Hirsau, one book. On Sin:

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On original sin, one book. Also some sermons. But he is said to have written many other works also, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1080.

Wilhelm, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, in the diocese of Speyer, of the Order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, to whom blessed Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, wrote several letters, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, inferior to no one among the Germans in his time, a philosopher, astronomer, and distinguished musician, most holy in life and conduct, since he is read to have shone with many miracles, reformed regular discipline, which had already collapsed, in many monasteries of Germany. Therefore, for the conversation of monastic observance, from the statutes of the ancients, he wrote:

Constitutions of monks, two books. “Since I, brother Wilhelm.” On music and tones, one book. “After, by God’s gift, [unclear].” One book. “Whoever [is] most truthful.” On the clock, one book. “If anyone in this necessary [matter].” On the correction of the Psalter, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. To St. Anselm of Canterbury, three letters. And certain other works.

He also published several other works, which through the negligence of the ancients have fallen into oblivion. He died under Emperor Henry III, but as king of the Romans the fourth, in the year of the Lord 1091, indiction 14, on the fourth Nones of July. He was buried in the middle of the church of the Apostles, with a great reputation for holiness.

Giselbert, provost of the monastery of Weltin in England, of the Order of St. Benedict, hearer and disciple of Anselm of Canterbury, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and skilled in the practice of secular [learning], and nobly taught in the disciplines of secular letters, a clear theologian and poet, ready in talent and cautious in speech, not ignorant of philosophy, sufficiently endowed in talent, made his name known to posterity by writing, while he composed certain necessary works, in which he exercised his talent magnificently. Of these are reported the following; [he wrote] splendid volumes, of which few have come to my knowledge. There exists his volume, written in elegant meter; the following are reported:

On the Passion of St. Cyriacus, one book. Life of Saint Bavo, one book. On the prophet Isaiah. And certain other works.

He flourished under Henry IV, with Anselm, in the year of the Lord [1090?].

Gunther, monk of Elno, of the Order of St. Benedict, skilled in the practice of the divine writings, and nobly taught in the disciplines of secular letters, a theologian and clear poet, sufficiently instructed by talent, excelling in verse and prose. Not ignorant of philosophy, ready in talent and cautious in speech, he wrote his name; he made [it] known to posterity by writing, while he magnificently exercised his talent in certain works. Of these splendid volumes, of which few have come to my knowledge, there exists his volume written in elegant meter; the following are reported:

Life of Saint Trudo, one book. “To the one and eternal first [one].” Life of Saint Remaclus. And certain other works.

And many other works. He flourished in the times of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord [1090?].

Theoderic, abbot of the diocese of Canterbury, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, a man studious and learned in the sacred writings, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, excelling in counsel and [unclear]. Nobly taught in philosophy, in proof of his sincere faith, he wrote in both styles. He wrote, under the name of Moses, what he had been as a Jew, and of Peter, what he had begun to be as a Christian, a distinguished dialogue, necessary concerning Christ, concerning the Church, and concerning the future life, which he entitled:

Against the Jews, one book. On free will, one book. On knowledge and philosophy. “You are said to wonder.” One book. Offense concerning priests, one book. Seal of St. Mary. Summary of histories, one book. “The army in the camps of the eternal [one].” Twin-spotted [unclear] of the soul, on the divine offices, three books. On the ima-

270 The Abbot of Spanheim

On the Image of the World, one book. “The world, therefore, is so called.” On the Song of Songs, one book. “At the beginnings of books.” On the Luminaries of the Church, one book. “Gelasius of the city of Rome.” On the Body of the Lord, one book. On the Hexaemeron, one book. On God and Eternal Life, one book. On the Soul, two books. The Ladder of Heaven, on the degrees of visions, one book. The Key of Physics, on the natures of things, one book. On the Whole Psalter, one book. Homilies on the Gospels, one book. On the Pope and Emperor, one book. A Dialogue from the little works of Augustine, one book. A Refutation of [unclear] on feasts, one book. Food of Life, on the saints, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published many other things, whose titles I have not been able to find. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Sigebert, a monk of Gembloux, of the Order of St. Benedict, a Gaul by nation, a man from his youth most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, and in secular letters second to none in his time in the territory of Liege, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote many volumes in both styles, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. He is reproached, however, for this: that, adhering to Henry, persecutor and rebel against the Roman Church, he wrote letters and little works against Hildebrand, Pope Gregory VII, which did not befit his purpose. What he wrote, indeed, he openly declared at the end of On Illustrious Men. When he had been placed in the monastery of St. Vincent at Metz to instruct boys, he wrote in heroic meter:

The Life of St. Theodoric the Bishop, one book. The Passion of St. Lucy, in meter, one book. On the Translation of the same, one book. The Life of King Sigebert, one book. The Passion of the Thebans, one book. The Life of St. Guibert, one book. The Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux, one book. The Life of St. Maclou, one book. The Life of St. Theobald, one book. Against Pope Gregory, one book. An Apology to the Emperor, one book. Against the Letter of Pope Paschal, one book. On Ecclesiastes, in heroic meter, one book. Histories after Eusebius, one book. On Illustrious Lives, one book. “Marcellus Marcivr.” Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published other things after these, which he did not mark together with the little works written above. He flourished in the times of Emperor Henry III, King Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1070. He brought his Chronicle down to the year [unclear].

Calixtus II, pope, a Burgundian by nation, brother of the duke of Burgundy, formerly archbishop of Vienne, sat in the pontificate after Gelasius for six years. He was a man learned in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular letters, a special lover of St. James the Apostle; in his honor he raised the church of Compostela to an archbishopric. He wrote, in well-composed speech and with the greatest diligence:

On the Miracles of St. James, one book. “Calixtus, bishop, servant.” Letters to various persons, one book.

And certain other things. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Stephen, also called Herrand, the fourteenth bishop of the church of Halberstadt, formerly abbot of the monastery of Ilsenburg, of the Benedictine Order, a German by nation, was a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech. He wrote little works not of contemptible reading, but few have come into our hands. In the person of Count Louis he wrote a very elegant and useful letter to Waltram, bishop of the church of Naumburg, defending Henry, rebel against the Roman Church.

A Defense of the Pope, one book. “As a good man from the good.” And several letters to various persons, one book.

And certain other things. He died under Henry V, in 1107, in the fifteenth indiction. And he was honorably buried in Reinsburg.

Bernard, the first abbot of Clairvaux, of the Cistercian Order, a Burgundian by nation, a noble and holy man, who was renowned for many miracles both in life and after death, learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect and adorned in speech, since he neglected nothing in his writings that could serve to adorn discourse. He published many distinguished little works, of which the following are reported.

Anselm of Laon, scholasticus, very devoted to the divine Scriptures, skilled through long practice, and in the disciplines of secular letters a notably acute teacher, scholastic in speech, distinguished no less in life than in knowledge, explained the Scriptures of both Testaments with an interlinear and marginal gloss, from the writings of the Fathers, in a new kind of exposition. He also wrote certain other little works which have come to me. It is reported. Commentaries on the Psalter, one book. And certain letters. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1110.

Hugh, priest and monk of Saint-Victor at Paris, of the order of the regular canons of Augustine, abbot there, as they say, a Saxon by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, inferior to none of the ancients in secular philosophy, who, like a second Augustine, was regarded as a most celebrated teacher in his time, subtle in intellect, adorned in eloquence, and venerable no less in conduct than in learning. He wrote many, almost countless, little works, of which few have so far come into our hands. A Summary of His Sentences, one book. On the Soul of Christ, one book. The Abbot of Sponheim

On the Hierarchies of Dionysius, 14 books. On the Praise of the Fathers, 1 book. On the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary, 1 book. On the Magnificat, 1 book. On the Love of the Bridegroom and the Bride, 1 book. On the Medicine of the Soul, 1 book. On Meditation, 1 book. On the Incarnation of the Word, 1 book. On the Wisdom of Christ, 1 book. He also composed many sermons and various other treatises. He flourished under Emperor Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1130.

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Deutz near Cologne, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, enlightened by the Holy Spirit through vision, not ignorant of secular letters, a monk of Saint Lawrence of [Traiectum], was taken from there by Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, on account of his incredible learning, and raised to be abbot of the monastery of Deutz. He composed many distinguished little works. For from the time when in his youth he entered the monastery, he had exercised himself so much in the holy Scriptures that not even when sleeping did he seem able to rest from those meditations, but his tongue and lips were moved as if in reading. Of his works I have found only the following at present. To Cuno, abbot of Siegburg and afterwards bishop of Regensburg.

On the Victory of the Word of God, 13 books. It begins: “Recently, when you as a guest...” On Genesis, 1 book. It begins: “Whoever to a faithful soul, while...” On the Song of Songs, 1 book. It begins: “He who against a man like...” On the books of Saint Job, 10 books. On the books of Kings, concerning David, 15 books. On the Holy Trinity in the Old Testament, 12 books. It begins: “That you also, venerable...” On the Apocalypse of John, 11 books. It begins: “Those things which through the cycle of the year...” Meditations on the Fire at Deutz, 3 books. It begins: “Behold how the accuser...” On the Twelve Minor Prophets, 14 books. On the Rule of Saint Benedict, 1 book. On the Gospel of John, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. An Apology for the Same Work, 1 book. It begins: “He was made...”

He wrote, moreover, works not contemptible in reading, of which I have only [unclear]. Finally, he is said to have written many other works, and to have explained the greater part of the New and Old Testament in many books; of these, up to the present, we have seen nothing except those which we have marked. He flourished in great holiness, gleaming with doctrine and miracles, under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1124. And he died under Lothar III.

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Limburg in the diocese of Speyer, of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, magnificently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, distinguished in life and conduct, so much so that he deserved to be visited by frequent divine revelations. For many years he applied himself to secular philosophy in the school of Paris and became a noble philosopher. But, considering that the philosophy of the present life was empty, he abandoned the study of vanity; returning to his homeland, he became a monk in the said monastery, and finally abbot. He wrote works not contemptible in reading, of which I have found only the following.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Song of Songs, 4 books. “Whoever [unclear] of his own matters.” On contempt of the world, 2 books. “The world by an undeserved name.” On St. John the Baptist, 1 book. “The evangelical historian relates.” Of his revelations, 1 book. “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation.” He wrote certain sermons on the saints whose bodies or patronages were held in the same monastery of Limburg. He flourished under Emperor Henry V, not without a reputation for holiness, in the year of the Lord 1124.

Rudolph, abbot of St. Trond in the diocese of Liège, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a German by nation, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures through constant practice, and not meanly learned in secular letters, strong in verse and prose, and an excellent musician, no less distinguished in work than in knowledge, wrote in both styles some little works not to be despised, of which there are reported: 7 books. Also a chronicle. Against the simoniacs, 1 book. Many poems. He also composed many chants in praise of the saints, in sweet and regular melody. He flourished under Henry V, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Franco, the second abbot of the monastery of Affligem, of the order of St. Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular doctrine, strong in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote both in meter and in prose certain commendable little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. While he was still a simple monk in the aforesaid monastery, at the command of Fulgentius his abbot he began an outstanding work, 1 book, which, after he had been made abbot, he later completed, adorned with learning and eloquence. On the grace of God, 7 books. On the state of future glory, in verse, 1 book. Letters to various persons, 1 book. Sermons on the Blessed Virgin, 1 book. And certain other things. He was elected abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Affligem under Emperor Henry V, in the year of the Lord [unclear], indiction 13.

Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, formerly a scholastic of Paris, surnamed Porretanus, a Frenchman by nation, a man much practiced in the divine Scriptures and magnificently learned in secular letters, subtle in talent and confused in eloquence by novelty of terms, was accused in certain matters of heresy by blessed Bernard, and, convicted in the council of Reims celebrated by Eugenius, is said to have renounced his error. There are those who excuse him, saying that the authorities introduced in his expositions were understood by some persons in a less sound way. But we, thinking with the Roman Church, confess that what has once been concluded by it may be infringed by no one. Gilbert wrote many little works, of which the following are reported: On the whole Psalter, 7 books. On all the epistles of Paul, 14 books. On the Gospel of John, 7 books. Books of Questions, etc. On Boethius, On the Trinity, 7 books. And certain other things. Several sermons. He flourished under Emperor Conrad III, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Lucas, abbot of the mount of St. Cornelius, of the order of the divine father Benedict, learned in the holy Scriptures by continual practice and sufficiently instructed in secular letters for his state, having obtained a noble talent for expounding the divine volumes, transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity by writing various treatises. But I do not recall that any of them have come into my hands. There is reported an outstanding work of his, addressed to Milo, bishop of the church of Thérouanne, likewise a very learned man, which I have not yet seen. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. Several sermons and letters. And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Lothar, the last emperor, in the year of the Lord 1130.

Wilbert, bishop of Chartres, studious and very skilled in the divine Scriptures, and inferior to none of the doctors of his time in the disciplines of secular letters, of talent and sufficiently adorned eloquence, notable in morals and life, and a special lover and worshipper of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, wrote an outstanding little work on this prophecy: “The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah,” 7 books. Against the Jews, 1 book. On the nativity of St. Mary, 1 sermon. Approved customs. Various sermons, 1 book. He is also said to have written a number of other things, which have not come to my knowledge. I believe that he flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Odo, bishop of Cambrai, a man learned in the holy Scriptures and nobly taught in humane letters, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, in composing and declaiming ho-

Abbot of Sponheim

[unclear] in homilies to the people, according to the custom, by no means undistinguished. He wrote a disputation which he had held with a certain Jew concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, in dialogue form, with the first letter of his own name and that of the Jew disputing with him noted.

To Wilbodo the monk, one book. On the Canon of the Mass, one book. On the steward of iniquity, one book: “There was a certain rich man.” Several homilies and letters. And he composed not a few other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Emondus, a monk of Canterbury in England, of the Order of St. Benedict, formerly a hearer and disciple of Archbishop Anselm, a man learned in the divine Scriptures through long practice, and not ignorant of secular letters, wrote little works not unworthy of reading, by which he benefited the edification of the faithful and made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant one volume on the discord which existed between William, king of the English, and the aforesaid St. Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.

On ecclesiastical liberty, one book. The life of the same Anselm, one book. And certain other things. He flourished in the time of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Gratian, a monk of Bologna or of Classe, of the Order of St. Benedict, by country, as some think, an Etruscan, a man most learned in the divine writings, burning with marvelous zeal, ready in talent, distinguished in eloquence, and notable also in life and conduct. After Ivo, bishop of Chartres, he wrote a distinguished volume of Decrees from the statutes, sanctions, and writings of the ancients, which professors of canon law use in the schools down to the present, approved by Pope Eugene III. Its title is:

The Concord of Discordant Canons, four books: “The human race by two.”

He composed certain other things. He flourished under Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Hugh, a monk of Corbie, of the Order of St. Benedict, called “of Fouilloy,” a man rich and learned in the holy Scriptures through the reading of the ancients, distinguished in talent, sweet in eloquence, and no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, made his name known to posterity by his writings. For he wrote a notable volume, for all religious persons fearing God not so much useful as delightful, divided into four little books, entitled as follows:

On the material cloister, one book: “On the ordering of the cloister.” On the spiritual cloister, one book. On the cloister of the soul, one book: “The cloister of the soul contem[unclear].” On the cloister of paradise, one book: “In the heavenly Jerusalem cloi[unclear].” And certain other things. He flourished in the time of Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Richard, a monk of St. Victor at Paris, of the order of regular canons of St. Augustine, a man most learned in the divine writings and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, scholastic in eloquence, and excellent in morals and conduct. He wrote many, almost innumerable, little works, by which he greatly benefited the usefulness of believers and consecrated his name to immortality. Among these the following are reported:

On the Holy Trinity, one book: “I have established my [unclear] from faith,” etc. On contemplation, one book: “Arise, O Lord, into thy rest.” On the twelve patriarchs, one book: “Benjamin the youth.” On the mystical ark, one book: “That mystical ark of Moses.” On the Song of Songs, one book: “In the little bed,” etc., “the soul which.” On the extermination of evil, one book: “What is it to thee, O sea, that.” On the advancement of good, one book: “Every head is sick.” Against the Judaizers, one book: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive.” On the tabernacle of the covenant, one book. On the forty-two stopping-places. On the four degrees of charity, one book. On the priesthood of Melchizedek. On the twelve apparitors, one book. On the study of wisdom. On the progress of monks, one book: “Since to thy question,” etc. On the threefold holocaust, one book: “Bring to the Lord, O sons of God.” On the authority of Peter, one book: “The things which in the Gospel.” On judicial power, one book. On diverse affections. On the difference of sins, one book: “In Da-” On the instruction of novices, one book. On the Apocalypse of John.
