On Ecclesiastical Writers

one book. A Chronicle from the beginning of the world, one book. [unclear] Daniel the prophet. On the double Passover, one book. 24 books. “O God supremely good,” etc. Of divisions or exceptions. On the vision of Nebuchadnezzar, one book. On the sacrifice of Abraham, one book. On the four winds. On the words of Isaiah, one book. “On that day a man will nourish.” On the words of the Apostle, one book. “You ask how,” etc. On the Acts of the Apostles, one book. “King Herod sent [unclear].” On violent charity, one book. “Purge out the old leaven.” On newness of life, one book.

He also composed many other things besides: letters, sermons, various treatises. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Guido, the fifth prior of the Carthusians, a man skilled through long study in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, gentle in disposition, clear in speech, and venerable no less in his way of life than in his learning, is reported to have composed several little works, by which his name has been bestowed upon immortality. Of these there survives an excellent work written in lucid style:

On the life of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, one book. On the institutions of the Carthusians, one book.

And certain other things. With diligent study he corrected, according to the rule of truth, the letters of the most blessed father Jerome, corrupted by the excessive fault of scribes, and brought them together into one. He died under the younger emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 1137, in the fifteenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris after being a scholastic, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and nobly learned, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, transmitted his name to posterity by writing with such great glory that, down to the present day, the school of theologians everywhere, exercised in his little works, names and holds him as Master with singular veneration. For with sagacious study he wrote, from the sayings of the holy fathers, a commendable work:

Sentences, one book. “Desiring something concerning.” On all the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books. “Since all the prophecies of the Spirit.” Various sermons, one book. “The beginning of things require [unclear].”

He also composed not a few other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Conrad III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Eckard, first abbot of the monastery of St. Lawrence, which is called [Vraugia], in the diocese of Würzburg in the Hercynian forest, of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and, in secular letters, inferior in learning to no one among the Germans in his time, excelling in verse and prose, wrote little works not to be scorned for reading, by which he made clear the liveliness of his talent. Of these I have seen only an excellent work, composed in a double style in imitation of Boethius, very useful and necessary for the instruction and consolation of monks and of all the faithful who fear God, which he entitled:

The Lantern of Monks, one book. “Concerning lives and virtues.” Elegant sermons, one book. He was buried in the middle of the church of the aforesaid monastery.

Engelbert, abbot of the monastery of Admont, of the order of St. Benedict, a German by nation, a man very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, clear in intellect and speech, and no less [unclear] in way of life than [unclear], in verse and prose, wrote in both styles certain excellent little works, whose authority has already long been approved by use in the Church. He was called Comestor, or Manducator, for this reason: because, by more frequently citing the authorities of the Scriptures in his sermons and little works, he as it were [unclear] the volumes into the belly of his memory and talent,

an excellent work addressed to William, archbishop of Sens, briefly and usefully explaining all the historical books of the Bible, which now by usage is entitled:

Scholastic History, twenty books. “Of the imperial majesty.”

276 ABBAS SPANHEMENSIS De laudibus sanctae Mariae lib.i. Sermones de tempore lib.i. Sermones de sanctis lib.i. Et alia complura lib.i. Claruit sub Frederico Imperatore primo. Anno domini 1160. PETRVS Dialecticus Parisiensis, dictus Abelardus natione Gallus, vir in seculati Philosophia eruditiffimus, &; in diuinis scripturis doctus, gaudens nouitate ter- minorum &; aliiora se serutari tentans, oppressus à gloria plures incidit errores, &; agente sancto abbate Bernardo in Senonensi concilio cum prauis suis doctrinis condemnatus. Ab hoc tempore Philosophia secularis facram Theologiam sua curiositate inutili foedare ccepit. Scripsit autem Petrus iste nonnulla opuscula, quibus si errores non miscusset, vtili- tati posteritatis profuisse poterant. E quibus extat volumen dialectica obscuritate subũm-18 bratum, multis sententiis varium quod praenotare voluit. Theologiam suam lib.i. Scito reipsum lib.i. Et quaedam alia. Claruit sub Conrado Imperatore tertio. Anno domini. 1140. ADELPHVS abbas ordinis S. Benedicti, vir in diuinis scripturís longa exercitatione peritus, &; secularium literarum non ignarus, regularis obseruantiae cultor indefessus, vt se verbo &; exemplo ouibus Christi sibi commißis vilem posset exhibere pastorem. Fer- tur ad earum vitilitatem nonnulla cudisse opuscula in quibus diues ingenii vena ornatum commendat eloquium. De quibus extant elegantes. Sermones ad fratres lib.i. Contra Saracenos lib.i.20 Caetera quae composuisse dicitur, ad notitiam meam non venerunt. GVILHEMVS abbas S. Theoderici &; postea vt dicitur monachus Clareuallensis sub diuo patre Bernardo ordinis Cistertiensis vir in diuinis scriptris studiosus &; eruditus, vita quoque &; sanctitate conuersationis infigns, &; ob id eidem singulariter dilectus, edidit non spernendae lectionis opuscula. De quibus ad meam notitiam pauca peruenerunt. In- cepit scribere, sed morte praeuentus non perfecit. Vitam S. Bernardi abbatis lib.i. Scripturus vitam seruitui. Speculum fidei lib.i. Aenigma fidei lib.i. Setentiarum fidei lib.i. Ad Theophilum de natura animae lib.i. De contemplando Deo lib.i. De natura &; dignitate amoris lib.i.30 De Sacramento altaris lib.i. Meditationes pronouitiis lib.i. Contra Petrum Abelardum lib.i. In Cantica canticorum imperfectum li.i. In epistolam Pauli ad Romanos lib.i. Et quaedam alia. Sunt qui dicant hunc Guilhelmum cum adhuc abbas esset S. Theoderici vulgatam ad Carthusienses illam scripsisse epistolam cuius initium est. Fratribus de monte Deiorien- tale lumen, quebeato Bernardo à multis adscribitur. Claruit sub Conrado Imperatorẽ ter- tio. Anno domini. 140. Et ante Bernardum cum vnum de vita ipsius librum complesset, moritur, cui Arnoldus abbas Boneuallis quatuor alios adiecit libros CONRADVS monachus Hirsaugiensis ccoenobii in confinibus Sueuorum, ordinis S. Benedicti, natione Teutonicus, Spirensis dicecesis vir in diuinis scripturis eruditissimus, 40 &; in secularibus literis valde peritus, Philosophus, Rhetor, Musicus, &; Poeta infigns, sub nomine peregrini mula praeclara composuit opuscula, in quibus ornata sententiarum dif- positio, &; venuti sermonis cultura, nulli veterum inferiorem suum declarant authorem. De his ad meam notitiam subiecta tantum peruenerũt. Opuꝫ dialogorum infigne sub no- mine peregtni presbyteri, &; Theodorae Deo sacrata virginis, quod praenotauit. Speculum virginum lib.i. Collaturo tecumo theo. In Euangelia per annum lib.i. Quia in litera veteris test. De vita spiritus &; fructu mortis lib.i. Cum omnis divinę pagina. Matricularius lib.i. Cum manifestum fit mun. Delaudibus S.Benedicti metrice lib.i. Luce velut solem. Diascalon lib.i. Quia se video diu va. De Musica &; tonis lib.i. Musica est secundum cuiusdam De caeteris nihil vidi. Fuit alius quidam declamator ordinis praedicatorum qui secun- dum modernorum consuetudem sermones ad populum composuit sub nomine Pere- grini, nostro multum eloquio inferior, &; tempore quoque posterior. Quicquid autẽ Con- radus iste scripsit Tullianam resonat eloquentiam, quod alter non potuit. Claruit sub Cõ- rado Imperatore tertio. Anno dominj. 140. ARNOLDVS abbas Boneuallis, ordinis Cisterciensis, beati Bernardi abbatis quon- dam

The Abbot of Sponheim

On the praises of Saint Mary, one book. Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. And several other works, one book.

He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

PETER the Dialectician of Paris, called Abelard, a Gaul by nation, a man most learned in secular philosophy and learned in the divine Scriptures, delighting in novelty of terms and attempting to examine things too lofty for himself, was overwhelmed by glory, fell into several errors, and, through the action of the holy abbot Bernard, was condemned with his depraved teachings at the council of Sens. From this time secular philosophy began to defile sacred theology with its useless curiosity. This Peter wrote some little works which, if he had not mixed errors into them, could have served the utility of posterity. Among them there exists a volume, shadowed over with dialectical obscurity and varied with many opinions, which he wished to entitle:

His Theology, one book. Know Thyself, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

ADELPHUS, abbot of the order of Saint Benedict, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures by long practice and not ignorant of secular letters, an indefatigable cultivator of regular observance, so that by word and example he might show himself a good shepherd to the sheep of Christ entrusted to him. He is said to have forged several little works for their utility, in which a rich vein of talent commends ornate eloquence. Of these there survive elegant works:

Sermons to the brothers, one book. Against the Saracens, one book.

The other things which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

WILLIAM, abbot of Saint-Thierry and afterward, as is said, a monk of Clairvaux under the divine father Bernard of the Cistercian order, a man zealous and learned in the divine writings, distinguished also by his life and by the holiness of his conduct, and for that reason singularly beloved by him, published little works not to be despised in reading. Of these only a few have come to my knowledge. He began to write, but, overtaken by death, did not complete:

The Life of Saint Bernard the Abbot, one book. Incipit: “About to write a life for the service.” The Mirror of Faith, one book. The Enigma of Faith, one book. Sentences of Faith, one book. To Theophilus on the Nature of the Soul, one book. On Contemplating God, one book. On the Nature and Dignity of Love, one book. On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. Meditations for Novices, one book. Against Peter Abelard, one book. On the Song of Songs, unfinished, one book. On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, one book. And certain other works.

There are some who say that this William, while he was still abbot of Saint-Thierry, wrote that well-known letter to the Carthusians whose beginning is “To the brothers of Mont-Dieu, an eastern light,” which is ascribed by many to blessed Bernard. He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord [1140?]. And before Bernard, when he had completed one book on his life, he died; Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, added four other books to it.

CONRAD, a monk of the monastery of Hirsau on the borders of the Swabians, of the order of Saint Benedict, a German by nation, of the diocese of Speyer, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, musician, and distinguished poet, composed many very excellent little works under the name of the Pilgrim. In these the ornate arrangement of the opinions and the cultivation of graceful speech declare their author inferior to none of the ancients. Of these only the following have come to my knowledge: a distinguished work of dialogues under the name of the pilgrim priest and Theodora, a virgin consecrated to God, which he entitled:

The Mirror of Virgins, one book. Incipit: “When I am about to confer with you, O Theo-.” On the Gospels throughout the Year, one book. Incipit: “Because in the letter of the Old Testament.” On the Life of the Spirit and the Fruit of Death, one book. Incipit: “Since every page of divine.” The Matricularius, one book. Incipit: “Since it is manifest [unclear].” On the Praises of Saint Benedict, in verse, one book. Incipit: “Like light the sun.” Didascalon, one book. Incipit: “Because I see myself for a long [unclear].” On Music and the Tones, one book. Incipit: “Music is, according to someone’s [unclear].”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. There was another declaimer of the order of preachers who, according to the custom of the moderns, composed sermons to the people under the name of Peregrinus, much inferior to our man in eloquence and also later in time. Whatever this Conrad wrote resounds with Ciceronian eloquence, which the other could not achieve. He flourished under Conrad, the third emperor, in the year of the Lord [1140?].

ARNOLD, abbot of Bonneval, of the Cistercian order, once of blessed Bernard the abbot

On Ecclesiastical Writers

...a close friend, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant also of secular letters, ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, conspicuous no less in conduct than in learning, made his name known to posterity by writing. For when William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, had died and left unfinished the work on the life of Saint Bernard, while that saint himself was already holding the heavenly realms, he wrote and composed:

The Deeds of Illustrious Men, one book. The Life of Saint Bernard. And certain letters.

He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Richard, a monk of Cluny, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters the most learned of all men of his time, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, who by writing and composing various treatises transmitted his name with great glory to the knowledge of posterity. Yet I do not recall that any of them has so far come into our hands. His notable and distinguished work is reported, however:

Histories of the Times, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He flourished in the times of Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Ganfred of Auxerre, a monk of the Cistercian order, formerly a hearer and disciple of Peter Abelard; but lest he should also become an imitator of his error, he betook himself to the teaching of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux. Under his discipleship, distinguished in learning and religion, he composed little works not contemptible for reading, by which he made his name known also to posterity.

Against Peter Abelard, one book. On the Apocalypse of John, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He flourished in the times of Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Peter, cleric of the church of Reims, called de Riga, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters most learned among all the doctors of his time; a grammarian and an outstanding philosopher, excelling in verse and prose. He wrote not a few volumes in both styles, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen only the notable metrical work on the Bible, which he entitled Aurora, as follows:

On Genesis, one book. It begins: “The beginning of the world, what sort...” “The twelfth of the fathers...” One book. “But the voice of the Lord Moses [unclear]” “God addresses Moses.” One book. “These are the words of God.” “After Moses, Joshua.” One book. “The Hebrew sins, he says.” “Solomon reigned.” “To Ruth [unclear] quickly...” “Dwelling on Mount Ephraim...” “Origen alone with [unclear].” One book. “After [unclear] and [unclear] for himself...” “You who read the history...” “Certain persons [ascribe] the book of Job to Moses.” “To Eustochium and Paula...” “As far as under the Ethiopians...” “Great Alexander.” “Herod flourished [unclear].” “In the nineteenth year of Tiberius.” One book. “These things concerning the new law...” On Grammar.

Joachim, abbot of the monastery of Fiore, of the Order of Saint Benedict, born in Calabria, a man devoted to and practiced in the divine Scriptures, who, since he was regarded as a prophet in his own time, even attempted to foretell future things. But he seems to me, if I may speak without prejudice to his own opinion or that of his followers, to have spoken more from conjectures of the Scriptures than to have prophesied. For, to be silent for the moment about the rest, he dreamed that Emperor Frederick would be a future enemy of the Church, whom all [unclear]. He wrote, however, in plain speech, a number of little works, in almost all of which, as though foreknowing the future, he wove in mystical prognostications.

The Abbot of Sponheim

On Jeremiah the prophet, one book. On the Gospel of John, two books. On the Apocalypse of John, three books. To Henry the Sixth, three books. “You piously ask something from ...” On the seven seals, four books. “The first time ...” The Psalter of ten strings, five books. “Of concord ...” On the fifteen pontiffs, one book. “Go up, bald man, that [unclear] ...” On future times, one book. “Since the general [unclear] of the world ...” Letters to various persons, one book. “Among all historians ...” He also published many other works, especially against the Jews and other adversaries of the Catholic faith, which have not come into our hands. But the treatise which he wrote against Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, was condemned in a general council, as is clear at the beginning of the Decretals, “We condemn.” He flourished under Henry the Sixth, in the year of the Lord 1100.

Rupert, monk of the monastery of St. Remigius in the diocese of Reims, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a Frenchman by nation, a man trained by constant study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular disciplines, distinguished in talent and clear in speech, wrote several small works of his intellect, by which his name became known to posterity. Of these I have seen only the deeds done by the Christians in the Holy Land in the time of Urban the Second against the infidels. A distinguished history, ten books. “Among all historians ...” Of the others I have seen nothing. He flourished under Henry the Fifth, in the year of the Lord 1120.

Roswitha, a noble woman born in Saxony, a nun in the monastery of Gandersheim, which is not far distant from Hildesheim, was distinguished by marvelous talent and learning, and admirable in both kinds of writing. For, exhorting consecrated virgins to chastity and continence, she wrote six comedies in the Latin language. On the deeds of the Ottos, a panegyric in verse, one book. “The sole hope ...” Also the passion of St. Dionysius in elegiac verse. Also several works on St. Gangolphus and other saints. She also had knowledge of the Greek language. She was a contemporary of John the Englishman, who by his learning deserved the papacy.

Dudechinus, priest of the church in Logenstein, a German by nation, a man learned through long practice in the holy Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, went to Jerusalem, in hope of eternal recompense, with many others under the emperor Conrad the Third; when they fought with the Saracens in a naval battle, [unclear]. Great in subtlety and distinguished in speech, he transmitted his name with glory to posterity by writing many and varied works. Of his small works few have come into our hands. These, however, are reported: A Summa of Theology, one book. “On the books of Dionysius ...” The Summa which is called Numerical, one book. “Those who rule well, pref. ...” On the celestial sphere, one book. “Our intention in this treatise ...” On ecclesiastical computation, one book. “Computation is the science of nume...” A beautiful calendar, one book. He furthermore published many other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

John, bishop of Chartres, by native place of Salisbury, formerly clerk and disciple of blessed Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, a man learned in the divine writings and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, and composed with beautiful grace, excellent in verse and prose, and venerable no less for religion than for knowledge, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he made his name known to posterity; but few of them have come into our hands. I have read his distinguished work on the trifles of courtiers and philosophers, which he wished to title: Polycraticon, eight books. “Most delightful then among many ...” A Penitential, one book. “Since the mercies of the Lord ...” The Life of St. Thomas the archbishop, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. He flourished under Frederick, the first emperor, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Ecclesiastical Description

Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, the close friend of the above-mentioned bishop John of Chartres, to whom he dictated some letters, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally instructed in secular letters, acute and forceful in talent, who knew not how to flatter the vices of princes and prelates but to rebuke them, held in esteem among kings, princes, and bishops for his learning and the uprightness of his life, wrote many little works. Of these the following are reported:

On Christian Friendship, 1 book. “For they have been diminished.”

On Salutary Penitence, 1 book. “You asked me that for you [unclear].”

1 book. “Who will give to my head...”

On Hastening the Passage, 1 book. “Your excessive [austerity?] of severity...”

1 book. “You are divided [unclear].”

On the Quality of Penitence, 1 book. “Your little exhortation.”

1 book. Against the Depraver, 2 books. “You have been chosen by your own.”

Exhortation to an Abbot, 2 books.

On the Office of a Bishop, 1 book. “You ask more urgently, reverend father.”

1 book. “Whenever I recall the words.”

1 book. “I give thanks to your grace.”

Letters, 194 in number, 1 book. “Asked by you, [unclear].”

2 books. He wrote many other works.

On the Danger of Prelates, 2 books.

On the Life of Court Clerics.

On the Deceptions of Fortune.

He flourished under Frederick the First, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Alexander, the third pope, a Sienese by homeland, after Adrian the Fourth sat in the chair of Peter for twenty-one years; a learned and vigorous man, who endured many injuries from Emperor Frederick, while he stoutly crushed the three antipopes raised up by him against himself, and at last, overcoming the emperor himself, trampled his neck with his foot as a sign of his subjection, saying: “It is written: You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk; you shall trample the lion and the dragon.” He wrote elegant works:

Letters to Various Persons, 1 book; and On Ecclesiastical Power, 1 book.

And certain other works. He died in the time of Frederick the First, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1181, in the fourteenth indiction.

Crisolanus, archbishop of the church of Milan, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular letters, distinguished in Greek and Latin eloquence, published certain little works of great authority, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity; none of these has come into our hands. His work is reported:

On the Holy Spirit, Against the Greeks, 1 book. On the Holy Trinity, 1 book.

Letters, sermons, and various other treatises, which are unknown to me.

Hugh Eterianus, a Tuscan by nation, easily the most learned in the holy Scriptures of all the learned men of his time, exceptionally instructed in secular letters, a philosopher and most eloquent rhetorician, perfectly equipped in Greek and Latin speech, whom all Greece admired as he wrote, most subtle in talent, a disputant second to none. He wrote many distinguished volumes, both in Greek and in Latin, by which he transmits his name with glory to posterity. Of these I have found only one work, brief indeed, but not to be despised, on the heresies which the Greeks lay upon the Latins:

To Cardinal Ardoinus, 1 book. “Careful prudence.”

On the Immortal God, 1 book. I have found nothing about the rest.

He flourished in the times of Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, with whom he was of great authority, under Frederick the First, emperor of the Romans, and Pope Alexander III, in the year of the Lord 1160.

Christian, archchancellor of Frederick the First, emperor, a Teuton by nation, a man most learned in secular literature, eloquent and industrious, whom the Italians in his time admired when he spoke, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, whom Leo the Tuscan, notary of Manuel, emperor of the Greeks, extols with praises. He wrote certain distinguished little works of his talent, of which there are extant:

The Deeds of the Life of Frederick the First, Emperor, 1 book. Various letters, or speeches, and certain other works.

He flourished under the same Frederick the First, in the year of the Lord 1170.

Leo, a Tuscan by nation, interpreter of imperial letters under Manuel, the great prince of the Greeks, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, an excellent cultivator of secular letters, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, whose office it was [to handle] letters sent to the emperor

380
136 ABBAS SPANHEMENSIS vel aliis mittendas de lingua transferre in linguam. Edidit quaedam praeclara volumina, quibus nomen suum etiam ad posteritatis notitiam transmisit. E quibus ego legi duntaxat opus egregium, quod praenotauit. De praeuaticationibus Graecorum lib.2. Graeorum intolerabilis. Contra errores Graecorum lib.I. Claruit apud Constantinopolim temporibus Frederici Imperatoris primi, & Alexan- dri Papae tertii. Anno domini. 1170. IOHANNES ecclesie cuiusdam Horit. archidiaconus, vir in diuinis scripturis eru- ditus et secularis literaturae non ignarus, Graeci et Latini sermonis peritus, ingenio prę- stans et clarus eloquio. Scripsit quaedam ad aedificationem fidelium non spernenda opu- scula, quibus nomen suum notificavit. Equibus extat opus insigne et praeclarum ad Ste- phanum regium quendam notarium contra Graecos. Epistolas etiam varias. lib.I. Multarotundo Craeco. De proceffione Spiritus Sancti Sed et alia quedam scripsisse dicitur, quae ad manus nostras non venerunt. GODEFRIDVS Viterbiensis presbyter, vir in diuinis scriptoris studiosus et erudi- tus, & secularis litteraturae non ignatus, ingenio praestans et clarus, metro exercitatus et profa. Scripsit non spernendae lectionis opuscula, quibus memoriam sui posteris reliquit. Equibus extat grande volumen ad Vrbam tertium earmine et soluta oratione mixtum, de mundi principio de vniuerso Veteri et Nouo Testamento, & aetatibus mun- di, temporibus gestis, ac historiis omnibus regum, quod praenotauit. Pantheon lib.IS. De mundo principio. De alijs nihil vidi. Claruit sub Frederico Imperatore primo, & Henrico eius filio. Anno domini 1185. ECKEBERTVS secundus abbas monasterii sancti Florini ordinis diui patris Be- nedicti, Treueniensis diccecesis, natione Teutonicus, vir in diuinis scriptruris studiosus et eruditus, & non minus conuerfatione quam scientia venerabilis, frater beatae Helizabet virginis abbatissae Schonaugiensis fuit. Hic anteab Bumensis ecclesie canonicus fuit, qui à sancta fotore ad Schonaugiam vocatus, primo: monachius, ac deinde abbas factus est. 30 Scripsit non contemnendae lectionis opufcula, quibus nomen fuum ad posteritatis noti- tiam transmisit. Equibus subiecta reperi. Aduersum haerefes lib.I. Prophetatum dudum tem. In principium Euangelii Iohannis. lib.I. Mysteria divini ser. Super Magnificat lib.I. Spiritus Domini super te ma. Super Mihius est angelus lib.I. Sermo Euangelicus omni. De obitu fororis suae lib.I. Virginibus Deo sacratis. Meditationes lib.I. Verbum mihi est ad te. Sermones per annum lib.IS. Erunt signa, etc. adiventus. Laudes saluatoris lib.I. Epistolarum ad diuerfos lib.I.40 Factum est in exordio. Alia quoque nonnulla edidit, quae ad notitiam meam non venerunt. Fuit enim decla- mator egregius, doctus et eloquens, adeo vt quandam haereticum quem nemo conclu- dere poterat, vnicà difputatione superaret. Claruit in coenobio pręfato sancti Floriniquod Schonaugia dicitur in diccecesi Treueniensi, sub Frederico Imperatore pimo. Anno do- mini. 1160. & propter religionem et doctrinam in precio habebatur. HELIZABET monialis et abbatissa fotorum coenobi Schonaugiensis, ordinis S. Benedicti (Sunt enim duo monasteria, vnvm monachorum alterum monialium, in fine Treuenensis diccecesis non longe à Rheno in Hircinia fylua constituta) foror Eckeberti abbatis supradicti, virgo sanctiffimae conuerfationis, quae multas reuelationes diuinitus 50 accepert, quas ad aedificationem posteritatis literis demandauit. Equibus legi ista. Viartum Dei vtile opus lib.I. Factum est in exordo. De II000.virginum Coloniensium lib.IS. Nobis qui pios affe. Reuelationum diuerfarum lib.I. Omnes qui lecturi funt, Ad fratrem fuum Eckeberturn lib.IS. Petis à me frater et Epistolarum ad diuersos lib.I. Ex epifcopatu Metenside. Ad sanctam Hildegardini lib.IS. Et alia quedam. Moritur sub Frederico Imp.primo Anno domini. I165. Indict. 13. Aetatis suae anno. 36. Conuer-

The Abbot of Sponheim

or to be sent to others, from one language into another. He published certain distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name even to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have read only the excellent work which he entitled:

On the Prevarications of the Greeks, 2 books. “The intolerable [unclear] of the Greeks.” Against the Errors of the Greeks, 1 book.

He flourished at Constantinople in the times of Emperor Frederick I and Pope Alexander III, in the year of the Lord 1170.

JOHANNES, archdeacon of a certain church of Horit., a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain little works, not to be despised, for the edification of the faithful, by which he made his name known. Of these there is an excellent and distinguished work, addressed to a certain royal notary Stephanus, against the Greeks.

Also various letters, 1 book. “[unclear] Greek.” On the Procession of the Holy Spirit.

But he is also said to have written certain other works, which have not come into our hands.

GODEFRIDUS of Viterbo, priest, a man zealous and learned in the divine writings, and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding and distinguished in talent, practiced in verse and prose, wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he left his memory to posterity. Of these there is a large volume addressed to Urban III, mixed in verse and prose, on the beginning of the world, on the whole Old and New Testament, and on the ages of the world, the deeds of the times, and all the histories of kings, which he entitled:

Pantheon, 15 books. “On the beginning of the world.”

Of the others I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick I and his son Henry, in the year of the Lord 1185.

ECKEBERTUS, second abbot of the monastery of Saint Florinus, of the order of the divine father Benedict, in the diocese of Trier, a German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, was the brother of the blessed virgin Helizabet, abbess of Schonau. He had previously been a canon of the church of Bonn; summoned by his holy sister to Schonau, he was first made a monk, and then abbot. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I found the following:

Against Heresies, 1 book. “Prophesied long ago [unclear].” On the Beginning of the Gospel of John, 1 book. “The mysteries of divine [unclear].” On the Magnificat, 1 book. “The Spirit of the Lord upon you [unclear].” On ‘The Angel Was Sent’, 1 book. “The Gospel sermon [unclear].” On the Death of His Sister, 1 book. “To virgins consecrated to God.” Meditations, 1 book. “I have a word for you.” Sermons through the Year, 15 books. “There will be signs,” etc., “of Advent.” Praises of the Savior, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. “It happened in the beginning.”

He also published some other works which have not come to my knowledge. For he was an excellent, learned, and eloquent declaimer, so much so that by a single disputation he overcame a certain heretic whom no one was able to refute. He flourished in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Florinus, which is called Schonau, in the diocese of Trier, under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1160, and was held in esteem because of his religious life and learning.

HELIZABET, nun and abbess of the sisters’ monastery of Schonau, of the order of Saint Benedict (for there are two monasteries, one of monks and the other of nuns, situated at the end of the diocese of Trier not far from the Rhine in the Hercynian forest), sister of the aforesaid abbot Eckebertus, a virgin of most holy conduct, received many revelations from God, which she committed to writing for the edification of posterity. Of these I have read the following:

The Ways of God, a useful work, 1 book. “It happened in the beginning.” On the 11,000 Virgins of Cologne, 15 books. “To us who [unclear] pious [unclear].” Of Various Revelations, 1 book. “All who are going to read.” To Her Brother Eckebertus, 15 books. “You ask of me, brother.” Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. “From the bishopric of Metz [unclear].” To Saint Hildegard, 15 books. And certain other works.

She died under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1165, in the thirteenth indiction, in the thirty-sixth year of her age.

Ecum Latinĩ sermonis esset ignata, tamen reuelante spiritu Dei omnia Latine et congrue dictauit, notariis excipientibus. Vidimus multas epistolas Conradi tertii &; Fre- derici primi imperatorũ, &; episcopeorum Moguntinensis, Treuerensis, Colonienfis, Bre- denfis, Hierosolymitanı, &; aliorum pene innumerabilium, qui ex diuersis mundi regio- nibꝰ fama sanctitatís &; reuelationum eius prouocati, se scriptis commendabant oratio- nes ibus fama sanctitas &; reuelationū solutiones querrebant. Carmelitis adhuc in terra sancta degentibus regulam dedit, quam iidem fratres iam in Eu- ropa constituti per Apostolicam sedem modificatam &; approbatam vbique profitentur, ad instantiam Innocentii Papae tertiī descriptit luculento sermonē &; veraci. Statut terrae sanctae lib.i. Regulam Carmelitarum Claruit sub Henrico Imperatore sexto. Anno domini. 1190. On Ecclesiastical Writers

Of her conversion, the twenty-fourth; but of the visitation of the heavenly splendor, the thirteenth. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July. Buried in the church of the monks of Saint Florin, in the middle of the choir.

Hildegard, abbess of the monastery of Saint Rupert the Confessor, opposite the town of Bingen on the other side of the river Nahe, in the diocese of Mainz, of the order of the holy father Benedict, German by birth, from the county of Sponheim, once a disciple of the blessed virgin Jutta, sister of Megenhard, count of Sponheim, our founder, a virgin of most holy conduct and enlightened from her childhood by divine revelations, whose life, approved by many miracles, spread the fragrance of her holiness into far distant regions, so much so that Eugene III, Anastasius IV, and Hadrian III, Roman pontiffs, visiting her very frequently by letters, commended themselves and the Roman Church to her prayers. And Eugene III, in the council of Trier, with Saint Bernard present, publicly approved her writings and small works when they had been read before all, and again strengthened her by letters to persist in the undertaking she had received. All the things that she committed to writing she learned by divine revelation.

Among these are the following:

On the Rule of Saint Benedict, one book. “And I, a poor little woman...”

Thirty Questions, one book. “Charity, which with abstinence...”

Life of Saint Rupert the Confessor, one book. “For, as in a true vision...”

Life of Saint Disibod the Bishop, one book. “In a mystical vision,” etc.

Fifty-eight Homilies on the Gospels, one book. “A certain man who...”

On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. “In a vision which of the soul...”

Scivias, a large volume, one book. “And it came to pass in the ninth year...”

Life of Merits, one book. “O crowd of men being born...”

Compound Medicine, one book. Simple Medicine, one book.

Divine Works, one book. “And it came to pass in the sixth year...”

To the People of Cologne, one book. “He who was, and who is...”

To the People of Trier, one book. “I, a poor little woman...”

Exhortation for Secular Persons, one book. “O crowd of men being born...”

To Her Sisters, one book. “O daughter, who the footsteps...”

To the Gray Monks, one book. “I, a poor little woman, in...”

Various Songs, one book. “Who are these who, as...”

And to Saint Bernard, one letter. “In the spirit of mysteries...”

Letters to various persons, 135, one book. “Every father, I, poor...”

She also wrote other things. In all her small works Catholic doctrine shines forth, which either confirms faith or instructs morals; nor did she ever say or write anything that could be called into doubt. And although she was ignorant of Latin speech, nevertheless, as the Spirit of God revealed it, she dictated everything in Latin and fittingly, with notaries taking it down. We have seen many letters of Conrad III and Frederick I, emperors, and of the bishops of Mainz, Trier, Cologne, Bremen, Jerusalem, and of others almost innumerable, who, stirred by the fame of her holiness and revelations from various regions of the world, commended themselves in writing to her prayers and sought solutions. She died under Emperor Frederick I, in the year of the Lord 1180, at the age of 82, in the thirteenth indiction, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October.

Albert, patriarch of Jerusalem, a learned and most holy man, who gave a rule to the Carmelite brothers while they were still dwelling in the Holy Land, which those same brothers, now established in Europe, profess everywhere after it had been modified and approved by the Apostolic See, at the urging of Pope Innocent III described in a clear and truthful discourse:

The State of the Holy Land, one book. The Rule of the Carmelites.

He flourished under Emperor Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1190.

Innocent III, pope, Campanian by birth, previously called Lotharius, after Pope Celestine III presided over the Church for eighteen years. He was very learned in the divine Scriptures, since from his childhood he had devoted himself to letters in the school at Paris, and he became a man no less upright than learned. He left not a few small works of his genius, of which the following are circulated under the name of Lotharius the Levite, or also of Pope Innocent:

On the Usefulness of the Human Condition, two books. “Why from the womb of the mother...”

On the Seven Penitential Psalms, one book. “There are three things especially in which...”

On the Office of the Mass, one book. On the Cloister of the Soul, one book.

On the Sacrament of Baptism, one book. Many Sermons. Let-

GILDELMVS Antisiodorésis vt ferunt episcopus, vir in diuinis scripturis eruditif- simus, & in seculari Philosophia nobilitet doctus, ingenio subtilis, sermone scholasticus, in gymnasio Parisiensi Theologicam cathedram ascendens, longo tempore clarus emicuit, & inter omnes doctores illius temporis maxima et opinione celebris fuit. 282 The Abbot of Spanheim, book I.

Letters to various persons, one book.

He flourished at the time of the discord which was between Philip, brother of Henry, and Otto, duke of Saxony, in the year of the Lord 1200.

William of Auxerre, as they report a bishop, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, ascending the theological chair in the school of Paris, shone forth with distinction for a long time, and among all the doctors of that time was celebrated with the greatest reputation and esteem. He wrote a very notable and useful volume, or

A Summa of Theology, "As the Apostle says, Faith," one book. On the divine offices, "On the divine offices," one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Cyril, priest and monk of Mount Carmel, and third prior general of the same order, by nation, as they report, a Greek, a holy man and illuminated with a prophetic spirit, to whom almighty God is said to have revealed his will by angelic ministry, when he was honored with silver tablets written by the finger of God. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote, to Abbot Joachim, On the Angelic Oracle.

The prologue begins thus, one epistle: "To the house of the whole divine..." But the Oracle thus, one book: "In the time of the years of Christ..." On the progress of his order. Several letters to various persons, one book.

He flourished under Philip and Otto, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Helinand, monk of Froidmont, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures through long practice, and nobly instructed in secular letters, keen in intellect and eloquent in speech, because of the excellence of his learning and the integrity of his life appeared not least among the ecclesiastical doctors of his time. For he wrote many things by which he gave his name to immortality. Of these the following are reported: from the beginning of the world down to his own age, a great and notable volume,

Histories, 48 books. On the restoration of the fallen, one book: "G. Lamentations and ve..." Several sermons, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

And many other things. He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Gilbert, monk of the Cistercian order, and afterward abbot of a certain monastery, a man studious in the divine writings and excellently learned, subtle in intellect and clear in speech. After the death of St. Bernard the abbot, he wrote, where he had left off, namely from that place, "On my bed by night," down to the end, 46 subtle and most elegant sermons.

On the Song of Songs, one book: "There are different kinds of lovers..."

And certain other things.

He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Aelred, abbot of a certain monastery of the Cistercian order, as one practiced by continual study in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, gentle in intellect, sweet in speech, outstanding in devotion. He wrote for the benefit of his brothers several little works, by which he both profited them and transmitted knowledge of his name to posterity. Of these there is extant a little work of great usefulness for religious men, filled with spiritual sayings, which he entitled

The Mirror of Charity, one book. On Luke, one homily: "When Jesus was of the years..."

And other things which I have not seen.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, around the years of the Lord 1209.

Maurice, bishop of Paris, very studious and learned in the divine writings, and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, as one who before his episcopate taught theology gloriously for many years at Paris, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, was of excellent application in declaiming sermons to the people. He is reported to have composed certain excellent little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there are reported, through the course of the whole year, both on Sundays and on feast days,

Sermons to the people, one book. On the care of souls, to priests.

But the rest which he is said to have written have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1190.

Papias, by nation a Lombard, a man most learned in secular letters, the most distinguished grammarian of all in his time, fully instructed in Greek and Latin speech, and also not moderately practiced in the divine Scriptures. He wrote in a twofold style in both literatures

DE SCRIPT. ECCLESIAT. tura quaedam egregia opuscula. Equibus pauca ad notitiam meam peruenierunt. De ordine dicendi lib.i. De linguae Latinae vocabulis lib.i. Omnium in hoc libro inne. Epistolarum ad diuerfos lib.i. De caeteris nihil reperti. Claruit temporibus Henrici sexti. Anno domini. 1200. IOHANNES Beleth, gymnasii Parisiensis olim insignis Theologus, in diuinis scri- pturis eruditus &; in seculari Philosophia sufficienter doctus, ingenio promptus, sermone scholasticus, interdoctores fui temporis non ignobilis, scribendo &; disputando nomen fuumad posteritatis notitiam cum gloria deduxit. Scripsit enim non inutilem. Summam de diuinis officiis lib.i. In primitiua ecclesia. Sermones quoque varios lib.i. Alia insuper non pauca scripsisse dicitur, sed ad notitiam meam venerunt. THEODERICVS abbas ordinis S. Benedicti, natione Teutonicus, vir in diuinis scripturis studiosus &; secularium literarum non ignatus, nec minus conuersatione quam scientia clarus. Fertur nonnulla composusse opuscula, de quibus ego tãtum vidi ad quos- dam abbates. Vitam sanctae Hildegardis lib.4. In Romana repub. Et quasdam epistolas. Claruit sub Henrico sexto. Anno domini. 12oo. Benedicti, vir in diuinis scripturis iugi ex- ercitatione doctus, ingenio placidus, sermone dulcis atque compositus, &amp; ad persuaden- dum satis idoneus, conuersatione deuotus et amp; laudabilis, ac regularis obseruantia zelator insignis,nomen suum scribendo posteris notificans, ad vtilitatem legentium quaedam de- uota composuit opuscula,de quibus ista feruntur. On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear] certain excellent little works. Of these a few have come to my notice.

On the order of speaking, one book.

On the words of the Latin language, one book. It begins: “Of all things in this book [unclear].”

Letters to various persons, one book. About the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the time of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

John Beleth, once a distinguished theologian of the University of Paris, learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, ready in intellect, scholastic in speech, not undistinguished among the doctors of his time, by writing and disputation brought his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. For he wrote the not unprofitable work:

A summa on the divine offices, one book. It begins: “In the primitive Church.”

Also various sermons, one book.

He is said besides to have written not a few other things, but they have not come to my notice.

Theoderic, abbot of the order of St. Benedict, German by nation, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, no less renowned for his manner of life than for his knowledge. He is reported to have composed several little works, of which I have seen only, addressed to certain abbots:

The life of Saint Hildegard, four books. It begins: “In the Roman commonwealth.”

And certain letters. He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Werner, otherwise Hirnerius, an illustrious and notable man, professor of civil law and a most distinguished interpreter, and an exceptional cultivator of humane letters, who was deservedly called the lamp of law, because he was the first to expound civil law with little glosses, and gave to others after him an unparalleled example of illuminating the law. And from this time professors of both laws have always flourished in abundance, and began to explain the volumes of his instruction down to the present day. He taught in both places, both at Rome and at Bologna, for a long time, where he had many distinguished pupils, who by their learning spread the fame and glory of their master. His glosses and splendid memorials on the laws are extant, very well known among professors of this field. He flourished in the time of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Peter, abbot of Cluny, of the order of St. Benedict, a man learned in the divine Scriptures through constant exercise, gentle in intellect, sweet and composed in speech, and quite fit for persuasion, devout and praiseworthy in manner of life, and a distinguished zealot for regular observance, making his name known to posterity by writing, composed certain devout little works for the benefit of readers. Of these the following are reported:

Accounts of many things, one book.

On the eremitical life, one book. It begins: “I have received the letters of love.”

Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published several other things, which have not come to my notice.

Peter Cantor of Paris, and afterward, as they report, bishop, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, gloriously presided for many years over the theological school at Paris and trained many distinguished pupils. He also wrote certain excellent [unclear], transmitted with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among his little works there is found a certain notable and by no means contemptible summa, which he entitled:

The Abridged Word, one book. It begins: “The abridged word.”

Another book of distinctions, one book. It begins: “Abel is called the beginning.”

The Grammar of Theologians, one book. Various sermons.

On certain miracles, one book.

Also On the Sacraments, three books. It begins: “The people went about.”

He flourished in the time of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Pileus of Modena, professor of both laws, very celebrated in intellect, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, renowned for knowledge and cautious in counsel, held in the highest esteem among the older jurists, by writing and teaching various things in that faculty [unclear]. His name [unclear] appeared first among the expositors of law, and by his example gave many both the spirit and the form of studying. He is reported to have written in that faculty certain splendid little works, by which he gave his name to immortality. Of these there is extant a brief summa on the Pandects, which is entitled:

Vento-

284 ABBAS SPANHEMENSIS lib.i. Ventosa Et quaedam alia. Claruit sub Henrico sexto: Anno domini. 1200. lib.9. STEPHANVS Anglicus gymnasi Parīsiensis quondam decus et rector in diuinis scripturis studiosus et eruditus; atque in Philosophia Aristotelica nulli suo tempore fecun- dus Theologiam multis annis gloriose docuit, & primus scripturam facram medullitus, & moraliter exponere coepit. Et hinc nos inoleuit vt magistri Theologiae diuinos libros suis lecturis in scholis discipulis lucidius aperirent. Scripsit autem iste Stephanus vt acce- pi subiecta opuscula. In quinque libros Moysi lib.5. Super C.lectura In Iosue lib.1. In libro quoque Iudicum lib.i. In Regum quoque lib.4. To In 12. Prophetas minores li.12. Alia insuper multa edidit, quae ad notitiā meam nec dum venerunt. Claruit circa tempora imperii Henrici sexti regis, Imperatoris autem à papa coronati quinti. Anno domini.1200. BAGOROTVS vtriusque iuris professor insignis et celeberrimus interpr̄s, aliarūm quoque literarūm secularium non ignarus, cuius apud antiquos Iuristas non parua autho- ritas erat, propter excellens ingeniu docendi, scribendo studio etiā posteris nomen suum notificauit, de cuius opusculis extat suma notabilis quam pręnotauit. Cauillationum lib.i. Cum periculo sum sit mi. De ordine iudiciorum lib.i. Precibus et Instantia. Alia insuper complura scripsisse dicitur, sed ad notitiam meam non venerunt. PLACENTINVS natione Italus, vtriufque iuris cultor et explanator celeberrimus, in monte Pestilano docendo et scribēdo magnā gloriam est consecutus, qui olim apud hu- ius artis professores inter pęcipuos doctores locum obtinuit, propter quędum commen- datiffima volumina quae composuit. E quibꝰ inter cetera extare dicitur. Summa iudiciorūm lib.i. Cumessem Mantua. Super codice quoque lib.i. De aliis nihil reperi. Claruit temporibus Henrici sexti. Anno domini 1200. ROFREDVVS patria Beneuentanus, doctor in vtroque iure clarissimus ingenio subti- lis, eloquio scholastico more compositus, ad soluenda dubia et iuris quaestiones longa ex- ercitatione satis idoneus. Scripsit in ea facultate studentibus non contemnenda opuscula, 30 quibus nomen et opinionem suum immortalitati consecrauit. De quibus tamen pauca potuimus inuenire quae et subiecimus, volumen perutile continens. Quaestiones iuris ciuilis lib.i. Si considerarem ingentum. Quaestiones iuris canonici lib.i. Super omnibus actionibus. Summam iuris lib.i. Quicquid amplius edidit, ad notitiam meam adhuc minime peruenerit, PETRVS archiepiscopus Senonensis in diuinis scripturis iugi studio eruditus et ve- terūm lectione diues, atque in secularibus literis doctus, ingenio subtilis et clarius eloquio. Scripsit non paruę vtilitatis opuscula, quibꝰ et suum ingenium excoluit, & aliorū aedificationi materiam pręparauit. Scripsit valde subtiliter sententiis patrum appositis. 40 In epistolas Pauli omnes lib.i. Sermones etiam varios Diuerfios etiā libros Bibliae diligenter exposuit, aliosque tractatus et varios et vtiles scri- psisse dicitut, qui ad notitiam meam non venerunt. Azo natione Italus est Bononiensi ciuitate orditus vitae originem, Iohannis Bosiani Cremonensis viri doctiffimi quondam auditor atque discipulus, iuris ciuilis famosiffimus interpr̄s, fons legum, copia verborūm, lucernia iuris, qui sua eruditione et scientia omnes Iuristas qui eum pęcesserant facile pręcellit, multa ad ius ciuile pertinentia opuscula edi- dit, quibꝰ laudem et gloriam immortalem acquisiuit. Summam iuris notabilem lib.i. Super Digesto veteri li:2 4. Super Codice quoque lib.9. Pręterea optimos in legibus apparatus confecit, & pluribus summis additiones appo- soit, ac varia scripsit quae à doctis non ignorantur Iuristis. Claruit temporibus Frederici Imperatoris fecundi. Anno domini .1230. Et multos insignes disciplinos post se reliquit, legibus imperialibus quam in alīs disciplinis humanitatis nobiliter eruditus, ingenio sub- tilis et clarius eloquio, in professoribus huius facultatis apud veteres magnae authoritatis doctor. Scripsit quędam pręclara in ea disciplina volumina, de quibus ego tantum vidi. De ordine iudiciorūm lib.r. In nomine Domini nostri Iesu De of-

The Abbot of Sponheim, book I.

“Ventosa,” and certain other things. He flourished under Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200. Book 9.

Stephen the Englishman, once the ornament and rector of the school of Paris, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy, taught theology gloriously for many years, and was the first to begin expounding Sacred Scripture inwardly and morally. And from this the custom grew up among us that masters of theology should explain the divine books more clearly to their pupils in their lectures in the schools. This Stephen, as I have learned, wrote the following little works:

On the five books of Moses, 5 books. A lecture on the hundred [unclear]. On Joshua, 1 book.

Also on the book of Judges, 1 book. Also on Kings, 4 books. [unclear]

On the twelve minor prophets, 12 books. He also published many other works, which have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished about the times of the rule of King Henry VI, but the fifth emperor crowned by the pope, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Bagorotus, distinguished professor of both laws and a very celebrated interpreter, not ignorant also of other secular letters, whose authority among the ancient jurists was not small, on account of his excellent talent for teaching, also made his name known to posterity by his zeal in writing. Of his little works there survives a noteworthy summa, which he entitled:

Of Cavillations, 1 book. “Since his danger is [unclear].”

On the Order of Judgments, 1 book. “By the prayers and insistence.”

He is said besides to have written several other works, but they have not come to my knowledge.

Placentinus, an Italian by nation, a most celebrated cultivator and expounder of both laws, attained great glory by teaching and writing on Mount Pestilanus. He once held a place among the principal doctors among the professors of this art, on account of certain most commendable volumes which he composed. Of these, among others, there is said to survive:

A Summa of Judgments, 1 book. “When I was at Mantua.”

Also on the Code, 1 book. I have found nothing concerning the others.

He flourished in the times of Henry VI, in the year of the Lord 1200.

Rofredus, Beneventan by homeland, a most renowned doctor in both laws, subtle in intellect, composed in scholastic fashion in speech, sufficiently fit, by long practice, for resolving doubts and questions of law, wrote little works not to be despised by students in that faculty, by which he consecrated his name and reputation to immortality. Of these, however, we have been able to find only a few, which we have set down below, a very useful volume containing:

Questions of Civil Law, 1 book. “If I were considering the talent.”

Questions of Canon Law, 1 book. “On all actions.”

A Summa of Law, 1 book.

Whatever more he published has not yet come to my knowledge at all.

Peter, archbishop of Sens, learned in the divine Scriptures by continual study and rich from reading the ancients, and also learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, wrote little works of no small utility, by which he both cultivated his own talent and prepared material for the edification of others. He wrote very subtly, with sayings of the fathers added:

On all the epistles of Paul, 1 book. Also various sermons.

He also diligently expounded various books of the Bible, and is said to have written other treatises, both various and useful, which have not come to my knowledge.

Azo, an Italian by nation, took the origin of his life from the city of Bologna; formerly the hearer and disciple of Johannes Bosianus of Cremona, a very learned man; a most famous interpreter of civil law, a fountain of laws, an abundance of words, a lamp of law, who by his learning and knowledge easily surpassed all the jurists who had preceded him, published many little works pertaining to civil law, by which he acquired immortal praise and glory:

A noteworthy Summa of Law, 1 book. On the Old Digest, [unclear] books.

Also on the Code, 9 books.

In addition, he produced excellent apparatuses on the laws, and added additions to several summae, and wrote various things which are not unknown to learned jurists. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230. And he left after him many distinguished disciples, nobly learned in the imperial laws as well as in other disciplines of humane letters, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, a doctor of great authority among the old professors of this faculty. He wrote certain excellent volumes in that discipline, of which I have seen only:

On the Order of Judgments, 1 book. “In the name of our Lord Jesus.” On [unclear].

ANTONIVS dictus de Padua,natione autem Hispanus ex Vlixbona ciuitate oriundi, ordinis minorum, beati Francisci discipulus, vir in diuinis scripturus eruditifimus

On Ecclesiastical Writers, book I. It remains now that concerning the office.

On the Office of a Notary

Various questions of law.

The other things which he composed have not yet at all come into our hands.

FRANCIS, founder and head of the Order of Minors, an Italian by nation, sprung from the city of Assisi in Italy, a man of most holy conduct and a most ardent follower of evangelical poverty, who by word and example converted many from iniquity and directed them into the way of Catholic justice, was so great a lover of Christ that in contempt of the world and of transitory consolation he scarcely had an equal. In his order many very learned men have already flourished, who for the usefulness of the faithful have composed almost innumerable little works. Francis himself, however, wrote a brief work:

The Rule of the Minors, book I, "The rule and life of the Minors."

A brief Testament, book I, "The Lord gave to me, brother."

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1220.

CAESARIUS, a monk in Heisterbach, of the Cistercian order, a German by nation, of the diocese of Cologne Agrippina, a devout man, outstanding in regular discipline, and by long practice devoted to the divine scriptures, composed for the instruction of the novices, whose instructor he was, some little works in a simple and open style, the reading of which is not to be despised by more simple devout brothers. Of these I have found only the following.

A lengthy work on miracles and diverse visions made in Germany in his own time, which he entitled in imitation of the holy Pope Gregory.

Dialogues on various matters, 12 books, "Gather up the fragments, lest."

On the Sunday Gospels, book I, "The cluster of Cyprus, beloved."

On the Gospels for saints, book I, "Our Lord and Savior Jesus."

Sermons to novices, book I.

Besides these he published several other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

WILLIAM, monk of the monastery of the divine martyr Dionysius of Paris, of the Order of St. Benedict, a Frenchman by nation, a man skilled in the divine scriptures by constant study and excellently learned in the disciplines of secular letters, clear in talent and eloquence, and a distinguished knower of times, not ignorant, notable in morals and life, was of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people; gloriously preaching the cross against the Albigensian heretics, by apostolic authority he signed many of the faithful against them. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which, writing and teaching various things, he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is extant:

A volume of Histories, 3 books. And many letters to various persons, book I.

He is said, moreover, to have published commentaries on the divine scriptures, which I have not yet seen.

JACOBUS de Vitriaco, bishop of Acre, afterward cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, bishop of Tusculum, a man learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, notable in morals and life, was of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people; gloriously preaching the cross against the Albigensian heretics, by apostolic authority he signed many of the faithful against them. He wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity.

The Eastern History, book I. The Life of Mary of Oignies, 3 books.

Against the Saracens, book I. On the holy women of Liege, book I.

Letters to various persons, book I. Besides these he composed some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1220.

BONAGUIDA of Arezzo, a man in both laws the most learned of all in his time, of great authority among the ancient professors of this faculty, subtle in talent, clear in eloquence. He wrote for the usefulness of students of law certain splendid volumes, by which he made himself useful to those present and known to those to come. Among these there is extant the noble summa which he entitled:

The Introductory Work for Advocates, 2 books, "Since the office of advocacy."

The Pearl of Law, book I, "Since after the invention."

Explanations of various cases. But he is said to have composed certain other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

PETER de Vineis, a German by nation, scribe and chancellor of Emperor Frederick II, a learned and eloquent man, but especially blameworthy in this, that adhering to that same Frederick and relying on his favor he foolishly barked against the Roman Church; by him at last he was worthily rewarded, when he had offended him in certain matters, and lost the light together with his eyes. He wrote certain little works of his talent, of which I have found only these:

Letters in the person of the Emperor, 6 books, "The pontiffs gathered."

On imperial power, book I.

He flourished in the times of the same Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

ANTONIUS, called of Padua, but a Spaniard by nation, sprung from the city of Lisbon, of the Order of Minors, disciple of blessed Francis, a man most learned in the divine scriptures

Abbot of Sponheim

[unclear], since before entering the order he taught theology gloriously for a long time at Toulouse, Bologna, and Padua, and left distinguished disciples after him. He was of such holiness that, living and dead, he shone with many miracles. He was moreover a most excellent preacher, so much so that the supreme pontiff was accustomed to call him the ark of the covenant. And St. Francis used to call him his bishop. Among other little works of his talent he wrote very elegant and most ardent works:

Sermons on the season, 2 books. “There shall be signs [unclear].” Also sermons on the saints, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230. And because of the frequency of miracles after his death he was at once enrolled in the catalogue of saints by Pope Gregory IX, together with Saint Dominic and Elizabeth, landgravine of the Thuringians.

Jordan of the Order of Preachers, after Saint Dominic, as they say, master general, a German by nation, a man sufficiently trained and learned in the divine Scriptures, an outstanding preacher of the word of God, venerable no less for holiness than for knowledge, by his own example and honey-flowing teaching instructed many in piety. He is said to have written some little works, the reading of which is judged not unprofitable for declaimers and devout brothers. Of these, from the office of the priorship, there are said to be, to the brothers of his order:

Several exhortatory letters, 4 books. Sermons to the people. On the institution of the order.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, at the same time as blessed Dominic, in the year of the Lord 1220.

Hubert of Bobbio, professor of both laws, a most sagacious interpreter, subtle in intellect, clear in expression after the scholastic manner, who among the old professors of this science was regarded as one of the foremost doctors, handed down his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity by teaching and writing, giving to others both an example of learning and an aid to advancement. For he wrote a notable summa, which he entitled:

On the order of judges, 3 books. “Because paternal piety.” Questions and determinations.

And not a few other things, which nevertheless have by no means come into our hands.

Bernard Dorna, a Provençal by nation, formerly a hearer and disciple of the very famous Azo of Bologna, professor and most learned interpreter of both laws, stirred by the example of his most learned teacher, applying himself wholly to letters, wrote various little works, by which he consecrated his name to immortality. Of these there survives a distinguished volume:

On the conceptions of libels, 1 book. And other things which I have not seen.

Accursius, an Italian by nation, born in the city of Florence, formerly a hearer and disciple of Azo, a man most skilled in both laws, and not among the least learned in the other disciplines of secular letters, subtle in intellect and famous in eloquence. How great his authority is at this time among professors of the laws, no one even moderately learned is unaware. He wrote many distinguished little works; he was the first to gloss the whole civil law:

On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. On the Code. On the Institutes, 4 books. “Since by imperial command.”

He published besides not a few other things, which are very well known to students of the laws. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Hubert of Bonacursus, an Italian by nation, a man skilled in both laws and not ignorant of secular philosophy, ready in intellect and clear in speech, who among the old expounders of law was of no obscure reputation. He composed in that faculty certain distinguished little works, of which I do not recall that any has come into our hands. There is said to be his:

On the preludes of cases, 1 book. Other useful and distinguished works.

We believe, however, that both these and his other works are not unknown to skilled jurists.

John of Abbeville, archbishop of Besançon, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, a Frenchman by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, a very famous interpreter of those same sacred letters, who in the Parisian studium taught theology excellently for many years, most excellent in declaiming sermons to the people; for this reason especially, from a master at Paris he was made archbishop of Besançon. He wrote:

Sermons on the season, 2 books. Sermons on the saints. Other things.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

He also published many other works, which have come to my knowledge. He also wrote the aforesaid sermons through the cycle of the year: first, brief readings from the Gospel and the Apostle, expounding them briefly; afterwards he published other sermons, both on Sundays and on festivals, so lengthy, introducing so many testimonies of the Scriptures, that they can scarcely be committed to memory; yet these have now, with newer ones coming in, partly lost their value.

RAYMUND of Pennafort, a Catalan by nation, [was?] provincial and third master general of the Order of Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, ready in talent, distinguished in knowledge of canon law; by writing various things he made his name immortal, and by his little works bound the church to be perpetually, so to speak, his debtor. For at the command of Pope Gregory he compiled the Decretals of law, in 5 books: “The peace-making king, by pious mercy.”

A Summa on cases, in 3 books: “Since, as Jerome says.”

The Constitutions of his order, in 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

ALBERTUS Galioti, a Parmese by homeland, a professor and famous interpreter of canons and laws, subtle in talent, cautious in counsel, scholastic in eloquence, who because of his learning and experience in affairs was held among the foremost doctors by the old jurists. He wrote certain little works in law not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with immortal praise. Among these there is extant a summa:

The Pearl of Questions, in 10 books: “When I, Albertus Galio.”

And Declarations of Judgments, in 1 book.

And certain other unknown works are held by various persons.

ODOFREDUS of Benevento, a hearer of Azo of Bologna, afterwards the teacher of Jacobus Balduini, a man most skilled in both laws, very subtle in talent, clear in eloquence, who left many distinguished disciples after him; on account of his learning and erudition, both in law and in the other letters of humanity, he was held in great authority among the ancients. Many little works of his are reported, by which he made his name known to posterity.

On the Formation of Libels, in 1 book: “After the work of notarial art.”

On Judicial Order, in 1 book: “In what manner Christ’s.”

On the Art of the Notariate, and other things which I have not seen.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

JOHANNES de Blanosco, a Burgundian by nation, a man most learned in both laws, sufficiently instructed in the precepts of secular philosophers, keen and ready in talent. He wrote in plain speech little works not to be scorned by professors of this faculty, by which the fame of his name became known then to those present and afterwards to those to come far and wide. Among these there is extant a volume of great usefulness, which he entitled:

“I, Johannes de Blano.”

On the Actions of Advocates, in 1 book. But the rest of what he composed has by no means come to my knowledge.

And Various Questions. A Genoese by origin, from the city of Fribourg by origin, John by name, a German by nation, much [unclear] from the divine Scriptures; bishop of Bosnia in Hungary, of the Order of Preachers, a man [unclear] in the divine [unclear] by the consensus of the fathers, much practiced and learned in secular law, excellently skilled in philosophy, who, because of his learning and holiness of life, had been taken from the order to the episcopate; later abandoning it, he returned to his order and, after Raymond, was made general master of the order [unclear]; he did many good things. He wrote a notable work:

Summa of Confessors, in 5 books: “Since the newness of doubts.”

And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230. He was buried in his convent at Strasbourg, once shining, as they say, with many miracles.

INNOCENT IV, pope, formerly called Symbaldus, an Italian by nation, [unclear] city.

On Ecclesiastical Power, in 1 book: “It is read in Ezekiel.”

Apparatus on the Decretals, in 5 books.

Rule of the Poor Clares, in 1 book: “The form of life of the order.”

288 The Abbot of Spanheim

Also the Authenticae, one book, and certain other works. He flourished under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250. [unclear] books.

Rolandinus de Romantiis, a professor of both laws and a very celebrated interpreter, and nobly learned in secular philosophy, was not among the least of the old jurists. In that faculty he wrote certain excellent opuscula, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only a summa, one book. It begins: “A little book begins: On the order of crimes”; Determinations and Questions.

The rest which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

Bernardus, priest of Compostella, familiar and chaplain of Pope Innocent IV, a man most learned in law, prompted by the zeal of the same pontiff, wrote certain excellent opuscula in law, which in these times are held in great authority among jurists. Of these I was able to find a few, namely an outstanding apparatus:

On the Decretals, five books. It begins: “At the beginning of this book.”

Cases of the Decretals, five books. It begins: “The peace-making king, by pious [mercy?]...”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under the emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Guido de Suzaria, a most skilled doctor in law, and sufficiently instructed in the other disciplines of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, ready and cautious in counsel, had great authority among the old experts in these matters. He is said to have composed certain excellent opuscula in law. Among them there exists a notable summa which he entitled:

On the Actions of Cases, one book. It begins: “On the ordering of cases.”

Also Various Declarations, [unclear] books. It begins: “Since, with [unclear] supporting...”

And many other works, which have not yet come into our hands at all.

Bartholomaeus Brixianus, a professor and very learned interpreter of canon law, and excellently learned in the other disciplines of secular literature, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote various excellent opuscula both in law and on other matters, by which he gave his name to immortality. Among these the following are reported:

A Repertory of the Decretum, three books.

A Chronicle of Italy, one book.

Disputations on the Decretals, five books.

And certain other works.

Letters to Various Persons, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Johannes de Deo, a professor and outstanding expounder of both laws, and sufficiently learned in the disciplines of philosophy, subtle in intellect and scholastic in speech, by the memory of his name came to the knowledge of many. Of his works only a few have come to my knowledge; for I found only the following:

A Summa of Cavillations, seven books. It begins: “To the honor of the highest [Trinity?].”

Another, entitled Judgment, [unclear] books. It begins: “May he be present at our beginning.”

A Table of the Decretum, [unclear] books. It begins: “The book of decrees, distin[ction]...”

A Concordance of the Decretum and the Decretals, [unclear] books. It begins: “For those wishing readily...”

Various Questions. A tractate on constitutions.

He taught in the city of Bologna, where he composed the aforesaid works and others.

Hugo Barchinonensis, of the Order of Preachers, made cardinal priest of the holy Church of the title of St Sabina, was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, who before entering the order had been a master of sacred theology and had many distinguished disciples. He wrote several outstanding opuscula, by which he consecrated his name to immortality. No less shining in conduct and religion than in learning, he remained in dignity the same man he had been before. The following books are attributed to him:

On Genesis, [unclear]; On Exodus, one book.

On Leviticus, [unclear]; On Numbers, [unclear] books.

On Deuteronomy, [unclear]; On Joshua, [unclear] books.

On Judges, [unclear]; On the Book of Ruth, [unclear] books.

On Kings, [unclear]; On Chronicles, [unclear] books.

On Ezra and Nehemiah, [unclear]; On Tobit, one book.

On Judith, [unclear]; On the Psalter, one book.

On the Book of Job, [unclear]; On Ecclesiastes, one book.

On Proverbs, [unclear]; On the Song [of Songs], one book.

[unclear] books. 10.

Scripsit ad quaedam deuota opuscula, quibus nomē fūum ad notitiam posteritatis deuenit. Equibus ista feruntur. Super regulam S. Augustini Omnis homo est exhortandum lib.i. VINCENTIVS Gallus natione Burgundus, ordinis praedicatorum dictus Belua- censis, vit in diuinis scripturus studiosus et exercitatus, ac veterum lectione diues, ingenio subtilis, & sermone compositus, tantum literis studium adhibuit, vt nullis vnquam labori- bus vigilliis vel occupationibus ab earum cultura potuerit euocari, quin semper aut lege- ret, scriberet vel predicaret. Tantus itaque fuit, vt post se necdum habuerit parem. Si atdua quae scripsit opuscula ex multis laboriose collecta, equa lance cum coeteris ponderemus. Nam petente et sumptus ministrante rege Francorum, grande et admirabile opus speccu- lorum de omni (vt ita dixerim) rescibili in multis voluminibus maximis laboribus com- portauit quod ita praenotauit atque distinxit.
