388 | Abbot of Sponheim … he rendered by his eloquence, excellent in talent, devout in life and conduct. He wrote many distinguished little works in both kinds, by which he made his name known far and wide. Of these the following are extant: A work in notable verse to Arnoldus Bostius, a Carmelite dwelling at Ghent, against Vincentius de Castronovo, of the Order of Preachers, On the Conception of Saint Mary, one book, “And to me a mind [unclear].” On the same subject, in prose, one book, “No Christian reli[unclear].” On the Wretched Condition of Man, one book, “Among the many things by which he [unclear].” On the Art of Composing Verse, three books, “Those things concerning the making of ver[ses?].” Many very elegant orations, one book. Also a book of letters, one book. And several other things. He is still living at Paris, residing at Saint-Mathurin, and is writing various works day by day to be published, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Harynghus Sifridi Sinnama, from The Hague, of Frisian origin, who is commonly called Hermannus, German by nation, professor of both laws and a most celebrated interpreter, and excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular philosophy; subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, ready and steady in counsel, whose authority is held in great esteem among princes and prelates of churches, easily holds the first place in teaching, writing, and giving counsel in the university of Cologne. He wrote, among other things, a large and very celebrated work, explaining legal titles with the utmost clarity, very useful and necessary for all beginning to study in both laws or in either one: On the Titles of the Code, twelve books, “And if verbosity without [unclear].” On the Titles of the Old Digest, twenty-four books, “Although the new pla[unclear].” On the Titles of the New Digest, fourteen books, “It will have to be known here in [unclear].” On the Titles of the Authentics, one book, “Because there are seven parts.” On the Uses of Fiefs, one book, “Although the constitutions [unclear].” On the Peace of Constance, one book, “Because this book of fiefs [unclear].” On the Titles of the Institutes, one book, “Because Emperor Frede[ric?].” On the Titles of the Decretals, four books, “Although from this book.” Certain other works are also extant, “Since, as the Emperor says.” He is living in the vigor of manhood in the city of Cologne, [unclear] that most learned [unclear], and under the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year in which we wrote these things, 1494, indiction 12.

Raphael Regius, an Italian by nation, a man most learned in every respect, a renowned philosopher, a celebrated poet, and a distinguished orator, skilled in both languages; excellent in talent and eloquent in speech. In the university of Padua he acquired the highest praise for his learning by teaching, disputing, and composing. He is said to have produced many distinguished little works, by which he made his name and talent known with glory. Of these the following are extant: Corrections on Quintilian, one book, “High-minded men are accustomed [unclear].” On the Praises of Eloquence, one book, “If ever anyone of distinguished [unclear].” On one letter of Pliny, one book, “In the inscription of this work.” Against Johannes Calphurnius, one book, “Although with very weighty [unclear].” A dialogue against the same, one book, “Yesterday you disturbed the boys.” Various orations, one book. Also many letters. And several other things. An Introductory Notice to the Fasti, one book. And certain commentaries. He is still living at Padua, as I have learned, and is composing various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Laurentius Bonincontrius, a philosopher and distinguished astronomer, and excellently learned in the other disciplines of the liberal arts; outstanding in talent and clear in speech, strong in verse and prose. He is said to have produced many distinguished little works, by which he has transmitted his name to the knowledge of many, but up to now I have not been able to see any of them. There is said, however, to be a notable work of his, through the circle of the year.

Johannes de Keisersberg, German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, in life and conduct

IOHANNES Picus, natione Italus comes Mirandulae et concordiae dominus, vir omnis bonae literaturae studiosissimus, & ficut praeclaro sanguine, ita diuino admodum, ingenio nobilissimus, magna familiae omnignum artium stipatus caterua, cum quibus literis et studis latinis, pariter hebraicis et graecis palaestram exercet, dignus et optime meritus, cuius profectionem Musae sequantūr, doctissimus nostra aetate philosophus est atque disputator acerrimus. Scripsit stylo elegantissimo nonnulla quae aetas nostratum comprobarē, tum vel maxime admirati habebit, quibus nominis et gloriae suae memo- riam non indigne sempiternam reddidit, de quibus iam prodiere Heptaphus super principium Genesis. Item: Nongentae conclusiones philosophicae. Apologia. Item super Psalmos lib.1. Et plura alia quae nondum conspectui nostro sese exhibuere. Viuit adhuc hodie inter ingeniosorum adolescentum suorum gregem apud Italos, neque altiora scribere, neque benefacere posteritiatis cessat, sub Alexandro sexto pontifice maximo, regeque Rom. Ma- ximiliano. Anno domini, quo haec scribimus 1494. IOHANNES Capnion, alias Reuchlin, natione Teutonicus, ex Phorcen oppido Sueuiae, legūm imperialium doctor eximius, illustrisque comitis Eberhardi de Wirten- berg confīt cum facundissimus tum iuris fideique integerrimus omnis antiquissima philosophiae et literaturae indagator solertissimus. Trium principalium linguarum he- braicae scilicet similiter et caldaicae, graeca pariter et latina interpres peritiff. Gallicanae etiam atque politioris linguae nostrae vernacula inprimis clarus. Et tam in diuinis scriptu- ris secretarius, quā in secularib. literis eruditissimus. Quin imo in omni genere doctrinae hac tempestate pręcipuus, puta qui Graecorum secreta mysteria multis iam annis enixissime penetrauit. Dignus profecto qui solis litteris, non etiam perfrepēti po- pulari curiae incumberet. Nullum enim nobis non modo Italia, sed nec seculum quidem nostrum huic tanto viro parem obliiceret. Scripsit nonnulla opera, quibus memoriam fui praesentibus commendauit et posteris. Ad episcopum Vangionum camerarium Dal- burgi, Dialogum in quo omnia secreta philosophiae graecae, hebraicae, & Christianorum portentisica verba explicat, quem praescripsit Capnion, vel de verbo mirifico, lib.3. De praeercitamentis rhetoris, lib.i. Est à veteribus. De diuersitate quatuor idiomatum graeca linguae, lib.r. Orationem funebrem in mortem Rudolphi Agricolae. On Ecclesiastical Writers

renowned for his conduct, a very celebrated preacher of sermons, who for many years has held the office of preacher in the cathedral church of Strasbourg. He wrote some commendable little works, but they have not yet come to the notice of our reading. His elegant works are reported to be:

Sermons to the People, 1 book. Various Orations to the Clergy, 1 book.

And certain others. At great expense and with long labor he collected the works of Johannes Gerson, many of which at last he brought to us from France, dividing them into three parts in a very handsome order, and making a very useful table; he gave the whole of this to be printed. He is still living in the German city of Strasbourg, and is composing various works, under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Johannes Picus, an Italian by nation, count of Mirandola and lord of Concordia, a man most devoted to every kind of good literature, and, just as he is of illustrious blood, so too most noble in an almost divine talent, surrounded by a great household crowd of all kinds of arts, with whom he practices the arena of Latin studies and letters, and likewise Hebrew and Greek, worthy and most deserving, whose journey the Muses follow, is the most learned philosopher of our age and a very keen disputant. In a most elegant style he wrote some things which the age of our contemporaries will approve and then indeed will hold in the greatest admiration; by these he has not unworthily made the memory of his name and glory everlasting. Of these there have already appeared:

Heptaplus on the Beginning of Genesis.

Also: Nine Hundred Philosophical Conclusions.

Apology. Also On the Psalms, 1 book.

And many other things which have not yet presented themselves to our sight. He is still living today among the company of his gifted young men among the Italians, and he does not cease either to write loftier works or to do good for posterity, under Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, and Maximilian, king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Johannes Capnion, otherwise Reuchlin, a German by nation, from the town of Pforzheim in Swabia, an outstanding doctor of imperial laws, and counselor of the illustrious count Eberhard of Württemberg, both most eloquent and of the greatest integrity in law and faith, a most diligent investigator of all the most ancient philosophy and literature. Of the three principal languages, namely Hebrew and likewise Chaldaic, and equally Greek and Latin, he is a very skilled interpreter. He is also especially distinguished in French and in our more polished vernacular tongue. And he is most learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters. Indeed, in every kind of learning he is foremost in this age, as one who for many years has very earnestly penetrated the secret mysteries of the Greeks. Worthy indeed to devote himself only to letters, and not also to the very noisy popular court. For not only Italy, but not even our age, could set against us any equal to this great man. He wrote some works by which he commended the memory of himself to those present and to posterity. To the bishop of Worms, chamberlain Dalberg, he wrote a dialogue in which he explains all the secret words of Greek, Hebrew, and Christian philosophy, wondrous words, which he entitled:

Capnion, or On the Wonder-Working Word, 3 books.

On the Preparatory Exercises of the Orator, 1 book.

It is from the ancients.

On the Diversity of the Four Idioms of the Greek Language, 1 book.

A Funeral Oration on the Death of Rudolf Agricola.

Of Epigrams and Elegies, 1 book.

Besides, for our common utility he translated many little works from Greek into Latin: Xenophon’s Apology for Socrates, Nestorius the heretic, the Confession of Cyprian, Proclus on the blessed Virgin, some of Lucian’s Dialogues of the Dead, a dialogue of the same author on the council [unclear] in verse, Epiphanius on the life and death of the prophets, Maximus Tyrius the Platonist [unclear]. That renowned Capnion makes the name more illustrious by his talent. In the year in which we write these things, 1494.

[unclear], monk of the monastery of Maulbronn, of the Cistercian order, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures, excellently taught in secular matters, a philosopher, orator, and poet not to be rejected, skilled, as they report, in the three principal languages, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote in verse and prose some little works by which he made his name known. Of these there exists a volume,

The Abbot of Sponheim

Letters to various persons, one book. Various orations. Many poems. And certain other things.

He lives to this day at Citeaux and persists in the study he has begun, under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord 1494, indiction 12.

Conrad Celtis Protucius, German by nation, born from Franconia in Germany, a man in every respect most learned, a distinguished philosopher, an eloquent orator, an eminent astronomer and cosmographer, and a poet laureate, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, skilled in both languages, excellent in talent and fluent in speech, wrote certain distinguished little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Concerning these he formerly read the following to me:

To Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans, on both rhetorics of M. Tullius Cicero, an epitome, that is, a compendium, one book. “Qui in concione quip.” On the praises of eloquence, one book. “Morine aeternis cele.” On the art of versifying, one book. “Accepi illustriss. prin.” On composing letters, one book. “Epistola seu apostolus est.” On the site of Nuremberg, one book. “Cum nuper relaxandi ani.” A Sarmatian journey, one book, to which he gave the name “volu.” Of poems, two books. “Urse doctorum specimen.” Of loves, which he inscribed according to the four sides, four books. “Scribere que nostrae fat alia.” A panegyric to the duke of Bavaria, one book. “Italicas tentare lyres.” On the life of Saint Sebald, in verse, one book. “Regiae stirpis soboles.” The situation of Germany, three books. “Germaniam scripturus.” Various orations, one book.

He published many very elegant letters to various persons, in verse and prose, and diverse epigrams; in cosmography, of which he is most knowledgeable, he wrote various things, which we trust will hereafter come to light. He is still living, thirty-five years of this age, and writes various works under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans, and under the supreme pontiff Alexander VI. In the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Petrus Bonomus of Trieste, protonotary of the imperial court, a man most learned in the Latin language, both very fluent and very practiced in composing every kind of poetry, as one from whose storehouse the tuneful Muses pour forth, and for that reason very celebrated by the fame of a great name, wrote very many works in prose and in verse of various kinds. Of these there are extant especially:

Books of epigrams. An unwearied mass of letters.

Nor does he ever cease to write. He is still living under his king Maximilian, devoted to letters and cultivating his talent with good arts. In the year in which we write these things, 1494, indiction 12.

Sebastian Ticio, otherwise Brandt, of Strasbourg, German by nation, distinguished professor of both laws, excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in the other disciplines of secular literature, by no means unskilled in poetry, subtle in talent, outstanding in speech, counsel, and action, who by his learning and literary labor wonderfully adorns Basel, the renowned city of Germany, wrote certain little works, both in verse and in prose, of by no means contemptible reading, by which he made his name widely known. Of these there are extant:

On the titles of both laws, one book. “Cum difficile.” A Sapphic rosary of divine Mary. “Stirpis humana.” Enigmas in praise of the Virgin, from the Old Testament. “Que parisi.” Proof that the virginal conception was possible. “Huc adez o.” The wonder of Mary when the angel came. “Quid tibi vis.” The salutation of the Angel. “Missus ab excelso.” On the [unclear] places of the blessed Virgin. “Si tu a virgo.” The virginal compassion. “Nare patris.” The consolation of Christ to his mother. “Quid gemis o.” On the blows given to Christ. “Respice que tulerim.” On the ingratitude of those eating manna. “Sorte sub hac.” In praise of Saint Sebastian. “Quid tuas coner.” The life of Saint Onuphrius. “Nostris carminibus.” In praise of Saint Valentine. “Laudibus o presul.” The beginning of a poem: “Vica.”

DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLES. Vita sancti Bernardi. In laudem ordinis Carthusiens. De contemptu seculi. Laudes beatae Christianae prope Basileam. Contra aduocatos calumniantes. De captiuitate regis Maximiliani Elegia in mortem Imperatoris Frederici Ad diuum Maximilianum regem. 10 Variorum epigrammaton. lib. 1. Commendaticia carmina in varias impressiones. Compilauit praeterea mira arte et ingenio, vulgari tamen et vernacula lingua libellum quendam, quem nauem Narragonię appellauit. In quo causam et radicem omnium stultiarum adeo eleganter expressit, mores hominum carpit, & quaedam salutaria remedia singulis tradit, vt non iure stultorum librum, sed diuinam potius Satyram opus illud apellasset. Nescio enim si quid tempestatis nostrae vsibus salubrius, aut iocundius legi posset. Aiunt eum magnopere anniti, vt et latine, carmine pariter et oratione soluta opus il-lud quamprimum prodeat. Viuit adhuc apud Basileam, annos habens aetatis 36. eiusque opera et industria impressores plurimum in exornandis libris suis vtuntur. Varia enim conscribit sub Maximiliano Rom.rege, quem singulariter diligens plura de eo et ad eum suauissimai (etiam secreta vt aiunt) condidit carmina. Anno quo haec scribimus 1494. 20 Iacobvs Wimpelingus Sletstetensis, natione Teutonicus, presbyter ecclesiae Spi-rensis, vir in diuinis eruditiffimus, & in secularibus literis egregie doctus, theologus celeberrimus, philosophus, orator et poeta omnium praestantissimus, primum apud Erfor-diam, ac deinde in Heidelbergensi gymnasio philosophiam, sacramque scripturam publi-ce edisserens, magnam eruditionis suae gloriam acquisiuit. Vir, inquam, undecunque do-tifissimus, ingenio subtilis, eloquio difertus, qui et metro excellit et prosa, scripsit vtroque genere quaedam praeclara opuscula, quibus nomen suum longe lateque diuulgauit. E qui-bus extant subiecta. Ad Bertholdũ archiepiscopum Moguntinũ opus celeberrimũ hexa-metro et pentametro versu elegatissime composuit, quod praenotauit de triplici cãdore. 30 In laudem diuae Mariae lib.i. Maxima nostrarum spes. Praecepta rhetorices. lib.i. Nescio si tuum Theoderi. Laudes Spirensis ecclesię. lib.i. Quemadmodum expect. De Spiritu sancto oratio. lib.i. Lustra iam octo fruenda. Ad regem Franciae oratio. lib.i. Carmina variis generis multa. 40 De arte poetica. lib.i. Et quaedam alia. Epistolas tam ad me quam ad alios multas, elegantesque composuit, quarum incertist est numerus. Ad instantiam Ludouici Spirensis epifco pi officium de compaffione beatae Marie semper virginis composuit, quod per eandem dicecesim annuatim solenniter per-agitur. Ad hunc Iacobum librum de luminaribus viris Germaniae iam pridem dedimus. Viuit aetate virili annos habens ferme tres et quadraginta, in inclýta ci-uitate Spireni, & varia conscribit, sub Maximiliano Romanorum rege. Anno domini quo nos haec seripsimus. 1494. BAPTISTA de Salis, ordinis fratrum minorum prouincie Ianuensis, vir in diuinisscripturis studiosus et eruditus, & tam in vtroque iure quam in seculari philosophia egregie doctus, ingenio subtili sermone scholasticus vita et conuersatione deuotus, & regulas disciplinae obsertuantia praeclarus, edidit quaedam ad instructionem simplicium sa-cerdotum necessaria opuscula, quibùs nomen suum longelatcque diuulgauit. De quibus extat summa de casibus in foro conscientiae valde utilis, quae iuxta nome autoris vocatur Summa Baptiftiniana. lib.i. Compleuit eandem summam sub Frederico Imperatore tertio. Et viuit adhuc eius fi-lio Maximiliano regnum tenente. On Ecclesiastical Writers

The Life of Saint Bernard. In praise of the Carthusian order. On contempt of the world. Praises of blessed Christiana near Basel. Against slanderous advocates. On the captivity of King Maximilian. An elegy on the death of Emperor Frederick. To the divine King Maximilian. Of various epigrams, book 1. Commendatory poems for various printed editions.

He also compiled, with wonderful art and talent, though in the common and vernacular tongue, a certain little book which he called the Ship of Narragonia. In it he so elegantly expressed the cause and root of all follies, censures the morals of men, and offers certain salutary remedies to each, that he would not rightly have called that work a book of fools, but rather a divine satire. For I do not know whether anything more wholesome or more pleasant could be read for the uses of our age. They say that he is striving greatly so that the same work may come out in Latin as soon as possible, alike in verse and in prose. He is still living at Basel, being 36 years of age, and printers make very great use of his labor and industry in adorning their books. For he writes various things under Maximilian, king of the Romans, whom he loves in a singular way, and has composed many very sweet poems about him and to him, even secret ones, as they say. In the year in which we write these things, 1494.

Jacob Wimpeling of Schlettstadt, a German by nation, priest of the church of Speyer, a man most learned in divine matters and excellently taught in secular letters, a very celebrated theologian, philosopher, orator, and poet, most outstanding among all, first at Erfurt and then in the Heidelberg academy publicly explaining philosophy and sacred scripture, acquired great glory for his learning. A man, I say, most learned from every side, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, excellent both in meter and in prose, he wrote in both kinds certain distinguished little works, by which he spread his name far and wide. Of these the following are extant. To Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, he composed a very celebrated work in hexameter and pentameter verse, most elegantly, which he entitled On the Threefold Whiteness.

In praise of the divine Mary, book 1. “Greatest hope of our...” Precepts of rhetoric, book 1. “I do not know whether your, Theoderic...” Praises of the church of Speyer, book 1. “Just as he expects...” On the Holy Spirit, an oration, book 1. “Already eight lustra to be enjoyed...” To the king of France, an oration, book 1. Many poems of various kinds. On the art of poetry, book 1. And certain other things.

He composed many elegant letters, both to me and to others, of which the number is uncertain. At the urging of Ludwig, bishop of Speyer, he composed an office on the compassion of the blessed Mary ever virgin, which is solemnly performed annually throughout that same diocese. To this Jacob we have already long since dedicated the book On the Illustrious Men of Germany. He is living in manly age, being about forty-three years old, in the renowned city of Speyer, and writes various things under Maximilian, king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Baptista de Salis, of the order of Friars Minor of the province of Genoa, a man devoted to and learned in the divine scriptures, and excellently taught both in both laws and in secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, devout in life and conduct, and distinguished in observance of the rules of discipline, published certain little works necessary for the instruction of simple priests, by which he spread his name far and wide. Of these there is extant a summa on cases in the forum of conscience, very useful, which, according to the author’s name, is called

The Baptista Summa, book 1. He completed this same summa under Frederick III, emperor. And he is still living while his son Maximilian holds the kingdom. In the year of the Lord 1494.

Engelhard Funck of Schwabach, an East Franconian, a German by nation, a learned man and skilled in every respect, a distinguished philosopher, orator, and poet, not ignorant of the divine scriptures and pontifical law, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, excellent in meter, [unclear]. In elegiac verse.

On the praise of his fatherland, book 1. Various epigrams. Several letters to various persons. And many other things.

392 The Abbot of Sponheim He is distinguished at Rome, as [auditor?] or advocate of causes, and composes various works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Johannes Langer of Bolkenhain, priest of Wroclaw, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, excellent in verse and prose, in life and conduct worthy of a priest. He wrote many excellent little works in both kinds of style, by which he made his name known. Of these there exists a distinguished work addressed to Georg von Stein, lord of Steynaw, which he entitled:

On [unclear] and [unclear], one book. “Today I am oppressed by a great [unclear].” Letters to various persons, one book. Many poems. And many other things.

He is still living in Wroclaw and writing various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Werner Rolevinck, of Laer, a German by nation, by homeland a Westphalian, of the Carthusian order, of the house of Saint Barbara in Cologne, a man most devoted to and very learned in the divine Scriptures, excellent in talent, devout in life and conduct, published many excellent little works, by which he made himself useful to the present and memorable to the future. Of these the following survive: a large work on all the epistles of Paul, which he entitled:

The Teaching of Paul, two books. “The teaching of Paul the apostle.” On the Life of Paul, one book. “Just as I was with Moses, so.” On the Value of Masses, one book. On the Rule of Princes, one book. On the Study of Theology, one book. The Bundle of Times, one book. “Generation and genera.” The Paradise of Conscience, one book. “The Lord God took the man.” Many sermons, one book. And many other things.

I once saw in his cell treatises, small indeed, but numerous and useful, whose titles oblivion has now taken from my memory. He is still living in the Cologne Charterhouse, of advanced age, and writing various works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494, the twelfth indiction.

Arnold Bostius, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Ghent, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and exceptionally learned in secular letters, a distinguished theologian, philosopher, orator, and poet, acute in talent, eloquent in speech, devout in life and conduct, of whom several letters to me survive. He wrote many excellent little works in verse and prose. Of these the following survive: a distinguished volume written in verse and prose, in which he clearly shows the prerogative origin and progress of his order in view of Marian protection; for that reason it was pleasing that it be entitled:

On the Patronage of Mary, one book. “You asked, most distinguished man.” On the Illustrious Men of the Carthusians, one book. “To the venerable and among [unclear].” On the Illustrious Men of His Own Order, one book. “Brother Arnold Bostius.” Against Vincent in the New Castle, one book. “How long always [unclear].” Letters to various persons, one book. On the Four Last Things, one book. Various poems. And many other things.

He is still living at Ghent, in vigorous age, and composing various works, and by his example and writings he summons many to sacred studies. In the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Heinrich Euticus, an East Franconian, an excellent professor of both kinds of medicine, has published many things which he prepares for posterity. Also, in a varied and pleasing character of poems, a very beautiful little work which he entitled:

Jests, or Urbane and Witty Jokes of Young Men. In Praise of the Blessed Virgin. And many other things. A Satire against Sophists and Dialecticians and Enemies of the Study of the Humanities.

He is still living, when we wrote these things, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Eytelwolf von Stein, a noble man, German by nation and Swabian, a man of great talent and a vigorous emulator of Roman eloquence, and for that reason having obtained great honor with the margrave of Brandenburg. He wrote to Georg von Stein, his maternal uncle, a man most devoted to letters:

On the Praises of Heroes and Illustrious Men, one book. A most polished letter. And

Anno domini quo nos ista scripsimus 1494 CAROLVS Phernandus, natione Teutonicus Brugis oppido Flandriae ortus, à partua aerate captus oculis, &amp; ob id elementorum quoqꝫ penitus ignarus, tantum sui mi- raculum praebet, vt velut alter Homerus poeta, musicus, philofophus et amp; orator celeber- rimus euafert, diuinarum quoque scripturarum fagacissimus interpres, carmine excel- lens et amp; prosa, ingenio subtilis eloquio difertus, vita et amp; conuerfatione integerrimus, qui à rege Gallorum publico et amp; perpetuo donatus stipendio in celebrimo gymnasio Pari- sien.multo tempore literas humanitatis egregie docuit, &amp; authores complures pulcher- rime exposuit. Demum contemptis omnibus, mundum cum suis stipendiis deferuit, & ante biennium ferme ordinem diui patris nostri Benedicti intrauit, in monasterio pro- be reformato quod Casale Benedictum appellatur, firum in quadam sylua deniffi- ma decem à Bituricensi ciuitate ferme millibus diffante, in quo vsque hodie perfeue- rat, magno feruens zelo animarum adeo vt dispensatione apostolica Leuita ordinatus, verbum Dei cum maximo omnium fructu et amp; admiratione publce praedicet, scripfit tam metro quam prosa multa graeclara volumina, quibus nomen fuum pofteritati commen- dauit.In decertationem metricam Ruperti Gaguini de puriflima conceptione facra Dei genetricis et amp; virginis Mariae, aduerfus Vincentium de Cafronouo ordinis praedicato- rum opus elegantissimum. Carmen Iambicum de eadem. lib.i. Quantum creatis antecel. Orationem de concep.ad Carthuf.lib.i. De S.Catharina orationem. lib.i. Epiftolarum multarum. lib.2. Carmina ferme innumera. lib.i. IOHANNES Phernandus frater praedicti Caroli, natione et amp; ipfe Teutonicus, vir- vndecunque doctiffimus philosophus, oratot et amp; poeta celeberrinus, &amp; diuinarum scri- pturarum non ignarus, ingenio subtilis et amp; difertus eloqiuo, quem rex Gallorum perpe- tuo stipendio donans sibi in musicum defumpfit, scripft tam metro quam prosa multi v- tilia et amp; deuotioni congrua opufcula, quibus nomen fuom ad multorum notitiam dedu- xit.E quibus extant subiects. 50

On Ecclesiastical Writers

And other works by which he will win great praise for Germany among cultivators of the Roman tongue. He is still living today under King Maximilian, in the year in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Rudolphus Langius, German by nation, canon of the church of Münster in Westphalia, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, a most learned philosopher, orator, and very celebrated poet, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote many distinguished little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he spread his name far and wide with immense glory. Of these the following are extant. To Hermann Langius, dean of the same church: On the City of Jerusalem, 2 books, “A certain most splendid [unclear].” To the dean of Cologne, Poems, 1 book, “Clear virtue, whom [unclear].” On the Siege of the City of Neuss, 1 book. A Poem on the Three Magi, 1 book. Several letters to various persons. Various poems also. And many other works.

He is still living, very old, in the city of Münster, composing many works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Sebastianus Murrho of Colmar, German by nation, priest and canon in Colmar, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and most learned in secular letters, an outstanding philosopher, orator, poet, and cosmographer, very skilled in three languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, celebrated for his knowledge of laws and canons, second to none in architecture, music, and the whole quadrivium, wrote, among other things, to Jacob Wimpfeling of Sélestat, whom we mentioned above, a brief but very beautiful work: Epitome on the Praises of the Germans, 1 book. On the Works of Baptista Mantuanus, 1 book. And certain other works.

He is living today in Colmar, where he is a canon, and is composing various works which we hope will be published day by day, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Carolus Phernandus, German by nation, born at Bruges, a town of Flanders, blind from earliest childhood, and for that reason also wholly ignorant of the elements, presents so great a marvel of himself that, like another Homer, he became a very celebrated poet, musician, philosopher, and orator, and also a most sagacious interpreter of the divine Scriptures, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, and most upright in life and conduct. Having been granted a public and perpetual stipend by the king of the French, he taught humane letters with distinction for a long time in the celebrated college of Paris, and explained many authors most beautifully. At length, despising everything, he abandoned the world together with his stipends, and about two years ago entered the order of our holy father Benedict, in a well-reformed monastery called Casale Benedictum, situated in a very dense wood about ten miles distant from the city of Bourges. There he perseveres to this day, burning with great zeal for souls, so much so that, ordained a Levite by apostolic dispensation, he publicly preaches the word of God with the greatest profit and admiration of all. He wrote many very distinguished volumes, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his name to posterity. Against the metrical contestation of Robert Gaguin on the most pure conception of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, against Vincentius de Castronovo of the Order of Preachers, a most elegant work: Commentaries, 1 book, “We do not doubt from the Apostle.” Praises of the Order of Carmelites, 1 book, “While the Parthian turns his weapons.” Odes in Praise of Christ, 4 books. On the Conception against Vincentius, 1 book. Iambic Poem on the Same, 1 book, “How much he surpasses created things.” Oration on the Conception to the Carthusians, 1 book. Oration on Saint Catherine, 1 book. Many Letters, 2 books. Almost innumerable poems, 1 book. Elegies on Contempt of the World, 1 book. And many other works.

He is living today, blind but most learned, in the aforesaid monastery, composing many and varied works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494, indiction 12.

Johannes Phernandus, brother of the aforesaid Carolus, himself also German by nation, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, very celebrated orator and poet, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, whom the king of the French, granting him a perpetual stipend, took for himself as a musician, wrote many useful little works, suited to devotion, both in verse and in prose, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of many. Of these the following are extant.

394 The Abbot of Sponheim

On Saint John the Baptist, one book. “Seek with the plectrum how ...” Many and varied orations, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Many poems and epigrams, and many other things.

He also wrote the Hours of the Holy Cross and of the compassion of Saint Mary in elegant verse; these, recently printed at Paris, are in circulation. He lives to this day with the king of France in the highest esteem, and is composing various works, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Hieronymus Donatus, a Venetian patrician, a most distinguished man, devoted to the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, a very celebrated translator of both languages, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, although he is now distracted by the care of wife and children, nevertheless burns with a wonderful diligence and incredible zeal for letters, writing many things day by day and translating many things from Greek; if another man, even one free from every care, were to compose them, they could be something of a marvel.

An oration to the king of Portugal, one book. Various orations also, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. And very many other things.

He translated into Latin John Damascene on the immaculate mysteries; also Dionysius on the Divine Names, and certain letters of his; also the volume On the Soul by Alexander of Aphrodisias the philosopher; and many other things. He lives to this day at Venice, thirty-seven years old, writing and translating various works, under Maximilian, the most illustrious King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Jodocus Badius of Ghent, German by nation, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very distinguished philosopher, rhetorician, and poet, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, who once at Ferrara heard Baptista Guarinus teaching Greek letters, and in that branch of knowledge also became learned. He now adorns Lyons with his learning, and reads the poets publicly and privately, instructing several sons of magnates. He wrote many excellent little works in verse and prose, of which the following are extant. A notable metrical work against vices, which he entitled:

The Moral Grove, one book. “Unhappy Vincent, and ...” Against Vincent also, one book. “What chorus of poets ...” 20 Psalter of Mary in Sapphic verses, one book. Many epigrams, one book. On grammar also, one book. Various letters. And very many other things.

He lives to this day, thirty-two years old, composing many different works under the renowned King Maximilian. In the year of the Lord 1494, indiction 12.

Helias Regnier, a very celebrated jurist, excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular philosophy, subtle in talent, distinguished in speech, cautious in counsel, who for a long time publicly taught law in the school of Poitiers, wrote certain excellent little works by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these I have seen only the following, a celebrated work which contains:

Cases of the Sixth Book of the Decretals, one book. “Boniface the Eighth established ...” 40 Cases of the Clementines, two books. “John, bishop, divide ...”

Of the others I have seen nothing. He is still living in the University of Poitiers, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Rutgerus Ventray, German by nation, of the order of the regular canons of Saint Augustine, from the monastery of the holy apostle Peter which, situated not far from Worms, is called Heyne; a man devoted to the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, practiced in verse and prose. He wrote in both kinds certain little works not to be despised, of which the following are extant. A Tetralogue, which he entitled:

On the Instruction of Boys, two books. “When you notice childish ...” 53 On the Inquiry into the Blessed Life, two books. “In the year in which Ceres ...” Hymns on Saint Mary, two books. “Behold, Mary, mother of God ...” On the Various Use of Letters, two books. “For knowing in verse ...” On a Marvelous Thing, two books. “Very many things to the mind, to the will ...” On New Matters, one book. “Most familiar in Christ ...” On the Kinds of Metres, two books. “This Tetralogue, which concerning ...” A panegyric to me. Various epigrams, one book. “To the reverend father in Christ ...” And certain other things. I hear

DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLES. 395 Audio eum ad me opus cudere de calamitatibus horum temporum, quod nee dum vidi. Epistolas tam ad me quam ad alios carmine ac oratione soluta plurimas perscipsit non inelegantes. Viuit vsque hodie et varia componit sub Maximiliano rege Rom. & Alexandro papa sexto. Anno domini, quo nos ista scripsimus 1494. IVDOCVS Beysselius regiae vrbs Aquensis patricius, natione Teutonicus, vir in scripturis sanctis studiofus, & in secularibus literis eruditiissimus, philosophus clarus, orator facundus, & poeta insignis, qui licet vxoris et rei familiaris cura sit necessario distractus, incredibili tamen amore feruet scripturarum, multa indies scribens et componens, E quibus extant subiecta, quibus nomen suum cum ingenti gloria vbique diuulgatur. E quibus extant subiecta, Dialogus pulcherrimus ad Hermolaum Barbarum, Platonicorum more, De optimo genere musicorum, lib.i. Perduxi vos ô Hermo. De Christiano ambitu, lib.i. Et si tibi omnia suppetunt. Epitoma stimuli amoris lib.i. Cum per hec Christina. Dero facea Mariae corona lib.i. Rosaceam Augustissime. Rosarium metricum, lib.i. Quisque amat roseam. Derosarii mysterii lib.i. Egredimini filia Ston. Rosarium de sacramento altaris, lib.i. Pane sub hoc modico. Gesta Flandrensum, lib.i. Orationes elegantiissimae. 20 Epistolae quoque plures. Carmina et epigrammata multa. Et quaedam alia. Viuit vsque hodie Aquigrani vtriusque iuris clariusissimus interpretes et varia conscribit sub Maximiliano Romanorum rege. Anno domini quo nos ista scripturus 1494. HIERONYMVS Balbus, vir celeberrimae opinionis, & in omnibus disciplinis bonarum artium egregie doctus, philosophus clarus, & rhetor facundus metro excellens et prosa, ingenio praestans, & disertus eloquio, qui docendo, legendo publice et scriben-do, magnam gloriam apud Gallos et Parisienses commeruit. Scripsit quaedam ingenii sui praeclara opuscula, quibus nomen suum post eritati commendauit. E quibus ego adhuc viditantur, volumen magnis eloquentiarum sibi bus conditum, in quo calumniis respondet cuiusdam Guilhelmi Tardiui rhetoris, per modum dialogi sub suo, Caroli Phernandi, Petrj Cohardi, & ipsius infensoris nominibus, cui titulum impofuit, lib.i. Inter ea officia quibus. Rhetoris gloriosi no Rom. rege illustriss. Anno domini. 1494 De alijs nihil vidi. Viuit adhuc in Gallia scribens et varia componens, sub Maximilia- ex epistolis Caetera me latent. Sancti Hieronymi presbyteri, lib.4. Viuit vsque hodie in ciuitate Cameracen. vita et doctrina celeberrimus et varia cõpositio, & etuditus, & seculari literaturae non ignatus, ingenio praestans, vita et conuer-satione praeclarus, & singulari deuotione conspicuus, edidit quaedam praeclara voluminibus, quibus nomen suum notificauit. E quibus extat opus celeberrimum omnii statuti ne-qua, quibus nomen sum notificauit. De quorum numero ceffarium quod mirabili industria, pulcherrimaque consequentia in vnum comportauit ex epistolis Historia Polonica contra Turcã.lib.i. Amorũ diuerso metro. lib.II. PHILIPPVS Callimachus, natione Italus, patria Florentinus, regis Poloniae secre-tarius, vndecunque doctiss. philosophus clarus, orator facunds et disertus eloqujo. Fertur multa praeclara eudiisse opuscula, quibvs memoriam sui posteris reliquit. De quorum numero subiecta feruntur. Opus insigne de gestis Attilae regis impii, quod praenotauit. Attulam. De moribus Tartarorum. lib.i. Et alia complura. Viuit vsque hodie apud regem Poloniarum maximo in pretio, & varia conscribit, sub Maximiliano Romanorum rege Anno domini, quo haec scripturus 1490. Indictione duodecima. PAVLVS Niauis, natione Teutonicus vir in literis humanitatis egregie doctus, diuinarum scripturarum non ignarus, philosophus et rhetor celeberrimus, ingenio praestans et disertus eloquj, docendo et scribere do varia in gymnasio Lyptzeni magnam nomini suo famam acquisiuit, scriptus enim quaedam praeclara opuscule, quorum lectio non venit contemnenda. De quibus subiecta ferūtur. Opusculum pro nouitiis religiosis. Cũ mego sepius cogita. De institutione latinizandi. lib.I.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

I hear that he is composing for me a work on the calamities of these times, which I have not yet seen. He has written very many letters, both to me and to others, in verse and in prose, not without elegance. He is living to this day and composes various works under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI. In the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Jodocus Beysselius, a patrician of the royal city of Aachen, a German by nation, a man devoted to the sacred Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher, eloquent orator, and notable poet, although he is necessarily distracted by care for his wife and household estate, nevertheless burns with an incredible love of the Scriptures, writing and composing many things every day. Of these the following are extant, by which his name is everywhere spread with great glory. Of these the following are extant:

A very beautiful dialogue addressed to Hermolaus Barbarus, in the manner of the Platonists, On the Best Kind of Musicians, one book. “I have brought you, O Hermo[laus]...”

On Christian Ambition, one book. “Even if all things are at hand for you...”

Epitome of the Goad of Love, one book. “Since through these, Christina...”

On the Rose-like Crown of Mary, one book. “Most august rose-like...”

A Metrical Rosary, one book. “Whoever loves the rose-like...”

On the Mystery of the Rosary, one book. “Go forth, daughters of Sion...”

Rosary on the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. “Under this small bread...”

Deeds of the Flemings, one book.

Most elegant orations.

Also many letters. Many poems and epigrams.

And certain other things.

He lives to this day at Aachen, a most distinguished interpreter of both laws, and writes various works under Maximilian, king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord in which we were about to write these things, 1494.

Hieronymus Balbus, a man of very celebrated reputation, excellently learned in all the disciplines of the liberal arts, a distinguished philosopher and eloquent rhetorician, outstanding in verse and prose, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, who by teaching, public lecturing, and writing earned great glory among the French and the Parisians. He wrote certain excellent little works of his talent, by which he commended his name to posterity. Of these I have so far seen [unclear], a volume composed with great [unclear] of eloquence, in which he responds to the slanders of a certain Guilhelmus Tardivus, rhetorician, in the form of a dialogue under the names of himself, Carolus Phernandus, Petrus Cohardus, and his accuser himself, to which he gave the title, one book. “Among those duties by which...”

[unclear] of the boastful rhetorician, under Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord 1494.

I have seen nothing of the others. He still lives in France, writing and composing various works, under Maximilian [unclear] from letters. The rest is unknown to me.

Of Saint Jerome the priest, four books.

He lives to this day in the city of Cambrai, very celebrated in life and doctrine, and [unclear] various compositions, and learned, and not ignorant of secular literature, excellent in talent, distinguished in life and conduct, and conspicuous for singular devotion. He published certain excellent works in volumes, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a very celebrated work of all [unclear], by which he made his name known. Of their number [unclear], which with wonderful industry and very beautiful sequence he brought together into one from the letters.

Polish History against the Turk, one book.

Of Loves in Various Metres, two books.

Philippus Callimachus, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by homeland, secretary of the king of Poland, most learned in every respect, a distinguished philosopher, an eloquent orator and fluent in speech. He is said to have published many excellent little works, by which he left his memory to posterity. Of their number the following are reported: an outstanding work on the deeds of Attila, the impious king, which he entitled Attila.

On the Customs of the Tartars, one book.

And very many other things. He lives to this day at the court of the king of the Poles in the highest esteem, and writes various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which he was about to write these things, 1490, in the twelfth indiction.

Paulus Niavis, a German by nation, a man excellently learned in humane letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, by teaching and by writing various things in the gymnasium of Leipzig acquired great fame for his name. For he wrote certain excellent little works, whose reading should not be despised. Of these the following are reported:

A Little Work for Religious Novices. “Since I have often thought...”

On the Practice of Latinizing, one book.

396 The Abbot of Spanheim

Vision of a certain hermit, one book: “A huge grove clearly.” Colors of the art of rhetoric, one book: “Once you wished, [unclear].” Dialogue of the idiot, one book: “When I often recalled [unclear].” Short formal letters, one book: “Great force is wont.” Letters to the same, of moderate length, one book: “I promised, good man.” Letters also of greater length, one book: “I conceive a great and [unclear].” And certain other works. He lives to this day in Germany, composing various works under Maximilian, most illustrious King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Bohuslaus of Hassenstein, a German by nation, a noble man and learned on every side, a distinguished orator and poet, who, contrary to the custom of the other nobles of this age, both handles arms and with remarkable zeal cultivates, fosters, and celebrates letters, so that, like a second Pliny, even while serving as a soldier he composes books and poems, wrote certain excellent little works both in verse and in prose, by which he made his name known. Of these the following are extant:

A distinguished work on the proper inventions of the Germans and Italians, one book. Various letters. Poems also, one book. Various letters. And many other works.

He lives to this day in his castle Hassenstein and writes various works under Maximilian, most excellent King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494, indiction 12.

Henricus of Northeim, a Teuton by nation, a man devoted to and learned in secular letters, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent and fluent in speech, excellent in verse and prose, wrote certain little works not to be despised in reading, by which he commended his name with glory to posterity. Of these I have seen only that distinguished work which he wrote in verse and prose to Frederick, Margrave of Meissen, and the dukes of Saxony, entitled Dimetronachia:

On the conflict of virtues and vices, one book: “Then you, laurel-bearing [unclear].”

Of the other things which he composed, nothing has come to my knowledge. He lives to this day, writing various works, under Maximilian, most illustrious king, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493.

Aquinus, of the order of Friars Preachers, having the origin of his life from Sweden, was devoted to the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, a celebrated philosopher and distinguished mathematician, excellent in talent and polished in speech. Imitating Boethius, he wrote a most highly commended work:

On the proportions of numbers and sounds, one book. Certain letters. And certain other works.

He lives to this day among the Bavarian dukes, in esteem with Otto, and writes various works under Maximilian, most unconquered king, in the year of the Lord 1494, indiction 12.

Albertus of Prusa, a Pole by nation, a collegian of the university of Krakow, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, also excellently learned in secular letters, a distinguished theologian, philosopher, and astronomer. Praised in a poem of Conrad Celtis for his skill in the stars, outstanding in talent and clear in speech, he wrote several little works not contemptible in reading, by which he made his name known. But few of them have come to my knowledge:

Commentaries on the Theoricae of Georgius Burbachius, one book. To the ephemerides of Königsberg, one book. And certain other works.

He still lives in the university of Krakow, composing various works under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1493, indiction 12.

Theodericus of Osnabrück, a Teuton by nation, of the order of Friars Minor of the province of Cologne, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures, a very famous declaimer of popular sermons, whose life all who have known him proclaim at this time to be most holy. In making sermons to the people he is illumined from God with such grace, speaks with such eloquence, and finally affects his hearers with such compunction and sweetness, that he has had no one like him among the Germans. Hence he was appointed general preacher throughout the whole province. Recently, while he was with me at Cologne, he read to me a distinguished little work, fitting for devotion, which he had composed at the instance of Hermann, archbishop of Cologne:

On the Passion of the Lord, one book: “Most reverend in Christ.” Manual of the simple, one book: “Because, as Augustine.” On the inner army, one book: “He who shall have persevered.” And certain other works.

He still lives in the province of Cologne, vigorously pressing on in the office he has begun, under King Maximilian and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493. Bartho-

LI

On Ecclesiastical Writers

BARTHOLOMAEUS of Cologne, German by nation, a man excellently learned in secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, a distinguished philosopher and poet, whose poems even the most learned poets admire and extol with praises. He wrote in both styles certain little works worthy of notice, by which he made his name known. Of these I have so far seen only a little work on the praises of philosophy, composed in meter, which he entitled:

A Woodland of Poems, book I. “Why [unclear] gold to Pluto.” On the Sect of Diogenes, book I. “Whoever desires [unclear].” A mythological letter.

There is, however, as is said, what he wrote on this book, which bore the sign of the cross, and through him [unclear]. Of the others I have seen nothing. He is still living today at Deventer, composing various works, under King Maximilian and Pope Alexander VI. In the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

JOHANNES Thurotus, a Hungarian, a man studiously trained in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine scriptures, excellent in intellect, renowned in eloquence. He is said to have fashioned some little works, by which he made his name known. Of these there exists a volume not to be rejected, which he assembled with much industry, containing:

A Chronicle of Hungary, book II. “In constant leisure in these years [unclear].”

And certain other things. He is said still to be living and composing various works, under King Maximilian. In the year of the Lord 1494.

HIERONYMUS of Padua, Italian by nation, a man studious in the divine scriptures, excellently learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher, orator, and poet, excellent, eloquent in speech. He wrote certain little works not of contemptible reading, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Of these there exists a very beautiful little book, entitled Jesuita, addressed in meter to Peter Donatus, bishop of the city of Padua:

On the Passion of the Lord, book I. “Greatest of the heaven-dwellers [unclear].”

Other works of his exist. He is said still to be living and composing various works, under King Maximilian. In the year of the Lord 1494.

FRANCISCUS Mataracius of Perugia, a man educated in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher, orator, and poet, highly skilled in both languages, excellent in intellect, eloquent in speech. He wrote certain distinguished works, book I [unclear]. Of these there exists a very celebrated little work addressed to the young man Petrus Paulus Cornelius:

On Composing Verses, book II. “The ancients [unclear] the poetic art.” Letters to various persons, book II. Many epigrams.

And many other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV.

DOMINICUS Mancinus, a man very learned in the divine scriptures and excellently learned in secular letters, excellent in meter and prose, subtle in intellect, renowned in eloquence. He wrote certain approved little works, by which he spread abroad his name. Of these I have read only that treatise which he composed in elegant meter:

On the Passion of the Lord, book I. “Not the praises of men, nor [unclear].”

He wrote other things. He is said still to be living and writing various works, under Maximilian, most noble king of the Romans. In the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

LUDOVICUS Brunus, Italian by nation, from the marquisate of Montferrat, a man most learned in every respect, a very celebrated professor and interpreter of both laws, a poet laureate, philosopher, distinguished orator, and not ignorant of the divine writings, excellent in intellect, eloquent in speech. He is said to have fashioned many distinguished little works in both kinds of writing, but none of them has come into our hands except that treatise which he described in elegant verse:

On the Coronation of King Maximilian, book II. “Holy through eternity [unclear].”

Of the rest I have seen nothing. He is still living, and is said to be writing various works, under the same King Maximilian. In the year of the Lord 1494.

JACOBUS Sprenger, German by nation, provincial of the Order of Preachers at Cologne, a man studiously learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, excellent in intellect and plain in speech, when he had formerly been appointed inquisitor of heretical depravity by Pope Innocent VIII, together with Henricus Institoris, a theologian of the same order, assembled and wrote, with the help of the same colleague, a volume against little women who are witches, instruments of the Devil, for the caution of the simple, which he entitled:

Statuta

Abbot of Spanheim

The Hammer of Witches, 5 books. He lives to this day in his convent at Cologne, under Maximilian, most clement king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1493, indiction 12.

Johannes Tholosus, a German by nation, born in Eastern Francia, which is called Franconia, canon of Regensburg and provost of Forchheim, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed in secular letters, a distinguished doctor of pontifical law, a very celebrated astronomer, cosmographer, and poet, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote certain excellent little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his talent to posterity. But I do not remember that any of them have come into our hands. Yet those who knew the man well report that he has, on various subjects:

Elegant Letters, 1 book. And certain works in mathematics.

And certain other things. He lives to this day in the city of Regensburg, in the province of the Norici, and writes various works, a very great supporter of learned men, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493, the twelfth indiction.

Adam Werner of Themar, a German by nation, a man excellently instructed in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a philosopher and no trivial poet, and a most distinguished interpreter of imperial law, outstanding in intellect and eloquent in speech, writes various works, playing in verse and prose, by which he has made his talent known far and wide. There are extant many of his writings, and poems addressed to me, 1 book, beginning: “To the reverend father in Christ.”

Also many letters. He composed for me, On Saint Anne, 1 book.

In addition he has written, and daily writes, many other works to be published. He lives to this day at Heidelberg, tutor of young princes, under Maximilian, king, in the year of the Lord in which we composed these things, 1493.

Johannes of Düsseldorf, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Strasbourg, a man devoted to and learned in the divine writings, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, a very celebrated interpreter of the faculty of theology, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in life, is said to write many things, but [unclear]. I saw certain treatises of his, whose titles I have not now been able to recall to memory. He lives to this day at Strasbourg, under Maximilian, most clement king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1493, the twelfth indiction.

Theodericus Visenius, a Frisian man of singular learning, persistent in poetry and oratory. Among his works are extant:

Cultivated Elegies. And other epigrams, 1 book. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

And many other things which will come down to posterity. He is still living under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Hartmann Schedel of Nuremberg, a German by nation, doctor of arts and medicine, and not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, outstanding in intellect and clear in speech, compiled and wrote, among other little works of his talent, from Jacobus of Bergamo and other historiographers, adding some things, especially concerning German affairs, a great and distinguished work, which contains:

Histories of the Times, 10 books. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He lives to this day at Nuremberg, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494. [unclear]

Johannes, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin the Bishop in Spanheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict, of the diocese of Mainz, a German by nation, a Mosellan by homeland, born from the village of Trittenheim in the diocese of Trier: although I am not worthy for my name to be placed among the ecclesiastical writers, because of the poverty of my intellect, nevertheless, compelled by the urging of friends, I have been forced at the end of this catalogue [unclear] also of my lucubrations [unclear] the priest of Autun, Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, who also placed themselves at the end of their treatises published on these same matters. Therefore I wrote, besides this work, also the following. And first, indeed, by command of the presiding officers of the general chapter, I abridged:

The Statutes

I AM nunc igitur post multos tandem labores operi nostro finem imponamus, quoniam si multi restant scriptorum illustrium catalogo digni, nobis tamen impossi- bile fuit omnium vel sola nomina inuenire. Eos vero quorum certitudinem habere po- rui diligenter consignaui, nec quemquam scienter omisi, cuius opuscula, ingenium tempora scire potuissem. Neque ignoro quam mulier erudinssimi viri hodie supersint va- ria componentes, quorum ego nullam feci mentionem, non quod eos iudicauerim indi- gnos, nostro catalogo, led propterea qđ opescula sua vel celare maluerunt, vel non vique adeo multiplicata sunt, vt in notitiam meam venire potuerint. Feci quantum po- tui, non quantum volui, quippe qui omnes quotquot sunt vel vnquam fuerunt (si licuis- set) scriptores mihi conciliassem. Relinquo posteris eam prouinciam, vt de sua vena ad, dant, ybi ego fatigatus defiti. Caeterum vos oro patres conscripti, qui coelica regna tene- tis, qui hunc nostrum catalogum vestris nominibus, ingenijs lucubrationibus exorna- tis, quatenus si vera, si iusta, si digna, si denique grata de vobis scripsimus, omnipotentis Deilectamentia pro nobis exoretis, vt culpas abluat, veniam tribuat, sanctum proposi- tum confirment, intellectum illuminet, affectum purificet, participes gaudiorum vestro. 40 num clementer efficiat. Quod si in aliquibus minus quam res ipsa requirebat potuimus, veniam nobis ô sacratiffimi donate, quoniam sicubi erratum est, vitium est ignorantiae, non voluntatis. Vos etiam ô clarissimi viri scriptores, qui adhuc vitam terrenam mor- talem agitis, vos interpello, vos obtestor oro, si quid minus vestris meritis, ingenijs vel lucubrationibus dignum in hoc catalogo peregimus, non voluntati, sed imperitiae nostrae apribatis, veniam quam petimus non negantes, quoniam sicuti defecimus, eorum culpa fuit qui nobis aliter quam se res habet, opuscula vestra vel ingenia descripserunt. Lectorem deinde huius catalogi monemus obsceramus, ne facile contra nos moueatur, si scripto- rum nomina, dignitates, patriam, vel opuscula secus exarata inuenierit, quam ipse forsitan alibi legit, cum historiarum transacti temporis dissonantiam, nemo vnquam potuerit 50 conciliare. Neque nos aliiquid scripsimus, qđ non multis locis vel testimonijs fuerit cõ- probatum. Verum sicut in principio huius operis professi sumus, libenter ce dimus opini- onal cuiuscunque beneuoli correctoris, quam veritas solidam, charitas reddiderit sin- ceram. Nouiffime vero nobis deridendi sunt aemuli, qui more canum ex cõsuetudine pel- sima lattantes, omnia damnant, omnia vituperant, omnia lacerant, quae vel ipsi non fece- rint, vel suis opinionibus inuenerint esse contraria. Mox enim vt vel modicum legere coe- perint, flomachantes, illud non verum esse dicunt, iudices temerarij priusquam examina- tores veritatis effecti. Sed quae nobis causa cum istis, qui nihil vituperãt nisi bonum, nihil laudant nisi malum? Contemnendi sunt igitur inuidi canes, non docendi. Nos autem si LI 2

Conferences, indeed, delivered both in general chapters and in observantine ones, or elsewhere, without fixed number, are partly extant and partly have been taken away, besides those which still remain unfinished in my hands; these I recall having written up to the present, in the thirty-fourth year of my age, the tenth of my assumption of the office of abbot, and the twelfth of my monastic life, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, when Alexander VI was supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord in which I have now for the third time corrected, enlarged, and completed this catalogue, having labored on it for nearly seven years: 1493, in the twelfth indiction.

Now therefore, after many labors at last, let us put an end to our work, since, even if many men worthy of the catalogue of illustrious writers remain, it was nevertheless impossible for us to find even the names alone of all of them. But those of whom I was able to have certainty I have diligently set down, and I have knowingly omitted no one whose little works, talent, and times I could know. Nor am I unaware how many very learned men survive today, composing various things, of whom I have made no mention: not because I judged them unworthy of our catalogue, but because they either preferred to hide their little works, or they have not yet been so multiplied that they could come to my knowledge. I have done as much as I could, not as much as I wished, since, if it had been permitted, I would have brought together for myself all writers, as many as there are or ever have been. I leave to posterity this province: that they should add from their own vein where I, wearied, have stopped.

Moreover, I beseech you, enrolled fathers, who hold the heavenly kingdoms, who adorn this catalogue of ours with your names, talents, and studies: if we have written things about you that are true, just, worthy, and finally pleasing, pray for us to the tender mercy of almighty God, that he may wash away our faults, grant pardon, strengthen our holy purpose, enlighten our understanding, purify our affection, and graciously make us sharers in your joys. But if in some matters we have been able to do less than the matter itself required, grant us pardon, O most holy ones, because wherever there has been error, it is the fault of ignorance, not of will.

You also, O most distinguished men and writers, who still lead mortal earthly life, I call upon you, I adjure and beseech you: if in this catalogue we have accomplished anything less worthy of your merits, talents, or studies, ascribe it not to our will but to our inexperience, and do not deny the pardon which we ask, because, insofar as we have failed, it was the fault of those who described your little works or talents to us otherwise than the matter stands. Then we admonish and beseech the reader of this catalogue not to be readily moved against us if he finds the names, dignities, native lands, or little works of writers set down otherwise than perhaps he has read elsewhere, since no one has ever been able to reconcile the discordance of histories of a time past. Nor have we written anything that has not been confirmed in many places or by many testimonies. But, as we professed at the beginning of this work, we gladly yield to the opinion of any well-disposed corrector, an opinion which truth has made sound and charity sincere.

Lastly, rivals are indeed to be laughed at by us: those who, barking like dogs from the worst habit, condemn everything, disparage everything, tear apart everything which either they themselves have not made or have found to be contrary to their own opinions. For as soon as they have begun to read even a little, in indignation they say that it is not true, made rash judges before they have become examiners of truth. But what cause have we with those who disparage nothing except the good, praise nothing except the evil? Envious dogs, therefore, are to be despised, not taught. But we...

Additions of Certain Men ...we may consider it glorious to displease the malicious, yet we judge it far more glorious to have pleased good and learned men; by them, if there had been error anywhere, we are gladly corrected, and, once corrected, are more fruitfully amended. Let love of the Scriptures excuse us, for whose sake we have taken this heavy burden upon an intrepid neck. End of the book On Ecclesiastical Writers of Lord Johannes de Trittenheim, Abbot of Sponheim. There follow additions of certain illustrious men.

An addition to the foregoing, of illustrious men, partly excerpted here and there, partly recently inserted.

Marianus, Roman by nation, [Genazzanensis?] by native place, of the order of the hermits of St Augustine, a most skilled theologian and prior general of the whole order, shone forth in this our age, like the morning star and a certain most brilliant sun, by his most exquisite declamations and by a certain new manner of preaching; and, offered to the world as if another vessel of election, he displayed such force of talent and strength in teaching that I would dare to say that no one could ever have been found in this century who [unclear] might be compared with him. Indeed he was of such quality and so great that nothing in any more polished discipline could be vainly desired in him. For in his declamations to the people he was so eloquent and sententious in choice words, and also so suited to the matter by his melodious voice, countenance, and other movements of the body, that you could add nothing to the full measure of praise. How great this man’s learning was, and how great the force and majesty of his eloquence, anyone can clearly gather in part from the sermons and orations most learnedly published by him. For he wrote various sermons; one book of orations; one book of letters. He died, moreover, with great loss to the Christian commonwealth, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Felinus Sandeus, of the most noble family of the Sandei, a native of Ferrara, a most accomplished doctor of both laws and not ignorant of the rest of good letters. First at Ferrara, then at Pisa, in the public university of those cities, he professed canon law to the great admiration of all. Summoned to Rome by Innocent VIII, he was placed in charge of the college of the Rota, where difficult and very important business is handled. Although he was occupied with a thousand affairs, because he was of almost divine and most consummate prudence in both laws, he published many little works and commentaries in it. And these indeed so clearly, so learnedly, so exactly, that he untied all the knots of this discipline, restored obscure matters to the light, and, with right judgment applied to doubtful matters, made them easy and open; in this he brought no small assistance to our jurists. The works which he sent forth are appended: first, on the books of the Decretals of Gregory: On Constitutions; On Rescripts; On the Office of the Ordinary; On Majority and Obedience; On Witnesses; On Compelled Witnesses; On the Credibility of Instruments; On Presumptions; On Oath-taking; On Exceptions; On Prescriptions; On Sentence and Res Judicata; On Appeals; On Accusations and Inquisitions. Additions to the Decretum, to the work begun by the abbot. One treatise On the Right of Patronage. A sermon On Plenary Indulgence, whose theme is: Today you will be with me in paradise, etc. In history, one little book On the Neapolitan Kings. There are also other commentaries of his. He flourished at Rome under Innocent VIII and Alexander VI.

Matthaeus Bossus, a native of Verona, of the order of the regular canons of blessed Augustine, a man excellently learned in every kind of erudition, but still more learned in elegance and gravity of speech, was held in great esteem among all, both from the office of preaching and teaching, in which he was long engaged, and from the various works composed by him, by which he so adorned and polished ecclesiastical dogma with rhetorical embellishments that you would find nothing more refined or more elegant. He wrote the following little works: a Dialogue on Enduring Adversities, divided into two books; On Bearing Office and Cultivating Justice, addressed to Johannes Ludovicus Bossus, jurist and golden knight, one book; Letters to various persons, one book. He also published certain other works, in all of which, since varied learning shines forth, and everywhere [unclear].

Nam inter caetera vitam obitum deiparae virginis ita deuo- te pie, copiose, luculenter, ac sancte cecinit, vt non mortalem eius poesim, sed diuinam prorsus omnes proclament. Ponticus Virunio, by birth, as they say, of Treviso, a most learned philosopher, a student of Latin and Greek literature, by industry, toil, and liveliness of talent, without any help from his parents, advanced so far in learning that, because of his enormous erudition, he was held in great esteem with Ludovico Sforza throughout all Insubria.

He wrote the following works: Commentaries on Claudian. Commentaries on the Sphere of Johannes Sacrobosco. Three books On Obscure Passages in Authors and Corrupt Names. Two books On the Misery of Letters, in verse. One book On the Praises of Beatrice, queen of Milan, in verse. Two books of elegies and epigrams. A commentary on the Chremata of Chrysoloras. A commentary on the Achilleid of Statius. Commentaries on Ovid's Metamorphoses. Commentaries on the works of Virgil. Sixteen books On the Art of Divination. He translated Homer's Odyssey into Latin. Four books of hymns of the same Homer. Six tragedies of Euripides. In medicine he translated Theophilus. On pulses and urines. Likewise Aeneus on pulses and urines. One book of Inventions. One book On Titlings. He translated Apollonius' Argonautica into Latin in four books. He also made and published many other Latin works. He flourished under Ludovico Sforza.

Nicolaus Leonicenus, the most elegant of all orators of his age, most accomplished in philosophy, not ignorant of natural things, treated many matters in medicine elegantly and copiously.

Likewise there is a little work in the same discipline, in which he taught that health and life can be restored and procured for all the sick.

Very many letters of the same man are extant, which display his very great learning and elegance. He flourished at this same time in Italy under Ludovico Sforza.

Ambrosius Calepinus of Bergamo, of the order of Saint Augustine, flourished in this age, a most zealous investigator of divine and human letters. Hence, by his own industry and with great labor, he made common to us a very large work, collected from almost innumerable authors, concerning knowledge of vocabulary and the interpretation of Greek and Latin prepositions, with attestation from the authors. In it not only those words which contribute very much to knowledge of literature, poets, and learned men, but also the words which pertain to physicians and philosophers, and also to ecclesiastical doctors, are explained learnedly enough and elegantly, so that in clearer light than in certain other works, where barbarous men had already made barbarous things, they may become Latin. But those things which among the doctors were being called into doubt now lie open, the cloud of uncertainty having been dispelled.

Petrus Burrus, a Belgian, by birth of Bruges, canon of Amiens, renowned in divine and human letters, flourished at Paris under Charles VIII, king of the French, where his youth, celebrated for good disciplines, virtues, most approved morals, piety, and religion,

...grew up. As very many people, and especially the Gandincourt family, would have wished to have this one man alone as teacher for instructing their children and many other rather noble youths. Nor indeed should one swear it, since he is one among the few in our age who taught how to join eloquence, poetry, and the other good arts with wisdom, and that the arts without morals, but morals without letters, are of no benefit. This, indeed, his works show; in them you would not know what most to admire: the weight of the most serious and most holy thoughts; or the variety of style and poetry; or the elegance of things and words; or the skillful joinings; or the pleasing texture of little words; or the flow and harmony that repeatedly mark the verse; or, finally, six hundred other adornments, so that one might deservedly say that all graces, charms, delights, and beauties of speech have been most abundantly gathered here, although nothing either swollen or inflated is seen. Therefore, if this Burrus had written in Quintilian’s time, he would certainly not have said: “Among lyric poets Horace almost alone is worthy to be read.” For this man is most worthy to be read even by holy nuns. Indeed, since he is wholly chaste and wholly Christian, which that man is not, he sweetly breathes forth the Christian religion. Yet no less than he does this man sometimes rise full of delight, grace, varied figures, and most happily bold words, as it is easy to discern from his works listed below and issued into the light. These, then, are the monuments of that most fertile talent:

Four books of Odes. One book of Hexameters.
